product_title: Steinberg Cubase Pro 8 Retail
review_body:
Okay, so what I received was not technically what I ordered. However, as far as I am concerned, it is probably much better. The four stars has nothing to do with the seller or really the product I got. Just that Cubase is not the easiest program to use and their documentation leaves a little bit to be desired. They do have good YouTube videos.

I ordered Cubase 7 Retail with an upgrade to 8 Pro from YRS Midi Systems. What I got was a Cubase AI Controller with Cubase AI 6 that automatically upgraded upon install to AI 8 with an upgrade to Cubase 7.5.. After registering and activating this, I installed the Cubase 7.5 Upgrade. It took a bit of messing around and a visit to the support forums to figure out how to activate it all. You have to get the AI 8 on the elicenser first for 7.5 to recognize there is an upgradable version. But once it does, It automatically upgraded to 8 Pro. Then I went to Steinberg to download the 8. So I did get Cubase 8 Pro, just not directly.

So here's the good part. I got a controller for free. Granted, they don't make it anymore, but it still appears to be supported. And I get a full version of Cubase Pro 8. For a lot less than I would have paid for the full version. It takes a few more steps to install. But it's not difficult. Of course, we won't talk about the hour or two it will take to download 8 Pro. LOL!

I have been using ProTools for many years. But they have changed their licensing process, and now require $200 a year if you want to continue updating. I am currently running 10/11 and I am happy, but if I'm going to have to pay that much, why not switch to something that would be more user friendly and that has something like Chord Assistant. and Intelligent composing - both of which I have been eyeing for a while. ProTools has neither. And buying another program to do it just adds on to the $200.

All DAWs are basically the same when it comes down to it. The plugins included may vary a bit, but they are mostly the same. Yeah, you will hear arguments about which is better. But I have used a number, and it doesn't seem to matter too much in the end. It ends up being personal preference. So I will try this out and hope we get along. :)the same. product_title: Remo SA0110-00 Hazy Ambassador Snare Drum Head,.
review_headline: Excellent general purpose snare side head
review_body:
While I mainly use the [[ASIN:B0002F53XC Remo SD0114-00 Hazy Diplomat Concert Snare Drum Head]], the extra mil thickness of this head works better than the Diplomat for when I am using 10- or 12-strand snares and want a more articulate, drier sound.

However the Diplomats are more one-dimensional than this head. I use those mainly for jazz and very light work. This 3-mil head works with everything from rock to ... well, everything.

The collars always seat perfectly, and the only time I have ever experienced any wrinkling is when using them on snare drums with very narrow and deep snare beds like those on vintage Gretsch snares. For just about every other drum these seat perfectly and allow quick, even tuning.

Bottom line: if you are using generic snare-side heads that usually ship with snare drums, consider replacing with this model. There is a difference, and this is one of the most popular general purpose snare side heads, making it a safe bet.

product_title: GBGS Led Uplight RGB PAR Light
review_headline: DMX basic addressing scheme for these PAR lamps.
review_body:
Basic addressing for these lamps is straight forward. In DMX 512, your controller assigns a channel number in increments of 16 decimal.

Chan 1 is 1
Chan 2 is 17
Chan 3 is 35 and so on....

Chain the lights together with DMX cable and use this basic addressing scheme by setting the bits 1 thru 9 on the dip switches on the back of the lamps. Bits 1 to 9 go left to right. You put in the binary equivalent of the channel as shown above in binary on the dip switches:

chan 1 is decimal 1 and binary 100000000
chan 2 is decimal 17 and binary 100010000
chan 3 is decimal 35 and binary 100001000

Bit 10 must be ON on these lamps if using a DMX controller, otherwise the lights will not respond to DMX signals from a controller and the internal controller for each lamp must be set manually on the dip switches.

The rather cheezy user manual that comes with these, is really only helpful if using them in stand alone mode.

A decent DMX controller, like a Chavet 10, will then control the 4 channels that each lamp has for Red,Green,Blue and effects with the channel sliders and give you all sorts of chase and effect capabilities. Hope this gets you started.

product_title: American DJ Micro Galaxian Laser Special Effects Lighting
review_headline: Beginner DJ's...GET THIS! All DJ's need this!
review_body:
Lets say your on a budget and a party is coming up, this is the buy you should go after! I started out with two speakers and a small mixer; once this tiny laser system was added to my system, my business took off even further. This little device fits on the palm of a single hand and encapsulates a few hundred red and green lasers that move in all different kinds of fashion. This is a spectacular piece of machinery and is ideal for weddings, dance parties, quinceaneras, anything you can think of! Personally, my next buy was a smoke system because once you have a somewhat fogged view of a room with this laser system in it, the lasers come ALIVE! Even without the fog machine, I was able to make much impact on most of my gigs. The system comes with a remote with easy instructions but I almost always have it on the mode that follows the beat of the song I am currently playing at the time. When everything is on beat, the customers are happy and notice things like that. You have the choice to prop the laser system on its two legs (as shown in the photo) or you can install it onto an O-Clamp (See my page for more info about that) which holds the system in place very well. The lasers do not shoot into the same position over and over; they seem to sweep through a series of modes to cover anything in front of you: top to bottom, left to right. Just know you really DO NOT need two of these, a single one of these can cover a gym when positioned correctly. But if you are a mad man or man woman and enjoy the illumination, please get two! Keep it centered where you are located and it will do the job well. Thank you American DJ, this Micro Galaxian Laser system is inexpensive, powerfully bright and effective for all to see!!!

Pros
1. Compact and lightweight
2. Impressive illumination of lasers
3. Internal fan keeps the device cool

Cons
1. Nothing really to say here but if you want the FULL effect of a laser show, GET THE FOG MACHINE. They are half the price of this laser system by the way.e half the price of this laser system by the way.

As essentially a beginner player, the guitar was good looking and to me, sounded like a professional instrument. The technician asked where I purchased it and told me that the bridge plate had begun to separate from the body and it was not worth a set up!  He told me to exchange it as it was defective.  I sent the vendor a message, he politely responded that too much time had passed (three months) and that perhaps Amazon could do something for me.  I contacted Amazon who very surprisingly offered to allow the item to be returned!  I really did like this product and have cautiously ordered another identical set.  I will take it immediately for a setup and if it should fail the inspector's test, I will return it and search for another guitar.  I wanted to give this vendor the opportunity to redeem themselves and I hope that the second guitar meets my initially held expectations.

review_headline: So glad I chose this one!
review_body:
[[VIDEOID:158610e5627c8fdedac361bfb342e66d]]Even better than I expected! I am so happy I chose this piano set to order. I was worried the stand would be flimsy as I saw in some reviews, but I actually find it to be very nice and sturdy - we haven't had any problems at all with it (even with 5 children using the piano). The piano was quite a bit larger than I was envisioning which is nice - it is close to a \\"real\\" piano size! My kids love it (and so do I), especially all the different effects that are available. As far as unpacking and setting up, it was pretty simple. I didn't read the directions thoroughly enough at first, and so I had to take the legs off the stand an embarrassing number of times to get it right. Basically, make sure you see that there are 2 different leg lengths. The shorter ones go on the top of the stand, and the 2 longer ones go on the bottom. Also, each leg has a short side and a long side - make sure the short sides are all facing the same way - that way you won't have to unscrew and screw again 15 times like I did! :P The stand is very easy to adjust heightwise and, athough I have seen some negative comments about the stand, I think it is rather sturdy and is holding up well for us. I don't see any reason to purchase a different stand, especially if you have the piano up against a wall like I do.

Sorry about the video quality (taken by my daughter), but I thought some might like to see the box, what comes in it, and what it looks like all set up. :)

review_body:
Below is a comparison between this Hohner and a Fender dreadnought guitar that cost twice as much.

The Fender does sound slightly better, but was frustrating for a beginner. Fender came with strings gauge and height that hurt my fingertips, so paid extra $50 for luthier to replace and lower strings. But strings separation remained tight, cramping my B7 chord. Each time I contacted Fender or its dealers regarding warranty coverage on strings separation distance, I got a run-around.

This Hohner looks like a computer-machine-precision-cut instrument--a mechanical rather than craftsman look. Still looks great! My fingertips hurt far less with the Hohner. Strings height was ideal for me straight of the box. Strings tension and height makes a BIG difference for the beginner players' fingertips and desire to practice.

Haven't had to thoroughly test Hohner's electronics yet. Some preliminary thoughts-- Hohner's microphone and preamp has an equalizer, which makes a big difference on my acoustic-amp-modeling feature of my electric guitar-amp.

Considering that the Fender cost more than twice as much and yet still required adjustments, I am very happy with the Hohner, which additionally came with a decent bag.

review_headline: Quality stand at a decent price
review_body:
I just got this stand in and set it up with my guitar. The build quality is quite good and the item does not feel cheap in any way. There are some nice touches, like the rubberized handle for tightening the height adjustment of the neck holder and swiveling rubber strap to close off the neck. The black finish on all of the metal parts is a very nice smooth matte finish. There is foam covering the parts where your guitar will make contact: on the swiveling base holder on below and on the neck holder. The one place that could use a bit more foam is the "leg" on the body fork. When you put your guitar in to the stand, it is easy to swing the body too far and then make contact with the uncovered portion and overtime that may create some nicks or scratches in the body of your guitar.

The legs fold up for a more compact shape for transport or storage, But once I put in the swiveling fork that holds the body of the guitar, It seem to lock itself in and I didn't want to break it by pulling too hard on it. I'm not sure if this is intended to be removable or not, but it does make it harder to store since it's not easily removable. The three legs of the stand have Nice rubber feet on them that plug up the ends of the tubes and help it grip the floor better. All of the tubes have nice rounded plugs on the ends so there are no exposed ends.

The attached tag includes a link to the company's contact information along with their three-year warranty info. One tip: I rolled up my card and stuck it inside the bottom of the base tube (see picture), where it is invisible but can stay with the stand and not get lost in case anything ever happens to the stand and I need parts or repair.

product_title: AGPtek® 10 Isolated Output 9V 12V 18V Guitar Pedal Board Power Supply Effect Pedals with Isolated Short Cricuit / Overcurrent Protection
review_headline: A great value! Small, affordable and full of POWER!
review_body:
No, this is not truly and isolated brick as the product states; see other reviews.

With that out of the way, I'd have to say this little thing is quite good for the price. I'll probably never the 12 or 18 volt outputs, but they're nice to have in case I've got a pedal that requires either voltage, or if I want to try one of my less expensive dirt boxes and see if it can handle a higher voltage for more headroom... Maybe not.

So that leaves 8 outlets for the rest of my board; one of which is a high current output of 500ma. I've got four TC Electronic pedals daisy chained on this output (Vortex, Corona, HOF and Flashback) and it handles those just fine. I've probably got enough juice to power one more.

I'm using the other five to power different dirt boxes, but I'll probably end up daisy chaining those too to free up some room as 100ma is more than enough to power 5 OD pedals as they draw a lot less current than digital modulation pedals.

I can honestly say that this thing produces a lot less noise than the wall-wart I was using before. Granted, it was a power supply that's seen better days and I had to reverse the polarity for it to work... This little guy is significantly quieter. If I turn goose the amp, and roll down the guitar's volume, there's just a slight bit of electrical noise compared to the white noise that I before. I can't say whether or not a Voodoo Power or T-Rex power supply would fare better in this area, but I'm a lot happier with this vs. my old supply.

Playing at normal volumes is also a lot cleaner that it used to be; it sounds like I'm not plugged into a chain of pedals. No noise comes through at this point.

The LEDs are a bit much, but they can be turned off via the switch on the front of the unit. That's really my only negative comment about this thing... It does what it's supposed to do rather well, but the excessive blue light is a bit much.

The footprint of this device is rather small, so it should fit easily on, near or around your board. I liked that the supplied cables are straight at one end and a right angled at the other; I've got some pedals where the power jack connects on the side (right below the patch cable) and some where it attaches on the top, so cable management is easy. Each cable is also long enough to reach my currently un-mounted powersupply.

I've not tested this particular unit as much as others have, but I've viewed You Tube clips where folks tested the voltage of each output and it was a constant 9, 12 and 18 volts with no spikes or drops. I expect mine to act in a similar manner, so I don't anticipate any issues. Some people have commented here and there that this will fry your pedals because it's made in China... blah, blah, blah... My pedals and amp were made in China, and they work just fine, as will this new power supply. I'm really, really, really not worried. I've put it through its paces for the past few hours, and with all of my effects on, it worked just fine AND I didn't lose a single pedal.

All in all, this is a great value as it's small, affordable, and powers a ton of different pedals. If you *need* an isolated solution, look elsewhere (the aforementioned VooDoo Pedal Power 2 or anything made by T-Rex), otherwise, this fits the bill for me!

product_title: Dean Vendetta XM Solid Body Electric Guitar, black satin
review_body:
Just picked one of these up lightly used for about $90 locally, and I am blown away by how good this thing plays and sounds. Mine has the brown natural finish, not the black, but honestly, I like both. I lowered the action a bit, adjusted the pups, and tuned it, and this thing was ready to go. After playing it all afternoon, I can honestly say I would not have been disappointed in this guitar if I paid $300; for $120-$150 new, it's a freakin' steal! It is VERY light, and that plus the bolt on neck can sometimes mean the tone is a bit thin, but this is clear and bright, and still has good bottom too. I think the tone stays fat because of the strung-through setup (not sure how the Floyd Rose models sounds, but I hate FR bridge anyway, so I'd never buy one lol). Obviously you aren't getting Gibson-fat or Telecaster-fat tone here, but for a bolt-on neck and light-bodied guitar with stock pups, I think this one would be hard to beat for under $800-$1000.

Either way, if you're looking for a great guitar for a song (ha!), this is it, and it's half the price of the cheapest Fender, Ibanez, Jackson, etc. Sounds better than the Fender Squire or Jackson Dinky (which is actually what I went to buy!). I'd also rate it favorably against any Ibanez, and in fact, I haven't tested anything under $800-$1000 that sounds or plays better.

product_title: On Stage DS7425 Tripod Desk Microphone Stand
review_headline: Manufacturing fault or deliberate product tampering.
review_body:
First product arrived with the mic screw adapter glued to the stand upside down and not able to be removed. Either some sort of manufacturing fault or deliberate intervention by someone along the manufacturing to delivery process. Thankfully Amazon agreed to replace the item at no charge, but this item could not be used for intended purpose and was disposed of.

Replacement item arrived today and there is clearly some sort of manufacturing issue with attaching the 3/8 to 5/8 mic adapter to the base. This time the adapter had been put on correctly but looks like the manufacturing equipment doesn't have a proper torque setting or gauge as it was screwed onto the base that hard that it had started to strip the internal thread. I eventually managed to get it unscrewed using some grips and rubber to prevent damage to the external screw mount. Of course little bits of metal dropped out where the thread had been damaged and tapered over from over tightening.

At least this one is useable and works as intended. Manufacturing problems aside this stand works beautifully for my intended purpose of holding a fairly heavy Rode Podcaster Mic. Extremely stable even with this heavy mic in place along with a shock mount and pop filter, quite impressive. Great portable stand and would highly recommend and give five stars if it wasn't for the production problems experienced.

On that note be prepared for problems with the screw mount adapter if you order.

product_title: Focusrite iTrack Pocket Portable Stereo Microphone and Guitar Input for iPhone Video Creation and Sharing
review_headline: Wonderful device when you know how to set it up!
review_body:
I'm using this for recording my guitar performances with both my iPhone 6+ and my iPad Air2.

The software is free and you can also use it with any other iOS video/audio software, too.

The recorded sound via the stereo mics is noticeably superior to the iPhone's microphone.

The recorded sound via the guitar input and mono mic is also really good and the video looks great!

Be sure you use the volume wheel on the side of the iTrack to adjust the signal level. You want a Green sound level indicator and not yellow or red but just into the green beneath the yellow volume to get the best quality of undistorted sound.

One challenge with this is that it is very light weight making it tippy when you put a large iPhone 6+ into it's slot.

Also, the iPhone has to be removed from it's case to fit into the slot.

And the iPad Air2 just falls over instantly. To solve this, I put the iPad Air2 and the iTrack next to each other on my music stand. This also works better with my iPhone (when it's in it's case), too. And my $12 conductor's stand is large enough to hold both my music and my iPhone/iTrack at that same time. Even if you are not a musician, get yourself a cheap but sturdy music stand so that you will have this adjustable platform for your video recordings.

I've even drilled a hole in my music stand for the rear camera to shoot through and I have a short bungee cord I use to keep everything from falling off of it. This is now a great/cheap (under $100 not counting my iPhone) setup for my video recording from either the front facing or the rear cameras.

The simplicity of using the free Impact app with the iTrack to capture great video and sound and then instantly upload it to YouTube is amazing!

product_title: Casio CTK2400
review_headline: Love It, Love It, Love It!!!
review_body: I don't have a lot to compare it to but I love this keyboard.  The sound is awesome and the range of different tones is incredible.  It has everything from classic grand piano tones to drum tones.  Each key becomes a different drum sound - from bass drum to snare drum to cymbals to triangle.  You can easily fool your neighbors into thinking that you have a full drum set in your house!  The teaching system is awesome - it will literally have you playing songs within minutes. It tells you which finger to use for each note (a female voice calls out numbers 1-5) and the display shows you where the note is and waits for you to play it.  As you learn the song and pick up playing speed, the system moves at your same pace so you can't get behind or ahead of the instructions.  Thanks to this keyboard, I now know how to play Fur Elise by Beethoven quite well. I played violin back in the day but never had any formal piano lessons so I'm amazed at what I've learned with this system. It comes with a book of songs with a nice variety- from American folk songs to classical to Christmas songs and the headphones are a fantastic perk.  You won't regret this purchase!

review_headline: psc=1&redirect=true&ref_=oh_aui_detailpage_o02_s02 and I'm pretty sure that that product is identical to this one
review_body: After posting a question (on this product page) about the use (misuse) of the brandname "Mighty Bright" in the AODE product headline, I decided to try the AODE anyway, since the responses to my question were favorable and since the price was so low. As you can see in the answers I received, nobody was bothered by the fact that the seller is illegally using the brand name of the original, "real McCoy" product. I'm here to say not only that Amazon should police and prevent this sort of thing (it is NOT a Mighty Bright), but also that the product provides much less light than the comparable (9 LED) Mighty Bright (I own one and compared it with several power supplies, none of which caused any variation in the brightness of the product, so that's not a factor). In terms of brightness, there is no comparison - and that's with both of them on the full bright setting. The provided cable with the AODE is also much shorter than what Mighty Bright (too short for my needs) - and, of course, no power supply with the AODE. If I were Mighty Bright, I would take action against this sort of thing and have in mind to let them know. It's also happening here, as well: http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00WLFXGQW?psc=1&redirect=true&ref_=oh_aui_detailpage_o02_s02 and I'm pretty sure that that product is identical to this one. As a further point, if you can buy the Mighty Bright with no power supply for the same price ($18.99).

product_title: Samson Expedition XP150 150-Watt Portable PA
review_body:
This is my first purchase of a PA system. I did a lot of research online before ordering. My expectations were met -- and in some ways exceeded.

The design of the system is well conceived: the amp/mixer nests in the back of one speaker and all the wiring fits nicely in the back of the other speaker AND the two speakers then interlock so that the entire unit is compact and easily portable.

More importantly, the sound quality is very good. I have used the system to play music at several outdoor parties, the largest being an event of approximately 90 people in an area about 2/3 of an acre in size. Even in this setting, I never needed to turn the volume up to anywhere near its maximum output.

A DJ who was a guest at one event commented that his (more expensive) PA system did not sound any better than the Samson Expedition XP308i and he had to rent or borrow a minivan to haul his equipment. A couple other people commented that this unit sounded so good, they'd love to use it in their home theaters.

I know that the 308i mixer board is not as sophisticated as other bigger, more expensive models. But for the price and performance, I feel this is an outstanding value.

review_headline: Tell your friends! These strings are very nice.
review_body:
Whoah! Okay, these strings need to get a bit more attention. I've been trying different sets of strings lately. I don't feel that a lot of the reviews out there are detailed enough. Also, it seems to me, people's expectations might be set a little high sometimes. I will try to give some good details on my experiences with these strings.
First, my experience; I've played guitar for more than 25 years. I've done solo acts, played in bands and now I'm a worship leader at our church and I play 10 - 14 hours a week.
I own several guitars. My performer is a Taylor 814 from 2001 that I use Elixir HD's on, but the guitar I used these strings on is a Takamine EG45C with a cedar top. This guitars has laminate back and sides.
My Takamine is my guitar that sits out all the time and I just grab and start playing. I tend to do a lot of finger picking and practice rifs on it. For this reason I prefer a little lighter string set on this guitar. I tried different strings from another manufacturer, but didn't quite find them to be a match. Some were too light. So after some research, I thought I wanted a set like 11-52. I decided I would try a set. I started with a popular manufacturer, but they were way too light. As a matter of fact, I think their lights are still too light. They just felt and sounded weak. I wasn't super concerned about volume although more is better. I wanted full sound more than loud. I want to enjoy playing the guitar for the hour or two I play daily. After trying the other brand (which I decided I really like their medium set on my AJ220), I decided to do a bit more research on string tension. I went to a website for personal opinions and recommendations and came away with a pretty nice list. I tried several of them. Some were really good. Then I tried these strings...WHOAH. So, here goes...
The set I put on my Takamine are the Phosphor Bronze 2086, Light 11-52. After my experience with the other brand, I thought the 11-52 might be way toolight for me no matter what brand, make or model. Well, I read a few reviews about these strings and quite a few people were complaining about the tension being way too high. I did notice, though, Dean Markley marked these 11-52 as "light". So I decided to try them and I am so glad I did. These strings made the low end really come to life. The wound strings feel like there's more mass and there's a lot of sustain. Very full sound and just the right amount of punch. I think these are the magic set for my Takamine. If you decide to try these, I highly recommend you go a set gauge lower than your usual gauge preference.

product_title: Shinp Stage Lighting Laser Light DL-55 Green Red Four Lens 260MW DMX512 for DJ Club Disco Home Garden Birthday Xmas Christmas Party Effect
review_headline: Scanner-based lasers just can't be made this cheaply and be effective. It's bright, but makes disappointing shapes.
review_body:
This is ridiculously over-priced at Amazon. It's available on eBay for $192 right now, and even that's a bit high for what you get. The one I have is actually quite bright, contrary to what the other reviewer said (that's its primary redeeming characteristic). For a scanner-based laser, I guess this is cheap, but you really can't get a decent scanner for this cheap ($1000 is considered the minimum entry point for a laser that can draw shapes with accuracy, and even that is toward the low end). The scanners in this device are slow and noisy (noisy both in terms of signal noise and audible noise), so the shapes are sloppy; nowhere near as clean as the shapes in the demo videos. The manufacturer is basically lying to you in those videos; they clearly have a much faster and more accurate scanner in the videos (this manufacturer makes some higher end stuff with faster scanners, so it wouldn't be difficult for them to pull such a bait and switch). The ones in this device make very sloppy shapes.

So, the good: It's bright (much brighter than any laser by a good manufacturer in this price range). It does do shapes, which very few low-cost devices can do, but the value of this is limited as they aren't very clean shapes. I'd rather have one of several laser models from American DJ or Chauvet in this price range, even though they aren't as bright and won't be scanner based (so no shapes like this one does). If you're using it with haze or fog and just want it to fill the air with laser beams, it'll work fine and for a quite large space (because it is so bright). The chassis is reasonable sturdy, all aluminum, with nice mounting options.

The bad: Noisy, slow, scanners. Shapes are goofy looking. Sound active mode is workable but unimpressive. DMX implementation is relatively weak (though many low-end lasers don't even have DMX support, so it's nice that it has it). If you're using it to put shapes on the walls or floor or ceiling (rather than beams in theair), you'll be disappointed. The shapes look like a toy made them, even though it's big and expensive very much unlike a toy. The chassis, while sturdy, contributes to the noise. The scanners, when vibrating, make the case rattle. A rubber washer on each of the connection points would probably fix this, but would cause a manufacturing cost increase of at least 8 cents, so will obviously never happen.

product_title: Fog Machine with Wired Remote Control
review_headline: It looked crappy doing this for a graveyard scene
review_body:
I got this product after reading many product reviews. It was used for an outdoor graveyard setup on Halloween night. I got the separately sold piece that controls it ( http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B00LKXYYVC?redirect=true&ref_=cm_cr_ryp_prd_ttl_sol_17 ), so I didn't have to manually set it off. I had the controller pushing the max fog (http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B004B470XG?redirect=true&ref_=cm_cr_ryp_prd_ttl_sol_16) it could. This machine covered our graveyard area (30 feet x 40 feet) without a problem even with a constant slight breeze. Once in a while a strong gust of wind would come by and push the fog down the street. This was hilarious because then those down wind could not see anything until the fog cloud passed (a few kids screaming). Initially I found it shot a straight stream of fog about 5-10 feet before it started to spread. It looked crappy doing this for a graveyard scene. I went to a local store and got a cheap fog machine cover (gravestone design) and the mesh material caused the fog to immediately spread out and gave the exact look I was going for. I used one lightening and thunder style strobe and three tiny basic strobes in the graveyard scene. It looked great and we got good comments all night. A full reservoir (half a bottle of fog) lasted about 3 hours.

DO NOT use this inside. It is way to good for an indoor party use! I thought I would use it for a Halloween party and decided to test it in the living room when it first arrived. After about a minute I could only see 2-3 feet in front of me. It filled about a 1,000 square foot area and set off the smoke alarm. I had to open all doors and windows for 3 hours to clear it out (30min of fanning the smoke alarm to shut it off).

If anyone has further questions feel free to email me at floridasheepdog@gmail.com

product_title: Epiphone EJ-200CE Acoustic-Electric Guitar, Shadow Preamp
review_headline: Best Bang For The Buck! Review of Epiphone EJ-200SCE
review_body:
REVIEW DISCLAIMER - Please keep in mind, this is a review of the most recent release of the Epiphone EJ-200, which is the SCE (solid cutaway edition) which offers a solid spruce top and laminate body and sides. The "CE" edition only offers a three piece top which is essentially three pieces of wood that have been wood glued together and planed down and finished to make the guitar top, while the "SCE" offers a one piece, solid wood top which greatly affects the sound and will better with age once the guitar begins to "open up". I have not tried the "CE" or standard, non-cutaway, dreadnought version of the EJ, which is just the EJ-200, so I can not speak for those instruments.

Now with the review - first off, this is a BEAUTIFUL instrument! The moment you look at it it just gleams! I can safely say that I've never seen a guitar this nice looking at this price-point in my life. From the gorgeous vintage sunburst finish to the crown inlays, mustache bridge and the ultra-high gloss shine, this guitar is a definite showpiece and will be the talk of any gig or jam session once you pull it out of the case (and I do RECOMMEND that you buy a hardshell case for this beauty if you want to protect the finish. Epiphone makes one specifically for this model). It's so nice looking that you almost don't want to play it, and rather just display it, until you strum the strings and hit that first chord and the thing just sings! It has a sound, unplugged, that is as good as guitars more than three-times its price. This is no joke. I've tried $1500 Martins and Taylors that don't sound as good as this. Now, I'm not saying that this sounds better than it's counterpart, the Gibson J-200, which sounds better for sure, but then again, that guitar is $3K+ and the difference in sound is actually not that much. The J-200 sounds a bit louder and deeper and sustains a little longer, but otherwise, it is almost the same guitar and at 1/8 the price the EJ-200 is probably the greatest bargain guitar outside the Epiphone Les Paul Standard (which, when the stock pups are replaced with a better set, like a Seymour Duncan Hot Rodded set or '59 set for instance, sounds just as good as a Gibson Les Paul right down to the signature chunkiness and sustain). I guess you can see where I'm going with this. Epiphone just knows how to make a quality instrument at an affordable price - period, and the EJ-200 is their flagship acoustic/electric. Yes, I know they also produce the solid wood Masterbilt series, but personally I like the EJ's sound and look much better.

The EJ-200SCE is a 25.5" scale guitar, with a solid spruce top, laminate body and sides , rosewood fingerboard with faux mother of pearl crown inlays, and gold grover tuners. The guitar features an eSonic 2 Pre amp and two pickups - a Shadow Nanoflex under the bridge and a Nanomag at the end of the fingerboard, and also features a built in tuner. The phase shift between pickups in the preamp system provides a serious, distinct range of sounds which makes the EJ-200SCE capable of playing any style of music from Jazz to Rock.

The Sound is amazing and will remind you of much more expensive guitars. The guitar is heavy and very well made and should hold up to the rigors of playing for years and years to come, whether you're a home musician or a gigging one, it will stand up to any kind of punishment.

There's really nothing more that I can say about this beauty, other than GET ONE, you won't regret it.

product_title: Pyle PWMA170 Dual Channel 400 Watt Wireless PA System with USB/SD/MP3, 2 VHF Wireless Microphones (1 Lavalier, 1 Handheld)
review_body:
I must say I took a chance on this one. The reviews were mixed but I needed an amp on short notice to perform an outdoor wedding and I was pleasantly surprised that the sound was both as clear and as loud as it is. This little amp is relatively easy to use and even on battery, it's Loud! All 3 wireless mics it came with worked perfectly (though you can only use one at a time) despite the fact that they are not great quality, and will require very gentle handling. But the range was good, no odd sounds or distortion, and no drop out.
Audio playback of music off a USB stick was likewise flawless. For a single speaker, the sound quality was unexpectedly good. As a bonus, if you have music playing on USB, the microphones work in conjunction (so you can speak along with music) and since they have independent volume control, you can keep the music volume low and mic volume up higher. REALLY nice feature.
It has two 1/4" Phone inputs as well, so I suppose you could use this as a portable guitar amp or add a wired microphone if you needed the additional channels.

Down sides: The microphones are cheap quality. They are inexpensive to replace if need be, but will probably not last.
Only one wireless mic can be used at a time
The "remote" is sketchy at best. It has to be pointed directly at the front of the amp to work and that was unreliable when I tested it.
There is Zero feedback suppression in this, so keep the microphone well back behind the speaker or the squeal will be remarkable.

All-in-all, this is a terrific buy for the price point, and I forsee getting a lot of use from it.

product_title: TC Electronic Flashback Triple Delay Guitar Effects Pedal
review_body:
I had a lot of trouble using my flashback triple when I played live (or even practicing at home). So much so that I returned it after a couple of weeks as not fit for purpose. It is a great (really great) sounding pedal but the tap tempo feature, that I use a lot, is not suited to anything but a very controlled studio setup.

I'll try to explain why. Imagine a song using one delay in the verse and two stacked delays in the chorus (sort of thing this pedal is built for).

When we start the song, I use Delay 1. Critical feature of the pedal here is that, when Delay 1 is enabled, it reverts to whatever tempo that preset was saved with (ignores Time dial and any attempt to tap in a tempo before enabling the delay). So I have enable Delay 1 and then tap in the tempo as we count in. Not a huge problem. All is fine.

Later in the tune I switch to or add a different delay (lets say Delay 2) but when I enable this second delay, it uses whatever tempo 'Delay 2' was originally saved with rather than picking up the one I am currently playing with (so Delays 1 and 2 are out of sync). This means having to enable the new delay and then tapping in the new tempo before I can start playing. If you want to drop in the second delay and play immediately, this means the first few repeats are a nasty mess (until tap tempo takes effect). It also means some fancy foot work to enable and then tap the tempo in.

When I then disable this second delay the pedal then reverts to whatever tempo 'Delay 1' was originally saved with rather than keeping the new tempo or indeed the tempo from the first part of the song. This means having to tap the tempo in again.

Hopefully you get the issue here. Basically, every time you add or disable a delay you need to re-tap the tempo into the pedal. This is a pain when playing at home let alone on stage (you look like an inept tap dancer half the time).

Unfortunately (I've checked with TC support onthis) there is no way to force all delays to pick up the current 'master' tempo rather than having to tap it in every time I enable/disable a delay. Even the relatively cheap Visual Sound Dual Tap Delay has solved this problem.

I guess the Triple might works in the studio but live on stage it is very difficult and I have not been able to use the pedal at all. The upshot was that I went out and bought a Strymon El Capistan, instead. This pedal has fewer voices but is much (much) easier to use and so I tend to get more use from it.

Real shame as the Triple is a great idea and a great sounding pedal just very poorly implemented.

review_body:
A capacitor has two plates with a voltage between them. In a condenser mic, one of these plates is made of very light material and acts as the diaphragm. The diaphragm vibrates when struck by sound waves, changing the distance between the two plates and therefore changing the capacitance. Specifically, when the plates are closer together, capacitance increases and a charge current occurs. When the plates are further apart, capacitance decreases and a discharge current occurs.

A voltage is required across the capacitor for this to work. This voltage is supplied either by a battery in the mic or by external phantom power.

Now has there been any mention of using a battery with this microphone? Apparently, many computer sound cards and other consumer equipment use plug-in-power to supply voltage for a condenser microphone through the Ring connector of the stereo plug. Huh, it's just that I'm a recording engineer that has been doing this for decades after schooling and apprenticeship and I had no idea, cool, I'm still learning.

This condenser microphone will plug into a 3.5mm microphone jack on your sound card or into many voice recorders or cameras or any compatible device. Not a headphone input, not a Tip-Ring-Ring-Sleeve 4 connector headphone/mic input, just a stereo Tip-Ring-Sleeve 3 connector, stereo microphone input, that provides line powering, plug-in-power. Don't ask me which devices will be compatible because short of trying this, I don't believe that there is any other way to know.

This mic will not sound good, but it's not real bad either and you could be upgrading from your other microphones with this one, and be able to provide the much needed cable for placing it also. I'm thinking of voice recorders and their mics here, but the idea applies to any recording through any recorder. You can probably get away with using a 10 foot extension on this cable for more reach. Microphone placement is a crucial step to proper recording, and it will change with different microphones and the type of audio that they're recording. This microphone is designed for recording from roughly 2-8 feet away from it when talking loudly and it's pickup pattern isn't wide.

review_headline: Very purple white channel and anti-adhesive material.
review_body:
I purchased two of these strips and just like many other reviewers mentioned, the colors are not even remotely close to each other. One strip's white channel was actually somewhat close to white, but it still had a purple hue to it. The other strip is absolutely, without a doubt purple. The RGB leds are much closer to each other in hue, but still vary noticeably.

If you only buy one strip, you might get away with it, but when you have two strips next to each other, the color mismatch is glaringly obvious on the white channel. I can actually get a somewhat neutral whiteish color if I mix in lime green with the RGBs when the white ones are on to counteract their purple hue.

The adhesive on the back is such a joke, and I'd actually prefer if they hadn't put anything there. I used Scotch (3M) 10 pound extreme double sided adhesive every two feet or so to keep them up, yet shockingly, the strips still manage to come down! You'd probably be better just leaving the paper on the back and using the tape on that, rather than trying to stick it to this apparently anti-adhesive material.

But for the price, I'm satisfied. This product isn't remotely professional, but it is a great novelty and provides some fun lighting effects. If you want to get decent strips, you'd probably have to buy multiple at a time, test them and match the closest ones and return the rest. It's a shame that there's such poor quality control.

product_title: TASCAM US-366 4-In/6-Out or 6-In/4-Out USB Audio Interface
review_body:
I got this interface mostly because of the excellent price point and the positive reviews. I needed an interface to do audio recording (both mic and line) and having a better DAC/headphone preamp a nice plus as well.

Installation was a snap. Just plug in the USB, get the latest drivers from the website and install. Get into Windows Control panel's Sound settings - make sure to set it as the default device and jack the sample rate up to 24bit/192khz! I Plug in my (modified) Grado SR-60i's, fire up foobar2000 (with SOX Resampler) and start spinning some reference hi-res FLAC and DSD tracks. Very clean and natural sound with great clarity and sense of space. Head and shoulders above the somewhat hazy and glutenous sound I was getting out of the computer's stock soundcard. I ran some distortion tests (feeding a sine wave from the output into the input) - the distortion is very low and so is the noise floor.

I took the thing apart expecting to find a pile of cheap capacitors begging to be replaced. To my pleasant surprise, I found nothing but high quality solid state caps, which have excellent sound quality and extended lifespan. The mic preamps use discrete transistors, too.

review_headline: Great for the right vocals, needs lots of gain
review_body: This is a great vocal mic for powerful vocals. It adds a thickness and richness that fattens up thin singers. In quiet lower registers, it can be a tad muddy even with the LF rolloff engaged and an HPF on the preamp. For quiet detailed vox you are better of with a condenser. But it is fantastic in the mids and upper mids when you're singing with power into it. Adds really nice color. You will need a clean, high-gain preamp to drive it. And, even beyond the preamp gain and noise floor, the sound quality of the mic is very preamp-dependent. Specifically, the input impedance of the pre matters a lot. My preamp has continuously variable impedance, and the tonal character of the mic varies significantly based upon these settings. If you set the impedance right, you can minimize the low end mud to some degree and really open up the overall sound of the mic, enabling you I relax your voice more as you sing into it and add vibrance and openness to the sound. In a nutshell, I'd want anothe option (a good LDC) for vox at my disposal in my studio as opposed to using this for everything, but it will give you a great texture and fullness like no other mic on certain vocal styles.

product_title: Chrome Dome Knob 6pc - 6 Pieces Chrome Brass Dome Knob for Guitar or Bass
review_headline: Good knobs for the money (but with a slight modification for CTS split shafts)
review_body:
I've provided this input in the "Answers" section, but will also post here for completeness.

Similar to another user, I had to drill out the middle slightly to make them fit a split shaft CTS potentiometer.

I upgraded my Squier Jazz bass to CTS 450G pots with a split shaft (formerly used Alpha pots). According to the spec sheet (http://www.ctscorp.com/components/Datasheets/450g.pdf), it's a 6mm diameter shaft (solid shaft is 6.35mm).

These knobs contain a middle black plastic insert with teeth. However, it appeared to be "coarse" instead of the 24 teeth "fine" that are on the CTS pot. I simply used a slightly bigger drill bit to make the knob fit (slightly loose but I used the set screw to tighten the knob. Make sure to align the screw with the opening in the split shaft). After enlarging the hole, the press fit was a little loose but the set screw seemed to help tighten the knob on the CTS pot.

Not sure how much the set screw actually helps because I couldn't tell if the inner plastic insert prevents the set screw from physically touching the CTS shaft. The screw might just slightly compress the inner plastic housing enough to friction fit the shaft.

The knobs feel heavy (not "plasticy"). Parts arrived quickly via Prime Shipping.

Happy with the purchase (although I had to make a small modification). The set screw was a major advantage.

product_title: Full Size Electric Guitar with Amp, Case and Accessories Pack Beginner Starter Package Vintage Sunburst
review_headline: Unexpectedly decent guitar and amp set
review_body:
I've purchase four similar-type guitars lately for practice in building electric guitars. This guitar is surprisingly nice. It should be considered a "starter" guitar-- but a good one. Here are the pros and cons:

- Has only one pickup and that's near the bridge. Don't expect rich, deep tone. This guitar is obviously designed to appeal to the younger generation looking for metal / distortion guitar playing... thus the location of the pickup.
+ But it's a rather nice humbucker and pulls the best sound possible out of this guitar, considering its location.
+ The body is pristine, gorgeously finished. The wood (at least on the one I received) was well-assembled with joint marks just barely visible and blended in with the transparent / grin finish. It's an attractive guitar.
+ A swirl-maple 1/16" veneer on the surface of the neck provides an attractive and durable surface
+ The neck is straight and sturdy. I did not have to adjust the guitar or action at all... rare with off-the-shelf guitars.
+ The amplifier with this-- although predictably "tinny" due to the small speaker size-- is surprisingly robust. The basic tone is clear and clean, even at higher volume. Hit the "overdrive" button and you can get all the dirt and grit you want. Overall, it is a much better amp than a similarly-configured competitors guitar set (which I also bought. In short... this guitar set is better).
+ I like that the bottom of the neck (where it joins the body) is rounded and smoothed rather than cut off straight as we see with some guitars in this price range.
+ Comes with everything you need-- guitar cord, strap, picks, tuner and gig bag.

In summary-- this is a nicer guitar set than I thought it would be when I first purchased it. You get the entire set for about the price of a Fender Squier and the nicer tone and power of a humbucker pickup (although of course, not the tonal versatility of a 3-pickup Squier). I consider this guitar set to be well worth the purchase price and a good choice for a beginning guitar player.-pickup Squier). product_title: New Drum Set Black 5-Piece Complete Full Size with Cymbals Stands Stool Sticks
review_body:
I am not a drummer nor am I a professional musician so let's get that out of the way. I bought this for my kids who suddenly became interested in guitars and drumming. The item was as described, and it is indeed a full-sized drum set (according to a friend of mine who is a musician and knows about drums).

From a non-musician perspective:
1. Love that the set comes complete to get you going as soon as you finish assembling out of the box.
2. Snare came fully assembled (and somewhat tuned)
3. Assembly was a breeze (for a non DIY dad). My 9yo daughter helped me put it together and it took us under 3 hours from unboxing to hitting our first "drum solo".
4. I have no knowledge of tuning drums so I just played it by ear and listened to the sound of each drum to get a "tone" I am comfortable with without it sounding like an echoing toy drum.
5. Fit and finish of the product looks very well made for a "cheap" set.
6. Cymbals are OK - not sure what that means really.
7. I added a pillow inside the bass to give it more "oomph" - seems to do the trick.
8. Adjusting the drum heads are as easy as inserting the included tool and going on a "STAR" pattern to tighten or loosen the nuts.
9. Comes with DVD instructions but didn't need it because there were plenty of online videos I found - highly recommended to watch first before tackling the assembly.
10. Started playing with the different "levels" of "stretching" the drum heads as my kids where playing them so we are now playing "in tune" sort of.
11. I bought a "stress mat" from Harbor Freight tools so I can sit the drums perfectly without messing with our wood floors.

From my professional drummer friend:
1. Kit is amazing for the price.
2. Definitely a beginner's drum set. Not a toy but a serious beginners drum set.
3. For the price, it sounds okay, so long as you don't decide to take it to stage.
4. Easily upgradeable to quality drum heads and cymbals.
5. Able to "tune" it without issues and fit and finish is pretty impressive for this price range.
6. Don't expect to sound exactly in-tune with professional drum kits you hear being played in the songs you hear on the radio.
7. Bass pedal is not designed for "experts" so be gentle, if that's even possible with drummers.
8. I'd buy this if I had very limited budget and want to practice at home or get started.
9. I had my reservations and definitely lowered expectations being that I am a seasoned drummer but I was impressed by the decent sound that comes out of this drum set.
10. Definitely, a great buy!

product_title: Shure Microphone
review_headline: EXTREMELY faithful vocal reproduction, broad enough range to record more than just voice!  GREAT DEAL!
review_body:
This is a stunning microphone designed for any kind of vocal work, but which will work well for any other sound with frequencies mostly around the human voice range.

Produces a warm, clear sound VERY faithful to the input. I can't stress enough how faithful its recordings are to the performer's vocals. It works wonders for speech, for singing, for chant, for beatboxing, and for turning regular sounds or instrument sounds into sound effects / sound fonts / MIDI instruments.

VERY shock resistant.

Heavy, and heavy-duty.

Con: The only 'con' I can come up with is that it's so true to the sound that you'll hear everything in your recording -- including windows, ceilings, furniture, anything that makes a hum, or anything else that will affect the ambient sound in the room. It picks up your local soundscape very effectively.

For about $100, I must insist this is a great choice for your recording arsenal. In fact, it's the ONLY mike I carry. I pair it with Blue Icicle for 96kbit recording.

Pretty good guitar for the money. When you recieve the guitar, the first thing you need to do it take off the strings and use lemon oil (you can buy it at your local music shop) to condition the fret board and bridge. product_title: Mendini 1/2 MV Solid Wood Violin with Hard Case, Shoulder Rest, Bow, Rosin and Extra Strings
review_headline: A few kinks, but great overall.
review_body: This arrived on time for our daughter's birthday, we ordered the 1/4 size. It was packaged very nicely in a big box stuffed with thick paper to prevent the smaller box (that held the violin itself) securely in place. We haven't tested it yet as far as sound goes, but I can say it will most likely need to be tuned up before use. The case it came in is wonderful and well built and has straps for easier carrying, on the inside there was small flecks of black lint which was easily removed. The rosin looks a little on the cheap side (thin and in a rectangular plastic piece). One of the things I was most disappointed with (reason for 4 stars) was that the bridge was cut unevenly. It's curves as it should be but one end is shorter and rounder while the other is taller and pointy, almost sharp. The f-holes also has white paint on the inside for some unknown reason. product_title: ION Audio Cassette Adapter Bluetooth | Bluetooth Music Receiver for Cassette Decks
review_headline: I think I might get it to work, eventually...
review_body:
I've wanted a bluetooth cassette adapter for years, and I finally put down the money for one. I paired it with my phone, put it in my car stereo's tape deck, my speakers exploded with sound (it's incredibly well-amplified, a welcome change from the wired cassette and FM adapters I've been using that are too quiet) for half a second, and then my tape deck spit it out, flashing a warning the manual interprets as "tape too tight". (Feels fine advancing the wheels with my fingers.)

So I opened it up and took out some of the gears inside that seemed like they might be offending. Tape too tight. Took out all the gears. New error "Tape is broken." Put back all the gears but the reverse-stopper and put it in other side up (a trick I had to do with my last wired adapter). Deck ejected it halfway and no farther. I got a pair of tweezers and removed it, spent another hour trying different combinations, never getting anything but "tape too tight" or "tape broken".

I'm giving it two stars because it's technically not the adapter's fault. With enough research into how the bloody tape deck is sensing this, I might be able to rejigger this adapter into something useable. From what I could tell in the brief moment it played, the sound was fine, if ear-splittingly loud, but you have volume controls for a reason.

product_title: 38" Acoustic Guitar Starter Package, Guitar, Gig Bag, Strap, Pitch Pipe & DirectlyCheap(TM) Translucent Blue Medium Guitar Pick
review_headline: Cheap "TOY" quality! Does not work for learning to play guitar!
review_body: I ordered this guitar for my my son's sixth birthday. His older siblings play guitar, but his hands are too small for a regular sized guitar. I figured this would be a good starter guitar for him to begin learning. It is not. This guitar absolutely will not work for a child who actually wants to learn to play guitar.  The quality is extremely poor and it is pretty much unplayable.  When I took it out of the packaging, I noticed the paint was worn off the bars on the guitar neck. The zipper on the case was broken. We went to tune the guitar, and the included pitch pipe was useless--doesn't hit the right notes, and makes such a strange noise, you can't even pinpoint the note it is trying to make anyway. I used our piano. The guitar was nearly impossible to get in tune well enough to play--the quality of the strings is poor, and the tuning knobs are poor, and the guitar is cheap and junky overall. After tons of tweaking, we were able to play a few very terrible sounding chords.  In contrast, my 10-year-old also received a guitar (about $100 compared to $45 for this one). The quality difference was VAST. Tuned in minutes and played a beautiful chord right away, and stayed in tune.  If your child just wants a guitar to play with and is not interested in actually learning how to play--then this TOY guitar may be fun.  This will not work for a child, or an adult, who is serious about playing the guitar. Get a nice guitar. You cannot learn to play on a "toy" like this. I would have given it one star, but if you want just a TOY, then it is worth two, I guess. Still had the paint issues and the broken zipper.

product_title: Focusrite Scarlett Solo Compact USB Audio
review_body: This is a five-star device for mic preamplification and USB connectivity.  The device is dead quiet including on the computer side of the USB connection, where two distinct channels can be brought into your DAW, and the device has all the knobs you need for preamping any mic properly.  I'm tempted to take away a fraction of a star, but I won't, because this device did not work properly when I first set it up, until I reduced the bitrate on my computer (set by default for some reason to 96000), but the specs for this unit state it supports 96k - still I admit I spent no further time troubleshooting or diagnosing and don't really know if it was my computer or the little red box complaining about the 96k.  As soon as I brought it down to 48, which is fine for me, the box worked perfectly.  I didn't toggle back and forth to try 96 again, but I would describe what it had previously sounded like was everything you were trying to record (my voice for example) sounded like it was in very slow-motion!  96k may indeed work; I'm only on a Macbook Air and don't need 96k recordings, so I did not pursue further.  The Scarlett Solo version I got has two ins and two outs, and two USB outs.  It may also go the other direction on USB, so you can monitor the computer through the Scarlett headphone jack, but this is the longest path to latency, if you will, and I did not try it.  It's difficult sometimes, I think, to derive from the product descriptions of all of these Scarlett products how many tracks go across the USB; in my little box, it's only two.  This generally is a professional-quality and sturdy box that does what it claims.

review_headline: This guitar looks gorgeous and sounds very good for this small size
review_body: I ordered one on eBay for 100$ (free shipping) and received it today. This guitar looks gorgeous and sounds very good for this small size. The abalone binding around the guitar edges and the sound hole are beautiful, not expected for a 100$.guitar. It is solidly built and the action at the nut and at the saddle are just right so the strings are easy to fret. If the action are not right, I would have adjust them myself and not rate the guitar bad due to this (some new guitars need a setup to get proper string height). The saddle is specifically compensated for this guitar to achieve excellent intonation (.i.e.  notes at fret#12 are exactly one octave above the free strings). It looks quite different from a compensated saddle for full size acoustic guitar. Both nut and saddle are in bone. It has a truss rod and a truss rod wrench is included. The nut width is a 1.5" and the scale length is 22-3/4", these two factors determine whether the guitar is suitable for a junior or adult. The total length and the width do not really matter on playability. The fret ends are just a bit sharp, not noticeable unless you know what to look for (expected for any low end guitar, so I will not rate it bad for this), I will file them to make them smooth. I am an adult with many full size guitars to play, and I bought this one for a different purpose (converting is to a mandocello).

product_title: Selmer BS203 Brilhart Bass Clarinet Mouthpiece, Medium
review_headline: Great mouthpiece for novice to intermediate players
review_body:
I had purchased this mouthpiece in addition to a Rovner 3RL ligature in hopes of improving the sound of a plastic LeBlanc bass clarinet that I have been renting. This mouthpiece has greatly exceeded my expectations, especially since my prior experience with Brilhart mouthpieces on alto sax were mediocre. This mouthpiece fixed magically fixed may issues that I had been struggling with beforehand. The throat register was magically more in tune, and I didn't have to work so hard in transitions into clarion. The clarion register took on a full, round sound that wasn't as strident as it was on the old mouthpiece. In all registers, the mouthpiece could handle as much diaphragm vibrato as I cared to push through it without pinching off or squeaking. I found it much easier to voice correctly in altissimo.

My playing preference: As a flute student, I own very little clarinet music to speak of, and consider my self an intermediate player at best on the bass clarinet. I can transpose very well, so I can readily read bass clef music on the bass clarinet. I also read flute and alto sax music as if they themselves were in the bass clef, making key transpositions when necessary. As such, I tend to play much more in the upper registers instead of the lower chalumeau.

From my limited experience, I find that the sound of the lowest notes is a little closed off on this mouthpiece, but this is the case for any other mouthpiece I have tried thus far. This isn't the best mouthpiece for, say, clarinet choir playing, in which you hang out in the basement range all the time, but for soloistic work, this is a great choice that doesn't break the bank! Then again, I play tenor sax reeds on the bass clarinet due to local music shops not stocking any Vandoren bass clarinet reeds. Playing such reeds certainly works well for me, and for many others, but they are a little narrower than bass clarinet reeds, so maybe that is where my lower register problems arise from. For the adventurous: I recommend trying out Vandoren V16 or ZZ tenor sax reeds on this if you are in search of a different sound!

I think everybody in search of a mouthpiece should try this one out. It is a budget-friendly option. If you don't like it, Amazon is very return-friendly, but I say give it a decent try!

product_title: Seismic Audio L_Wave-15-Pair Pair of Powered 2-Way 15-Inch PA/DJ Molded Speaker Cabinets
review_body:
I bought these because they were less expensive than JBL EON's one of my peer musicians had, and were more powerful. I knew when I bought them they are heavier and bigger than the JBL's at 51 pounds, compared to the JBL EON's approximate 35 pounds. I spoke to a customer service rep at Seismic and asked why they are so heavy, and he said they use an older, analog technology that is heavier, but less expensive. He said they are more durable and may even sound better than a lighter, digital PA Speakers.

I noticed you can lay them down on their side and they point upwards at 45 degrees or so, like monitors. So they can act as a monitor or a PA speaker, in my opinion. You do have to install the feet on the bottom of the speakers when you get them -- you simply drill the feet into the polypropelyne housing, where a starter hole is provided. One of the screws stripped the housing so the foot wasn't tightly attached to the speaker. I thought this might become a problem so I got a bigger screw and that solved the problem.

No manual -- get it off the Seismic site. The customer rep at Seismic told me that if you send an amplified signal to the speaker, you void the warranty. I think you should make sure you educate yourself on how to use these speakers so you don't blow them. For example -- there is an output jack on the back of the speaker -- can you send a signal to a passive speaker from the amplifer in the Seismic L Wave speaker I am reviewing here? Will this blow its amplifier due to too much draw from the Seismic's power amplifier? These are questions I still need to answer for myself. But for now, I can go directly out from a mixer and get lots of loud sound without having to use an amplifier.

Update 6 months later.

These speakers are still holding up. I have used them several times now and they did the job. The guys in the band(s) I work with gave them a clean review based on their sound, although no one likes the heaviness of the speakers. With no manual, there are a few things I learned after calling Seismic.

First, there are three kinds of outputs from the powered speaker -- a 1/4" line output, an XLR output, and a Speakon output. The 1/4" is just a line output and sends an unamplified signal to another speaker. The XLR output does the same, and is the output you use to send an unamplified signal to another powered speaker. The speakon output is for sending a powered signal to a passive speaker. Don't send a powered signal to another powered speaker or you will blow it. I made this mistake early on, and later found there was no damage to the speaker, although it was making horrendous noises during our performance and I thought I had blown it at the time. It took a trip to an audio repair place to discover the powered speaker that received the amplified signal from the Seismic LWave was actually OK, but was making "blown" noises only due to be overdriven at the time I sent a powered signal to it. I was lucky it wasn't permanent.

I did notice that there is a bit of a hiss if you turn the gain way up. I had to mitigate it by turning the treble down on the speaker. I'm not unhappy with the speakers though, but at times, sort of wish I had bought the JBL EONS since the EON's are lighter and smaller, but pack similar power. But the price of the Seismics makes them hard to say "no" to for the gigging musician. I paid about $225 per speaker shipped to my door. Which at the time, was a great price as the JBL's were about $140 more expensive each.

product_title: Samson SMS150 Mixer Stand Holder
review_body:
I purchased this from a different source, but am overall pleased with it. First, you need to know that this is basically a piece of painted sheet metal with an open back and a microphone stand attachment, with four sides.

The sides are made from bends in the piece of sheet metal. Although one of the product photos (at the time of this review) show a boom post, that is not included. Still, the convenience that this holder provides is well worth it to me.

Note that while the XP150's mixer is not particularly heavy, I do not recommend attaching this holder to a boom on some of the budget boom stands because their locking mechanisms may not take the total weight of this holder plus the mixer. I found this out when I tried it on a fifteen dollar stand and the weight with the book halfway extended caused the boom to dip significantly. Bottom like here is if you do plan to attach it to the end of a boom as shown in the product photos make sure you have a beefier stand or you do not extend your boom more than a quarter the length.

This is perfect for just about any straight stand. I tried it on both tripod stands and an [[ASIN:B0002MJTZ8 On Stage MS7201B Round Base Microphone Stand]] with excellent results. I prefer the round base style stand because it is stable with this holder and XP150 mixer and adjusts to a good working height.

Overall, if you own an XP150 this may seem pricey for a piece of sheet metal and a female threaded adapter, but it's definitely convenient and - to me - worth every penny.

product_title: HWP H-BSTB Brass-Saver Trombone Brush Set
review_body:
I am an advanced high school trombonist, and after buying a beautiful, barely-used Blessing B-88 (with closed wrap F-attachment) I knew I needed a new brush to keep it clean. My old brush, with an unprotected(!) metal spring core, couldn't even attempt to navigate the tighter turns of my F-attachment.

Let's start with the good: this brush easily cleaned the entire length of the inner, outer, and main tuning slides (yes, it's long enough to pass through the bow), and it passed straight through the closed rotary valve (not through the F-attachment) like it wasn't even there. It got through the tuning slide of the F-attachment and the short half of the attachment with only a little difficulty, but nothing to complain about. In addition, possibly best of all, the brush is very absorbent, so after you've cleaned your trombone and dried the brush (I used a microfiber towel) you can (slowly) pass the brush through again to get the inner tubes dry as a bone.

I only have a couple of problems. As the brush passed through the tight bend of the F-attachment tuning slide and the open rotary valve (through the F-attachment), the resistance it put up seemed to untwist the leading end of the brush (like a can of Pillsbury dough). I'll update this if the problem gets worse, but I don't think that it will. In addition, it couldn't quite get the first length of the inner slide (the dirtiest spot, right where your mouth is) clean because the brush part is too soft, but it did better than my old brush. These are relatively minor problems, though; my main issue is that the long half of my F-attachment had one too many tight turns for the brush. If you go in from the screw, the core isn't firm enough to get through the last bend; if you go in from the attachment, it isn't flexible enough to make the turn in the valve. I bent the core trying to get it through (FYI, even when it's bent halfway along the length it works great everywhere else), but I simply couldn't getthe core through the long half of my attachment.

All in all, though, this is the best brush I have seen on the market. It is flawless if you have a straight trombone or an open wrap attachment, and it does far better on a closed wrap than any metal spring core brush could (at least it can clean the short half!).

product_title: Rode Microphones RODE PSA1 PRO STUDIO ARM,
review_body: So I was extremely uneasy on getting this for a number of reasons. One reason was that this is rather expensive, but another is that I wasn't sure if it could support the weight of my Blue Yeti with shock mount. And I have to say, I can see why this is expensive. Because this thing really does work, even for some of those REALLY heavy microphones out on the market. This boom arm also supported my buddy's MXL USB .009 which is also rather heavy. So, let me explain how this thing works. It has 2 mounts that you can use to mount this on, one mount is a clamp which you just tighten onto your desk. Another is one where you drill a hole and then you can mount it it your desk. So I use the clamp method so I can reposition the clamp and don't want HUGE holes in my desk everywhere. So onto how this supports the microphones. As you probably already know, stands similar to this use a spring-loaded method where the stand is spring loaded so with no load, this thing will just spring up like an erection(Not a very good comparison but there you go). And that allows it to support lightweight and heavyweight microphones without sagging and still have the ability to lower or raise the height to your preference without ANY sagging. Now, something that some people look at when buying stands, is vibration control. And if that's what I was looking for in this, I would not like it all too much since it does let in quite a bit of vibrations(Varies on your surface). However, no desktop mic stand is meant to act as a shock mount as well. But it does reduce ALOT of vibrations compared to just having the mic on top of the desk with the included mic stands that come with the Blue Yeti and MXL 009. Overall, the price tag is definitely worth the quality since this will get the mic out of your way, looking cool, and will last a LONG time.

product_title: Allora ATR-1301 Aere Series Plastic Bb Trumpet Red
review_headline: Recommended for those that want a cheap trumpet.
review_body:
I gave this a try not expecting much. I played brass trumpet throughout my school years so I can compare the two. It is very lightweight and actually sounds pretty much like a trumpet should sound. However, I find that the tone is pretty "airy" in the lower registers. Also, there were some flaws on the one that i received right out of the box. There were minor scratches here and there and one of the valve tops is slanted slightly off axis. Also, you will definitely want to pick up some valve oil and slide grease. I was worried the slides were not even functional because they seemed stuck in place at first. After pulling on them with some force they popped off. I applied a coating of slide grease and they are now functioning as smoothly as my old brass trumpet. The valves were also pretty sticky after the first play session. Standard valve oil did the trick as the valves are actually made of metal. The case and stand it comes with is surprisingly nice, though. The plastic mouthpiece is a 7c and is decent, but more experienced players will want to definitely pick up a standard metal mouthpiece. That may help the tone problems I've been having. I haven't tried one with it yet. Once I got back into the hang of playing i was surprised with how nice it can sound. At this price point, this is a great pick-up for someone who may have played in the past and wants to see if they still "got it"...or a young beginner who may not invest the time in picking it up full time. The fact that it comes in different colors is a nice plus as well. I was VERY skeptical as there aren't many reviews out there on these plastic instruments...but considering what I paid and the low expectations I had (I feared it would be a total piece of trash), I'd consider myself satisfied.

EDIT 4/22/15. I upgraded to a Blessing (brand name) mouthpiece and the sound is better now. I get a less airy tone. I'd recommend using a standard metallic mouthpiece over the plastic one.

product_title: Blueridge Historic Series Dreadnaught Guitar
review_headline: Outstanding Guitar With Golden Era Specs
review_body:
The BR-180A is a fantastic sounding beauty. I purchased one of these guitars with the Adirondack spruce top & you can't find anything remotely as good for twice the amount they cost. After I bought the 180A, I AB'd it against my Martin D41, Gibson Singwriter Deluxe & Taylor DN3. It sounded just as good as the Martin with just as much bass & sounded better than the Gibson & Taylor. It's very high quality, has fantastic tone & more abalone bling than you can imagine. The secret to it's tone is the pre-war forward shifted X bracing & Adirondack top. Adirondack is extremely articulate and produces crystal clear notes. Bass, mids & treble are equal through the spectrum. Adirondack is extremely hard to come by and has the best tone quality. It's for that reason that Martin used the Adirondak and forward X bracing before WWII during the golden era of guitars. Now if you want a pre war reissue Martin, you would have to spend 4 times what the BR180A costs. The Blueridge BR180A is a steal at this price & definitely a keeper. I understand that Blueridge guitars are garnering praise & high reviews from the likes of Acoustic Guitar & other guitar magazines. They will raise the prices soon so grab yourself one!
* UPDATE- I've had the BR180A for a year now and it's really opened up in the last 6 months. I actually set this guitar in front of my stereo speakers allowing the top to vibrate and speeding up the "OPENING" process. It vibrated to the point that you could hear the stings ringing out. This is an old trick that I've known about for a longtime. This guitar now has the most beautiful open sound of any guitar I have ever owned. If you buy one, the Adirondak top for $150 more is well worth it. My Martin owner buddies jaws drop when they hear this canon! Buy it you will be glad you did!

After about 30 hours of breaking in however I started getting a warmer and fuller bass end and the whole speaker over all, warmed up and now has very warm, clean, clear, articulate even tones. product_title: Bogner Alchemist 112 Tube Guitar Amplifier
review_headline: One minor change... but otherwise perfect!
review_body:
Amazing amp if tweeked just a tad. You dont need to change the power tubes, just the preamp tubes which dont need biasing. Switch out the EH V1-V3 stock tubes with a JJ5751 in V1 and JJ12ax7s in the other 2 and it tightens up the bass and rolls off the ice picky high end that the Celestion V30 naturally has. The low mid emphasis also helps round out the sharp upper mid spike the v30 has as well. The clean channel opens up fuller and the gain channel is tighter. Stock, it is a little loose and unrefined. I didnt even notice the darker flare that JJs tend to have. Granted, i use a darker guitar so i always keep the bright switches on for each channel. If youre using a tele or strat then it may still be fine without. So change the first 3 to JJ and the other two can be EH. The stock phase inverter is a pice of crap chinese one so Eh is an upgrade. The 5751 also makes it take pedals a little better with more clean headroom. I tried tungsols and ruby and ehs, but JJd helped the overall tonality of the amp the best. Just dont put a JJ in the phase inverter. Not so good there in any amp really.
But other than that the channel and boost functions work great and the delay and reverb are above average.

review_body: I was prepared for this mouthpiece to not fit perfectly because an earlier reviewer mentioned it. And it would not fit most of my barrels.
