product_title: Jensen Vintage Ceramic Speaker
review_headline: Break it in and then drive it.
review_body:
One of my favorite speakers, and I've tried a bunch. This 12" C12K 8Phm speaker came in my Deluxe Reverb amp stock.
I'm a tone chaser so I've tried just about everything else too...
Greenbacks, Creambacks, V30's, Jensen P12Q Alnico's, Jensen C12N's, Eminence GB128 Legends, Eminence Patriots, Swampthangs, Eminence Cannibis Rex, and even other sizes from 6" to 15".

This is a great and versatile speaker, and a good price point at $95-$100. The biggest difference between this Jensen and most of the others is that it has what Jensen calls a "tight" low end. Most of the others have a looser low end that can be a little farty (P12Q comes to mind.)

The only downside I see to this speaker is it is a bit heavy at 9.65lb. That big heavy magnet is the price of the tight low end. The other feature that could be a downside or an upside depending on your specific application is that it is fairly efficient at 99.1 db sensitivity, so it can be a bit louder than some other speakers at the same volume setting.

Give it 75-100 hours of good "stage volume" break in, and she'll mellow out and sing for you. Jensens are sometimes a bit harsh until broken in. (As are many other speakers but Jensens in particular.) Does good with distortion, overdrive, and every effect I've put through it. Overall, this is a great sounding speaker that cuts in the mix, and gives great sounds across a variety of genres and styles of play. I keep trying to find something I like better and I haven't been able to, although I haven't tried those creamback 65's in the deluxe reverb yet so those are TBD still.

It's hard to find a more versatile and balanced guitar speaker, in my opinion. Sparkling cleans, chunky low end, and takes distortion and overdrive well.

Highly recommend you listen to the sound samples on the Jensen site for tonal differences between speakers. Just be aware that those samples don't demonstrate weight differences, or sensitivity differences -- they normalize the volume in the samples.differences, or sensitivity differences -- they normalize the volume in the samples.

product_title: Casio Learn-To-Play Quincy Jones Keyboard Bundle with Playground Sessions
review_headline: I wish I had this when I was younger
review_body:
I wanted to learn to play the piano but have no musical training. Within a couple of hours of setting this keyboard up, I was able to play the right hand part of "Somewhere Over the Rainbow". It took me a couple of more hours to get the timing of the left hand to match up to the right, but now I can now play a song on a piano with only 4 hours of practice and no teachers. That impressed my wife, who grew up playing piano and the pipe organ at church.

The songs range from very simple to extremely difficult, so you can pick and choose what works best for you. Probably the best part is the ability to slow down the song or have it only progress when/if you hit the correct keys. If I had this as a kid, I would be able to play all sorts of music today.

If you have a kid, you can convince them that learning a song is like playing a game. The keys light up and you remember which ones they were and type them out in the same order and speed. "Follow the bouncing ball".

The display screen shows you the actual notes on a sheet of music so you can learn to read music as well. It also shows you which fingers you should be using to hit each key. Unfortunately, the little screen is too dark. That is probably my biggest complaint about the keyboard. I plan to purchase Synthesia software to connect this with my computer after I exhaust the keyboard's features. Although, that might take a while.

As for sound quality... this is what I would call a 'learning keyboard'. It sounds 'good enough' to learn to play the piano. If you want to perform at a concert, you'll need to upgrade to something considerably more expensive.

If you want to show off your new skills to your friends and family, there are lots of accompaniment options and even a Karaoke feature.

I am extremely satisfied with my purchase of the LK280.

review_body:
[[VIDEOID:1c5bf7c8225588db4f46b83df66910fa]] I've had a pretty negative experience with this product overall. I would not recommend you buy this, and I will not be buying anything by Gemini again. You've probably heard that people have had problems with this unit. You might be thinking, \\"Oh, they just got a defective unit.\\" At least that's what I thought when I purchased mine. But please heed the warnings and be very careful about purchasing one of these. If you somehow manage to get a fully working one, it will probably work just fine, but there are some things about this product that are pretty big design flaws that make even a fully functioning unit a disappointing experience.

My CDMP7000 had major issues.

When you use a USB stick, the master output produces static. I didn't encounter any problems with static interference when I used an SD card or CDs in this thing. Quite a strange thing indeed. I tend to use CDs over USB sticks so it didn't bother me too much, but in no circumstances should a device like this produce static over the master outputs. Imagine playing a house party with this thing.

Seek mode sucks. When you have vinyl mode off and use the jog wheel to search the track, it messes up the waveform on the display, so it doesn't match the music that's actually playing. This can be a major issue for people who use the waveform to help beatmatch. When this occurs you have to reload the track from the beginning to get the waveform to match up with the track again. It's also really slow and skippy, making it impossible to seek accurately with vinyl mode off. Which brings me to my next problem.

Vinyl mode causes the jog wheel to malfunction and ruin a mix. The surface of the jog wheels are touch sensitive. But it my experience they are more accurately \\"warm air\\" sensitive. You can literally hold your hand 3 or 4 inches away from the jog wheel and it will cause the track to stop and skip around. I'm actually not joking. I made a video. There were times when I'd be 30 minutes into a mix and the thing would just start bugging out for no reason. I wouldn't even be breathing on it and it'd start acting like it does in the video. Oh, sorry for the vertical video btw.

You also see in the video how unresponsive and garbage the touch screen is. Notice how it takes me a good 5 or 6 tries just to seek in the track.

The play and cue buttons only work about 90% of the time. This is a serious problem and can seriously screw up a mix if you plan on introducing a track at a certain time. I've heard from other places on the internet that these buttons will just die in a few months time.

The scroll nob for browsing through your tracks is pretty poor. Sometimes it will skip 2 or 3 entries, sometimes it will just bring you all the way back to the top of the list. If you go slow, it doesn't do it nearly as often. This is a minor problem, but it shouldn't be a problem at all. This is easy stuff, guys.

But all that being said, if you manage to get a unit without the static when using USB, and the issues with Vinyl mode, and play and cue buttons that work every time, then you actually have yourself a decent little dj controller that would make a good beginner set of decks. When everything is working the way it's supposed to it's a blast to use. I would only buy this if you can get it used from someone who will let you test the thing out for a few days before committing.ng. I made a video. There were times when I'd be 30 minutes into a mix and the thing would just start bugging out for no reason. I wouldn't even be breathing on it and it'd start acting like it does in the video. Oh, sorry for the vertical video btw.

You also see in the video how unresponsive and garbage the touch screen is. Notice how it takes me a good 5 or 6 tries just to seek in the track.

The play and cue buttons only work about 90% of the time. This is a serious problem and can seriously screw up a mix if you plan on introducing a track at a certain time. I've heard from other places on the internet that these buttons will just die in a few months time.

The scroll nob for browsing through your tracks is pretty poor. Sometimes it will skip 2 or 3 entries, sometimes it will just bring you all the way back to the top of the list. If you go slow, it doesn't do it nearly as often. This is a minor problem, but it shouldn't be a problem at all. This is easy stuff, guys.

But all that being said, if you manage to get a unit without the static when using USB, and the issues with Vinyl mode, and play and cue buttons that work every time, then you actually have yourself a decent little dj controller that would make a good beginner set of decks. When everything is working the way it's supposed to it's a blast to use. I would only buy this if you can get it used from someone who will let you test the thing out for a few days before committing.

review_headline: Very good quality, a couple cons as well.
review_body:
These were my first set of "audiophile" headphones. I received the special edition set, and was overall happy with my purchase. The package came with three different cables, a short straight line cable, a long straight line cable, and a coiled cable, this helps to be able to use in different situations. The overall build quality was very good, I definitely felt I was holding a premium product after unboxing. The fit was pretty tight out of the box and I could definitely feel the headphones getting tight after maybe 20-25 minutes of use, which isn't good, but I read that they can be stretched out over time to have a better fit. Another con was the cable lock mechanism. In theory, you will only be able to use the cables that came with the headphones or cables from the Audio Technica website. If you had a cable with a small connector plug in then it could possibly work, I didn't try. The cables are very good quality, they are very thick and I don't see them breaking or ruining anytime soon.

The Audio quality was very good as well. The bass was a little bit on the stronger side. The bass was by no means even close to Beats headphones, but it was strong when it comes to the other respectable audiophile headphones and brands. The treble was a little sparkly which I didn't like, but maybe burn in will bring that down a little bit. The overall sound quality was warm with the bass having a little extra, which I like. I am using these for gaming and music. I would recommend these to purchase.

product_title: Haz Labs MutronIII Plus Envelope Filter Pedal
review_headline: Not for everyone, but not bad either
review_body:
The large size isn't for everyone, it is a monster, but I love the retro design. The cost is high and if you don't want to deal with a 9v battery then it requires a special power supply that costs even more money. The controversy about whether this is really a true Mutron or a shady stolen design will drive many away, but after trying it I can testify that this is an excellent envelope filter. Compared to a Mutron style envelope filter like the Keeley Neutrino which I own, the Mutron III Plus does some things better and some things worse. It is better at producing a consistent enveloped sound under all playing styles and all settings than the Keeley. It is worse at producing a juicy funk laden sound. The Mutron III Plus is more conservative and controlled. I've heard some call its sound wooden. I wouldn't go that far, but it does have less heart and more of a dry sound. The Keeley is awesome but it fills its pots up after a few hard hits of the strings and lays down for a few notes before bouncing back. The Mutron III envelops every note but without the moxie of the Keeley. It is a compromise that reduces its overall impact in order to deliver that consistent enveloped note.

After trying both the Mutron III Plus and the Keeley Neutrino, I kept the Keeley because of its smaller size and more extreme sound despite the flaws. I wish I could afford both. The company that sold this to me allowed me to return it and issued a refund. They were really cool about it so buy with confidence.

product_title: Audio-Technica ATH Professional Studio Monitor Headphones
review_headline: Good entry level audiophile grade headphones...
review_body:
I bought these headphones most likely due to the same reason most people bought it - the rave reviews on the internet, how these headphones are the greatest price for the money, which I can attest to, but there are certain things I think people may have over hyped:

The comfort, is decent, not "WOW THESE ARE LIKE PILLOWS!" it's more along the lines of , it's comfortable to a point it won't make you not want to wear them again, but after a while the clamping starts to chafe your ears, and after you take them off you definitely feel it.

The sound, is moderately flat and balanced, save for the slight bassiness, and yes it does sound really, really good but, no, I'm not an audiophile, I have much better things to indulge my life with that trying to find out the best sound for audio is, because at the end of the day sound is just a subjective thing that I think people just lie about the details that they hear and if you don't hear it your ears are "broken" or something...

The build quality is plastic, and seems to hold up very well, but I'm not going to try bashing it on the ground or throwing it around. I will say the cables look very sturdy and well made, and don't seem to have any defects in it. In addition to that there is a spring on the gold plated cable connector that takes the stress of the bending wire, where most of the fraying occurs

The design looks phenomenal, and I wouldn't have to second guess if I could be caught outside with these headphones, because the problem with these audiophile grade headphones in the market is that they always seem to pump out good sound, but lack on the design, but again that's just an opinion on what looks "good" and "bad"

This is just my opinion and take on these headphones, they are definitely worth your money if you can't or don't feel like spending too much on decent audio quality, definitely grab these.

review_headline: A terrific value, good sound, rugged construction
review_body:

I did need to purchase the "speakon" cables for this, but everyone is changing to this system, or else amplified speakers, it seems, so that wasn't a big deal. They look great, have metal grills on the front, tower slots on the bottom for tripods, and are a quadrangle shape, narrower in the back, with rubber feet if you want to set them on a table or on stage. They could, I suppose, also be used as large monitor speakers, but I'm using them for mains. They can handle plenty of power and have good tone and frequency response.
My only complaint that keeps them from getting 5 stars is the felt-like covering. This is good protection, but I have a cat and her hair is all over these cabinets, deeply embedded in the fabric covering. I would have liked a more leather-like covering, even though it gets scratched up more, which is probably the reason they went with this fabric. The price was great, too. I needed a simple, quiet "cough" button that could be wired to mute the primary voice microphone in my small audio studio. Among other things, the button had to be quiet (no button click noise that the microphone might pick up), and it had to be of suitable quality to handle line level audio signals. I added a shielded five foot audio cable with a phone plug to the switch that allows me to plug it directly into the "insert" jack on my voice microphone's audio processor device. Now, when I need to clear my throat or make a brief noise while recording, pressing this handheld switch mutes my microphone's audio signal quickly and silently without pops or clicks (or my cough) reaching my recording.

The Shure A120S switch can be set easily by the user so that the pushbutton on top is either momentary or latching (push on, push off) simply by rotating the dial on the switch's face. Build quality is good. The solid plastic case halves are held together by screws that allow easy interior access for wiring. Good soldering skills are a must in order to properly use this device. A pocket clip on the back allows mounting to clothing or belt.

Highly recommended for audio or other low voltage, low current switching applications where a handheld momentary or latching pendant-type switch is needed.

product_title: Handy USB Cassette Player and Tape-to-MP3 Digital Converter
review_headline: Mediocre sound quality.  Time consuming.  There are better ways to do this and get better sound quality.
review_body:
THIS IS SOLD UNDER MANY DIFFERENT NAMES. This exact module is sold by many different companies who give it different names.
The prices can vary from $16 to $30.

THERE ARE OTHER WAYS TO DO THIS THAT WILL GIVE YOU BETTER SOUND. If you already have a good quality cassette deck or a portable device like a Walkman, you can use that. There are two ways to do this:
-You can buy a Behringer Uphono, or similar device. You plug the cassette deck into the Uphono, which you plug into your computer. The Uphono is a high quality digitizer. The procedure for digitizing cassettes is the same as buying this unit.
-You can plug your cassette player directly into the sound card of your computer and the computer can digitize the music. This just requires a cable. It depends upon the sound card in your computer how good the results will be.
-There is free software on line to help you with either method. Audacity is the most popular but there are others. This cassette player comes with Audacity software on a mini CD.

This cassette player is of mediocre quality. It is definitely not as good as any home cassette deck. And, most portable Walkman type players I have heard are better than this. Beside not having great playback, this unit sometimes adds in additional noise. The noise can be bad sometimes, sounding like a helicopter. I get my best results if I don't put the cassette player on the computer.

But, if you don't already have a cassette player, then this might be worth getting. The quality of most prerecorded tapes is poor to begin with. You could make a lot better sounding cassette tape at home by recording an LP with a tape deck than if you bought a pre recorded tape in a record store. So, even though this is not a high fidelity unit, you really aren't loosing that much because the sound quality of most cassette tapes is poor. In the early 1980s, cassette tapes sales surpassed LP sales by a wide margin. What boosted the CD is that it was so much better than cassettes and quickly killed the cassette business.

This unit comes with a mini CD with Audacity software. Audacity is free software that you can download for free from the Audacity website. The Audacity software lets you capture the music on to your computer and also lets you edit the music files to improve the sound. The benefit of loading the Audacity software from the mini CD instead of the website is that the mini CD sets up all the correct defaults.

Digitizing cassette tapes is long, tedious work and not for the computer novice. Here are the steps;
-Load the Audacity software and set it up as instructed.
-Plug cassette player into computer with USB cable.
-Play cassette and push the record button on the Audacity software to record the music on your computer.
-->From here, you can either record individual songs or you can record the whole side and then split up the songs later. Either way is tedious.
Here is how I do it:
-Record the whole side of the tape.
-Import the whole side as a WAV file (the Audacity software will show you how to do it).
-Load the file back into Audacity.
-Run the noise reduction software to eliminate the tape hiss and the extra noise this unit sometimes adds.
-Separate the songs out one by one. With the Audacity software, it is easy to tell where one song starts and ends. You then just cut out all the other songs.
-Export the song. Use the song title as the file name.
-A window pops up asking for song info, such as album and artist. Fill that in.
-Repeat for all songs on that side.

But, with the poor quality of cassette tapes and the work involved, you got to wonder if it is worth doing this.
Well, I am because my wife had a bunch of cassette tapes, she does not care about sound quality and she is not worried about me wasting my time on anything as long as I am doing something for her.

product_title: Squier 'Mini'
review_body: I bought this guitar for traveling and as something that would be easy to grab and play on the couch.  I am an intermediate player with a number of $1000 guitars - including an American Stratocaster. I also bought it so I could toy with the electronics - something I wouldn't dream of doing with my big dogs. I am sure this is a fine guitar for a beginner, but am focusing this review for someone that wants a good travel guitar.  There are no flaws with this guitar.  Like everyone says, changing the strings to 10's is the first thing to do.  I agree for someone that already knows how to play.  The 9's are way too \\"bendy\\" and you have to play with a light touch to get a reasonable sound.  I played a while with the 9's but eventually switched to 10's.  Yes - change to 10s - for sure.  For the beginner, 9's may be ok, but put new ones on if you want a better sound.  Like everyone says, the tuning machines are cheap but they are passable.  Definitely had to retune more often than usual with the 9's. With the 10's the added tension may keep the guitar in tune longer - we'll see.  I did not setup the guitar - no fret buzz and the string height is ok - even for a beginner.  I will eventually lower the strings a bit, but I'm in no hurry.  The smaller fret board forces me to be slightly more precise in my fingering and when I go to my full scale guitars, the fret board seems huge and roomy.  So the smaller scale may have advantages to the veteran players as well as the smaller/younger player.  Out of the box and after tuning - you are ready to play.  How about the sound?  Much better with the 10's and probably would be much better even with new 9's.  Hard to say much about sound without talking amps.  Sound is fine and it gets the job done for me - I tend to use headphones (with VOX preamp) or a cheap small amp (Honeytone). I definitely recommend for folks that want a nice smaller guitar.  (Edit: I got the black color)

product_title: Sony MDR7506 Professional Large Diaphragm Headphone
review_headline: Sony MDR 7506 - The Honda Civic of Heapdhones!!!
review_body:
Have you guys ever heard of "Wirecutter?" You should go there. It's not the Bible of Tech, but it's a pretty decent reference.
Lauren Dragan of Wirecutter, after researching & reviewing 75 other cans with 5 panelists, concluded that these $80 cans are the best $150 headphones. Let's see...

So, of course I had to check these out. Funny! The first time I checked these out were on Anna Kendrick in "Pitch Perfect" (maybe I was checking Anna Kendrick very closely... haha). Well, she was sporting these cans throughout the movie.

HEADPHONE BUILD: 6 out of 10
You wouldn't quite call these over the ear headphones. The pads pretty much sit on your ear. The exposed wires near the headband doesn't promote too much confidence. Knowing my clumsy ass... I'm gonna snag it on something & break these headphones... Despite that, the stories I've heard is that they're a pretty durable pair of cans.

CABLE BUILD: 4 out of 10
It's not a detachable cable. Boo! It's a long coiled cable. Uhhh... not all of us are DJ's. (Actually I used to be... haha! I forgot.). The 3.5mm jack ends with a straight cable (my least favorite).

ISOLATION: 5 out of 10
It sits on your ear... so it's not a complete seal. Sound definitely seeps through. Probably 50% is passively canceled through the ear pads.

COMFORT: 8 out of 10
The clamp is perfect. It's tight enough to hold, but not tight enough to give you a headache. The headphones are really light. So even though there isn't much padding on the band... it doesn't matter. The pads get warm... but hasn't been sweaty.

SOUND: 9 out of 10
These headphones have been an industry standard for a reason. They do sound great! I own a pair of ATH M50x, Vmoda M100's, & Sennheiser Urbanite XL's. The MDR 7506's are cheaper than all of these, but they hang with all of them. I think the Sony's have a cleaner & clearer sound signature than theUrbanites easily. The highs are most definitely better represented on the 7506's. The Vmodas, however, hit way harder of course. The V in Vmoda is for the Vshaped sound signature (probably... I don't know). But the lows on the Sony's are pretty tight. Zreviews on Youtube states that "these headphones sound exactly the way a good sub should sound." Now, my favorites are the ATH M50x's. They have a milder V sound signature. The Sony's are 2nd to the Audio Technica's in my book (out of the cans I own).

PRICE: $100 on Amazon for the refurbished or the one's "like new". Sadly these headphones are discontinued. :(

I've been likening each of my headphones to a car.
Guess what? I'm gonna call these the Honda Civics of the audio world. They don't look durable, but they last forever. They're not the most exciting drive, but they drive for the long haul. I guess reliable is the new sexy (especially when Anna Kendrick is wearing them). :)

product_title: KRK KNS-8400 Studio Headphones
review_headline: Great for music creators, a debatable buy for everyone else
review_body:
There are two possible types of customer reading reviews for these headphones. One, music listeners, and two, music creators. I fell into the latter category, and for my needs, these headphones are incredible.

Let's make one thing clear right away, these are monitoring headphones, which means they are not manufactured for music listeners, they are designed for music creators. If you want artificially "enhanced" sound, look elsewhere. If you want bass, I would suggest in ear headphones with a good foam earpiece. All over the ear headphones I have tried do not match a tightly sealed in ear headphone when it comes to bass response. JVC HAFX34 are my choice for casual listening for dirt cheap. Shure makes a compelling pair of in-ear headphones for casual listening as well, but they are more expensive. Neither are designed for music creation. I started making music that way, years ago, when I was just messing around and learning how to play, and after listening to the tracks I had made on other headphones, I feel pretty pathetic. They sound awful, which I now fully understand because listening to anything on these KRKs makes flaws jump out at you. These headphones do one thing very, very well - play back the music like a monitor: flat, uncolored, with all its imperfections.

Am I a seasoned audiophile who has tested every monitor out there? Hardly. But I have a discerning ear and am building my own home music studio, piece by piece, when I am not writing books. My tracks from the last year at youtube dot com slash ninthcinemadown and the album "Sleep of Reason" by Jabberwocky should give you an idea of me just starting out with these headphones. I am a hobbyist musician, but I assume some of you are as well. I am just now finishing breaking in these headphones, and I'm still teaching myself how to use Logic Pro X, so the quality of the tracks I make will only increase. I don't feel like these headphones will hold me back in any way as I progress. My next upgrade will not be another set of headphones, it will be KRK Rockit speakers, because that is how one should monitor music tracks, with external monitors, not headphones.

These headphones are designed for vocal recording, where you do not want sound bleed into the mic when tracking, some instrument tracking, and edits on the go. They are not made for full-time mastering and production. However, right now, that is what I am using them for, and I think one can get by using them that way, as long as they test tracks on other speakers before releasing them to the public. One should always reference their work on multiple systems before publishing it, anyway. These headphones work well for me as my full-time production sound system for now, until I complete my studio. I am sure many pro musicians are cringing at the idea of using just headphones in the production space, but I cross-reference tracks with external speakers, on a thousand watt home theater and a premium Infinity car audio system, and until I invest in soundproofing and adding external KRK monitors in my studio, these headphones cover my needs. In an ideal world, I would have a lavish studio with Genelecs, soundproofing, and producers on hand to cater to my every production whim, but alas, I make music as a hobby, not a professional career, and I don't have unlimited sums of money to throw around. Professionals should appreciate these headphones and their flat response for vocal recording and quick, mobile edits. Less-than-pro musicians will likely find these suitable for complete music production, if they find themselves in a position where external monitors are not practical or possible.

Casual music listeners will likely not be overly amazed by these headphones. They are comfy, they are decently constructed, even if the plastic feels slightly delicate, and the inline volume adjustment is awesome, it never crackles or tarnishes the output. However, the bass response is lacking if you are a bass head who likes music that stimulates. These headphones are great for mixing and tracking, but they are less than thrilling for your casual listening pleasure. Much like AMOLED and overly-saturated LED screens are beautiful to look at for casual viewing, and make images pop, but are poor for artistic production. Sometimes even in the production environment, the lack of bass in these headphones makes it hard to determine how much thud or thunder to add, but you quickly get a sense of things once you listen to various test mixes across your other, familiar external speaker systems. I say this as a heads up for what you are getting here - a flat monitoring headphone. Do not let this turn you away if you are a music producer. I am a bass freak, I want bass so heavy it will dislodge my teeth, and I consider the Sennheiser headphones I owned briefly tinny pieces of crap, which is why up until these headphones, I refused to wear over the ear models, and only worked with in ear headphones. These do not have quite the bass that the Rockit external monitors have, but some professionals think the Rockits are too bass-heavy anyway. These headphones make for an excellent mixing experience, and a moderate, unexciting casual listening experience for those who prefer huge bass. Certain casual listeners will appreciate the detailed and separated sound, but I think those customers are limited.

So, if you are a casual music listener looking for extra rich sound, these might not be for you. The sound here is not rich, it is flat. Flat, and detailed, which makes it excellent for tracking vocals, and showing subtle flaws in a mix. If you're looking for richer than average sound, Bose has a good reputation for non-professional, higher-quality mainstream sound systems, I would test their headphones first before spending your money on monitoring headphones.

However, if you're a music creator, and are looking for monitoring headphones to step into the professional pool, I would say these would augment (KRK's) external monitors perfectly. Outside *slightly* stronger bass, a little more robust construction (I don't feel like these would survive being stomped on or thrown violently against a wall repeatedly, my measure of durability) and a bigger, premium leather carrying bag (this one is very cheap faux leather), I cannot find a single fault with these headphones in the year or so I have owned them. Most of the respectable reviews I read said these headphones are great, but flat, designed for monitoring and studio use. I concur. Being a bass freak, I hesitated, but am very glad I chose these, and would buy them again in a heartbeat. They form a great seal without glasses, and a good seal with glasses. Their sound is accurate, and accuracy outweighs artificial thump in the production environment for which they are designed. These headphones have a very pleasing sound, and are very comfortable. They may not look the greatest stretched across my oversized head, but they fit well, and sound great whenever I step into the home studio. I think that covers all the concerns and questions I would have had when shopping around, I hope I helped you decide if this product will fit your needs. It sure fit mine. product_title: DiMarzio DP152 Super 3 Guitar Pickup Black Regular Spaced
review_body:
This is a fantastic pickup, and thus deserves a review. Here is a copy of a review I wrote for a guitar website I belong to, because it all applies.

The Super 3 was kind of an impulse buy for me - I like trying the pickups that are a bit off the beaten path. I'm mostly a metal guy, and have worked with a ton of different pickups, and DiMarzio is quickly becoming a favorite brand for me. The pickup I replaced with this was a Seymour Duncan JB model (which certainly has its merits, I was just looking to try something new) in the bridge position of a Jackson RRT-5 Pro. Amp rig is a Marshall JVM410H and 1960 Vintage cab. The sound of the pickup is supposed to be designed for players that scoop their mids - it allows for a bit more treble without getting "hissy" sounding, and I can attest to that. It's a great pickup for metal - it's hot and responsive, helps fatten up the tone a bit (it helped to warm up the alder body tone of my Jackson), and really handles overdrive/distortion well. But metal is not its only quality, as I've used it for many different settings and styles, and it works great. I wouldn't say the cleans are the worst I've heard (try a bridge model Dimebucker or EMG 81 for cleans. Yuck.), but I will say I don't make a habit out of using it for clean settings.

Reliability & Durability: I find it hard to damage any pickup beyond use or repair, so all I can say is that as long as it's wired in properly (which it is), you should never have any issues, barring any factory defects. It's made just as physically well as any product from DiMarzio, Seymour Duncan, Bare Knuckle, or what have you. It don't see why it wouldn't last as long as I care to use it, so I'm not particularly worried about the longevity.

Overall Impression: As I stated, I'm a metal player for the most part, and I've been playing and experimenting with pickups for 16 years, and for all the pickups I've used in all the guitars I've had, the Super 3 is near the top. Hot, but not too hot. Responsive, but not fussy. Simple, to-the-point installation. Cleans aren't fantastic, but mostly I use the neck pickup for that anyway. I have only used about six DiMarzio pickups in my day, but they have all been satisfying, wonderful sounding pickups. If something DID happen to it, I would get another. It might not be as popular as some of the other pickups out there, but the Super 3 is certainly worth looking at if you need a versatile, high output bridge pickup for any type of rock or metal.

product_title: BEHRINGER ULTRA-G GI100
review_headline: Usable DI box, and Explaining the Hum/no hum issue
review_body:
I just received this and tested it but felt the need to review to clear up the buzzing/hum issue. First off, this thing feels solidly build. Nothing cheap feeling about it. It mounts in the rear of my rack with velcro tape nicely. The cab sim sounds very good - better than the pod HD cab sims to my ears, which is what I plan to use this box in place of (the lousy pod cab sims) if my power amp dies during a gig.- so this is a backup (for now- more on that later.). Also with this box, i can use my usual pod patches that have no cab sims and just plug into this, using the same patches without having to add cabs to the patches if my power amp were to die at a gig, since i'll then need to go direct to PA - this box will provide the cab model for all my patches. Again the cab sim sounds plenty good on this box..

I plugged my Pod HD unbalanced out into this, and then the bypass on to my power amp, so i am sending this box a line level signal - when used in this manner, it's dead quiet - NO hum. Only when used as a load box, from a power amp speaker out (the manual says this is designed for it if desired) does the box produce hum. If i needed a true load box, i would not expect a $40 box to pull this off, but as a true DI box using a line level signal, it works great, no hum, and the cab sim is excellent.

It is promising enough that at my next gig i'm going to try running direct for a set, and compare this setup (pod -> G100 -> PA) to my usual (Pod -> Tube power amp --> V30 loaded guitar cab miced up) for another set and see which sounds better to the sound guy. If this box sounds better, i've got some changes to make on my rig!

review_headline: While I love the guitar (especially after swapping out the pick ups ...
review_body:

Like another reviewer mentioned, it's cut too deeply and your guitar can flop around inside. You'll need towels or thick foam to keep the guitar somewhat secure. The latches and hardware feel flimsy and loose and the outside of the case is adorned with with gaudy "Schecter Guitar Research" logo written in giant gothic letters. For those who bought the Ultra III partly because they like the cool retro Fender Jaguar meets Italia Guitars look, the cheesy death metal aesthetics of the case really seem like a poor choice.

It seems no one else makes a hardshell case that fits the Ultra III guitar either. The lower bout is wider than other offset guitars like Jaguars, Jazzmasters or Gibson Firebirds. I suppose a completely custom case is the only option if you want a quality hardshell case for the Ultra III and that's going to be really expensive. Really a shame that Schecter hasn't redesigned this case.

product_title: Yamaha DTX-450K Electronic Drum Kit
review_body:
Before deciding on this set, I researched other low cost electronic drum sets from various manufacturers extensively. This was pretty much the cheapest set that got the best reviews across numerous sites. After having owned it for a little over a month now, I can definitely see why the reviews are so positive. I've been a musician for 15 years now, but always wanted to play the drums before anything else had I not been introduced to the guitar first. That being said, this is a great starter kit that is well suited for beginners such as myself to learn the fundamental techniques of drumming, and I'm sure any experienced drummer will be able to find something to love about this set, even if that something is only that it's quieter than a normal drumkit.

Despite the rather simplistic looking "brain" or control panel, the set is actually very highly customizable in many different ways which includes downloading and installing new kits and even songs from Yamaha so that you're not stuck with the default kits or songs. You can visit the Yamaha website to look at the manual in PDF form, and you can also visit YouTube to see a few reviews where these features are covered. There's too many for me to list.

In the end, I'm glad I decided on this kit as opposed to any of the cheaper kits in the $300 range. Not only that, but I felt the extra money was worth it since Yamaha is generally regarded by many as one of the most high quality manufacturers out there, especially when it comes to electronics.

EDIT: I've had this set for a year now and it's still going strong. No problems, no complaints and no regrets.

It's important that you place the soundhole humidipak in the case while playing your guitar and of course, that the case is kept closed. If you're playing your guitar and just leaving the soundpaks in an open case, you're cheating yourself out of longevity for the product. It's not rocket science.

Ease of use is unbeatable. Place one pak in the headstock area and the double-pak in the soundhole and you're done.

I use this humidifier system for my favorite guitar..... my Taylor 814ce. I trust this humidifier system because I've tried it and seen the results for myself. A little common sense and the Planet Waves Humidipaks is all you need.

product_title: Shure Sound Isolating Earphones with Quad High Definition MicroDrivers and True Subwoofer
review_headline: The best of the best 100% sound for 300% price.
review_body: This is a very interesting product for me. I think it is important to know my audio background before I can start talking about this product. I started listening to music on a pair of first generation Ipod Touch headphones. I then upgraded to a pair of V-moda ear buds which served me well for about a year. I then acquired a pair of Audio Technica ATH-mx 50 studio headphones that I used for studio monitoring, as well as a pair of Bose 2i2 earbuds for exercise. After several years my Bose buds broke due to a cable failure. With no option to replace the cable and an expired warrantee, I was forced to start perusing for a new pair of ear buds.  That is when the Shure earphones came to my attention.  I purchased them with the intent to use them for exercise and monitoring live performances and studio recordings. So far they have given me mixed results. First of all the sound isolation is really top notch; almost too much so. I recently used these in the woodshop while running a handheld power sander, I couldn't hear the sander at all and the music was just as amazing. This is good because the music is all you hear no matter what, this is bad because it can be unsafe while exercising, walking, driving or doing anything where you need to hear ambient sounds for safety reasons. This is just something that should be noted before you decide wither or not to purchase.  The sound that these produce is absolutely stellar (as one would expect.) They provide exceptional clarity and all frequencies come through to provide an amazing sound signature. I have found some interesting attributes with some modern tracks that I am used to listening at a high volume. In the past I would turn the volume up rather loud to provide maximum awesomeness and a healthy dose of distortion. With these headphones, you can turn the volume up as high as you want and there will be absolutely NO healthy distortion. All of the sounds are crystal clear at all volumes, which is a good thing but something toget used to.  These earbuds are very comfortable. The over the ear cable provides an extra level of secureness on ones head.  If you are not used to in ear headphones you may experience some discomfort in the first few weeks but this discomfort will surely pass. They include two different cable lengths that come in very handy for different applications in the studio and on the go. If you can't find a well fitting set of tips from the selections included, you have bigger problems. Huge variety of tips that provide different acoustical qualities and different feels. These headphones are highly customizable.  Another note: ya' know that hair raising tingling sensation that goes from your head all the way to your toes when you are listening to the best part of one of your favorite songs? Yeah, that happens at least twice as often when I'm listening on these earbuds. It's really weird, I keep thinking there is something wrong with me. But day after day, repeat after repeat I keep achieving the same results. Shure has clearly done something very right here.  Overall there is diffidently a time and place for these headphones. If you've got the cash and you are willing to spend it these are definitively the best of the best; these are the 100% sound. If you are the average consumer looking for a 90% sound for everyday use I would go with the Bose 2i2. The only reason I gave it four stars is because of the price; sorry I forgot to mention that. This is a perfect product for certain applications, with in an imperfect & elitist price tag.   Hope you found this review helpful, I am happy to answer questions to help you decide if these are for you!

product_title: TASCAM DR-70D 4-Channel DSLR Audio Recorder
review_body:
This is an outstanding little recorder. The most important feature on any of these field recorders is the mic preamps. They are clean and they have plenty of gain for use with dynamic mics. The unit can also drive a line output if you want to record sound on your DSLR at the same time.

This recorder is very solid. It's made from die cast METAL. Not plastic. It's a bit heavier than you might expect. But that's the price you pay for a METAL enclosure. The front panel is a bit cramped. I wish the gain controls were knurled. (They are smooth.) And these gain knobs seem to operate an internal electronic gain control. There is a very slight delay in operation of the gain knobs. It's like they are damped for smooth fades.

I did notice that the built in mics do seem to suffer from the "zipper" effect that plagued the DR60. When you move the gain knobs on channel 3-4 with the internal mics assigned there is a faint zipper noise when you move the gain knobs. If these same inputs are assigned to the the XLR inputs there is NO zipper effect.

So Again... The gain controls work smoothly with NO zipper effect on all 4 XLR inputs. The preamps are clean and very quiet with plenty of gain.

The headphone amp is adequate. Not super great but it's loud enough to drive most headphones well.

I think this is the best DSLR pre-amp recorder option available today for under $1000. It lets you record 4 discrete channels simultaneously. It has 24/48 volt phantom power. It has clean mic preamps. It has effective limiters. It runs on AA batteries or an internal USB battery. (Or both with automatic switchover.) It's compact & rugged. Only things I wish it had were a slightly more powerful headphone amp with a clip indicator and a slate mic. Otherwise I think this little device has just about everything you would need. And you can't beat the price!

product_title: Sony MDR7506 Professional Large Diaphragm Headphone
review_headline: Unless you only listen to Hip-Hop or demand mega bass, get these
review_body:
These could easily be rated 5 stars, but I haven't ever given out a 5 star rating because I find it difficult to say that anything is perfect. These are great but aren't necessarily perfect for everyone. These have been reviewed so many times that there probably isn't a need for another review, but since I enjoy and benefit from reading other reviews, I wanted to add my own to the mix.

The first thing that I want to point out is that these headphones can and do reproduce a good bass sound IF the bass is in the music. If the song was recorded with a lot of bass, these cans do a good job producing the bass without it being muffled like so many other headphones do. I actually enjoy using these headphones listening to heavy bass songs like Days Go By by Dirty Vegas, In Da Club by 50 cent, and Low by Flo Rida. What these headphones don't do is artificially add a lot of bass. After reading a lot of reviews, I was hesitant to get these as I didn't think they had any bass. Some reviews actually stated that very thing, which is just false. It greatly depends on the music that you are listening to.

I think there are some songs that don't contain much bass in the original recording (some old James Taylor songs come to mind)that sound a little better with additional bass that can be supplied with some headphones, but that's not to say that these headphones are defective. They are doing what they are supposed to do which is reproduce the sound as it was originally recorded. For songs like these without a lot of recorded bass, you might get a better sound with the Sony MDR-V6.

I listen to a wide variety of music, pretty much everything: classical, jazz, rock, hip-hop, country, you name it. I have tried seven different headphones and still own four of them. For the price, these and the similar Sony MDR-V6 model are both very good. For those of you looking for great headphones for under $100, I would choose one of these three: Sony MDRV6, Sony MDR-7506, and Audio-Technica M40X. Each one has a different sound and tends to be suited better for certain genres of music rather than all styles although some cans are more versatile than others. Anyway, if you only listen to hip-hop or music that sounds best with a heavy bass emphasis, then you might prefer something else. For some music I want more bass emphasis, but I don't like super heavy bass no matter what I am listening to.

I have one pair that I use when I am listening to hip-hop - Sennheiser Momentum. A great versatile good all-around headphone that does well with most types of music is the Sony MDR-V6. The Sony MDR-7506 and Audio-Technica M40X while both being versatile, I think are best for classical, jazz, acoustic guitar, vocals, and some rock. So what kind of music do you listen to? If you like classic rock bands from the seventies you will like these headphones. I think they sound great for Eagles, Fleetwood Mac, John Mellencamp, Little River Band, Kenny Loggins, Neil Young, CSN, CCR, Steve Miller Band, Kansas, Supertramp, Tom Petty, Van Morrison, etc.

After listening to these headphones, you may find that your other headphones (that you thought sounded so good before)sound a little muffled in comparison. These are really clear and crisp without being tinny. The more I listen to them, the more I like them. If you want a pair with just a slight bass tweak for a little bit warmer sound, then I'd go with the Sony V6 model, but both are very good and hard to beat. What are you waiting for...the sound is great and the price is great too. I'd look for a price of $85.

product_title: Cakewalk Sonar X3 Studio Music Production Software
review_headline: Cakewalk Sonar X3 - could be the best DAW on Windows.
review_body:
I've been a Cakewalk user since way back when there was no Sonar, no audio, just a MIDI sequencer. Sonar X3 is the current version of the product and IMHO it has really come into its own with X3. Sonar is a powerful DAW but has a great interface for most tasks. Now with this version the base version and Studio are not crippled in any way. You get the same core software as the Producer version with unlimited tracks. The differences are in what add-ons are included.

product_title: Thomastik-Infeld Spirit Violin Set
review_body:
Spirit strings are a good deal if you can't spend any more than this. They bring out a nice sound from your instrument. They have a little more power and gusto than Pirastro Tonicas, which is their primary competitor (similar product at exactly the same price point). However, the Spirits are not as responsive as Tonicas, and they aren't as pitch-stable off the bat. The Spirits would be great for someone learning violin. You can make lots of beautiful music with them, as long as you don't want them to speak really fast. For only slightly more money, the regular Vision strings from Thomastik-Infeld are a HUGE step up from these Spirits, at least on my fiddle. The Visions have way more dynamic range, focus, subtlety, and super fast response. However, every violin responds to different strings differently, so YMMV. If this is your first experiment up from cheap steel beginner strings, you'll definitely notice your fiddle sounding much nicer with these strings. However, there are LOTS of string options out there, and they will all behave differently on your fiddle!

I only gave three stars primarily because of the slow responsiveness issue, especially notable on the aluminum-wound A string.

Also, for what it's worth, the product description claims that these Spirit strings have a "low tension" but they actually are not that low compared to other synthetic strings.

Just for the heck of it, I searched \\"Bouzouki Strings\\" on Amazon and look who shows up as a result? D'addario. Could this be a mistake? Is their some other Bouzouki I'm unaware of? The gages looked right so I figured what the heck. Yes folks, these strings work PERFECTLY on a Greek Bouzouki. That snappy aggressive and rustic tone is there in spades and the tuning is rock stable. D'addario, you are one of my favorite companies ever and will always have my business because you make a great product. For ANY instrument.

product_title: Planet Waves Lemon Oil
review_body: I've used lemon oil for years on my hand-made guitar's ebony fretboard and this is the real deal, pure and simple.  A small bottle can last a lifetime.  I looked everywhere to replace my old bottle of lemon oil I bought in 1979, and I couldn't find anything that was simply lemon oil without additives, petroleum products or other un-named oils.  I bought this as an add-on and its perfect for expensive, fine woods.  I use a dampened cloth to rub this on my fretboard.  It lifts and cleans the dirt and finger oils while replenishing the life of the wood.  Buff it dry and you have a shiny, fast fretboard.  I also use it on my rosewood bridge.  Use it every time you change strings.  You can also use this to restore life to dead strings and to lift dirt stains from the finished surfaces of your guitar--it will clean dirt without lifting the finish.

product_title: Gibson USA Solid Body Electric Guitar
review_body:
I currently own a 1993 Gibson Les Paul Standard and I love it. This guitar is of premium quality and has ranked my top guitar after 30 plus years of playing. I had a chance to play a friends Gibson SG premium and I absolutely loved playing it. I decided to purchase the Gibson SGM since it has 24 frets like the Gibson SG premium, but without the huge price. Anyway, I know Gibson guitars are the highest quality, so I purchased the SGM with confidence.
Review: The first thing I did not like was the e tuner constantly making noise as it tuned and tuned and tuned again. I could not understand why it made such a racket. I took it to a guitar tech and come to find out the nut is not right. The e and a strings buzz and even with truss rod adjustment the two strings still buzz. Also, when the e string is tuned it gets a perfect tune, but constantly loses tune. When the f is fretted it is not an f, but f #. I finally replaced the e tuner with Grover replacement machine-heads, but still have the problem with the sharp chords on e and a. I have taken my guitar to several guitar techs and still the same old story. The Gibson authorized tech said it was good enough... Really? and the other guys did a nut job for me, but still did not get the buzz out. I absolutely love this guitar, but I think I got a lemon. I would have never believed I could get a lemon from Gibson, but here we are. I own several Gibson acoustic guitars and now the two electric guitars and still am a huge Gibson fan. I just wish this SGM would have been better. I think buying at a dealer allows you the chance to play the guitar and pick the best one to buy. If I had it to do all over I would recommend a dealer and not online purchase. Also, I would spend the extra cash and buy the SG special. Good luck!

This is designed as a guitar/live music speaker, obviously,for it has very poor excursion, maybe 2.5 mm Xmax and will hit only 60hz, very high Q (stiff suspension) like 1.0 so requires larger enclosure. Tried a ported 1.0 cube foot (42hz tuning) and was way to dampened, building a 2.0 ft cubed now (50hz tuning) so will update when tested. It does play frequencies up to 5khz (estimated) before break up in full range due to it's light paper cone so could cross high but I just used Parts Express's pre built 2nd order crossover at 800hz (higher would be more beneficial). Also used the Pyle PDMR5 I picked up for $12 here on Amazon and it matches well. Midrange needs a Zobel filter though, peaks about 1500hz. It might sound fine in an air suspension enclosure (sealed) but being a guitar speaker open air might even be an option; idk, not familiar with guitar enclosures; perhaps a musician could enlighten us!?!
Cutout= 9.25", 10.125" overall. 8ohm.
Questions welcome
Simon

product_title: Shure Sound Isolating Earphone Hi-Definition Micro Speaker with Tuned Bass Port
review_headline: Fantastic, accurate, well made product....be sure you get a good fit!
review_body:
I bought these because I was looking for a good set of portable, high quality, reliable and well built, in ear monitors. I am an audiophile and a high-end audio electronics engineer and manufacturer. I bought these not as an audiophile but for daily use at home, the gym and when traveling.

I read with interest, the numerous reviews here, before I made the purchase. I have to say that the reviews are spot on and I am VERY pleased with them. The removable wires are great and allow for excellent fit and adjustment. They are also of very good quality and rugged. I expect them to hold up very well.

The caveats are ALSO true, especially about them fitting properly and how much this impacts their performance...especially bass. These are accurate and produce the ACTUAL musical event very well. Many cheaper headphones and especially ear buds or in ear monitors, purposely boost the bass. These do not. My first impression was that they were forward, bright and lacking bass. This changed quickly as I first determined the right fit sleeves for my ears. They also needed to break in for a day or so, upon which time they further improved. I first compared them to a $20 pair of skull Candy ear buds that my son uses and I thought WOW, there is the bass. I listened more and I realized that the cheaper ear buds just had REALLY exaggerated bass and no resolution otherwise. This is very important to keep in mind, as you may be dissatisfied with these at first listen, if you are comparing them to other inexpensive ear buds, but DON'T give up on them. Find the right fit, let them break in and then decide. They still may not be your cup of tea, but my conclusion now, after using them for less than a week, is that I am VERY satisfied and I initially considered returning them.

I looked at the 200 series as well as the 400 and 500 series products. I decided that for $200, the 300 series should give me what I am looking for without spending toomuch and yet not leave me dissatisfied. I am very satisfied with the performance for the investment. If anything, I am curious how much better the 500 series would be. It appears that they DO go deeper, with two additional bass drivers. I would certainly consider them in the future and possibly if I decide that I want a pair of 'monitors' for more serious listening at work, where I would be doing extremely critical listening.

I also have a pair of Grado SR325 headphones and they are great. I have also recently auditioned the Audeze LCD-X headphones. The Audeze headphones are exceptional! They are also very different than in ear monitors and cost $1600. I wanted a good pair of in ear monitors for their portability and convenience. I mention this only as another point of reference. In ear monitors are different than headphones and really cannot be directly compared.

I used them for several hours at the gym today, both running and lifting weights. They stayed in, even while I sweat, and the noise isolation was very good!

Regarding their noise isolation properties....exceptional! In fact, they do such a great job that I have to either mute my music or take them off if I need to interact with family or exist outside of my musical isolation....not a bad thing!

I don't typically write product reviews, but I have been SO impressed with these, and I also didn't want people to almost make the same mistake as myself and dismiss them without a proper fit.

If your goal is to enjoy music with great resolution, exceptional noise isolation, comfort and great build quality for everyday use, I cannot recommend them highly enough!

product_title: Yamaha DXR8 Powered Speaker Cabinet
review_headline: Nothing Touches It In It's Class
review_body: Measuring in at  27.8 x 22 x 29.9 inches, this is not a large subwoofer. It's heavy (90 lbs.) because it's made of real wood with internal bracing. It's a bandpass design which maximizes bass output (decibels) while sacrificing frequency bandwidth (Hz). In other words it hits louder like 2-3 regular speakers but sacrifices the really low bass (30 Hz and below). To produce 30 HZ and below at high SPL's you would need more power, and if you tune a bandpass to do that, it will be larger and it will sacrifice the higher frequencies (80HZ and above). This subwoofer (engineered by NEXO for Yamaha) is a perfect engineering feat. Producing smooth frequency output with incredible volume. The laws of physics are rigid, but NEXO somehow flexed them a bit.

product_title: Fender FCT-12 Color Clip-On Tuner - Black
review_headline: Easy to Use and Consistent Tuning
review_body:
We're using this to keep our electric guitars in tune. It was purchased to replace existing audio electronic tuners that required that we use the amp while tuning. This became inconvenient with two guitars and barking dogs!

This tuner clips onto the head of our guitars and swivels and tilts to make it easy to read while tuning. Response is pretty fast and very consistent. It tunes both the high and low E strings easily unlike some tuners which can't seem to hear the low E string very well.

Because it tunes using vibrations on the guitar, it ignores conversation, other players tuning, and even our dogs when they decide to get rowdy during our practice sessions.

We finally bought a second tuner so we wouldn't fight over who got to keep this tuner.

Update:

This tuner allows it to be put into various modes like Guitar, Bass, Violin and Ukulele. In the guitar mode, it displays the string number and note it expects. For example, it will display 6E for the #6 E string, then show the tone accuracy. The other instruments also show the string number and note, for example, 4G, 3D, 2A, 1E for a violin or 4G, 3C, 2E, 1A for an ukulele.

There seems to be a small, but definite, difference between tuning for a G with the tuner set to key of C and 2G in guitar mode. It isn't much, but for some reason, the guitar mode seems to want to tune to a slightly higher frequency than the Chromatic mode. Either seems accurate to me, but I'm not a professional musician and my guitar teacher doesn't seem to care which tuning I use in my lessons, so I use it in Chromatic mode all the time.

Update 2:

Tried this on an acoustic guitar and, like many others, it has a hard time "hearing" the low E string on my acoustic guitar. I have to strike the string firmly in order to get it to register. I may try the Snark series to see if they do any better on an acoustic.

review_headline: HD 380 Pro vs. Sony MDR v6
review_body: I bought these for the looks, good reviews, and great one day pricing. In person they look equally as good and seem to have a high quality build. I did back to back testing between these HD 380's and my 15-20 year old Sony MDR-V6 headphones which Sony still makes! The old pair still looks great and works perfectly. The verdict?: The MDR V6 are lighter and much more comfortable to wear (they disappear whereas the HD 380s have noticeable heft on top and pressure around the ears). Note that I had replaced the ear pads once on the Sony set with velour pads (Beyer DT250) that are soft and cushy.The comfort of the Sony set allows me to enjoy the musical experience more.  The Sony is dead quiet when turning my head whereas the HD380's amplify a rubbing sound (from the earpads?). Sound quality wise, the Sony set is as good or better at high and mid range but I'm undecided on bass (sometimes liking one then the other better). If the sound quality had been noticeably better, I may have kept the HD's but this comparison has renewed my appreciation of the Sony set and I'll be shipping the Sennheiser HD 380s back.

product_title: Peterson StroboPlus HD,
review_headline: A good unit but a bit difficult to use.
review_body:
I bought this mainly for the unit's ability to offer "sweetened" tunings, especially since I use a capo everywhere from the 1st to the 7th fret, and as most acoustic guitarists know, this usually requires retuning at each new position.I envisioned just pushing a button for each position- well, in theory the unit has the ability to do this, but there are a fews issues- first, the rotating ring is sensitive- you can get a short spin in both directions before it hovers near the "in tune" point, and then still moves a bit (both ways)making it hard to know if your tuning is EXACTLY right (any cheap tuner will get you CLOSE) Second, unless the unit is plugged into a USB port,the backlight shuts itself off when the note starts to decay, which to me is very annoying. I'm sure it saves battery life but I would prefer it to say on while I'm tuning. There is only a rechargeable battery, so bringing along a laptop or some other device just to keep your tuner working at an open mike is quite inconvenient, IMO.The menu is a bit complex but the online tutorial is helpful. It appears well made and came packed in a thick cardboard box with a magnet latch for future storage, a nice touch. After several hours of experimenting with it I went back to my $25 Snark clip on, and will just have to trust my ears for the sweetening.....
So I am returning it, but will say that it is a good product and may suit someone else's needs perfectly...........

product_title: Sennheiser HD 650 Open Back Professional Headphone
review_headline: Thousands of listening hours later, WOW -- what a great purchase!
review_body:
I've owned my HD 650's for about 6 years now, and probably have listened to 10,000 hours of music with them during that time. They sound just as fantastic today as they did when I first bought them. They are still in great condition physically, too. The black felt material that covers your ears has turned a little brown over time, but it's really no big deal. The HD 650's are the best music investment I ever made. I didn't realize how much better music could honestly sound before I got these. I had been using the standard iPod headphones that everyone had years ago, and I could seriously never go back now. The sound is extremely full-sounding and gives the perception of coming from a wide range of directions. I would characterize these headphones as roughly neutral in character. In my opinion, they don't overly emphasize the low or high frequencies in any particular way.

BUT, make sure you also invest in a quality headphone amp too in order to get the best out of them. The Schiit brand of products in particular is excellent.

product_title: Pacific Drums by DW 700 SERIES BOOM CYMBAL STAND
review_body:
For sure one of the best stands at this price. Easily holds an 18'' or smaller sized cymbal, can hold most 20'' cymbals (unless they are super thick and heavy), haven't tried any larger sizes; my guess would be that if you have an expensive 22'' inch you want to stay put just spend some extra $$ for a heavier duty stand to be safe. Either way note that if you do use it for a larger or heavier cymbal you shouldn't hang anything else off this stand b/c it already has enough pressure on it. Still, I was really impressed that this stand held an 18'' crash, as well as a 20'' ride that was hooked onto the lower level of the stand with a cymbal arm attachment. The only thing I had trouble with was my using a tom holder clamp on the stand to hang my 12 x 8 tom tom - the stand kept sliding down and got shorter within seconds of the drum being on it.

I like that this stand can be a boom stand or straight stand by inserting the boom arm back inside the stand, but it's much better used as a boom stand and can't be lowered as much as a straight boom stand. It breaks down fairly easily but I can tell that after years of intense use it might start to get stiffer and need more muscle to break it down and reassemble it. So if you gig constantly and you want a strong long term stand I would invest in a higher end model. For general uses (i.e. for practice or home use, only as a crash cymbal stand, putting smaller or lighter cymbals) it's an excellent stand!

IMPORTANT DRUMMER TIP - to avoid your cymbals ever falling down with the stand or falling towards you if you hit it too hard, ALWAYS have one of the legs of the cymbal stand facing towards you, in the same direction the cymbal is being angled for you to hit (so don't have the cymbal boom adjusted so that it falls in between the gap of two cymbal legs, hope that made sense) I know it can be a burden with optimizing floor space, but it's something that all pro drummers do for a reason.

product_title: Neutrik NL4FX 4-Pole speakON Cable Connector
review_headline: Worked well in the end, but not without frustration.
review_body:
I used a pair of these to split up a 100 foot speaker cable into the odd lengths I needed. I can honestly say that these connectors were designed for a much lighter gauge speaker cable than you'd typically find in 4-pole long-run speaker cables. I was using 12 gauge cabling and had to shave off quite a bit of the stripped end of the wire to fit into the tiny wire-clips provided. I found that screwing the wire clamps in place tended to push out the larger gauge more than it bit down, a big minus that I didn't find on other such connectors.

In the end, the connection was solid, but not without frustration.

Big plus for the connector: +2 and -2 poles were labeled on the outside of the connector for easy visibility (why not +1 and -1?), and the blue ring doubles as a wire-strip-length gauge. Love those features! Great use of the space on the connector.

product_title: Vics 3 Band EQ Equalizer LED Chromatic Tuner Ukulele UKE Piezo Pickup
review_headline: high hopes...low results.....UPDATED!....from one star to three.
review_body: I have to say i had real high hopes for this product. The delivery was very fast and arrived ahead of its estimated time. I did speak to the seller about the unit, specifically the pickup. They were very nice and prompt. The unit looked great, but did not come with any instructions. The pick up was very thick and would not fit under the saddle unless I really did some major cutting into the saddle. I first connected everything to do a dry run without installing it inside the ukulele and found that the pick up did not function properly or so I thought. after connecting everything to my amplifier to test out the base the mids and the treble, I noticed that there was no proper sound modulation through the pickup that was provided so I decided to replace it with a Piezo pickup. I built a disc piezo to install inside the uke under the sound hole.  once I installed the unit is there a ukulele I noticed that it did not work correctly. I thought it might be the new pickup...so I built another one and tried again. thinking that I had fix the problem I went ahead and installed the equalizer unit and the cord or plug in and then you pick up into the ukulele. Once I connected everything I noticed that the equalizer and volume would not work properly when the pick up was connected to the equalizer unit so being the person that likes to fix problems I opened up the equalizer and found that the plugin (for the pick up) was broken in the back and just glued back with hot glue. once I reassembled everything and reconnected everything back inside the ukulele I noticed that when equalizer was turned on the pickup did not work but if I turned off the equalizer the pickup would work perfectly fine but I could not use the equalizer settings nor could I use the tuner settings if I turn on the tuner the tuner would work but I could not hear the piezo pick up. I am NOT going to return the item mainly because it would cost me more to return it. Also because I open it and replace the pick upwith my own one, i dont think it would be fair to the seller. I dont think it was their fault, rather it seems that it was a manufacturing problem. I had high hopes for the equalizer but sadly it did not work now I have a ukulele with two nasty hold on I will have to somehow repair if I cannot find another equalizer here to replace this one.      UPDATE!!! UPDATE!!!  So I was able to fix the internal part that was damaged (piezo plug) and after removing some debris that was inside and the extra hot glue  on some of the circuit board the EQ worked better...still a hum and buzz, but its minimal. the Humming and the buzzing seem to dissipate depending on the speaker system or amplifier system that you are using and can be controlled. on this particular unit that I received if you turn up the volume to the highest maximum setting the buzz goes away and I can control the output sound using the other amplifier.  After installing the new home made piezo it sounded nice and the EQ settings worked nicely.  A buddy of mine told me that some EQ/tuners will shut off the amp to allow tunning without the sound feeding into your PA or speakers. This would have been nice to know about this unit, but it came with no instructions. The unit looks nice now that it is installed properly to my Uke. Once all the strings were in place, wound and ready to fine tune, the tuner worked very well. One more thing, I like the added slight weight and it seems to balance out the feel of this particular Uke. I used an off brand uke my wife bought for me (my first) and with some TLC and hard work is now sounding better than ever.  The Vicks EQ Tuner was a welcomed addition and for someone who enjoys a new challenge and learning experience the price was right.   So I have decided to change the ONE STAR TO  THREE!  I would have gone to four, if the batteries had not drained after only a couple of days,  of just sitting there.   If the piezo had worked better (forgot to mention that the mono jack was too long which pushed too far into the mono plug and could potentially cause damage).  For the price...still not bad.

product_title: pBone PBONE1OR Jiggs pBone - Plastic Trombone -
review_headline: Excellent sound and feel to this trombone
review_body:
Excellent sound and feel to this trombone. It sounds very "brassy" for being made from plastic and carbon fiber. The main slide is very smooth and needs no lubrication. The tuning slide is also amazingly smooth. Almost TOO smooth - if you're not playing and tend to hold the instrument by the counterweight, you can easily end up moving the tuning slide. The plastic mouthpiece I could take or leave. It's an 11C. Helps a little for hitting the higher notes. I also grabbed a Blessing 6 1/2 AL to go with this as my primary mouthpiece. *edit* I'm really warming up to the mouthpiece. I'm finding it gives me a more stable embouchure and really helps me hit the higher notes that I'd always struggled with in the past using a 12C or the 6 1/2 AL.

All in all, it's a very playable instrument, sounds great, is exceedingly light, has lots of fun colors, and won't break the bank. My only real beef with it (and it's not much of a beef) is that it's got some issues as a marching horn. The throat where the mouthpiece goes in won't accept a standard trombone lyre. Also the slide attaches to the bell with a friction fit - there's no screw nut to clamp the two pieces together. Combine the two and you can have issues if you grip the instrument by the bell, holding a marching flip folder. The natural backwards pressure to keep the mouthpiece solidly against your lips can cause the bell section to separate from the slide section if you're not careful. That can get a bit awkward in the middle of a performance.

review_headline: Extract All The Detail From Your Fine Vinyl Collection!!
review_body: If you want to hear all the fine detail embedded within the grooves of you fine vinyl collection, this is the cartridge for you. You may want to roll off some of the treble and turn up the bass a bit on some systems because this one is very bright. If you have very worn records it might be a bit too much. The cantilever is very delicate and very susceptible to damage, so take precautions during installation. Tracking angle is crucial for setup and alignment is crucial on this one. You might be able to get by with some leeway on a cartridge with an elliptical stylus, but this one is rather particular, so it is best to use an alignment gauge or protractor to set up the cartridge on the head shell. Tracking force is optimal at 1.5 grams. So far i have enjoyed everything I have played so far. It is hard to go back to a cartridge with an elliptical stylus since I have listen to this one, since it extracts more of the detail and distortion is minimal. This is one the finest cartridges that you can get in the Moving Magnet design. If you can't really afford to upgrade to a Moving Coil cart, this is a good choice.

review_headline: This was the best product I've purchased for my guitar in years
review_body:
This was the best product I've purchased for my guitar in years. I've spend close to a thousand dollars on an amp and pedal system for my apartment, but rarely use it due to the volume it produces and complexity of setup. I never liked using headphones with my setup because I was limited in range of motion.

I purchased the Vox lead guitar amp as a test and I'm incredibly thankful I did. The sound is AMAZING given how small it is and that it's battery powered. The sustain is fantastic - you can easily hold a note for 15 seconds+. High frequencies are also fantastic - mid and low leave a little to be desired, but this is a "Lead Guitar" amp after all.

Despite my expensive setup, I now use this 90% of the time and play guitar way more than I used to. This product has reunited my love affair with an old friend (Fender Strat) and for those of you looking for a plug-and-play solution that's powerful and has great tone, this is your answer.

In the future I hope they add a button that switches between overdrive and clean - moving the dial is hard to do on the fly.

product_title: ISP Technologies Decimator II Noise Reduction Pedal - (New)
review_body:

My particular setup for testing this was with a 2014 Gibson Melody Maker and a Fender Mustang III V2 modeling amp (set to a VERY high gain preset). Needless to say, this setup generates a LOT of buzz, thanks to those P90 pickups in the Melody Maker. The guitar is plugged directly into the Decimator, which is then plugged directly to the amp... not using the effects loop or anything like that. With the Decimator set to a position of about 11-12 o'clock, the 60 cycle hum is gone, just like magic!

From what I can tell, the tone isn't affected in any way when the Decimator is turned on. I still get tons of sustain, and a very graceful degradation of the signal when it gets to the point where the noise gate cuts in.

Overall, I'm extremely happy with this pedal, and it is really a must have for anyone that uses P90 pickups (or any other single coils).
