review_headline: I feel it's an excellent mouthpiece but my band student doesn't like it
review_body:
This is an excellent mouthpiece, so I felt the need to give it five stars, but I hope that others will read this review above and beyond the star rating, because my son has had a lot of difficulty playing with this mouthpiece versus the one that came with his clarinet. First of all, the cork on this one made for a very tight fit on my son's clarinet. I actually expected this, as all of the corks on his clarinet were VERY tight when first purchased, and this was easily remedied with some sanding and cork grease. However, for some reason he just has a lot of difficulty getting a good sound with this mouthpiece compared to the one that came with his clarinet. Even using the same reed and ligature. I also played the clarinet since 6th grade, and I don't have a problem with this mouthpiece at all, but I'm sure my son won't be the only one. I purchased this mouthpiece because his original one has a tiny chip on one corner of the mouthpiece, so I thought it would be a good idea to replace it before it became a problem. He's back to using his old mouthpiece, but I decided to keep this one in case the old one eventually gives up the ghost completely. Hopefully he can learn how to play on it should he ever need to.

My other son plays sax and I bought him a Yamaha 4C mouthpiece for it and he loves it and plays it much better than the mouthpiece that came with his sax.

Overall, I highly recommend this mouthpiece, but don't be surprised if your young band member doesn't like it so much.

product_title: DigiTech RP55 Guitar Multi-Effects Processor
review_headline: Incredibly good value for the price
review_body:
I'm torn between rating this 4 & 5 stars (because it isn't \\"absolutely perfect\\")... but finally decided on 5 because for the price (currently 38 bucks) this is an incredible value. You get far more from this device than would be expected.

This is a terrific effects pedal. It can make the cheapest electric guitar sound great, even when sent through a small amp. It comes with several pre-programmed effects (guitar / amp sounds) and you can program your own-- giving this pretty much unlimited versatility.

The pre-prog effects range from standard mellow-blues to heavy metal distortion to \\"voice wah wah\\"-- an impressive range. This is one of those well-designed items that allows literally millions of possible sound effects. It also allows bypass (no effects) so you can use it as a basic pre-amp; it really improves the volume of passive-preamp or piezo-based guitars.

The only downside *as other users stated)-- it is made of plastic and not intended for on-stage heavy \\"stomp-box\\" use. This is intended primarily for studio effects, not slamming down on it with a heavy boot. On the other hand it does have a jack to add an external stomp-switch which would allow it to take about as much punishment as one would want to give out. Just stick this on a stand or on top of your amp and use the external switch to trigger it. It even recognizes effects from different types of external switches and adapts accordingly.

Some reviews say their box gave out after a few months. I would suspect that would be possible if taken on gigs or on the road if it was manhandled or not packed in a safebox. And as stated, it's not made of titanium steel. But if it is treated like any other technical piece of equipment (which is exactly what it is)... well, mine has lasted for years and still works as well as the day it was purchased.

They do make these in much sturdier floor models ranging from about $120 to $300. So there is option to pick the model specific to one's needs. It's not really right to buy a $40 personal studio box and complain it doesn't stand up to active stage use. Use the right tool for the job. ;)

Recognizing that the shell is plastic and the RP55 doesn't cost $300, it's a superb low-cost special-effects device that is incredibly versatile. review_body:
I have been a saxophone player (alto & tenor) for nine years now. I was skeptical at first about purchasing this tuner/metronome because it was more advertised for guitar/bass, but I soon found out that the chromatic tuner works well for all instruments. Since I've purchased this tuner/metronome, I have had no serious problems with it. The controls are very simple and the device is easy to use overall. I find the metronome has been very effective in my practices, with the volume playing loud enough to hear over my instrument or having the capability to plug in ear phones to hear the beat more closely. In addition, the metronome has many different rhythms to choose from along with different time signatures.

On the negative side, the one main thing I have against this is that the chromatic tuner is auto tune. Other tuners, I have used, work by selecting a concert pitch and tuning to that pitch, whereas the auto tune sometimes will tune (display) to the wrong note. I have found that a little stressful. But it's not that big of a problem.

So, I would recommend this tuner/metronome to others. It is small/portable (roughly the size of a deck of cards), works well and is very reasonable in cost.

review_headline: Good sturdy budget guitar for any player, with some qualms.
review_body:
Ok first off I have been playing guitar for about 10 years now, I'm no Hendrix but I do know a little about guitars. First off the good, the guitar is really solid it's made of pretty good quality wood although all of it is made of laminate wood including the top. Don't worry about that though people will tell you only solid tops sound good but the technology to make guitars and the wood that goes on it has come miles.. After I got the guitar out of the box I had to set it up, by that I mean adjust the rod and tune, there is more I have to do to it but right now as is I would give the over all sound and tone a 9 pretty close to my guitar that cost way way more then this. Also it seems to stay in tune well from what I can tell, I also really love the overall look of the guitar it looks premium even though it's not, really love the inlays and the cool head stock!

OK now the bad, this is a very good cheap guitar but the Chinese manufacturing does show unfortunately! First off while over all the finish is very beautiful and super glossy (some may not like this), how ever it was obvious as soon as I took it out of the box some places had no gloss specifically around the sound hole and on the headstock my quick fix for this was some of my wife's clear nail polish it will due but I'm still not impressed, also around the neck and on the neck there is cracking in the gloss. My next complaint is that the neck is too thick, I could never wrap my thumb around to the E string even if I wanted too, maybe if you have bigger hands? Any way it's perfectly playable but just not to comfortable, although I think it may be better for new players as it will give them better grip.

To wrap it up, this is a really decent cheap guitar one that I don't think any one new or old that's looking for a starter or beater guitar should pass up. The sound quality sounds way way better then the price you pay, the thing feels super solid like it would survive thedrops and bangs a used guitar will take. It's looks super cool, way cooler then most budget guitars, and Sawtooth that's a pretty cool name right? Just watch out for the finish and that thick neck experienced players or people with smaller hands will Hate this!!!

Sound 9
Playability 6
Look 10
Quality 10 for the price remember this is laminent, who would expect any thing else for this Price?
Glossy finish is a 3 disappointing at any price range

product_title: John Pearse D'Angle Guitar Hanger
review_body:
This thing is great, really clever and built to last forever. It does take some getting used to, and will drop your instrument if bumped by a dog, clumsy guest, etc, so it's not the absolute safest way to hang your precious or fragile instrument, fyi.

I've had mine for years, and now I usually hang it on one of those chrome wire NSF shelves, which has a lip at the edge that makes it super secure. On a shelf without a lip, it's perfectly stable unless jostled, in which case it can and will slip off and tumble. If you hang it in one place all the time and your surface is slick, maybe stick on a piece of something sticky, tacky, or a little ridge to catch it, for ultimate security. This will work with headless instruments, and looks almost like an optical illusion when suspending a Steinberger, but it's even less secure with a headless because if the friction fails for a second, it'll plummet right through, so don't bump it!

The limitations aside, it's really cool, clever, very robust, and ultra portable unlike any other stand, really. I'm generally dextrous, but I had a few fumbles learning to handle this thing smoothly; I guess the utter simplicity just baffled me, so handle it cautiously until you get the hang of its leverage and friction actions, which are unique.

product_title: Dunlop DHCN1048 Heavy Core NPS Electric Guitar Strings
review_body: These are my first ever Dunlop strings, and I feel they were an excellent investment. I got the heaviest gauge, and they sound and feel great in standard, drop-D, D-standard, and drop-C, when applied to a 24.75\\" scale length (standard Gibson scale) guitar. I was surprised when I opened the package and found the .012\\", .016\\", and .020\\" strings were marked as plain steel acoustic-electric, but they were in the sealed package from Dunlop, so those are the right strings, and they're excellent. They have a very chunky sound and thick windings that give them almost a bass feel on the bottom 3 strings. One thing I find interesting is that, when playing through a clean channel, the lower registers have a nice, resonant reverb going on, and I know it's the strings, because none of my amps have reverb on them, and none of my previous strings had that effect. I'm sure these would be ideal for modern deathcore/power metal players, but they are equally  effective for thrash riffs. As to the longevity, I haven't had them that long, but the sound and feel have held up better thus far than the Gibson, Ernie Ball, and GHS strings I've alternated between for years. In short, they're well worth a try, and inexpensive enough that, even if you didn't like them, the loss would be negligible

product_title: Blue Microphones Yeti USB Microphone
review_headline: Classic Looks, But An Even Better Sound
review_body:
I bought this mic because I got some crazy idea to do a podcast. Well... I'm now five episodes into the Unified Republic of Stars (with another three in the can) and I have to say, I love this freak'n thing.

I bought it because it looks like the mic Larry King had on his desk. I mean, come on. It's freak'n classic looking. But, unlike that one, it's actually functional and sounds amazing.

It needs a pop screen, of course. But, when you set it up with one and speak about a hand's width away from it, people who listen will honestly ask you, "Is that your voice?" Because it really grabs a nice rich tone. And I have a voice that's pretty freak'n far from Orson Welles.

Another nice thing about it was that it was literally plug and play on my Mac. No drivers, no anything. Just plug it in and start recording.

Also, it's solid. I mean, I was surprised by its weight. I've owned other mics for other projects but this sucker has heft. Which is nice because it doesn't feel like something disposable for once. If your goal is to run around with it, it may not be the mic for you. But if you're speaking into it from a sound booth or a desk, it's amazing.

In fact, if I have a gripe or two it would be these: 1) The base is also really solid. Very solid. It's not going anywhere unless the incline is sixty degrees. But it's so solid that it picks up the vibration of me leaning on my desk when I speak into it. So I put a towel under it and, hey, problem solved. 2) I can't stop recording because I like using it so much. My girlfriend now calls herself a podcast widow because I'm either recording new casts or writing ones so that I can record.

Okay, maybe I have a third. The USB cable they sent was seriously long. I mean, it's right in front of my computer. Why do I need a six foot cord? But... whatever. A rubber band latter, cord management is solved.

Seriously, if you're thinking about starting a podcast or want to croon into a classic looking piece of hardware, this is the sucker for you. It sounds amazing, its nothing to set up, and it looks great. I leave it sitting around when I'm not recording because it's practically a conversation piece, what with the way it looks.

product_title: On-Stage Stands Folding Heavy-Duty Dual-Tier Z Stand,
review_headline: At last an alternative to expensive, short lived stands!
review_body:
I'm giving this stand such a high review because after 30 years of dealing with expensive Ultimate Support keyboard stands whose fittings and clutches crack and break with the occassional clumbsy handling of newbie crew members...as well as myself...or just the wear and tear of use ...finally a stand that can take a bit of a beating. See I can forgive the cumbersome aspects, weight and the lack of adjustments in the 2nd tier because they make up for it with 2 vital facts for me. 1) no plastic/carbon fiber joints, all metal, and 2) I can get it up to my height while standing (I'm 6'4") without sacrificing stability of the resting points for the keyboard. That means if I want my heavy digital piano at the maximum height it won't be balancing on two tubes a foot apart but at almost the whole length of the keyboard. I have been through conventional "A" frames, Apex and ICQs. and when parts broke, guess what? "Sorry, we no longer manufacter parts for this item." With this stand I can probably have a friend reweld or fabricate a part for repair.

It has one weak point with me. The brackets where the tiers swivel to fold the stand are thin and the outriggers/tiers can bend too easily when folded. I fixed this with gluing a velcro strap on each foldering part to keep them aligned during transport and will be buying the OEM case to further solve this.

I gladly traded the short commings of this stand for the expense and frustration of having gone through 4 much more expensive Ultimate Suppost stands over the past 30 years

product_title: BEHRINGER MS40
review_body:
Ahhh, computer speakers. Sometimes they're wonderful and sometimes they sound like tiny critters screaming inside a soup can! Fortunately for me, I got a set of the wonderful ones when I purchased these MS40's.

They came packaged in a huge box with a little crunched up packing paper and whatever was inside was sliding around and bouncing off the interior walls of the box. Uh oh!, I thought...but as it turned out, there was another box inside with the speakers and that one was securely packaged, probably to survive anything the shipping carrier could throw at it! :)

When I opened the speaker box I found two good sized speakers and three sets of cables. One was for connecting the two speakers together, one was to plug into an audio source with a 1/8" plug and two red and white rca plugs for the speaker amp. Then there was the power cable WITHOUT one of those irritating wall wart thingies. Just a normal power cable. Impressive!

The setup was easy peasy. My desk is almost seven feet wide with a 42" Vizio HD tv that I use as a monitor and the speakers fit nicely on the sides with a little room to spare. AND the speakers are shielded which means there will be no adverse affects to the tv. The shielding was one of my major concerns and added to my zeal to purchase this speaker set.

The cable that connected the two speakers together was plenty long and there is still a little slop in case I want to move them farther apart.

I plugged the audio cable into the lime green audio out jack on the back of my computer and took the speakers for a spin around the net. I watched part of a low quality movie on youtube, listened to a song on live 365 and generally enjoyed the speaker experience.

Then, I tried it all again with my headphones plugged into the little speaker amp and YIKES!...the sound was amazing! It nearly rivaled my Denon stereo receiver in fidelity and I was waaay past being merely impressed...I was stunned! Now I can use the MS40 speaker amp as my main audio amp and give the Denon a well deserved vacation.

Okay! All this wild stuff went on for a few days and then I was watching a video on youtube and I noticed that the sound was only coming in on one side of my headphones. I figured maybe I had a loose connection in one of the cables, so I turned everything off and set about re-seating the cables. Then I turned everything back on and started a song that I had on my desktop and guess what? The same thing happened. The sound was still on one side. PANIC!

Well. What can I do now? So I shut off everything, again and checked all the cables, again. Only this time I figured I would try some different cables. Heck, I had a box full of patch cords left over from my hardware hacking days (and no, I won't fix your computer), so I tried one of those audio cables with the two rca things and then started up the machines once again. This time things were a lot different. I started up the same song and YES...it played great and I was back in the game!

So, thats that! Except for a faulty cable, I have a great sounding system and I am not going to deduct a star from my rating because of a pissy thing like that. :)

Am I happy with my purchase of the MS40's? Absolutely. Would I recommend them to the world? You Betcha! :)

product_title: Namba Gear Shaka High Perfomance Laptop Messenger Bag for Musicians and DJs (Midnight Blue) SLM-BL
review_headline: A fantastic bag ruined by a cheap and non-detachable strap.
review_body:
This is what happens when you make a great product and then cheap-out on a critical component. It's too bad, because the bag itself is excellent. It's large enough to hold two 15-inch laptops plus plus power cables, and it's well padded. Someone accidentally knocked it off a chair while my laptop was in it, and the computer was fine. It has numerous compartments, as well as compartments within compartments. I was actually a little overwhelmed by the number of places to store things. The bag looks great too, and I've received many compliments on it. The stitching is excellent, the zippers are smooth, and the pull tabs on them are strong and well made. In almost every way, the bag is excellent.

I write \\"almost\\" because I have two small gripes with it. First, the top flap. It has a zippered pocket, which you can see in the product photo. Inside the pocket is a smaller pocket that could be useful for holding keys, subway passes, bus tickets, etc. Unfortunately, this smaller pocket doesn't have a flap on it to secure the items you place inside it. As a result, anytime you lift the cover flap to insert or remove items in the bag, whatever is in the pocket falls out and winds up jumbling around inside the larger zippered pocket. This could have been fixed by adding a small flap to the pocket that could be closed with a Velcro tab or a push fastener.

Second, the top flap can be secured to the bag with a side-squeeze buckle. The male end of the buckle is plastic, but the female end is metal. If you choose not to latch them, the metal end bangs noisily against the plastic end. Why not just make them both plastic? It would be quieter and weigh less as well.

But what absolutely ruins the bag is the strap. It's made of cheap nylon, just 1.5 inches wide, and it has no shoulder pad. Worst of all, it can't be removed because it's sewn on!

When I say \\"cheap\\" nylon, consider this: after two months of use, the strap developed permanent creases from the weight of what I was carrying (one and sometimes two laptops for subway trips no longer than 30 minutes, and only two or three days a week). At just 1.5 inches wide, and with no shoulder pad, the strap cut painfully into my shoulder when carrying it. In addition, the strap is attached to the bag at one end with a metal guide. The guide has twisted under the weight of the bag's contents so that it's now turned 90 degrees from its normal position. This, in turn, has creased the strap beyond saving.

I've used several messenger bags in the past, and I know from experience that a high-quality two-inch strap would have made all the difference, and a shoulder pad would have made carrying the bag more comfortable. Better still, Namba Gear could have made the strap removable so that buyers could substitute a better strap if they wished to. As it is, I can hardly use my bag anymore, and it's all down to the cheap strap. What a shame.

product_title: Zoom H4N Handy Portable Digital Recorder - 2009 Version
review_headline: recording quality is marred by hardware and software design flaws
review_body:
After owning and working with this device for a few weeks there are good and bad things associated with it. The recording quality is very good, the flexibility of formats and controls are decent.

However, there are a few flaws IMO:

1. Boot-up time is ridiculously long.

This device is completely unsuitable for spontaneous dictation or recording - forget about it. If you power this thing up to capture something impromptu, you'll either forget what you were going to say or the event will be over before the device is ready to use. I don't know if there's a tiny floppy disk it's reading during boot up but I cannot explain why it takes 30+ seconds for a device to become ready. It's ridiculously slow - it may not seem like it, but when you're on top of a ladder and getting ready to turn on an ambient recorder for a live show capture, you're hanging up there for awhile before the recorder will be ready.

2. Battery life is lousy

I put new batteries in this device and it didn't last more than 2 hours or so. I got this device to record ambient audio to be used to sync multiple video camera shots of live performances. I stick the recorder up on a light truss and turn it on.. it didn't last long and turned off. I discovered there is a "stamina mode" you can put the device in, and that helps but I'm not sure what difference there is between the two modes.

3. Date/Time is lost every time you change the batteries.

We have been in the era of non-volatile memory for decades. Why can't this device remember the date at least, when the batteries are being replaced? This ruins time-stamps on the files.

4. Inflexible file hierarchy

Speaking of files.. the system uses an impersonal file system that cannot be renamed or made more human-friendly. folder01, folder02, folder03, etc... really? I renamed the folders to something more descriptive and the device ignored them and re-created the same un-descriptive folder hierarchy for storing its files under. How difficult is it to at least be able to read the SD card and use the existing file folders? It would be really useful if I could create my own, more descriptive folder names on computer, stick the card in the device and read them. folder01, folder02 doesn't mean much.

review_body:
For what it is designed for, decent. You are getting a USB mic with its own little stand, and it plugs right in with no drivers or playing around with settings. If all you want is a bit more control and quality than the onboard microphone on your laptop, fine. If you are looking to record your string quartet, forget it.

From a quick listen, it has the same 6-8KHz emphasis of a lot of inexpensive settings using generic capsules. Voice was crisp and intelligible, ukulele was brittle and horrible. Again on a quick listen, the cardiod pattern is wide, and handling noise is low. Inside, there is a little foam to break up some of the plosives and wind noise, and the capsule is nicely isolated on three rubber standoffs. The build is generally robust...with the caveats noted below.

I had USB drop-out on mine and had to open it up to repair it. The main board turns out to be balanced precariously on two narrow headers, meaning USB connectivity was marginal until I modded it with a few blobs of hot melt glue. product_title: Donner Yellow Fall Vintage Pure Analog Delay Guitar Effect Pedal True Bypass
review_headline: Unbeatable delay for the price, or any price less than $120
review_body:
There’s no delay, new or used, that comes close to this at this price - or even two, three, or four times the price.

A couple of years ago I got back in to playing, and in the past year, I’ve been through close to a dozen delays trying to find one(s) that inspired me. Cool tones abound, but I often spent too much time twiddling knobs and digging through presets rather than actually losing myself in playing.

For $35 (same price as the power supply for one of the delays mentioned above), the Yellow Fall changed all that. Within minutes of plugging in, I’d going from programming my pedal to actually playing again. Inspiration, instinct, interaction, immediacy - all of the things I look for in a good piece of gear. And this certainly falls into that category.

That said, it’s not a one trick pony either. The control set is elementary, the building blocks of what you need for straight head classic surf, rock, and blues tones, up through more experiment and ambient textures are all right in front of you.

It’s less than a cost of a movie, and likely more fun. Haven't had it as long as some of my other pieces of gear, but it looks, sounds, and feels well build. No loose parts or connections. Surprisingly nice packaging for such a low dollar item.

Can’t lose.

product_title: Yamaha SB5XC Silent Brass System for Trombone
review_headline: Best version of Silent Brass, by far!
review_body: This is the third Silent Brass system that I have used, and it is definitely my favorite. I used the very first model in our music store nearly twenty years ago and was blown away. The reverb settings made me feel like I was playing in a big church. At the time, the price was out of my range. When Yamaha released the smaller, cheaper system years later, I bought one in a hurry. I was extremely disappointed. The sound unit had one reverb setting and it sounded terrible. The mute was front heavy and was hard to keep in the bell. I sold it very quickly. When I heard about this newest model, I immediately went to the forums and saw nothing but praise, not only as an electronic system, but as a basic practice mute. I ordered one right away and received in a few days. The mute, by itself, is great. I fits IN the bell, so I don't have to find a place to keep it. The response is similar to the Bremner Sshhmute, which means it feels pretty quick for a quiet practice session. The sound processor looks great, but feels quite cheap. The volume knob, switches, battery compartment, and jacks feel quite delicate, but as long as they last, that doesn't bother me at all. Because the wires and headphones are poor, I also changed those out. New headphones (ear buds in my case) make a big difference. I would use something bigger and better, but I want to be able to throw these in my instrument case, so smaller is better. The two reverb settings are perfect. One sounds just like you are playing in a normal room. The other sounds like a large concert hall. If I could make one change, it would be to increase the volume, as I felt that it was pretty weak. (I could always use an inexpensive inline headphone amplifier). From an outside point of view, I played out in the living room and my wife was able to hear me in our bedroom, but it was only a muffled noise. Now, I just need to get a pickup mute for my euphonium, which costs more than this entire system. If you're a trombone player, and want some practice time without disturbing others, I highly recommend this new system!!ant some practice time without disturbing others, I highly recommend this new system!!

product_title: Audio-Technica ATH-M50x Professional Studio Monitor Headphones
review_headline: These are one of the most recommended set of headphones out there for good reason
review_body:
If you're looking for your first general use over ear headphone under $200 then STOP. Add this to you cart, checkout, and carry on with your day. When you hear these for the first time you will understand why Beats by Dre are a fashion accessory and not a headphone.

These are one of the most recommended set of headphones out there for good reason. It doesn't matter what you listen to, unless you're an enthusiast audiophile these will probably do it better than what you currently have. Even better, we no longer have to choose between a coiled cord or a straight cord that's far too long and ends up getting tripped on, run over by chairs, and chewed on by pets.

I edit photo and video quite a bit, I also have a pretty good collection of 24 bit vinyl rips and lossless audio. I bought these so I could mix track levels and listen to music while I worked at comfortable (for my ears that did not make it out of the army completely preserved) levels without disturbing my neighbors. These are smooth and balanced, they have clean bass and detailed enough highs. I have usually had Focal and JL Audio components/subwoofers and in my vehicle and I own a set of Focal studio monitors for my loft. When I'm not in my car, or can't turn up my desktop speakers these fit the bill. They lack a great soundstage but that's the trade off you make when using closed headphones for decent bass and privacy. If you care about soundstage then look into open ear headphones, but at that point I would prefer to switch over to my monitors anyways.

product_title: MXR Custom Badass '78 Distortion
review_headline: ehh... Solid pedal that comes down to personal preference.
review_body:
As with most pedals, it really depends on your personal preference, your rig, your other pedals, your guitars, and even the tone of your band mates' instruments. I love heavy music but I play in a Christian rock band and various praise band groups so my board and rig goes from nice cleans with chorus and delay to overdriven (MXR Zakk Wylde pedal is my favorite) to a more classic rock tone (this pedal) to a nice juicy metal tone (I have a cheap Joyo pedal now, but soon to be replaced with an MXR Full Bore).

My rig: I'm using an Orange Micro Terror (20W tube pre-amp) going direct into a Behringer GI-100 with speaker cabinet emulation enabled. This allows the guitar to be mixed well with no blaring guitar cab in churches and provides minimal transportation. The guitar I usually use with this pedal is an LTD H-351 with a Floyd Rose and active EMGs (81 and 85). I also use an old Ibanez RT 450 with Seymour Duncan JB and Jazz pickups as a backup of sorts.

I am off and on with liking this pedal. One day it sounds great to me, and the next I can't dial it in nicely. I'm thinking of ways to make room on my board to fit my old DS-1 on there for the off days. I do believe that the MXR 78 is a better pedal than the DS-1, especially for leads. For just power chord punk-ish stuff, I'd prefer the DS-1.

The tone knob provides a good range of possibilities to fit your rig and sound. With just my guitar playing, I can dial in a pretty sweet tone with my Zakk Wylde Overdrive pushing it, however when playing with the band, the keys and other instruments/vocals in the mids can kind of crowd the sweet spot of the pedal and produce a high end, almost Slayer-sounding scoop coming through the mix that I do not like. To combat this, I usually dial the tone knob back further, which works pretty well but doesn't have the sparkle when playing full chords by itself anymore. I know you'd probably argue that the problem comes down to the keyboards playing in the same range, which I can't really argue with but coming from the situation, we can't really fix that up.

I do want to point out that my favorite guitar tone is a thicker metal sound like Phinehas, Haste the Day, Skillet, or War of Ages, but that obviously doesn't fit everywhere. If you love classic rock and you think guitar tone died after the early 80's, you'll love this pedal.

I can't really decide if it should be 3/5 or 4/5. I'd really like to give it a 3.5, but since I'm keeping it on my pedal board, I guess it gets the round up. Despite my rambling, I realize that this was a pretty vague review. I wanted to approach it a little differently than the other reviews. If you have any more precise questions on the pedal itself, I'd love to try to help you out.

product_title: Seismic Audio Tremor_18-PW - Powered PA 18-Inch Subwoofer Speaker Cabinet
review_body: Let me start by saying I didnt purchase this unit through Amazon, I instead used the Seismic Audio website, but as an Amazon user, I felt it pertinent to add my review here as well. I have a huge PA setup, all purchased from Seismic, from the amp rack and amps to cables, mics, passive towers and floor monitors, even stands, all of it is from Seismic. I have not had any issues with the quality or durability of any of the gear I have owned (a little over 3 years now with a LOT of use) and the few times that I have had a concern, the customer service at Seismic has been stellar. So when it came time for me to add a sub to my setup, my first place to look was Seismic Audio. I am extremely happy with this unit. The sound is phenominal and build quality is great, as always. The amp will clip at low levels if you are trying to use the sub volume control to increase the bass. The trick here is the sub low pass needs to be set to the desired level, and the volume needs to be set to where it doesnt clip, then when you turn up the volume from your input, it wont clip. At least, that was my experience. Another thing to remember is to use BOTH inputs. The unit outputs much better if you use a left and right input over the MONO input.  I had this unit in a 2000 sq ft open hall and it was PLENTY of bass. I was the DJ and played everything from big band to classical to hip hop and rap. At no point did I have to adjust any of the settings on this sub, and it performed flawlessly all night. I also used it to power two satellite speakers set up 75 ft. across the hall, and it handled that with no issues. If anyone has any questions, feel free to contact me. I would not hesitate to recommend this product, or an other Seismic products. They are a quality company with quality product.

product_title: Yamaha FG700S Folk Acoustic Guitar - Natural
review_headline: if you play 10 of these you will find that 2 stand out above the other 8 and that 4 will sound like utter crap
review_body: Every guitar is different no matter who makes it, every top has its own grain, and the wood makes the sound in any guitar. All kinds of things affect the sound of a guitar including how many coats of finish laquer are sprayed on it, too many coats will kill the tone.if you play 10 of these you will find that 2 stand out above the other 8 and that 4 will sound like utter crap, and the other 4 will be mediocre at best. This is just the nature of acoustic instruments, they all have their own personality and none are going to be exactly the same. Set up also affects them in many ways. If you set it up with low action , you will nkt be able to play with as much volume and therefore you will not get as much tone out of it. If4 you change the saddle and string nut to bone you will get more tone than with the cheap plastic. If you pick a guitar with a tight grain in the top, you are more likely to get a better sounding guitar th7an one with6 wider grains. If you use phosphor bronze strings like D'Addario's , you will get a crisper more responsive tone. In other words with a little education about what makes a guitar sound good you can pick a good one from any manufacturer who uses real solid spruce tops and some descent qaulity strings. Now, with all that said, I personally recomend playing a few of them and picking the best one out of the bunch. I did that at my local music store and the one i picked sounds as good as some Martin D-18's that i have owned in the past. But of course i have set it up with a slightly high action, some medium bronze D'Addario strings , and a bone saddl and nut, so now it is a little different from what it was straight out of the box, and it sounds great. By the way i have been playing multiple acoustic instruments since i was a teenager, i grew up around proffessional musicians and my father is a Luthier, which means he builds instruments for those of you who dont know the lingo. In short this is a great guitar for the price, it needs a littlework straight out of the box, but picking an acoustic instrument is like picking a girlfriend,  pretty is as pretty does and they all have different attitudes any where from pretty and sweet to looks good but sounds like a train wreck. You cant fix crappy wood. All manufacturers use whatever wood is on top of the stack for each guitar, gone a1re th6e days when a small luthier shop would hand pick quality wood4s for each individual guitar and try to turn out only the best. Unfotunately even Gibson , Martin, Fender, and all the other major players build just as many crappy instruments as they good ones. Its all about Dollar bills now, no more pride in their craftsmanship. So go through them and pick the ones that accidentally got some good wood and you will get a better guitar

product_title: Behringer Light 3000 W Amp With Dsp
review_body:
While I cannot speak to its full range performance, as a subwoofer amplifier the NU3000DSP is fantastic for the price and flexibility.

Currently I have it bridged powering one Dayton Ultimax in a sealed box. After much configuration of the included parametric EQ, I have it flat to 20hz with useable output below 18hz. The DSP is powerful and well worth the extra cost over the non-DSP version.

The only downside for home use (aside from the fan, but that horse is well beaten) is most people will need a -10/+4 signal converter between their consumer receiver/pre and this pro amp. There are many options like the ART Cleanbox Pro and ROLLS, or my choice, the Aphex 124A/124B. Without a converter, your amp will receive a weak signal leading to distortion.

If you plan to use bridge mode, you need a 4-pole speakon connector, then wire its +2 terminal to the negative on your sub and the +1 to positive.

product_title: Wattson Classic Electronics Fuzz
review_body:
Great box! When I purchased it, it had waay too much of the octave effect, and made the box sound pretty harsh.
After adjusting the internal trim pot to reduce the effect, it got a lot less screechy and more 'rounded' tones.
I use this box all the time as it can be adjusted in a variety of ways from input gain control to balance, to fuzz level, to amped gain settings. It sounds big, bold, and very much like the original Univox without the gain drop when you kick it in like the Univox model did. So I view this as an improvement over the original as well.
I would recommend trying this pedal. I've had mine for a couple years now, and would for sure buy one again if necessary.
I installed a power off switch and a power on led to remind me not to leave it on, and bypassed, as there is no indication power is still on even bypassed. Still, a very nice sound and pedal. Well constructed and nicely wired as well.

review_body:
I purchased this as a replacement for the stock speaker in a first year Epiphone Valve Junior combo. I also swapped out the 12AX7 in the preamp for an old US made 12AU7 (tried a 12AT7 too). These both made a dramatic difference on the tone. Previously, the tone was thick and muddy- with the new tube and speaker the tone is clear and bright with a nice tight bottom. I did sacrifice over all volume and dirt, but that's fine because the amp sounds so much better!

There are plenty of mods you can do to a Valve Jr, but nothing is quicker and easier than swapping a speaker and a preamp tube, and inexpensive to boot! I highly recommend this speaker for a Valve Jr!

The biggest problem with this wireless system is when moving around with the microphone you get a very loud "swoosh" or static sound when it momentarily loses signal. Also, when you turn the transmitter off there is a very loud static coming from the receiver. So when someone using the mic then turns the switch off you have to turn the sound off at the mixing board. All this happened within 8 to 30 feet from the receiver with no obstructions. This is a serious design flaw.

I purchased an Audio Technica ATW-802 VHF wireless system that works great and had great range. Surprisingly, I also purchased an Audio Technica UHF wireless system for much more money that had the same issues as the AKG WMS40. My cheaper VHF wireless systems seem to perform better...

product_title: Schecter OMEN-8 8-String Electric Guitar, Black
review_body: This guitar was my first introduction to the extended range family of guitars, and what a wonderful choice! Right out of the box, the guitar was set up perfectly, something that I have never seen before. The first thing you will notice about this guitar (  besides the quality ) is how thick the neck is, but even with such a massive neck it still manages to be very playable and after a few hours I was flying down the neck as quickly as I would have if it was a six string. The pickups, although not active, are very hot and will pick up even the softest of playing, this is either a love or hate thing, but I love it, with the pickups as such it allows for many different expressions to a single note, a big plus for me. This guitar is great for metal music in particular, it allows for some incredibly deep rhythm notes, even rivaling a bass, but with the extra strings you no longer have to drop down the tuning which, again, leads to a lot of variety in a single instrument. Although it seems to be more geared towards metal music, the extra strings lend themselves well to a wide variety of genres, from picking individual strings for some extra country twang to a buttery soft lullabye sound this thing does it all. One thing to mention is that the strings are closer together than on a regular six string, not a problem just thought it should be mentioned. Overall, if you are in the market for an extended range guitar, this would be my pick, I honestly doubt you could find one of better quality and sound for the price.

product_title: International Measurement Standard String Action Ruler Gauge Guitar Luthier Tool (Style 1)
review_body:
STA Online has the shipping down pat. I received a email today from STA stating that, I should have received or will receive shortly, my order.
When I checked the mail, it is here.
I could have ordered this item from a supplier in the States. However, I would have paid three times the amount plus shipping.
Yes it came from China and it took 22 days from the date of the order, but I "got what I did not pay for". That is, I did not pay for expediency.

Anyway, the product is as advertised. It's about the size of a credit card, so if you expect bigger you now know better.
Solid little piece though. Well marked and engraved so the measurements are easy to see, even for someone like myself. ( I wear reading glasses). Measurements are in metric and Imperial/ US Customary Units (inches), so do not think you will need one of each, as some vendors sell.

On one side of the String Action Gauge you will find a chart for "string action at 12th fret". Personally I will use manufacturers recommendations as a base and set up from the base to my preferences.

Anyway, all n' all very handy.

P.S. On the String Action Gauge you will find a plastic film (similar to what covers the screen of a new phone or iPad) on both sides. It's hard to see, especially if there are no scratches. From the corners, the film will peel off easily.

I gave 4 stars as I have yet to use it. I'm sure it will be fine and then I can rate it 5 stars.

review_body:
The Ion Party Rocker is a fantastic gift for a teenager. When my granddaughter opened the box, she was overwhelmed. I have never seen her so happy. She is an average 14-year-old teenager. It was easy to connect via bluetooth. Within a couple minutes, the kids were rocking out. The unit includes a microphone for Karaoke and announcements. This unit supports bluetooth 4.0, which supports high-quality audio (iPhone 5/5s).

The sound quality is pretty good as log as you don't turn the volume up too high. We set up the unit in a large living room with arched ceilings. The volume was plenty. However, if you leave the mic connected and turned up, you will get a lot of distortion from audio feedback. The light show is pretty good, compared to other party lights. The case is built to be hauled around. It will last.

The most important attribute is that the kids absolutely loved it. An adult audiophile? Maybe not so much. There is only one speaker, so no stereo. The unit is not suited for critical listening, but it is designed for parties. I gave the unit 4 stars because you can only turn the volume up about half-way before the sound distorts. product_title: BEHRINGER MICROPOWER PS400
review_headline: Significant Hiss when Paired with AGPtek HA0016R Condenser Microphone and Tascam DR-05 Recorder
review_body:
Using a Tascam DR-05 digital recorder, the PS400 worked extremely well with a Martin Panger DM-11 and a Naxa NAM-982 microphones on the 48V setting with no discernible hiss or distortion. Unfortunately, I purchased the PS400 to use with a AGPtek HA0016R condenser microphone. The HA0016R was a much more sensitive microphone, necessitating a big decrease in recording volume on the DR-05. Recordings had a noticeable hiss not present with the other two microphones. All the microphones had profound distortion at the 12V setting when paired with the DR-05.

Pairing the devices with a desktop computer instead of the DR-05, the PS400 and HA0016R performed well without hiss or distortion at both 12V and 48V, but both the DM-11 and NAM-982 did not produce adequate dB output at either 12V or 48V. Performing the same test with a Surface tablet returned the same result as the desktop computer.

Overall, I am happy with the PS400. It will perform well with the HA0016R providing I use a tablet or laptop for remote recording, but given I got it to do remote recording with the HA0016R and DR-05, I am disappointed. I know this is a unique situation. I have done no testing with any other condenser microphones or digital recorders

Troublesome for people with sausage fingers. But a minor inconvenience compared to benefits of compactness such tuning design allows. String change was not as painful as I expected.

I use this guitar to continue learning whilst traveling, both to increase my skill and maintain my fitness. product_title: Yamaha Digital Piano
review_headline: I prefer this to our upright piano
review_body:
I bought this for my son who is taking piano lessons, but can't practice when his little brother is napping (which tends to overlap with the exact time he is free to practice). This has weighted keys that feel very close to an actual piano and has a headphone jack, so he can practice accurately without disturbing anyone. I play piano a little myself and have gotten to the point where I almost prefer playing this to the real thing in our house. Our upright (Yamaha) is nice and all, but it's ever so slightly out of key (even after being tuned) and the keys are starting to feel a little mushy.

It is a bare bones, no nonsense piano, which I love. There aren't a million features that you'd never actually use (like silly accompanying chord riffs or jazz drum lines). Maybe other people actually use stuff like that, but I don't. Plus, it has basic sounds. Pianos, organs, vibraphones, choir, and I think that's about it. If you want more, you can hook your Mac laptop up via a midi interface and play a million midi sounds through Garage Band. But we don't do that yet. My son has to get good at the instrument before he can go exploring the synthesizer sounds of the 1980s.

Very pleased with this instrument.

APPEARANCE
this thing has amazing finish. Beautifully crafted. Definitely does not look like you spent this little on it. It is not a standard sized guitar. slightly smaller in all ways from thickness, length and depth. Very good for smaller fingers especially when learning the complicated chords. Fret is flat. Wires are closer together making it narrower. Fret is also closer together, so if a grown person were to play this, you will definitely hit the neighboring frets and wires.

SOUND
Remember, this is smaller, but boy, I have heard larger guitars sound worse than this. definitely enjoyable to listen to. If you are not going to be picky and expect a professional sound, this is awesome!! Very easy to tune. No issues at all.

CONS
Why it's four stars. Doesn't come with anything except the guitar. There is only one button for the strap, the butt end of the guitar and nowhere else. So the other end you cannot hang. this was designed for kids, so even if there is a way to hang a strap, kids should be able to attach the straps easily by themselves.

OVERALL
Awesome guitar. My daughter loves it, sounds wonderful, my wallet is not broken! Go for it!

product_title: Kala Solid Body U-Bass SUB - 4-String, Fretted, Sunburst 2013 Model with Gig Bag
review_headline: Great Start, but was updated for good reasons
review_body: Keep in mind that the 2013 Kala solid body bass is a discontinued model.  A buyer can save money by purchasing this model rather than the updated model, but the 2013 version has some issues that have been addressed with the new models.  The bass I received had convincing tone, playability, good fit and finish and was fun.  The first problem I noticed was that one of the control knobs fell off and could not be securely reinstalled.  I emailed Kala's warranty department and was told that the model was redesigned and that Kala was aware of issues.  The changes for 2014?  The electronics have been changed to a different manufacturer, including improvements to the control pot shafts and knobs.  The nut is now Graphtec instead of rosewood.  The bridge has been improved to be compatible with the new electronics. The neck now has an adjustable truss rod.  The control cavity is now screwed on instead of being held on with magnets as with the 2013 model.  The street price for the 2014 model is within $50 of the discontinued model.  Kala bases in general are just great and are serious instruments despite their diminutive size.  Both my wife and I suffer from Osteoarthritis and these bases allow us to play pain free compared with playing a full sized bass.

product_title: QSC KW181 Powered Sub Woofer 18" 1000w,
review_body:
As a mobile DJ who averages nearly 120 events annually, I love my KW181. I've had the first one for a little over three years, and it has a six year factory warranty. I didn't purchase it from Amazon (I have a friend who is a dealer), but since I'm always shopping on Amazon, I wanted to share my opinion with others. It has clear sound, and really adds quality to your audio.

I purchased a second unit from Craigslist, so now I can couple them together for dramatic low end at events like prom, homecoming, etc. Low power consumption, I can run a KW 181, two K10's or two k12's, my computer, and my turntables off of one 15 amp circuit with no problem. Of course, it has XLR in/out, so you can chain your audio signal from speaker to speaker. It also has the "bass boost" switch (can't remember the correct name for this), and a polarity switch. It also has a switch to turn on/off the blue LED on the front of the cabinet, or to have it only turn on if you are clipping. There are LED's on the back to show if you have audio input, power, and clipping.

I would suggest getting the bag to protect your speaker and keep it looking nice. It's $100, but brides really care about how your gear looks. The KW181 has heavy duty casters, and with the bag on, I use the sub as another "cart"... I throw speaker stands or road cases on top and use it to roll gear in and out of the venue.

Expensive? Yes. Worth it? Absolutely!

product_title: Pyle-Pro PDWM96 Lavalier Wireless Microphone System
review_headline: Stay Away-Trouble using 2 microphones at same time.
review_body: Well here we go. Just got this item yesterday. I bought 2 wireless Lavs to connect to my H4N Zoom. They got here quick and no problems. Coming in my expectations were not very high. I just needed a set of microphones to use on the boat for a fishing show, So if they get damaged it is not a pair of $600 mics down the drain.    Well here is the review part... As expected the plastic was very thin and one of the battery covers to a receiver was actually already broken. Nothing a little duct tape couldn't hold together. Also the sticker on the top that said \\"volume power off on\\" was pealing off.    The batteries were a joke and held a terribly weak charge. The antenna was very thin and looked like I could break it if I wasn't careful. All of this and I was still okay with it because heck it was only $12 each.    Individually, I was surprised how good the quality of the mic was. Now again, I had them plugged into my Zoom so I could make the adjustments that I needed to make it sound better. The mic had a small hiss, but once I put into adobe premier it sounded very good. I tried using them outside and they were not too bad against the wind. I would recommend buying a lavaliere wind sock for these things. The range for these things was best from about 1-10 feet. The farthest I got without any hissing was 8-10 feet which is not that bad. The mic would lose signal completely around 28 ft. Once I got past 10 ft i would get static spikes every once and a while and some interference. So while it does work up to 25 ft, I wouldn't recommend filming or recording from that far away.    NOW THE PART THAT UPSETS ME CAUSING THE 2 STARS!!!!......  As stated, I bought 2 sets because I need these to use on a fishing show with two people. I noticed individually the lavs worked great. But when I connected them simultaneously, one would drop out. The mic would drop in and out of signal, and then go go completely dead.    I looked at the instructions again and saw under \\"attentions\\" it said, \\" If two wireless microphones are used at the same time, you should use them with one red and another green lamp and can't use them with the lamp of the same color.\\"  I was like okay here is the problem. Let me switch one of these receivers to RED. Well, there is no red option. The LEDs on both the mics are green. There is no second red channel or anything. So I now have to google \\"how to turn PDWM96 red\\" and I get nothing but Amazon reviews stating the same problem I am having. So It seems like the manufacturer builds red and green light receivers, but Amazon does not give you the options to choose when purchasing.    I just called Amazon and they offered me my money back. They said I can send the microphone back and once they receive it they will refund my money and then I can purchase the correct microphone that I want. I told the lady named Mickey that this option isn't a very good one as it does not address the issue. If I try and buy another microphone, I will still be in the same situation because there is no option on the site to choose RED or GREEN. She then told me she could give me the manufacture's phone number and to call them. She said if they can't help then to call Amazon back so they can refund my money and I can buy the correct microphone. Did she not just listen to what I said was the problem? I feel like I have been made a fool by Amazon because I only find out these items will not work together AFTER I purchase them. Also, though there are reviews of this issue. Amazon has put the consumer in an inconveinent situation by not addressing the issue nor informing consumers at time of purchase of a red and green receiver.    As far as the product goes, individually they work very well considering how cheap they are made and the price. You just have to take very good care of them. I don't like the fact that the receivers can not work together and there is no option for an alternate channel. So if you only need 1 mic and a great deal then I suggest this mic. If you need two, I would try and find other options unless Amazon can inform the consumer on the website and give them the option of red and green.      ********    Update 8-26-14  I was never able to get the correct receivers I needed. I figured I would just keep the mics and use individually and just have one a a backup.   I went out and filmed with the mic receiver connected int my h4n Zoom. It was picking up the signal fine. As soon as I recorded I noticed the signal would just drop out after random times. This was with me standing a mere 5 feet to 10 ft away from the base. The wires are so flimsy. The green light on the receiver would go dim and look like power loss. I put brand new batteries into the transmitter and receiver. I would still get a drop in signal. sometimes it would record 30 seconds fine, sometimes 4 minutes fine, and other times I couldn't even get a signal. The signals were so sporatic. There was no phones or other wireless devices around as we were recording in the woods and our phones were all off. When the signal was there, the quality of sound wasn't bad. The biggest problem was I couldn't get through a segment without sound loss. We ended up having to use the onboard camera mic and the zoom mic separately. I just disconnected the Pyle-Pro and threw it back in the car to become trash. I may keep the lav itself to use on other recording devices, but as far as the transmitter and receiver, they are garbage. The plastic is very thin and like I said, did not even get through a complete session without losing signal. I tried both microphones I bought with the same issue. I urge you to look elsewhere for a cheap mic as this one will only frustrate you. If it works it's good for the money, but I apparently had 2 duds that couldn't hold a frequency signal. I will just have to save money and invest the cash in a good wireless lav. This is what I get for trying to go cheap I guess. Good luck everyone..If needed I may even do a video reviewto show how it drops signal..

product_title: ErgoPlay Tappert Classical Guitar Support
review_headline: Good for some body types and gravity is a plus
review_body:
There are a slew of guitar supports out there and this is just one of the more traditional ones. The device fastens on via suction-cups. Get some static cling wrap (Suction-Cup Protector) if need be as any tiny grooves in your polish can un-suction the suction. These feel pretty good, places the guitar in a nice spot and allows the guitar to be movable. I've had mine for years and you can buy new suction cups if they wear out...so durability is good.

Only problem might be if you have suction-cup problems during a concert #nofun. If the suction cup comes off on this model at least you still have gravity to help you. That is one of the better points of this model, even if the suction cup comes off your guitar will still stay in place if you are careful.

I’ve seen many people using these in combination with the footstool, very likely to get the perfect position. That’s the key with these things: getting the position you want not the one it sets you up with. Not that foot-stools are any different.

One thing I've found, and keep in mind that I'm quite short, is that I can not get the guitar very close to my left leg and therefore not as upright as I'd like. The support is just too bulky for my body type (I prefer the Gitano). However, I think taller people in particular do well with this support. I've seen this used successfully by hundred's of guitarists so it's a proven product but just not for me.

product_title: Tama HP910LWCB Speed Cobra - Midnight Special LTD
review_headline: Best DK pedals I've ever played on!
review_body:
I've been playing on DWs and Axis (back and forth) for over 15+ years, and I was pretty sold on the quality and usability of these products, but I've recently felt that there's something missing from these brands (especially Axis direct drive/longboard). At a recent gig I was expressing my issues and the soundguy (also a drummer) said: for your style and power, get the speed cobras. Hands down best pedal for the money. I had never played on any Tama pedals, so I checked some out at the local GC. I was pretty amazed at how fluid both pedals felt on a "practice pad". There was no loss in power/drive from the left pedal. Admittedly, my left foot is a little lazy, so I decided to order the Midnight Special.

After adjusting these pedals to my kit and my stance, I can say that after playing double kick, on dual kick and double pedal, that these pedals are the BEST piece of equipment I have ever bought. The chain drive construction and just the overall feel of the longboard pedals just instantly becomes a part of your feet. I don't do a lot of super fast or even that intricate of kick work, but this thing opened up my ability by giving my feet/legs a TRUE feeling of fluid motion. I've never had a piece of drum gear just be "perfect" right out of the box. Granted, every drummer has their preference, but if you're in the mood to try something new, double kick wise, you will NOT be unhappy with this purchase.

And...these ones are BLACK! Metal!

product_title: Red Witch Analog Famulus Distortion
review_body:
OUTSTANDING PEDAL!
Played with Gibson LPs' ('57 classic hum-buggies) through a Two-Rock Studio Pro 22. (clean amp, through the front)

1. Versatile dual gain: Overdrive to distortion (may not be for metal players)
2. Tone, tone, tone: Great "eq", my gear still sounds like my gear.
3. Extremely low noise floor: Very acceptable even with both gains cranked.
4. Easy to use: Start with everything at 12 noon and go from there. No need for 20 switches & dials, it's all right there. (easy)
5. Seems to be very well made: All the controls "feel right."
6. It's ......................... "A KEEPER!"

I kept one low gain pedal on my board to go along with the Famulus, this way all bases are covered. If desired, it stacks really well, again keeping a low noise floor, sustain forever going into "fuzz type territory." Remember, with regard to the low noise floor, this is with humbuckers through a clean amp. Single coils through a cranked "Boogie or Marshall" with definitely yield more noise, I can't say how much more, because I don't have a high gain amp here to run it through.

I'm sorry I didn't find this pedal sooner, it could have saved me a lot of wasted time and money. Very happy with it!

product_title: Blackstar HT-METAL Guitar Effects Pedal
review_body:
This is easily one of the best pedals I've ever owned. It exceeded all my expectations. It's range and tone is just phenomenal. You can get everything from light tube breakup on the clean setting of channel 1 to pure fury on channel 2. The ISF knob is a tremendous feature that really lets you tweak the midrange voicing extensively. I had never really heard much of Blackstar before this or given them any real consideration. This has totally changed my view of them. I still know very little about them but this pedal is cutting-edge. It's a tube amp in a box and it sounds even better with a tube amp. It's a portable/alternative preamp section.

I've played it for a few hours now but I was able to dial in exactly what I heard in my head within minutes of turning it on. I couldn't be more pleased. I know this is not a cheap pedal. But here's the deal -- it's not a cheap pedal in any sense. It sounds expensive, and feels very well built from the knobs to just the heft of the thing. Even the tube they put in it is a really good one.

If you are looking for authentic, rich, robust overdrive/distortion with all the gain you could ever want -- this is your pedal. But it's more than that -- it's a garden of classic amp tones that you can spend hours tweaking, from Mesa recto to classic Marshall. The ISF knob along with the EQ combined with the slightly different sounds of channel 1 and 2 give you an almost infinite range of tones. And it's 100% pure tube driven.

This is really a cutting edge pedal worth every penny. I just love this thing.

I personally prefer to record my audio separately, off camera, with a zoom or a tascam, and then sync back in post, but i have found that for certain situations (especially run and gun type filmmaking) that is not always possible, and it's nice to have a good backup of at least decent quality audio with the rode on the camera at all times, just in case something goes wrong with my other audio options.

I almost went with the shure vp83, because it looks to have better (metal) build quality for the same price and a couple of other cool features, but rode's super impressive 10 year warranty kept me with them, that's awesome.

With the rode videomic pro, you can get some pretty great audio, essential especially for the times you can't rely on other externally recorded audio options.

product_title: Zoom Q2HD Handy HD Video Recorder with 2GB SD Card and Two AA Batteries
review_headline: Wanted a high quality Sound and Video audition / industry demo device
review_body:
I've been in the music business for more than five decades.

I've was a "signed act" and had songs published in the mid-to-late sixties.

Now I do lease/license releases for myself and the industry.

Many years ago I would record potential players or singers with a stereo reel-reel... later with a multi-track, particularly for drummers... to use for later review.

Additionally I would record myself for an "industry shopper" - for my songs... something I do as an interim product, before and/or instead of, what's commonly called a "Demo".

Having produced a substantial amount of product (mostly for others) that was meant to image well and therefore convey it's recording environment, I have, since my introduction to the Format/Technique, been a huge fan of "Mid-Side" micing... partially because it also reproduces an essentially perfect phase correlation for surround sound which many of us have recorded in/ for - since the late sixties. Led Zeppelin, Hendrix, etc., having put fully correlated surround sound phase processing onto many of their records since about 1966.

Enter Zoom Products for field-video AUDIO recording - amongst their various attributes; Zoom offers interchangeable "Mic-Heads" for some of their products. Among the various choices offered are "Mid-Side" mics.

I already have a reasonably good (though limited) HD video recorder... and as you might imagine... I have about any audio device I might need - as well as having computer programs or traditional means of syncing their outputs if required. OK as far as it goes, but an awful lot of hassle for some of the more moderate things that I [and all of us] do on a day-to-day basis.

The Q2HD is seemingly the exactly right product to fill that niche... quick set-up, outstanding audio, remarkably good video and no additional processing required for almost all of the basic projects for which any of us would use it. 1- record your band live for YouTube or DVD... better than you have any right to expect for the effort, 2- make a simple song-demo... with or without video... etc, etc.

Not only is this a pretty amazing Audio Device - partly because of it's mid-side adjust-ability for "room-focus" [mono to wide in many steps] and partly because of its remarkable sampling flexibility, but also because the actual mics that are built-in are well beyond what you have any right to expect at this price-point... you could easily pay more for just the mics, than the entire Q2HD, and still not get as good a sound quality.

Then there's the video - at this price it's almost just a "bonus" yet it has substantial flexibility in terms of Zoom/Framing, lighting and format - from pretty darn good... up to very, very good.

And --- although for me, thus far, it hasn't really been an issue one way or the other; the fact that the entire package not only fits in my pocket... I can even close the button-flap on an ordinary shirt so it can't fall out... is pretty cool for portability, I'd say.

Last-but-not-least; the menu is a jewel. well lit, easy to use, logically laid out and very flexible. In addition the metering, which comes up in the menu window is excellent and useful. Lastly, although, like the entire unit; the video viewer is small, it's nonetheless entirely usable.

It's a ZOOM product - I expected it to be very good. It's actually better than that. quite an impressive product. the Only hope I could have for "better" would be a mufti-channel version -- with, at best, the interchangeable mic-heads. Dreaming? Maybe not. Could be just around the corner.......... and I'd still be glad I have this (stereo) version as well!

product_title: Fender Standard Stratocaster Electric Guitar - Flamed Maple Top - Maple Fingerboard
review_headline: A lot of guitar for the money
review_body:
I have been looking for a Fender Stratocaster to get that Strat sound through my new Marshall MG30CFX (also reviewed on Amazon). I have heard good things about the Mexican Made Strats and went to a store to check them out. The American Standard is a tad heavier in the body and the pups are a bit more crisp. The American Standard also has a 22 fret neck where this one is 21 frets. Other than some minor hardware differences this guitar is just as playable as it's more expensive counterpart.

The finish is what sold me in the end. The Tobacco Edges which almost have a hint of wine color fade beautifully to a Honey finish over an awesome Flame Maple Top. The back of the guitar allows the wood grains to show through and the Rosewood Fingerboard adds a soft look and feel to the smooth Maple Neck. I can find absolutely NO FLAWS in the finish. The chrome input jack has a few small rough spots, but that is about it.

The guitar sounds good as is and is playable out of the box. Down the road a piece I thought I would end up replacing the stock pups with an upgrade, but after getting used to these pups, I think I'm very pleased with just staying with the factory pick-ups. For the $$ I doubt I will ever find another Brand New Guitar that is set up like this. The lowest priced American Standard is still going to set you back around $800 and will have just a basic finish. If you are wanting a Strat but unsure of getting a Mexican Made unit because of quality, IMO this should suit you just fine.

review_headline: Fantastic for the price point. (audiophile review)
review_body:
I got these for my mom, so she could use them with her iPad and Sansa player I got and filled up with her favorite music. However, I did burn them in and listen to them just to see what they sounded like. The cans I will be comparing them to are the famous (or infamous, depending on your point of view) ATH-M50s. Now, is that fair? Of course not, but it's what I use myself, like many other \\"budget Audiophiles\\". Quick review:

Highs: as to be expected, the highs are more tinny sounding and not as clear. These are much cheaper headphones, so go figure.

Mids: the mids are less recessed than the M50s, which are known to have that issue, however they are not as clear. Again, go figure.

Lows: it's surprising how close these come to the M50s in this department - the bass is there and it is fairly clear

Volume: these headphones would not be suitable for me (aside from the sound quality) simply because they're quiet in comparison to the higher end ATH headphones. However, she doesn't like to listen to music loud so for her, they're perfect. I will note that they aren't as quiet as everyone is making them out to be, and with a small headphone amp you could boost them and make them sound better in the process.

Soundstage: this is where these headphones really shine and why I'm giving them a five star rating - the soundstage is pretty much equal to the M50s. Really, really, really good.

Comfort: just as comfortable as the higher end ones.

Anyways, yeah. You get what you pay for, but looking at competitors, I'd say that by far these are best for the price. These were 24 dollars for me and 30 when not on sale - that makes the competing headphones things like the Sennheiser HD-202s. They're by far better than other headphones at this price, but that's not all. Obviously the sound is different but in terms of sheer quality, I'd say these are about 25% less than the Sennheiser HD-280s (with a much better fitthough). So, akin to how the M50s are ~150 dollar headphones that rival ~200-250 dollar headphones, these effectively rival ~50-60 dollar headphones with the right setup, and for 24 dollars (apparently they're 21 now, too) that's a tremendously good deal. They're not going to satisfy anyone who has heard better headphones, but they're a great gift for people who haven't really heard good sound at all. One last note: ignore the people saying \\"these have no bass\\" about any Audio-Technica products. They're looking for artificial bass from overpriced Beats headphones or something because the bass response is fine.

product_title: Evans EC Reverse Dot Snare Drum Head
review_headline: Mediocre... chokes the drum too much
review_body:
I bought this to put on a Pork Pie 7x14 Cherry/Bubinga snare. I keep this snare tuned medium to low, to compliment my higher tuned metal snares. So, since I am a huge fan of the Power Center Reverse Dot head, I thought I would try this one for a meaty, low tuning. I figured the EC ring would cut some of those hard-to-control overtones, and 2 plies would add durability and allow lower tuning.

Well, it didn't work. At low tunings, it just chokes. It loses all tone and sounds flat and dead, no attack, no pop, just like hitting a wet newspaper. On top of that, it actually sustains much longer than, say, a G2, but in a bad way. It's not a ringy, overtone-rich sustain, which I like. It's a tom-like dry sounding sustain, more of a booonnngg sound that I have to add even MORE dampening to shorten. Yeesh.

At medium to medium-tight tensions, it works well. It does fatten up the sound and increase brightness and fatness, at the expense of attack.

Overall, I think it's just too much. 2 plies, overtone ring, center dot. The head has an identity crisis. There's too much mass and it makes the drum limp and ugly. I a/b tested with a G2 in a studio, same tension etc, and the G2 destroyed this head at low tunings. At medium tunings, I liked both for different reasons. So, this head goes in the closet with my Genera Dry to collect dust.

product_title: Zweiss Pro-Grade Rotary Valve Baritone Horn with Designer Hardcase
review_headline: I would not get this for a beginning player, everyone else is okay.
review_body:
I've played the Baritone for 25 years. I started with trumpet when I was 8, and I switched to Baritone TC when I was 14. I played in Jr High, High School, College & the Military. Today, I am in the largest permanent marching band in the USA. Most of the guys around me are all DCI champions, ex music teachers, composers, and guys like me. Everyone has been playing for at least 25 years.
If you've never played anything like this, you really might want to consider a piston valve horn.

I've had this Baritone for 3 months now, and overall, I'm happy with it. I practice 10-15 hours a week, w/o any issues, and I have 2 hour long marching band practices, 5-6 times a month. Its very light & easy to move around, but the material is very thin, so I worry that the bell will dent easily. There are 2 places to attach a strap, and plenty of open spots for your left hand to rest on. My only issue is where they put the spit valve, its on the side & not the bottom, you have to turn the horn on its side (not good in tight spaces), or for dumping it on your neighbors shoe (without being noticed).
Not that I'd ever do that.

A few things to keep in mind: Its not a $2000+ horn, don't expect the finish to be perfect!! I like that though, that way, if it does get scratched, dented, etc., I won't be thrilled... but I won't be as upset as I would denting a $2k horn.

I had to spend a lot of time adjusting the rotary valves, so make sure you have a small screwdriver handy, and a small soft brush to help get rid of the extra junk coming out of the valve joints.
I use rotary valve oil & piston valve oil.
(Did you know that sewing machine oil, is the same as rotary valve oil?)
Since this is a new horn, you're going to want to use a lot oil!
Everything is much smoother today, then it was when the horn first arrived. Take your time, make tiny adjustments on the valves as you break it in, and I'm pretty sure you will end up with a horn you will be happy to play.

Which gets to the main issue, sound.
For a relatively inexpensive horn, it sounds really good!
I was happily surprised when I first played it with 11 other Baritones. It does not sound cheap, its very warm & bright, and so far, it has a 3 octave range. A little more power is needed on the highs vs a Euphonium, but it drops really low with ease.
The case is pretty decent too, so you're set on that-

I'm about to order a different mouthpiece, and if you ever decide to do the same, you'll need one with a small shank.
I just saved you return postage.

Please feel welcome to ask me any questions. If I do not know the answer, I've got 11 other Baritone players I can ask.

product_title: Vic Firth VKB3 Fleece-Covered Felt VicKick Beaters
review_headline: Similar but not identical to Vater's Vintage Bomber
review_body:
This beater is made for feathering bass drums, so there is little attack. What you do get is the 'felt-but-not-heard' effect when played correctly. For higher volume work (still acoustic or in a lightly amplified setting) this beater will allow you to product notes instead of thuds with your bass drum.

At a glance this looks identical to the [[ASIN:B00080SEAU Vater Vintage Bomber Beater]], but there are some subtle differences. Physically they are close: this one is 8.125 inches long, which is .125 longer than the Vater, and the oval head is identical at 3x2.75 inches. Both are covered in a fleece like material that resembles lamb's wool of the vintage beaters.

The key difference is this has a medium felt core that provides a little more momentum than the Vater's lighter cork core. To be sure, the difference is subtle. If you play a lot of jazz in acoustic settings, or if you are a big band drummer who feathers your bass drum then you already know the basic characteristics of this beater.

While I prefer the feel of the Vater, that is subjective. I have friends who prefer the feel of this one, and it all comes down to individualized factors. For example, I have been playing the Vater for over five years, so have an ingrained feel for its every nuance, so I can tell the difference between the two. If you are new to these old school beaters, though, either will probably suffice and you should go by price and availability.

One final note: If you are looking for a beater for quiet gigs, but want more attack because of the music you play, you may be better off with the [[ASIN:B0088737SY Ludwig Lambs Wool Beater]]. That model is shaped like the traditional felt beaters of years past, with a lamb's wool head. You will still get the attenuated notes, but with a degree of attack that this beater will not provide.
