The sound you get out of this relies heavily on what you put into this. I have a hollow body, so not having built in reverb on the amp isn't the end of the world. Throw a multi-effects into the mix and you've got a very portable, fantastic little practice amp for less than $100. If you're looking for something to shred with, I'd probably look elsewhere, but if you want a great bluesy/jazz/50s rock amp, this is a great option.

A speaker under warranty needed repair. 3 months passed, during which they sent 2 defective replacements. They acted like they had no accountability.
I bought a pair of speakers made by Behringer on Amazon in January 2013. In late October 2013, the tweeter on one of the speakers began to buzz. I was still under warranty so I contacted The Music Group (whom handle Behringer warranty) and was told I could take it in to a local certified shop for repair. I called the shop owner and he told me that The Music Group was going to send a replacement speaker since the part he needed was unavailable. The replacement arrived in January and when I plugged it in it did not work. I contacted The Music Group again and they told me they would swap it for another one. I sent the defective speaker back and another one arrived in early February. This speaker was also defective. I called The Music Group and they informed me that they had been sending me refurbished units, which they had not informed me of before. I asked to have a new speaker sent to me since by this point I had been waiting for two and a half months for the issue to be corrected. They declined, saying it was not possible for them to do that. They then told me that the best they could do is send me another refurbished unit. I begrudgingly accepted because it was the only option I had. Two to three weeks passed and I still had not received my replacement. I called in again and they informed me that they had not sent me a replacement and that my original speaker was to be repaired and sent to me. They never tried to contact me beforehand to give me this information. By this time I had been fed up with their unacceptable customer service. Finally an agreement was worked out where they contacted Amazon to arrange a return for refund. A supervisor from The Music Groupcalled to tell me that Amazon would issue me a refund and that I would be able to keep my speakers as well (the other one being sent to me after it was repaired) which was a lie. I accepted, but when amazon contacted me via email they made it clear that I was to return the speakers in order to receive a refund. I once again called The Music Group and they acknowledged the error. I was hoping to get a new pair of the speakers, however the price on Amazon had risen from the original price of $230 to 300$ a pair. When I told The Music Group about this, they basically told me tough luck and to just, I quote, "shop around". I then asked how long I would have to wait for my speaker to be repaired because at this point I just wanted it back. They told me it would be another eight to ten weeks before they even got the part they needed. This was absolutely unacceptable seeing as I had already been waiting three months. As a last resort I called Amazon customer service to see if I could simply exchange the old speakers for a new pair. Unfortunately Amazon could not do that as my refund had already been issued but they could give me $70 dollars off a new pair to match the price. Amazon was able to do in ten minutes what The Music Group couldn't in three months(or even longer). The Music Group then sent me an email asking whether or not I would want my broken speaker shipped to me or directly to Amazon. I replied that I would like it shipped to Amazon. product_title: Aquila Red Series Tenor Ukulele String Set Low G Tuning, 88U
review_body:
It's been recommended here that you not rush, but instead take lots of time to string these carefully onto your uke. However, the Red Series strings are prone to snapping regardless if your uke's nut slots do not happen to be the proper width to accommodate these great-sounding but somewhat brittle strings, especially the 1mm-thick G string. Mine snapped right at the nut while in the case, after only about a week, probably because I didn't have a luthier file the slot a tiny bit wider and also \\"radius\\" (i.e., round off) the slot's edges on the fingerboard side of the nut, as some sellers recommend.

Aquila has conceded that these strings may require uke modifications. Aquila also makes special recommendations regarding installation methods, e.g., use two fingers to hold the string above the nut slot until nearly all the slack is wound onto the tuning post; fold the tuning end of the string over itself and twist into a rope-like, double-thickness bit that'll go through the hole in the tuning post, so there'll be a less acute angle against the possibly sharp edge of that hole on the first winding.

I'm replacing my broken Red with a very well-reviewed low-G string that's sold singly: the flat-wound, \\"squeakless\\" Fremont Soloist, which is .76mm thick, i.e., about one-fourth thinner that the Red G. (Worth-brand fluorocarbon low-G strings, even though they're .91mm thick, are long-lasting on my same uke, despite its unmodified nut.)

Responding to breakage complaints, Aquila reformulated the Red Series to be more snap-resistant but did not rebrand the product or change its labeling to indicate \\"new and improved\\" or \\"2.0\\" or the like. The only indication you've received the 2.0 version is the little, white date sticker on the back of the string pack: If it says \\"12/2013\\" or later, you've got the reformulated Red Series strings; any earlier and it's the more snap-prone 1.0 version.

product_title: Kala KA-SSLNG Soprano Long Neck - Solid Spruce Top / Mahogany Ukulele
review_body:
I purchased the Kala SSLNG soprano after playing a whole selection of Ukes at a local store even though I walked in without the intention of adding another soprano to my collection. I was actually testing out concert models to replace one that I will be presenting as gift to a family member

The next thing I discovered, I couldn't put it down once I picked it up. Hands down one of the best sounding ukes I've personally played. And surprisingly, it is as loud as a concert, yet has a smooth well balanced tone with a unexpected push in the bass and mid-range. This is probably due to the curved back design on the instrument.

Fresh from the factory the string action on this uke is great and does not require any additional adjustments. And although it looks sort of \\"plain Jane\\" because of the light solid spruce top and black binding, the aesthetic of the uke is the least important aspect of why I was compelled to own it. There is something about the balance of the tonality, volume, projection, fullness of the sound (without sounding boomy or boxy) that grabbed me instantly.

Despite being a soprano, the long neck (super soprano) aspect makes it so much easier to play for those with larger hands. Yet it still fits comfortably into my standard padded soprano ukulele gig bag. A plus indeed! Addendum (June 18): it will fit the Roadrunner soprano gig bag--which I recommend--available from Guitar Center but not most other cases. I believe that the Kaces Kuks-3 soprano case from Amazon will fit as well.

It's priced perfectly for an instrument that has a solid spruce top and quality construction and is a FANTASTIC deal compared to other more expensive models and brands out there.

Tone: Warm and balanced yet sufficiently bright and crisp

Volume: Comparable to a Concert size

Projection: Excellent

Playability: Excellent. Great string action

Construction: Excellent. Frets are smooth. Neckis straight. No blemishes or unevenness in the glossy finish

Looks: Simple and understated

Intonation: Very Good! The notes a ever so slightly sharp as it's played up the net to the 12th fret. However, that happens to instruments I've played that are twice the price.

I highly recommend the Kala SSLNG for all level enthusiasts because it's an incredible price for a ukulele of this quality.

review_headline: Oh my I should have picked something better.
review_body: I was torn over the high price of USB isolators.  So I chose this one, which cost less then half of what's out there.  I needed an isolator for interfacing with a microcontroller programmer/emulator that I use to develop embedded code on prototype hardware so I don't accidentally blast my computer (excessive voltage or EMI).  Unfortunately, just like the previous reviews, the device cannot be recognized.  I've tried a USB mouse and not even it can be recognized.  The only thing that works are USB memory sticks!  There are two issues.  1) The internal isolated power supply is very weak, so it won;t work with things requiring moderate power from the USB like mice.  2) There are data rate limitations, and the isolator IC inside seems to be configured for the lower of two speed options.  Very disatisfying, I recommend shelling out several hundred dollars for a real isolator.

product_title: Blue Snowball USB Microphone (Textured White)
review_headline: Ok, but not what I expected or wanted
review_body: This microphone is decent in overall sound quality and construction. However, I did have my griefs with this little (-massive) thing. First, the microphone is pretty big, roughly the size of a softball. Second, I had ordered the microphone in white and the box arrived with a "color white" icon on the bottom. I opened it up and out came a brushed aluminum snowball. Poor packaging quality control. I don't know if this is a common occurrence but henceforth be warned. The brushed aluminum was pretty nice even though it was not what i ordered. AND finally number three, The microphone had zero projection. I had to be right in front of the thing (no more than 2-3 feet) for it to pick up my voice. I bought this mic to be used for vocals and occasional instrumentals. The omnidirectional setting was terrible. It had zero gain and could barely pick up anything in the room. My voice amplified through a PA was barely louder than a whisper no matter how close or at what angle I positioned the microphone in relation to the PA speakers. This mic is hurting for an adjustable gain switch. It is possible that I received a defective product but I cannot be 100% certain. Overall I would say, if you are on a tight budget and need a microphone for podcasting ONLY this will fit your bill. Although, don't bother with settings 2 and 3 if you want any sort of distinguishable volume. I returned this mic after one day and bought the Blue Yeti instead. If you have a bit more cash laying around in your wallet, I suggest you do the same. The Yeti is everything this mic has ever hoped to be and then some. You will not regret this decision.

product_title: Beyerdynamic DT-150-250-GREY Closed Dynamic Monitoring Headphone for use in Loud Environments
review_body:
The DT-150 is a nice warm and balanced sounding set of headphones that tilts slightly slightly toward the dark side of neutral regarding the low mids and bass.
Compared to the B&W P7, the Beyer DT150 has a wider sound stage, has a deeper and more natural musical presentation, and a slightly sweeter sound overall. It does not reproduce quite the same clarity, or extend the trebles and bass, or roll back the mids the same as the B&W P7 but the Beyer DT-150 does sound \\"bigger:\\" and more frequency neutral, and has a better sounding bass response.
Build quality is very good and solid, and its comfortable to wear even tho its sort of \\"low tech\\" in its bulky '70s aesthetic design.
Its one of those phones that does nothing great but handles everything well, and does sound good.
Its not going to give you AKG 702 clarity and no bass, and it does not punch out the mids or overly extend the treble as does the KEF M500s.
Its unique and neutral analog and slightly dark@soft sound is very enjoyable.
Not for Bass Heads and not for Treble Junkies.
Will sound best with an amp.

product_title: JJ Electronics T-6V6-S-JJ-MQ Vacuum Tube Spiral Filament Matched Quad
review_headline: Replacement tubes for Dr Z amplifier
review_body: I purchased these as a replacement set for my Dr Z JAZ20/40 amplifier.  These are the same tubes that Dr Z uses, and the new ones came well-packaged and all tested out well with no issues so far (been playing them for a couple of weeks).  I've had good experiences with JJ tubes.  These power tubes are good for lower-gain amps as they have a nice break up when you turn up the volume and I've found that they are not as harsh as some other tubes. On a related note, their ECC83 tubes can handle higher voltages so if you have a tremolo circuit on your amp they work better and are quieter in that position.  I do not like JJ tubes in the gain stages very much, however, as they just don't have the tonal qualities of a TunSol, Mullard or Ruby but I'm betting they would last a lot longer.  This seller seems to be reliable and they deliver what they promise.

review_headline: Not that great for casual listening.
review_body: If you're looking for headphones for movies and music then these are not for you. I had them for a week and wasn't really impressed with the sound. The treble is sharp and the bass is weak. Listening to music was really harsh experience that made my ears ring something fierce. After seeing all the gaga reviews about these I thought maybe I just didn't possess the ability to appreciate good headphones. I was going to keep them to see if they grew on me but unfortunately the right side started buzzing at certain frequencies so I chose to return them. I looked around for a pair of headphones that would be more suitable for music and movies and ended up buying a pair of Beyerdynamic DT 770 PRO's and I was blown away! They're very pleasant sounding, the bass is nice and not over bearing, and they're VERY comfortable. If you're willing to spend about $50 more or so (I got mine new for $130, hold out for a deal!) then I really recommend the DT 770's as an alternative choice to these Sony's. If that's a little out of your price range I have friends who swear by the Grado SR80i, which go for about $99. Good luck!

product_title: CAD Audio AS32 Acousti-Shield 32 - Stand Mounted Acoustic Enclosure
review_body:
I am a professional VO Actor but since moving to a new apartment, I needed to create a 'home studio' that provided quality recording results without being able to build a sound/recording booth in a rental property. I set this up in the upper loft that I use as my office. I re-recorded some voice-overs and listened to the before and after. I noticed SIGNIFICANT IMPROVEMENT in sound without actually doing anything else other than having a standard cardioid microphone with a pop filter. It eliminated all ambient background noise from any echo, bounce and surrounding white noise. I couldn't believe how clean the vocals came out just by adding this CAD Audio Acousti-Shield. I am glad I selected this one after much homework, reading reviews, comparisons with other products (even looking at Guitar Center-which charged much more).

I prefer standing up to do recordings so that I can get full use of my diaphragm and had a boom microphone stand. I found that with a couple tweaks, you can make this work with a boom stand. I purchased a 6" Extension Tube (AD-8B) & an Adapter to turn a male-male extension tube to a female-male (AD-5B) from Atlas Sound to work with my standard 'On Stage Stand' microphone boom stand.
See pictures of my set up. I plan on adding some additional sound improvements to the wall and ceiling but this alone was such an amazing sound improvement, I was most definitely impressed. I wanted to add a few images of my set up but I don't see where to add images. So when I can do a video review I will update this to show my setup.

product_title: Takamine GC5CE Classical Acoustic-Electric Guitar,
review_headline: A great guitar for the price
review_body:
I picked this guitar up from Sweetwater. Didn’t’ come with a gig bag or case but I had one at home.

So I picked up the guitar when I was a teen. A few years later I realized that if I wanted to play in bands, I needed to take up something else besides the guitar. So I picked up the electric bass when I was 21. Fifteen years later, I decided to pick up the classical guitar again and do some home-made recordings just for kicks. The guitar is not my main instrument so I didn’t want to spend too much on it. I had read lots of good reviews on Takamine classicals.

I got so used to the oversized neck of the 5-string bass that I was a little worried about adjusting. But this Takamine has a nice, wide neck. Two inches at the nut.

I’m sight impaired so I can’t read the tuner. That’s my only complaint and why I can’t give it a 5-star rating.

For the price, the electronics sound nice and clean. One of the dials was making a static-noise when I moved it. Maybe it just needs a cleaning. The string height was a little too high for my taste so I had to take the saddle out and sand it down. Traditionally, classical guitars don’t have fret marks. So I looked into having pearl inlayws put in. But I think it may be less money to just paint a dot on the 7th and 12th frets.

Overall, I’m real happy with this guitar. Was great for the price.

In use the keyboard is excellent - it feels well made and looks stylish as well as considerably more expensive than it is, plus, it is also quite light. The feel of the keys is really nice - they are soft touch but have decisive feel and are well spaced. In addition, there are a number of useful extra keys for functions such as search, home, play, volume etc. - the availability of some of these functions obviously depends on the operating system you are using. This OXA keyboard represents an excellent use of Bluetooth to achieve a versatile design and is very usable because it is so well made - I have come to like it a lot in relatively short period of time. Recommended.

product_title: Beyerdynamic DT-770-PRO-32 Closed Dynamic Headphone for Mobile Control and Monitoring Applications, 32 Ohms
review_headline: My first Hi-Fi headphones coming from a USB "Gaming" Headset, never going back
review_body:
This review is for the Beyerdynamic DT770 PRO 32 Ohms.

First a bit of a backstory:
For the past 3 years I had a Logitech G35 headset which I wore all day. I loved the sound quality of that headset. Overall it was an outstanding product. The only problem was, it was very heavy on my head which made it uncomfortable to wear all day. Also USB audio often had conflicts with other programs. I figured it was time for a new headset. I wanted something a little high end and not a dedicated "Gaming" product. I had originally set my eyes on the Sennheiser HD598s which I ordered. They sounded amazing and were so comfy to wear in addition to looking nice. I live in an appartment with 3 other people, and as I had feared, the noise from the "open acoustics" of the HD598s leaked too much noise for me to be comfortable. I had to sadly return them. Unfortunately, most of the Hi-Fi headphones are open acoustics so I was having a tough time finding some good closed headphones with the exception of the super expensive DJ headphones. A friend of mine told me about the DT770s, this brings us to today.

I have had the headphones for about 2 months now and I am nothing but pleased. I have gained a whole new appreciation for music. Going back to my old headphones, music just sounded like a wall of sound. With the DT770s, I can individually hear each instrument, I have found myself just laying down and listening to my music since getting these. Needless to say, the sound quality is top knotch coming from someone who only knew USB gaming headsets. And the bass, oh god the bass... my earlobes rumble when listening to some bass heavy music like Pendulum or heavy metal like Fear Factory. Just as a note, get yourself an amplifier to really use these headphones. Yeah onboard will work but an amp should almost be necessary. I ended up getting an internal Xonar DGX soundcard/headphone amp, I avoided a USB amp due to my freaky USB situation.

Being someone that talks in games and VOIP applications a lot, moving to headphones without a mic felt weird. With these headphones you either get a desk mic like a Yeti Blue Snowball or you improvise, which is what I did. I salvaged a mic boom from some old call center headset from the 90s and clipped a zalman ZM-Mic1 on the end and zip tied the wires to my headphone wires, then velcroed the mic boom to my headset. A little bit of improvisation will allow you to get amazing headphones without having to settle for one with an integrated mic.

Build quality is top notch. The headphone band is made of nice solid yet lightweight metal wrapped in leather. The ears are nice solid hard plastic. The earcups are leatherette on the 32 ohm. The 80 and 250 ohm come with the velour pads. Beyerdynamic sells both the leatherette and velour pads on their website if you ever want to switch them. The headset makes no creaks or rattles. Compared to something like the HD598s, they do sit a little heavy, however they are studio headphones, so this is to be expected. Beyerdynamic also makes their headphones easily repairable and interchangeable, so I have a feeling these will last for a while.

Soundstage is great, but not as precise as the USB "gaming" headphones. However, the difference is not massive, and having the exponentially better sound quality is worth the tradeoff of a slightly smaller soundstage.

One final thing to note, the cord is rather short. This is perfect for professional applications where you are moving around with it, but for someone like me who works from their computer all day, it was too short. Its worth it to buy an extension cable.

Overall I am very happy with my purchase, I have had no regrets. If these headphones ever die 5-6 years down the line I will most definitely buy Beyerdynamic again.

product_title: RhythmTech RT7350 ProTorq Drum Key
review_headline: Imperative tool.. in theory. Lacks effectiveness in practice.
review_body:
For a drum key, this essentially stock standard. In context of tuning drums, I'll stick to tuning by ear. The tonal differences between say lugs 1 and 3 (following star pattern) are night and day when adjusting based on torque.

Despite following various techniques found on the internet, fine tuning is just out of the question. Not to mention if you follow the directions included with this key, (starting at one lug, torque to full, move to next) you'll never achieve equal tension on the head full circle.

Now the Evans key may prove to be adjusted better, but I'd advise against torque keys as a whole. In fact, the only tool which has proven to get perfect tuning without going by ear are the drum dials and head pressure gauges.

I bought this Rhythm Tech key to experiment with and to see if it lives up to the function which it is supposed to do and I feel it's achievements at tuning a kit are luck luster at best. Best advice is to learn to tune by ear, but if that's not working out invest in a drum dial.

product_title: Korg Kronos X 88-Key Music Workstation
review_headline: The best music production tool on the market.
review_body:
I was a little bit skeptical as to whether or not I wanted to shell out the money for this product's hefty price tag, but now that I actually have the machine, I can say without a doubt that it was the best investment I ever made for music production - I do a lot of work with electronic music in my spare time, and I recently decided to step up my game with the wider palette of sounds that this machine offers, and I got so much more than that - this instrument uses NINE different synthesis engines - whereas a keyboard such as the Motif would only use sample playback, this keyboard actually comes with unique on-board synthesizers that generate sounds catering to specific instruments - there's one specifically for piano, string modeling, drawbar organs, a bunch of different classic synths, electric piano, and of course, sample playback. You could spend months studying the collective complexity created by having all of these tools available in a single instrument, and I highly recommend you take a look into Korg's page for this product for a better description of each of the individual sound engines.

Some of the other highlights of the product include 3 GB or RAM, a 64 GB solid state hard drive, extensive MIDI control options (it has a control surface with 9 sliders, 16 buttons, and 8 knobs, a regular joystick, a vector joystick, and a touch-sensitive ribbon controller.. wow!), POLYPHONIC aftertouch (which means each individual key responds to aftertouch all on its own - it's not all meshed together into one signal for the whole keyboard like it is for assignable aftertouch), well over a thousand different programs (I can't remember the exact number, but the diversity of sounds contained within is just a marvel modern music instruments), and a huge touch screen display - it's like having an iPad built-in to control any parameter you want. Oh, and there's also sampling, two balanced inputs, and drivers and software that allow you to use your Kronos with your DAW!

There are, of course, a few areas where the product falls a little bit short - while the keys really do feel great, I've noticed that a few keys are a little bit loose - not in position, but how the weights were attached to the inside of the keys - there are a few keys where the weight jiggles around a little bit more than the others. Most people probably wouldn't notice it, but if you pay attention, you can definitely feel it when going up and down the keyboard. I don't really consider it to be that much of a problem, as you hardly notice it in the midst of playing a piece.

The built-in sequencer is very difficult to use when coming from any computer based DAW environment, as there's simply not a lot of space, and while it is fully functional, I found it very difficult to navigate, and I would recommend that you instead stick to using a computer based DAW.

The one thing that drove me absolutely insane was that Korg has not released an ASIO driver yet for the Kronos - ASIO is the standard that most Windows-based DAW software uses to communicate with external interfaces, which means that if you're going to be using the Kronos on a Windows machine, you have to install ASIO4all before you can actually communicate audio signals between the two - it drove me crazy trying to find a proper driver, and when I found out that there was none, I was very disappointed. MIDI signals are still fine without ASIO4all, though.

However, I think that what the machine does offer in the music production setting far outweighs any of the minor inconveniences that pop up here and there with virtually any product in any category - I believe one of the slogans they used in the initial advertising campaign went something along the lines of "imagine being able to create any sound imaginable", and I think this product is the closest that humanity has ever gotten to reaching that goal in a single instrument. You won't be disappointed. Make sure you read the manuals! There are several. :)

review_headline: Good all-purposes strings, better suited to some guitars than others
review_body:
These are good all-purpose strings. I'd be hard pressed to think of any style you couldn't play reasonably well with these strings and the right guitar.

I had been using Slinky 9s and 10s on my guitars for years. I recently got a 24.75" scale guitar for metal and classic/hard rock, as well as jazz and blues. I threw a set of 10s on there. It sounded good, but I was missing the low end tightness and clarity. The low end on the regular 10s was a bit muddy (not terrible, just a tad muddy) due to the scale. I switched to a hybrid (Heavy Bottom 10-52) set, and (after some action and truss rod adjustments) found the sound I was looking for.

I should also say that the longest I've had a set of these strings was 2 years on a single guitar. I wasn't playing seriously during the period (though I still played everyday), and was pretty much just waiting for the strings to break before I changed them. They never broke. I only switched them out because I started gigging again. These Slinky 10s are some of the most reliable strings I've ever used, more so than the 9s.

All in all, good, reliable, general-purpose strings, but if you have a particular genre in mind, you might be able to find strings better suited to it.

product_title: Golden Gate MP-12 Deluxe Tortoise Style Mandolin Pick - Rounded Triangle - Dozen
review_headline: Took me some getting used to but I like the result
review_body:
For about three decades playing mandolin I've used large triangular picks (well, rounded triangles, but I'll leave that to the geometers) of different thicknesses looking for a sound I like. As a result my right hand got used to having a larger pick in it, so playing with these smaller picks takes a bit of an adjustment for me.

I have to say, though, that the thickness and shape give me a most satisfactory tone -- there's less \\"plinkiness\\" (if you know what I mean, and mandolinists probably will) and a richer mid-range sound as opposed to a thinner treble. I'd add that the curve of the striking tip doesn't click so much against my fingerboard extension (not scalloped), so I'm more confident picking closer to fretboard and able to capture those tones better. (I suppose I was clicking before due to a flaw in my technique, but this pick seems to have solved it for me).

These strike me as rounded a bit more even than Dawg picks, so the sound is a bit different and and the cost is a bit less. So I like the results and after more practice with them I expect they'll be my regular tool.

review_body:
First of all, I bought it when it was over $400 for a double clarinet option. I previously had the buffet attache case for two clarinets and it did a far better job of holding everything I needed. This Bam X Light does NOT have enough room for all of my accessories. As another person mentioned, my clarinet stand does not fit in the bell or anywhere in the case. Only purchase this case if you are ONLY concerned with carrying your two clarinets and NOTHING MORE. If you're looking for ANY storage this is NOT the case for you. I would more so recommend (as previously mentioned) the Buffet Attache. That case has enough room for your reeds, cork grease, metronome/tuner, some reed modifier equipment, your stand (if you have a single one of course), and even some sheets of music. If you want to carry it over your shoulder there are some great secondary bags that allow for you do so, which still are cheaper together than the original cost of this case.

In addition (how could there possibly be more), I tried to return this case and although when purchased the return policy gave me 90 days, the offer was rescinded. I am now stuck with a $400 piece of equipment that I don't want and doesn't meet my needs. I even asked for a simple exchange for a lower price case because this one is so inadequate and I wasn't even offered that. I am very disappointed and am warning anyone who is searching. Regretfully these cases are hard to find and you don't have the option to try them out until you receive them. I would be more than happy to answer any additional information about this case for anyone who is looking to purchase one. It is an extreme shame when it costs just so much. review_body:
If this is your first uke, keep in mind that nylon (plastic) strings are standard even on professional instruments, and that they will need time to stretch (at least a day and up to a few weeks, depending on how much you play) before they will stay in tune.

MATERIALS
I wasn't expecting much at this price point, so I was pleasantly surprised.
+ The body seems to be made of actual wood rather than the plastic-wood laminate I was expecting. Plastic is easier to care for, but wood gives a richer sound.
= The frets and tuning gears are made of real metal.
= The binding, nut, bridge, strings and knobs are made of genuine plastic.
= The strings (high G at the top, followed by middle C, E and A) do come with a cardboard Aquila tag attached, as in the picture. The main selling point for Aquila strings is that they bring out the best in a cheap ukulele, but I'm not sure if that's necessary in this case.

WORKMANSHIP
This is where it seems the manufacturer cut corners to keep the price low. Most of the defects are only cosmetic, and the rest were easily fixed.
- Inside the body, at the top and bottom edges of the sound hole, there were some splinters. It was easy to remove the splinters without damaging the instrument, and that got rid of the buzzing I'd experienced the first few times I played.
- The fret wire ends are not completely smooth or flush with the wood. The burrs aren't big enough to scratch me or interfere with playing, but when I run my hand up and down the neck I can definitely feel them. I could fix this in a few minutes with a bit of sandpaper, but it doesn't bother me that much.
- The tuning gears look and feel very cheap. There's nothing wrong with them; they work, and will hopefully continue to work, but I won't be surprised if I need to replace them eventually.
- I can see some irregularities in the glue where the neck joins the body.
= The finish is very thin; you can easily see and feel the grain and flaws in the wood. I think this gives the instrument individual character and makes it look more "real;" someone else might compare it to scratches and dents in a car. It doesn't affect the sound either way.
+ Frets are correctly spaced. (This is very important, especially in a beginner instrument.)
+ Fretboard is straight and flat, as it should be.
+ Nut and bridge are at the correct height.
+ Strings were properly installed.

PLAYABILITY
I am very happy with the way this instrument sounds. It has a good, clear tone, and has not buzzed at all since I removed the splinters. The fretboard and string spacing are just right for small hands. Compared to a steel-stringed guitar, it is very easy to correctly fret the notes and learn new chords on an ukulele.

product_title: Sennheiser HD 380 PRO Headphones
review_body: I use the Sennheiser HD 380 Pro for audio production in for my classical record company. As a result, I need headphones that are flat, meaning they do not add to or subtract from the music. These headphones are very flat so if you are expecting that they will ramp up the music. you should look elsewhere. At the same time, I need phones that produce very detailed sound for editing. This is especially important for editing live performance recordings. They are so clear that an excessively noisy damper pedal in a a piano recoding can easily be heard, which I can then correct. Assuming your hearing is capable will be able to hear the vibrating of the lower octave strings in a piano recording. They do require a burn-in period. My only complaint is that they are a little tight but that is part of their passive noise canceling ability. I wear glasses and when I am engrossed in editing I don't notice the tight fit. This might be problematic for anyone using them for casual listening. In short, I highly recommend them if you keep in mind the caveat about their sound reproduction being flat.

product_title: Lexicon MX300 Stereo Reverb/Effects Processor
review_headline: Beautiful sound but Buyer Beware of a BIG Lexicon oversight
review_body:
I own this machine and the sound is great, but Lexicon have really mucked up here. When using Cascade mode (serial mode), i.e. putting an electric piano into the l&r inputs of the MX300 and the MX300 out to a l&r input on my mixer, the Effects 1 engine feeds the Effects 2 engine. That is fine, except there is no way to adjust the volume (balance) level of Effects 1 and 2. In other words, you can have a delay in Effects 1 and a Reverb in Effects 2 but if you do not like the volume balance between the two effects you cannot adjust it. This is a massive problem. Of course, you can adjust the wet and dry mixes of both effects from 1-99, but all that does is make the effects or reverb wetter or dryer, it does NOT adjust the volume or balance between the two effects. I wrote to Lexicon about adjusting the balance between effects and their reply is as follows:

\\"The only way to do what you are trying to do is by setting the mix routing to dual mono. Then adjust the send or return level from two separate mono aux sends or returns. The only level control is the one knob on the front of the MX 300.\\"

Now, if like me you only have two Aux Sends on your mixer and you already use one for pre-fader and one for post-fader then you cannot use the MX300 in the way Lexicon recommend here. It really does make the Cascade mode pointless when used in Serial mode. Even if I could use Dual Mono as they recommend, that is pointless as each preset I load between songs would then need me to adjust the Aux levels to get the right Effects balance I require on that preset before performing the song. I do NOT want to keep adjusting the Input Level control on the MX300 as this is gain structured to peak at the same time as my Post-fade Aux send and is set perfectly at around 10 o'clock (not 12 as they recommend in the manual). Gain structuring is SO important from mixer to speakers.

I also own a TC Electronic M350 and that has two Effects engines. However, you can use the balance knob to adjust between the effect levels and store them as presets. Perfect, but I want to use the lush Lexicon reverbs instead sometimes.

Lexicon has really missed the point badly when using Cascade mode. When using Stereo mode, where there is only one effect being used, it is a perfect machine apart from once again not being able to adjust the volume level - unlike the TC Electronic machine.

product_title: Dayton Audio iMM-6 Calibrated Measurement Microphone for iPhone, iPad Tablet and Android
review_headline: Perfect for a low-cost Laptop Real Time Analysis system
review_body:
This is a great value and very useful microphone. You can download a device-specific calibration file from Dayton based on your serial number. I bought this to use with a real time analysis program on my laptop that has a TRRS connector instead of separate headphone and microphone jacks, which is more common these days. With the headphone out jack you can send test tones through the auxiliary input of your system. I used it in my car for audio system calibration. I used True RTA software but you can also get REW.

I also purchased a mic/headphone Y splitter cable (StarTech MUYHSMFF 3.5mm 4-Pin to 2x 3-Pin 3.5mm Headset Splitter) to loopback for system calibration, and a long 3.5 mm auxiliary cable for plugging in to my system (StarTech MU6MMS Slim 3.5mm Stereo Audio Cable - M/M, 6 Feet STARTECH.COM ) and an extension for flexible microphone placement (StarTech MUHSMF2M 2m 4 Position TRRS Headset Extension Cable ) All for less than 40 bucks and you have a high quality RTA system. Worked great in my car and picked up the factory crossover points in my speakers. Microphone works in my Windows Phone as well, but there aren't many useful RTA programs like Audio Tools for WP. Too bad, it would be a great tool. Loading the calibration file into the iPhone is a joke.

Edit: FYI There are now Windows phone RTA apps available but I haven't yet tested with the microphone.

product_title: Line 6 M5 StompBox Modeler
review_body:
I have to admit up front that I plug my guitar into a digital recorder using the recorder's built in effects for most of my production work. Not so great sounding, but I spend most of my earnings on rent in crowded San Francisco, thus I have to be budget and neighbor friendly, so no Amp, big rack unit and live sound recording for me!

So one night, I was out drinking with my girlfriend at our neighborhood bar when someone mentioned this line of Line 6 pedal board emulators. This mention was from someone who makes big money playing heavy metal, plus he and his wife bought my girlfriend and I drinks, so I paid attention. Being a drunk fool, and poor, I ordered this low end unit without doing any research once I got home that night, hoping for something to improve my weak sound when I record.

When it finally showed up (not from Amazon) I just plugged it into front of the my digital recorder's input, jacked my Godin guitar in, dialed up the Tube Comp and started wailing away while recording. My experience that drunken night tells me that I made a good purchase, if only for the compression effect alone. I have a few cheep and not so cheep compressors, but this digital model was tight. It was worth the $129 just for the one effect alone, and a steal when you add in the tuner.

I agree with other reviewers that in a live situation this pedal might have limitations, but I will never play live given my style of music, so what do I care. For an old punk rocker who records at home, it is a good way to add variety to my sound. I admit, I have not used any of the other effects due to my love of the Tube Comp model thus far, but at some point, when I am not bar crawling and having fun, I will give some of the other presets a try. I am sure they will be equally pleasing.

product_title: TASCAM DR-60D Linear PCM Recorder for DSLR Filmmaking and Field Recording (Discontinued By Manufacturer)
review_headline: Complements, but does not replace DR-40
review_body:
I previously owned a DR-40 before receiving this unit, and this gave me a chance to compare the two. So far, I have seen that both are designed for and serve different needs, and might complement each other.

There are three important differences between the two:
- DR-40 packs a pair of internal microphones, which are very useful for on-the-go recordings, like stand up interviews. However DR-60 completely depends on external ones, or the ones in your camera. Frankly the mics in my cameras are not so good.

- While they have similar technical specs, and same recording formats, DR-60 comes with an upgraded sound processing circuitry, and much better physical controls

- The lack of mic is more than compensated in DR-60 with the additional I/O ports. It not only has the regular dual XLR/TRS inputs, there is a mini-jack for 3/4 channels (which might be hooked up to the camera or a PC), and a camera pass through. Additionally the there is now both a line and amplified (headphones) monitor output.

Overall DR-60 is a welcome improvement for more professional line of work. It will hook up nicely with existing sound systems, regular and condensing microphones, and produce great audio quality. However if you need a more portable recorder without carrying a secondary mic DR-40 is still a great choice.

product_title: Behringer UMC204 Audio Interface
review_body:
Installation was easy even without instructions. Does not come with the driver. You need to go to the Behringer website to get it.

Works well for recording. Well, it did for my 2 short tests trying to get the volume up.
Playback will consistently get out of sync and skip. It's internal clock (sampling rate) will change on it's own. Not sure if it matters. It does matter when it finally goes to an invalid value and stops working. I'm getting the clock value from a tool that installs with the driver. You can reset it with a power-cycle by unplugging the USB cable and plugging it back in. I went on a 4 hour quest to get this thing to work by trying all the output bit-depths and sample rates that Windows offered. Even tried other ASIO drivers like ASIO4All which didn't recognize it.
I gave them the benefit of the doubt on the first one. I had the same result from the other 2 we ordered.

Thankfully, I found a PCI-E to PCI converter so can continue using our Gina 3Gs.

We also ordered a Seydel Blues Session C harmonica. Guess what? Exactly the same problem! That further confirms our manufacuring line defect hypothesis.

The sound of the other holes is excellent. But, two bad holes out of ten is pretty terrible. Three Seydel harmonica failures in a row is too much for us, we'll be headed back to Hohner Harmonicas.

product_title: TASCAM DR-60D Linear PCM Recorder for DSLR Filmmaking and Field Recording (Discontinued By Manufacturer)
review_headline: Professional sound at pro-sumer price addresses gap in camera capabilities....
review_body:
If you're tired of really crappy sound in your videos, or want to do something professional (Wedding videos for example) then you need to upgrade your sound from the stock microphone, particularly if you're using a DSLR for video capture.

I've assisted in event shoots (weddings, etc.) with pro-level DV camcorders and do a fair amount of video recording and editing on my own. I started off with a Sony Mini-DV camcorder with 3-CCD and although it came with external mic inputs, I never needed them since the built-in mic was good enough. Unfortunately, as camcorders get smaller the microphones have been getting much worse for wind noise and isolation (At least you don't have motor noise to deal with anymore) Most of the video I shoot now is with a Nikon D5100 and a GoPro Hero3+ Black. Sound quality is marginal on the first and really, really poor on the second, even with the skeleton back in place. The other problem with using the internal mic is that it's typically omnidirectional - you catch coughs from the camera person much better than the bride and groom 20 feet away. Again, no wind noise protection, poor range and sensitivity.

After testing this out for a couple of short weeks, I have to say it's a fantastic piece of kit, but probably a good step or two above what most people need - there are several other ways to upgrade your sound before resorting to a separate 4-track sound capture:

1) On-camera mic. If your DLSR has a separate mic input, you can get a camera mounted mic like the RODE Videomic or the Audio-Technica PRO24. Much better, directional sound and tracked straight to your video

2) Off-camera mic - same benefits as on-camera mic, but you have the ability to boom-pole to get much closer to the source and isolate unwanted sounds. Azden ECZ990 or Sennheiser MKE400

3) Separate audio capture with the DR-60D or similar device. This gives the best sound capabilities both in capture settings as well as post mixing, but it's also the most expensive and heaviest option, On- or off-camera mic with separate audio capture - allows you to tune your sound input, separate sound track allows mixing in post. You do need to sync your video in post as well, so plan ahead.

*LIKES*
- \\"Safety Track\\" allows you to record a second track at lower gain - think of the difference between spoken wedding vows and the organ..or non-amped speakers vs applause.
- Beefy mounting bracket - very confident and secure.
- Control buttons - very tactile yet also silent
- Mini-stereo input - some people have dinged this for having only 2 XLR inputs, but mini-stereo (IMO) makes a lot of sense since this is the default for on-camera mics from which many people will be transitioning.
- Protection on the front for control panel
- Very readable display, even in sunlight

*DISLIKES*
- Back of case and right side could be stronger. Stuff gets banged around on shoot and you don't want things getting broken.
- Eats batteries. Would love if a lithium pack was available

Some thoughts
- This will really increase the weight of your rig if you shoot solo
- Budget at least $200-$300 for a decent pair of condenser microphones
- You'll probably want a cardioid or super-cardioid (directional) as opposed to a unidirectional mic.

product_title: Fender 500K, Split Shaft Potentiometer for Volume or Tone
review_body:
I ordered this to replace a dying volume pot in my Squier Strat thinking it would fit. I was wrong, it doesn't fit. The body of the pot is much larger than the Squier stock pots, and while the shaft fit through the hole in the pickguard, I doubt I could get the pick guard back in place. The contacts for the wires also come from the shaft side of the body and angle towards the bottom of the body, as opposed to the configuration of the stock Squier.
Finally, the shaft on this pot is longer than the stock Squiers. It fit the volume cap, but left about an eighth of an inch of play between the knob and the pickguard.

Four stars because I'm sure it's a quality product, and it's my fault that I ordered the wrong part. I'll post clearly labeled pictures comparing this pot to the Squier pot after I replace it.

After recording something, if it doesn't work the next time you try (maybe because you pulled the USB connection to listen to the recorded track on your PC), just close Audacity and reopen it; the program seems good at recognizing audio settings when it starts up.

My biggest con, however, is that one of the channels stopped working after maybe 40 hours of use. Yes, I have reversed the input connections and determined the problem is the output from the interface. Since it was about 15 days beyond the warranty, I took it apart and looked for loose connections or an obviously burned component on that part of the board. No dice.

product_title: Alesis DM7X Session Kit Five-Piece Ultra-Compact Electronic Drum Set
review_body:
I've always wanted to learn to play the drums, but grew frustrated with my early efforts--toy drums and rockband-type video games just aren't the real thing. But while I don't have the space in my home for an entire analog drum kit, I decided on this Alesis electronic drum set and have been very happy with it.

The kit was easy to put together, and contains a rack to hold all the equipment, 3 toms, 1 snare, 1 kick drum, 3 cymbals, a foot control for the high-hat, wire ties to keep your cabling neat, 1 pair of practice drum sticks, and the electronic control center. I was surprised at the high quality of the components. The only thing you need to add is a stool to sit on and either speakers or headphones so you can hear what you are playing.

You use the electronic control center to select from the many included drum kit sounds, or you can model your own drum kit and save your settings. You can play along with included rhythms and record your own playing. I also found the metronome very useful while learning.

In the first episode of the new show The Tim Ferriss Experiment, Tim tried to conquer learning to play rock and roll drums, and at the end of the episode he actually got to play with the rock group Foreigner on stage for a song. I might not ever get to play on stage with Foreigner, but I know I'm going to have fun playing drums on this electronic drum set.

review_headline: Even I sound half way decent now!
review_body:
I just retired and I find myself with a lot of free time. I was spending way to much time playing video games on the PS3 and felt I needed a change. I have played the guitar for most of my life, but not very often the last few years, so I decided to get more serious about playing and songwriting again. I invested in a new Ovation acoustic/electric 2778AX guitar and needed some accessories to go with it

My set up now consists of the guitar with the Fender Mustang IV guitar amp, Powerwerks PW100T PA amp and the TC Helicon Voicelive 2 and MP-75 mic. The Mustang amp is fantastic but a bit too much for living room playing so I send the output of my voice and guitar from the Voicelive 2 to the Powerwerks PW100T. This turned out to be a great setup for my living room (or music room) playing and is also perfect for a solo guitar/singer playing small to medium sized venues.

I have spent about 3 days now getting familiar with the Voicelive 2 presets and how to modify them to my liking, and I am very impressed with the amount of control I have. If you feel you have screwed something up though, it's very easy to reset the unit back to its factory presets. I still have a lot of experimenting to do but so far I am very happy with the results I am getting.

Another feature that the Voicelive 2 is supposed to be capable of, (that I want to try out) is the ease of connecting it to my laptop computer via the supplied USB cable. With the appropriate software, I should be able to record any songs or new music I write.

All in all, I am very pleased with this product and feel it will be a tremendous aid to my creative processes.

product_title: Kala KA Bundles
review_body:
I’m no expert on Ukuleles -- ask me about guitars, I’ve owned a dozen or more. But this is my first uke, bought somewhat on a whim, and I wasn’t sure what to expect for my modest cash outlay.

Now that I’ve spent a little time playing it -- and comparing it to other ukes in local music stores -- here are a few observations:

1) I’ve picked up baritone ukes that sound richer, and have a nicer feel. But they cost at least 50 percent more, on up.
2) As shipped, it needed to be set up and the action lowered. That’s to be expected. And after that was taken care of locally, the instrument was much more playable. Not as good as some, but decent.
3) It stays in tune reasonably well.
4) The fact that a hard case, tuner and other accessories were included in the deal was part of the reason I went for it, since otherwise I’d have had to buy those separately. I was concerned, though about how the uke fit in the case supplied. It seemed to slide and knock around a bit. I ended up adding a small piece of one-inch foam between the bottom of the uke and the case. Now it fits fine.
5) My verdict that it was decent quality for the price seemed to be shared by the guys at the music store that set it up, who I presume would have rather sold me one of theirs.

I bought a baritone uke partly because I travel from time to time, and it seemed an alternative to lugging one of my full-sized guitars. I considered a “travel guitar” instead, but the ones I like are twice the price of this uke. Now that I’m playing the thing and listening to other uke players, I’ve come to appreciate it on its own terms.

If I had it to do over? I might have opted to spend more money on an instrument I could really fall in love with, sound-wise and aesthetically. Still, I’m not disappointed -- just not delighted.

product_title: Yamaha FC4 Piano Style Sustain Pedal
review_headline: Will start to creak in half a year
review_body:
First and foremost, ditto all the other compliments in other reviews in terms of feel and function. It feels great to press, and works properly. There was a bit of a surprise with reversed polarity when I first hooked it up, but I quickly figured it out.

However, I encountered an issue nobody on here has mention: after about 5 months, the pedal began to creak pretty noticeably whenever I pressed it. This is a really annoying sound when you're trying to play. I took it apart to see what was going on, and internally there's a simple arm mechanism holding up the pedal, and when you press down this arm slides along the pedal a little bit as it bends down, then it springs the pedal back up when you release (think of how a cuticle cutter works, it's exactly the same mechanism). The problem is that there's only a bit of grease between these two metal parts, and when that grease wears out (or is rubbed aside), it starts to creak.

I tried adding a felt furniture pad to the arm mechanism, but it slid out of place within a few weeks. I was going to replace it again more securely (perhaps super glue), but at this point the screw heads which held everything together were totally stripped, making it impossible to disassemble again (apparently the screws are made of a very soft metal and are VERY easy to strip).

So, I'm now dealing with a very creaky sustain pedal, probably looking into getting another one :-(

product_title: Behringer Xenyx 802 Premium 8-Input 2-Bus Mixer with Xenyx Mic Preamps and British EQs
review_headline: When you pay peanuts, you get monkeys.
review_body: I was about to give this product 2 stars, but I decided that wasn't entirely fair considering how cheap this product is, so the point is: you get what you pay for.    Now, don't worry, just heads up, this isn't going to be some horror story about how everything went wrong. Just being honest here.    I've owned this handy little mixer for about 2 years now, and honestly, it was great when it arrived. Heh. It sits on my desk, taking in the outputs from my computer soundcard and my audio interface, and routing them to my monitor switcher, and to my headphones. It really completes the setup, and makes life easier.    Before getting it, I did my research on Behringer products, and of course saw all the fuss. \\"Why?\\" I asked myself. I couldn't exactly wrap my head around it, and then I saw all the positive reviews on their products from people who just bought them, and trusted the actual product reviews more than the people who never really had the products for themselves (probably) and were just feeding the negative hype. So, since it was so cheap, I decided I may as well buy it.    Like I said, when I got it, it sounded great, really low noise, no hum or anything, worked fine. Didn't understand the hate at all at that point! Knocked it off as hype.    Then, a year and a half later, the noise. It was very gradual, but it got worse. So barely, over time, it grew, along with this humming, RF interference...    And I know what you're thinking: \\"this guy uses s*** cables\\", or \\"this guy doesn't know his way around balanced/unbalanced and line levels\\". Well, you're wrong. Because that's the first thing I thought was the problem, and boy did I do thorough research. While I'm happy now to know so much about audio connections (very important for what I aspire to do), it only made me one thing: it's the mixer.    So, bottom line is that it'll work just fine probably the first year, maybe longer if you don't use it daily like I did, hah. Just don't expect it to age well. I think that's the catch here. But still, it's cheap, y'know?

product_title: GruvGlide GRUVGLIDE DJ Package
review_body:
I have a ritual when I buy used records. 1. If they're really, really dirty I'll wash them carefully with distiller water mixed with a little windex; to get off the grease, hair, and fingerprints. 2. GruveGlide. 3. Slide the clean record into a new Mobile Fidelity Rice paper sleeve. 4. Put the whole album into a 3 mil plastic cover. If the record isn't too dirty, I'll skip the wash.

Does GruvGlide really work? Maybe. It does appear to do a nice job for minor cleaning and eliminating any static. It does appear to restore some sheen to the vinyl making it appear new. Or at least, newer. However if you spray too much it will actually dull the sheen of the record, so use sparingly.

Does it actually make records sound better? Does it actually protect the record? Not sure. It may be more of a psychological effect based on having a clean shiny record. Still, I use it anyway. I'm on my third can!

One warning. The can/cap/nozzle are cheaply made. So be careful prying off the cap. I forcefully pried off the cap once and the whole can jumped out of my hands and dented the nozzle. It leaked and dribbled the contents. Just open the cap with care.

review_headline: For the money, you can't go wrong!
review_body:
This guitar is every bit the equal of some of the more well-known guitars (Gretsch, Guild, and Washburn) and a great deal especially when discounted by Amazon.

I feel no need to replace the pickups or tuning machines. Both are perfectly adequate for the task at hand.

Is this guitar the equal of a Gibson or Japanese-made Gretsch? Of course not! But for what it is, it's excellent. Mine arrived with straight neck, only requiring a final locating of the bridge in order to achieve good intonation.

A nice thing about the Bigsby is that you can turn the tremolo bar around so it faces the back of the guitar and is out of the way. There is a stop on the casting that prevents it from making a full 360 degree turn, and by adjusting the tension on the bar, you'll have no problem getting it to stay where you want it.

I did replace the (not so great) factory strings with light flatwounds. I think that the next time I re-string it, I will go up to medium weight ones. The guitar can handle it, and I think it will both sound and feel even better.

Well worth a look for those that want a jazz/rockabilly guitar on the cheap.

product_title: Samson VR88 Velocity Ribbon Microphone
review_body:
The Samson Ribbon Microphone is great, very sensitive, perhaps to much so outside of a studio. The microphone picks up the ceiling fan, the fan in the computer, everything, but it also picks up nuances in the voice. Ribbon microphones work by having two super thin magnetic strips with a strip of aluminum between that vibrates with air circulation. Ribbon microphones can be fragile and are best with mid range acoustic instruments and voices, although I did read that if set at a 45 degree angle one can get decent sound even with wind instruments.

The Samson is a great microphone. My son worked at his college radio station and he tried it there, in the more sound proofed studio the microphone worked like a champ. We are using a Shure X2U XLR-to-USB Signal Adapter which works great with the three pronged cord that is used with the microphone. The shure allows us to record and turn our computer into a recording device for the Samson.

The manual is an excellent guide on how to handle ribbon mics, carefully and gently being the key ideas. For anyone wanting to set up a studio but affordably, this microphone would be an excellent addition.

The possibility of the TC Flashback and Jamman consuming more than 9v (i.e. 2x9=18v + 9 = ~27v) has been considered but the voltage and current draw of the three units doesn't seem to be inordinate based upon manufacturers specifications for time of operation based upon pedals in use. Not to mention idle pedals vary in their voltage and current needs.

The stayed 36 hrs. of operation for a full charge was not realized. And even if I could have made it through 1/2 of the or 16 hrs. I would have consider that acceptable. Frankly the inability to make it through one show (4-5 hrs.) is not acceptable.

product_title: TASCAM DR-60D Linear PCM Recorder for DSLR Filmmaking and Field Recording (Discontinued By Manufacturer)
review_headline: Useful form factor, RELATIVELY good audio
review_body:
I am using a Shure KSM 42 mic for vocal recordings. Into a sub $500 2 channel tube/transistor hybrid mic preamp, the sound is pristine. With that setup, the sound is full bodied, detailed and warm. Using the same mic into the Tascam 60d is a different world. Many reviews of the Tascam 60d talk about the clean, low noise preamps (which it has). Don't come away with the assumption that this recorder will give even low level studio quality - it does not. The sound is narrow and a bit harsh. It IS a clean, low distortion signal. It is NOT a warm, full, detailed sound.

The format of the recorder works very well under a camera and has strong gain, enabling you to clearly hear your subject.The controls are easy to navigate and the unit seems reasonably sturdy.

\\"it is what it is\\"

Update - Many reviews have praised the excellent signal to noise ratio of the Tascam dr60, which it has. However, as noted above, the sound quality, even with a good mic seems narrow and shrill (various gain levels). I tested dr60 against the H6 by Zoom using a Shure KSM 42 and Rode NTG2. The Zoom H6 did not have as low a signal to noise ratio as the Tascam. However, the sound quality was noticeably fatter, capturing the nuances and subtle coloring of sound significantly better. The Zoom Mic capsules were surprisingly goo and along with 4/6 xlr ports the increased versatility is nice. Finally the ability to use the recorder while attached to a DSLR is overblown. You want the mic and recorder (short cables), as close as possible to the sound source; who cares if it is mounted to your camera in most instances. The Tascam dr60 is a well thought out, nice piece of gear. Too bad they didn't use better preamps and analog/digital converters.

review_headline: AKG K712 Pro review (comparison to Q701)
review_body:
Blur did a great job on the first review, so I'll just add a few comments. Mine are still <<burning in>> but after 24 hours of burn in and a couple of days of listening, here are my observations. The first thing you really notice over the Q701 is a major improvement in comfort. The bumps are gone, thank goodness. I never could quite accommodate those, even after trying an embarrassing amount of different kinds of padding for my nearly bald pate! Second thing that has really changed are the ear pads. The memory foam makes them much more comfortable and takes away some of the clamping feeling I used to feel with the Q701 pads. The comfort improvement is substantial, and a serious step in the right direction. The bass is full, accurate, and tight. It's not exaggerated in any way, but it is there, and is very full. It's not rattling the ear drum, thudding bass. It's accurate and fast, and tuned tympani in particular really shine on these. The stereo image is quite different than the Q701. It's less extreme, and the kind of unnatural "hole in the center" of Q701's is now miraculously gone. The highs and midrange are similar to the Q701's, but I find I'm never reaching to turn the volume down when the soprano aria comes up like I used to do with the Quincy Jones. Maybe because of the new bass response I'm not listening quite as loudly. But they're smooth, and extremely well-focused. On paper, they have a similar frequency balance to the Q701's, but in practice, they seem much, much smoother in the midrange and highs. They're not as revealing as my Stax Lambda's but they're plenty revealing on their own, and have a more natural balance than the Stax do. The better comparison might be to the Sennheiser HD800's but I haven't had a chance to do direct comparisons with the same material yet. The K712's might actually find themselves getting used more often for critical listening and mixing than my venerable K340's... In short, I was on the fence for awhile vs the Q701's, but I'm glad I went with the K712's. The Q701's are really a bargain at the price, and can get equalized or modded to offset their shortcomings to a great degree, but they're quite outclassed by the K712's. I'm mostly a classical listener, and the less outrageous soundstage and smoother bass make them pretty much an ideal headphone for that kind of listening. I did play Mike Oldfield's "Tubular Beats" on them also, and found them to really shine on the low end. Terrific sound, great balance, and extremely transparent. They can simultaneously render deep bass and fast cymbal attacks with no problem. No lower midrange/upper bass blurring whatsoever. These are really great headphones for listening to music, and the comfort improvement is considerable.
They aren't really difficult to drive, they sounded great coming out of the headphone jack of a Denon receiver, but I found them more confident in the bass using a dedicated DAC headphone amplifier (I used a FiiO E17/E9 base). They also sounded spectacular at 24/96 or 24/88 using an Apogee Duet DAC. product_title: DharmaObjects Tibetan Meditation Om Mani Padme Hum Peace Singing Bowl With Mallet
review_body:
Overview:
This is my first bowl, so I wanted something to try out that wasn't too expensive. Mine came looking like the picture, with the mallet AND the cushion. The paint job is not perfect, but I didn't expect it to be, and I like the way it looks. I think that with continued playing, the paint will wear off on the mallet some (a little bit of paint is already on my mallet), but I am looking forward to seeing it worn and used. The cushion is sewn well with some nice embroidery, and the mallet is a nice size for my hand. The bowl did have a very odd smell that gave me a headache when I first unwrapped it, but after I wiped it down with white vinegar it was better. I have read that many bowls contain lead, so be sure to wash your hands after playing just to be safe (and before you play, why not).

Sound:
The sound is nice and very clear. I didn't know at all what pitch to expect since the reviews have different answers. Mine ended up being a high D (D5 in scientific pitch notation, if you want to look it up). I suspect there may be quite a bit of variation with these bowls in terms of pitch. Striking it with the mallet causes a sound that lasts about ten seconds. I followed some video guides on YouTube to get the bowl to sing, but ended up having to do a lot of trial and error on my own to get it to work. I can get quite a loud, sustained sound out of the bowl if I run the mallet over the widest part of the bowl very fast to get it started. I can slow down a little once it has started singing, but I have to keep the mallet at the widest part of the bowl instead of at the rim. It's not difficult to get it to sing, but I still have to move my arm a lot faster than in the videos I've seen, which doesn't exactly create a peaceful and relaxed feeling. Perhaps my technique will improve so that in future my playing will more closely match the videos, but I suspect that this bowl is just not of the quality of those bowls--this bowl is thicker than it appears in the picture, and looks thicker than many bowls I compared it to online, which affects the ease of vibration.

Bottom line: In the future I think I would prefer to spend more money on a much larger bowl that is lower in pitch and easier to play, but this bowl is affordable and works well enough for a beginner like me.

product_title: Shure SRH440 Professional Studio Headphones (Black)
review_body:
I bought these 3 years ago. At the time, I got them for only $72. First off, these are very good headphones, especially for the price I paid. I find it pointless to try and describe specifics of sound quality to people on the internet, so I'm going to try to focus on other aspects of the headphones in this review. I'm going to touch on a few things I didn't like about them first.

- I did not like the coil cable. I've always had a hatred for coiled cables. Just a preference, not really a flaw since I know a lot of people like them. However, since the cable is removable, it can always be replaced with a straight one. I never cared enough to do that though.

- I found these uncomfortable, and that is the main reason I no longer use them. They mostly just felt tight around my head, and I couldn't wear them for long periods of time. For comparison, I also own an Astro A40 headset for gaming and a pair of Beats by Dre Studio headphones and both are much more comfortable to me.

- This wasn't a problem for me, but i didn't like how exposed the wires are that lead into the ear cups. It seemed like it would be easy for something to rip them out or cut them accidentally. It does come with a leather bag to store them in, so if you plan on being mobile with these, I would advise using it.

Sound quality wise, these are excellent and an overall great value. If this is would be your first pair of reference headphones, you'd be hard pressed to find a better deal. I no longer use these, but I gave these to a friend of mine and he loves them too. If you've only ever used the awful ear buds that came with your phone, you will be very happy. Keep in mind, if you only have 128kbps songs on your computer, or primarily listen to music from YouTube, don't expect to be all that impressed. Bad quality music will only sound worse through these. It's a lot like watching standard definition programming on a 60" LED HDTV and expecting it to look better because your TV is so good.

Also, I did buy a cheap amplifier after about a year of owning them and it did help out a little, especially since I like a little more bass in my music than these provide. Just remember, some people like these because of the mids and highs, and some people hate these for the lack of bass. Likewise, some people love Beats for their emphasis on lows, and some people hate them for their lack of quality mids and highs. It all comes down to what you want out of your music.

Are these worth $300? No. Are they worth $150? I think so. Are they worth the $72 I paid? Absolutely.

product_title: Mooer MAC1 Akoustikar Acoustic Guitar Simulator
review_headline: Acoustikar - Waaaayy better than the Boss AC-3!!
review_body: Alright, I feel compelled to review this pedal being there are currently no other reviews.  Lets first get this out of the way:  Any acoustic simulator is just that--a simulator.  Any acoustic simulator will NEVER sound nearly as good as a real acoustic.    Although I'm mainly a MXR guy, I had a Boss AC-3.  I don't dislike Boss by any means--they make a great product.  However, the Mooer Acoustikar is simply outstanding.  Anyone that's owned the Boss AC-3 can testify to the loud, annoying hiss you get with that pedal.  I also personally could never pull a tone out of the Boss that I liked.  I instead 'settled' with a tone on the Boss until I came across the Mooer.    This pedal is actually quite quiet.  There is a VERY faint hiss as you turn up the 'top' knob.  This hiss however is almost unnoticeable especially when compared to the Boss.  I had a very easy time arriving at a tone I was happy with too.  I also feel this pedal sounds just a bit more 'natural' for an acoustic sound.  The three-way toggle at the top switches between a Standard, Jumbo, and Piezo sound.  All three settings are quite different from one another.  The 'top' knob adds a nice about of treble, while the 'body' knob adds a nice bass boost/cut.  Again, I found it quite easy to arrive at sound that I'm truly satisfied with.    One word of warning: there is a very small drop in volume when this pedal is engaged.  Nothing drastic, but enough that it's noticeable--even with the 'level' knob the whole way up.  It probably wouldn't hurt to place a clean boost pedal (if you have one) after this in the chain.  However, I would not say it's actually necessary.    I play guitars with high-gain passive humbuckers through a 5150 III amp.  I play mostly hard & classic rock and use this pedal for acoustic intros (think Diary of a Madman, Can't Kill Rock and Roll, Fade to Black, Tesla stuff...)    I'm quite happy with this pedal, and at almost $80 it's well worth it.  I'd highly HIGHLY recommend this over theBoss AC-3.

product_title: Zoom G5 Guitar Effects and Amp Simulator with Z-Pedal
review_body:
Okay, I am 50 years old and have been playing for 33 years. I have owned a lot of gear over that time and both recorded and played live in many studios and venues. I use Les Paul's, Strats, Explorers, Charvels, Jackson's, Tokais...pretty much everything. I have used Vox and Line 6 products for modelling in the past, but I started out with full stereo Marshall stacks back in the 80s.
I have always struggled with the Line 6 equipment, can't quite put my finger on it, but it just doesn't feel right. I have not really had much opportunity to try the latest HD series, but although it has an enormous amount of flexibility, I hear that getting good working tones can take some time - I need something which can quickly and easily get a working sound out.
My Vox Tonelab SE is a great bit of kit which can handle a wide array of great useful tones - and until now I have found nothing to compare (for less than £500) I use it all the time.
But, this relatively cheap unit has great sound quality and flexibility...really quite impressive.
The looper and drum rhythmns combine to make a great practice tool - it is even quite possible to make loops and jams on the fly to use live if you feel brave enough.
Amp models all sound great and there is a huge selection of pedals to choose from - so many that you really need to edit patches using the Edit& Share software - it just makes the whole process much easier, trust me.
The unit seems quite robust (often a criticism of Zoom kit) - and the Z-pedal is useable!
Negatives: manual is very spartan - it really does not do the G5 justice. It is capable of much more than the thin manual hints at.
Some patience needed when navigating the pedalboard to get the banks, loops and assignments you want - not impossible by any stretch (and more flexible than first appears) but would have been better to include more controls.
No dual amping - Line 6 are the only folks really doing this, and the results arequite impressive..but do you really need it?
Haven't quite had the time to test it as a preamp front end on my Bogner power amp and cab yet - I am expecting great things, but fingers crossed!

product_title: QuNexus Smart Sensor Keyboard Controller
review_headline: The most indestructible Swiss Army Knife of mini-controller keyboards.
review_body:
I have had every possible flavor of mini-controller, and the QuNexus is my favorite by leaps and bounds.

I am a 3rd-year college music major, and I live inside Ableton and Finale. The QuNexus takes up no space in my backpack, and I can pull it out in the library or a practice room and immediately noodle out composition ideas. Further, the transport controls for Ableton are brilliant. I can whip through my ear-training in no time at all. For keyboard players, the arrangement of keys takes a little bit of getting used to, but it isn't dramatic--and the extra functionality you can gain from additional touch controls is more than worth the geometry trade-off.

I also have a collection of vintage and modern synths, drum machines, and samplers. I was stunned to be able to use a modern mini-controller to connect to modular CV gear, with just a couple of cables. And, using the MIDI Expander, the QuNexus happily talks to my Elektron Analog Four, Yamaha FS1R, Blofeld, and Tetra. The QuNexus will even convert signals between protocols (see the manual for more on this).

Finally, this thing is completely indestructible, from what I can tell. I have dropped it, stepped on it, crushed it under 10 books in my locker, and it seems oblivious to damage.

I am going to get a QuNeo now.

With Amazon, I knew they were returnable if I was not satisfied. I finished the project last night. I haven't been able too put the guitar down. The tone that these pickups produce is amazing. They drive the clean channel of my Delta Blues amp, without a pedal, for some of the best blues tones I've ever heard me play! When I kick in the Full Drive pedal....wow....it's \\"off the chain\\"! I have A/B'd the Eric Johnson, which is my \\"go to\\" guitar. For the Blues sound I was looking for, the $85 Korean, with the Tonerider Classic Blues pickups nails it, head to head with a $2500 Strat. To be fair, I changed out all the controls with Fender OEM controls, wired exactly as the \\"Johnson\\".

One thing is for sure.....ALL MY FUTURE PROJECTS WILL CONTAIN TONERIDERS!!!!
