product_title: Azden(r) Wlx-Pro+i Wlx-Pro System
review_headline: A Reliable Wireless Lav System For a Reasonable Price
review_body:
The Azden WLX-Pro is a wireless lavalier microphone system which includes a transmitter (with a clip-on omnidirectional microphone) and a receiver. The transmitter and receiver have two channels to choose from. If you are receiving interference on one channel you can switch over to the other one. That about summarizes the features.

I've read a lot of reviews and watched a lot of videos regarding the WLX-Pro, and a lot of people are complaining about it's lack of functionality when used at long distances. Or they complain about a lack of channels, battery indicators, and other things commonly featured on high end systems. One of the key points that they (and you) need to keep in mind is that this is a $150.00 product. If you want to spend $625 and buy into a top shelf Sennheiser system, by all means. But for a fraction of that price, this unit will give you basic microphone performance. And that's pretty much all I needed. I use the Azden WLX-Pro when shooting YouTube videos. It has thus far functioned flawlessly. I'm shooting the videos in my office, standing about 8 feet away from the camera. And I've never had so much as a hiccup from this wireless unit.

There's one point I do need to bring up. The 1/8" jack is mono. During playback, all of your sound is going to come out of one speaker only. To remedy this, you need to go to Radio Shack and purchase a mono to stereo converter (which costs about $3.50). Using that will split the signal. It's still monophonic, but now the sound will come out of both the left and right speakers.

For people who feel the need to walk long distances away from the receiver and still be heard clearly - this isn't the product for you. But if all you're doing is shooting simple videos and you're going to be within 25 feet of the receiver, this is more than good enough.

One more thing. I had a question about the product and called the company. The guy in tech support I spoke to was very nice, very friendly and patiently fielded all of my questions. I really do appreciate a company who does that for their customers.

I'm giving the Azden WLX-Pro a 4 out of 5 rating. Why not 5 stars? Well, I think they should've made it with a stereo plug. Other than that, it's a great product and highly recommended.e to was very nice, very friendly and patiently fielded all of my questions. review_body:
Exceeds my expectations. It's quiet and has good mike quality and range. Unobstructed range is over 250' and it's dead quiet all the way.

NOTES:
1. Unless the 1/8\\" plug on your lav. or head mike cord is a low-profile, *right angle\\" plug, it will stick up too far next to the antenna and shorten the range significantly. I simply folded the wire down and taped it to the plug to keep it out of the way.
2. If using a mixer, back all unused gain controls down to zero to prevent troublesome hiss.
3. Read the simple directions. Where possible, open the antennas to make a 90 deg. vee, elevate the Receiver box, and keep it clear of metallic objects. When I need max range, I bungee mine down on a music stand head adapted to a 6' mike stand.

product_title: HRT Music Streamer II
review_headline: Great upgrade for PC-based music system
review_body:
I already use the HRT Music Streamer II + as the sole DAC and input device on a hifi system in another room. I was looking to improve the audio in my living room HTPC setup, so I looked to the less expensive HRT Streamer II and I'm very pleased.

Setup is stupid simple. It is a good idea, if this will be your main audio output, to go into the sound settings in windows and disable any other sound output devices.

I was just using the Motherboard audio output with a mini plug to RCA adapter into the back of my inexpensive Onkyo stereo. The sound was pretty bad with noticeable noise in the line. I plugged in the Music Streamer II and the difference is incredible. I was able to audition my old setup with the Streamer II on different inputs of the Stereo Amp while playing the same music through each input simultaneously. This allowed me to switch between the two inputs and the difference is very pleasant and immediately noticeable. The noise floor is dramatically lower. There is much better detail and space in the music, with more detail in the whole dynamic range. It can play my 96khz/24bit files downloaded from HD Tracks! This is all running through a pretty inexpensive setup of a budget Onkyo amp and some Boston Acoustic bookshelf speakers! I think this (relatively) inexpensive USB DAC cost more than my amp! But I think it is definitely a worthwhile upgrade; I would argue it is an upgrade that you should do before you buy a new amp or speakers since you want a good clean source.

I haven't auditioned this against my HRT II+ on my hifi setup in my office. If I get around to doing that I can update this review.

product_title: Applause by Ovation AN13-4 Acoustic Guitar
review_headline: Can't buy better for the price
review_body:
As an Ovation and Applause owner for over 20 years I have to say this is my favorite brand of guitar. I've owned my Applause Classical for over 2 decades. I paid $500 for it brand new and it is an excellent instrument.

In this particular model one must realize this is the least-expensive guitar Ovation makes. Even so, it should be flawless in production. If there is any flaw noticed (which is always a possibility in any mass-produced instrument) one should take it for granted it's a defect and return it immediately for replacement.

As far as the guitar goes: it is considered a 3/4 size guitar. A standard Ovation is 41\\" long head to tail; this one is 35\\". I learned some time back that 3/4, 1/2 etc doesn't really mean anything as far as proportion. For example, a half-size guitar is usually 30\\" long (not 20\\" as one would expect).

The Applause/Ovation line is known for having a slightly narrower neck in the nylon (classical) guitar than is standard. It is however wider than a standard steel-string neck... somewhat of a \\"happy medium\\". I like the width of the neck; it fits my hand perfectly.

As for the sound, that composite-resin-back body just can't be beat. The curved shape pushes the sound through the chamber and right out the sound hole, as well as reverberating throughout. The face of the guitar is made of quality woods (spruce, cedar, mahogany depending on color and sound preference and guitar model).

At this time this guitar is selling for around $160 to $170. As such, I don't think anyone can buy a better 'student' guitar. But in addition it makes an excellent performer guitar. I've recorded three CDs and done several concerts using the electric version of this very guitar.

Definite 5 star instrument. I believe the lower ratings are a result of 1) someone getting a defective guitar, which I can surely understand-- should have returned it for replacement immediately and 2) Not being aware of what a \\"3/4 size guitar\\" actually means (it just means it's significantly shorter than the standard 40 to 41\\").

PS. Fretboard measurement is as follows: the distance from the nut to the 12th fret should be identical to the distance from the 12th fret to the bridge. That's the \\"golden rule\\" of bridge saddle placement. So there won't be a lot of difference in the length of the fretboard between a full size and 3/4 size guitar. There will be a bit more difference between a full size and a \\"half size\\" (30\\") guitar.

As an additional \\"fun fact\\": a half-size guitar (30\\") is commonly coming to be known as a \\"guitalele\\" or \\"6 string ukelele\\" because of its smaller body size. product_title: ZT Amplifiers Lunchbox Amplifier with Internal Speaker
review_body:
I'm one of those 'no tubes, don't want it', not interested guys. That is, until I decided to embrace a small but loud, ZT Lunchbox Amp.
I ordered it mainly because I found a like new, return that was discounted because the box had been opened. I guess some of my no tube, no play thru it brothers got it and sent it back. Hmmmm.... their mistake... my gain.

Well, much to my surprise, I received the amp in a most timely fashion.... just in time for the local monthly Blues jam.
My usual rig is a '72 Deluxe Reverb and a CS '51 Nocaster with Don Mare pickups.
I opened the ZT Lunchbox, that arrived about thirty minutes before time to leave and loaded it the car headed for the jam. First time I heard it was when I set it up on stage.
Played it all night and am still shaking my head at the uber responsive circuit from a Solid State amp no bigger than my gig tool box. Tiny but BIG voiced, it was not covered up by my bandmate's 50 TUBE watts 4-10- Peavey classic 50.
I was amazed at the tone and volume of ZT's answer to portability,with monster tone. The Nocaster RI really smoked thru it. Is it a fix all for portability and tone? My first impression was formed at this OUTSIDE stage gig. The ZT Lunchbox held it's own, with aplomb.
My buddies were kinda wondering if I'd lost my mind showing up for an open air gig with such a tiny, little, 'cute' amp. They were all as surprised, as was I. Slack jawed, comes to mind, here. Yep, I'll drag this around for small, even open air gigs. Needs a bit more bottom, but a single 10'', Solid pine finger jointed, ported at the bottom cab, with my Altec Lansing 150 watt speaker should fix that. Funny... me playing a SS amp and loving it. I'd have never believed it if not for my own ears.

Kudos to ZT Amplifiers for a major step in the right direction for very usable Tone from a 'no tube' circuit.
There's a ZZ Top VH1 video series on youtube. The have the Lunchbox and extended cab in the vid. I'm thinking ,on review of the vid, it is the Club 30 12\\" speakered ZT amp in the ZZTOP vid. I'll have one of those soon, too. Sounds great. I'm sure Billy has some secret pile of mojo in his pocket, but the Amps sound great. More bottom end would be nice, but 'as is' will certainly fill the bill. Did I mention I played just the bridge pickup all night. Killer tone and one trip to the car for load in/out. Mini humbuckers on my Wilshire sounded great, too. They are custom wound with AlNico 3 magnets. Gotta love the ZT Amplifiers' Lunchbox.

product_title: Stagg GAMP200-BK Junior Electric Guitar with Built-In Amp
review_body:
Amazon had this on sale, and I like little guitars for travel, practice, and for my kid to use, so I took the bait.

First, the good news:

It works!

The nut width is about 1.65\\", which is great for an adult as well as a kid.
The scale length is a bit over 21\\", which means very slinky tension. Easy fretting for a kid, easy bends for everyone.
It's solidly built, and I love the neck. It appears to be maple. No idea what the fretboard is made from, but it seems nice. Definitely not a plastic toy.

Now, the bad news:

Made in China (or someplace with a similar alphabet). Eh, it is what it is.
Fairly cheap Chinese tuners, but they seem to work well and the buttons are actually nice. I don't love the cheap sheet metal plates, though.
Sharp fret ends. Not the end of the world if you have a fret file.
The speaker works, but it's not hi-fi by any means. It sounds like an old AM radio, but what were you expecting, right?

But the worst thing about this guitar is the intonation and the complete lack of intonation adjustment. I may try to experiment with adding material to the bridge to change the intonation, but in the meantime, there's just about no way to play this guitar without it sounding out of tune. This will annoy some people more than others. I can probably live with it for practice and travel.

Bottom-line: it won't replace a REAL guitar, but it's not bad for the intended purpose -- learning, travel, practice, goofing off. Much better than a plastic toy.

9/13/2013 update: I replaced the bridge with a hardtail (65mm wide), and now I can control intonation. This $7 replacement bridge helped a ton! It plays in tune now! Heavier gauge strings (I plan to try 11's) might also help by reducing the amount of unintentional bending when fretting.

product_title: Yamaha FC4 Piano Style Sustain Pedal
review_headline: Not compatible with my Yamaha keyboard
review_body:
I have a Yamaha keyboard, so I bought a Yamaha pedal and guess what? They aren't compatible. The sustain function is on only when you DON'T press the pedal, and it goes off when you press the pedal. I would expect Yamaha branded components to work together better than this. I suppose this is easy to fix by cutting the cable and reversing the wires, but why should I have to do that?

UPDATE: Okay, after reading \\"Jim\\"s review (highest-ranked review when sorted by Most Helpful), I discovered the trick of not plugging it in until after it's turned on. Sounds stupid, but the obvious thing to do with this when you get it, it seems, it to turn on your keyboard and THEN plug it in.

UPDATE 2: The trick, it seems, is that if you hold down the pedal while powering on the piano, the pedal senses this and reverses its polarity! All you have to do is keep your fat foot off the pedal while powering on, and it works fine. ☺

Okay, so I'm still going to knock off a star b/c the pedal came without an instruction manual. But now that it works, I'm happy with it.

product_title: M-Audio ProFire 610 Firewire Audio Interface
review_body:
I spent a couple weeks going back and forth the support personnel at the m-audio forums, and they could not suggest anything that would get this product to work with my computer. In fact, they claimed the Profire 610 works well for many people with my operating system (windows7 x64). I tried every release of drivers, every trick I could find on every forum I could read, and everything the support guy suggested. I even tried (as a last resort) purchasing an expensive firewire card from their "approved list" but that did not work either.

My computer would recognize when the card was turned on or off in the sound control panel, and I could play audio out of the digital output absolutely fine. However, M-Audio's control panel would refuse to see the card and would not open, so I could not adjust any of the analog settings or use any of the analog inputs or outputs. So the hardware worked and was clearly communicating with my computer, except the company's software was completely useless. What a waste of time and money.

I thought all the other negative reviews were a bunch of people that didn't know how to troubleshoot anything and were written by a bunch of mom'n'pop users. I guess that's not the case, because I'm pretty proficient at this stuff and I'm still unable to get it to work. So don't be stubborn like me and think "oh I'm smarter than everyone else and I can make it work" ... because you won't.

product_title: Fender Hot Noiseless Strat Middle/Neck Pickup
review_body: I plugged the yjm fury pickups, neck and bridge into my american standard strat. These come with the fat 50s. Awesome pickups, that it took me months to make up my mind to change the middle one: the hum. I figured people will not remember the exact tone of the pickup, but the hum will always be there, so I decided to find a substitute. This (the hot noiseless) seems to be a bit less bass heavy or dramatic between the highs and bass than the 50s, which I solved with the pick up height. If you heighten the treble side, you will get a sound pretty close to the fat 50s, but without the hum. Look for the bass omf sound, and the icepicky clear treble when setting the heights. Do not try to remove the covers, chances are many covers will not fit the pickups, plus you can damage the structure. They say there is an adhesive that makes the cover stick more to the pickup, in order to prevent people from damaging them. They are good, but I do not know if they are the best of noiseless series, since I have not tried them all, but one thing is for sure, I do feel the stratty sound with this in the middle position, since this is the only one I can review.

product_title: Audio-Technica ATR3350 Omnidirectional Condenser Lavalier Microphone (Discontinued)
review_body:
Love the audio quality of these mics so much I bought a 3rd just as a back up. I've compared the audio recordings I've get with these mics from numerous handheld dynamic microphones, and condenser microphones such as the MXL 840 ($100 for 2). The MXL 840's are slightly crisper, noticeable mainly when recording paino. However, because they are XLR, they require me to upgrade to a recorder like the Tascam d40 (which I do NOT recommend) that can accept XLR inputs. Anyway, after basic cleanup in Audacity (eg: noise removal and normalizing), I and my family have a very hard time hearing any significant audio improvement from using the MXL mics vs these. These mics are much better (less noise) than dynamic mics.

Note that I'm completely misusing these mics, as I have two of them taped at the front of a community theater stage to pick up the actors -- and they work very well for that purpose. If you aren't willing to spend a few hundred $ per microphone for better mics, then I'd suggest just using these. They work great.

review_body:
I only use mogami and canare in the studio. I usually roll my own cables, but, in the case of this purchase, I was out of raw cable and needed to get some gear inline immediately, so I bought these premade cables.

Mine were the genuine article, though I've never had any reason to use the mogami warranty. I would advise, if you have concern, to just be sure you are buying from a known source (musicians friend, amazon themselves, any other reputable MI store, not, for example 'XYZ premium cables'

there's not much I can say about mogami here anyone who's done even a bit of research already knows. they are terrific cables that are quiet, well built, have phenomenal range, and are professional in every way. there's always some who prefer other brands - I personally only use mogami or canare - and I avoid the mess of monster. product_title: Kala MK-SD-LBLBURST Makala Dolphin Soprano Ukulele - Light Blue Burst
review_headline: Good Tone, but most have Fret Buzz
review_body: Sweet tone, full midtones, well balanced tonally between strings (with added expense and work of installing Aquila Nylgut strings and a new bone saddle). The nut slots are too high. You should lower the nut slots with a needle file but research youtube first and be careful because if you go too low the string will be unplayable. I bought 6 of these as gifts and have spent alot of time fixing fret buzz due to uneven frets on most of them. Some required only a few frets to be corrected, some needed alot more. This will always be a risk when buying cheap ukes, and can be fixed but requires skill (there's a youtube video of guy teaching how to dress/level frets by measuring only 3 at a time rather than leveling the whole neck at once; this is a much easier and safer method of correcting fret buzz; I use narrow strips of grey sanding paper to level the fret at its high point, protecting the wood fretboard with strips of thick tape). I bought a range of colours, pearl white, sunburst pink, sunburst orange, plain yellow. The plain yellow one had no soundhole decal and the inner rim of the soundhole was unpainted. It's lighter and has a slightly thinner feeling neck than the others and it might sound a little thinner but this could be psychological. Overall, a good sounding uke if you are prepared to spend time correcting its imperfections.

product_title: Peavey Bandit 112 TransTube Amplifier
review_body:
If you're a working musician, you can appreciate this amp. Of course, most open minded people can.

It has a good clean sound and a decent gain channel. It takes pedals well. The bandit isn't brilliant at anything but it certainly does a lot of things convincingly enough. Oh, did I mention that it's crazy loud for this size? On top of all that, they're tough as nails.

It's not pretty, and it's not a boutique tube work of art. It doesn't have a million presets or built in effects. It simply won't let you down, and considering how spotty live sound can be, it's often better to have a good loud amp than an amazing quiet one.

If you're tied of not being heard, or of changing tubes, or programming presets- this will fix that for you.

review_body: This pedal along with the digital reverb/delay, reverb machine, and compressor/sustainer pedals by Behringer all worked great for the first two day I had them. The second night while using them they all one by one started malfunctioning. They would cut on and off and produce unpleasant sounds. I replaced the batteries thinking although the batteries should last longer than two days perhaps that was the issue (which it was not). I realized I got what I paid for, cheap poor quality pedals. I almost gave these products 2 starts b/c while they were working they sounded fantastic, how ever there is no point in guitar pedals that can't maintain working order after such short time. I didn't handle these pedals roughly nor expose them to any harsh environments that could warrant defective behavior. Simply had them on my carpet floor in front of my amp. These pedals were practically undistinguishable in sound from the higher end pedals they are based on and it was truly a tease to have thought I found a cheaper alternative to them. I will NEVER purchase any products from Behringer after this experience.

product_title: KEDSUM® USB to DMX Interface Adapter DMX512 Satge Lighting Controller Suport MAC
review_body:
A very compact, effective device at the right price.
I had a small gig with simple 4 par cans and a DMX Eliminator (ED15) dimmer. Controlling with my PC was just the right thing and this did the job.
I had a little problem configuring the device and the included freestyler software because I was completely new to DMX. The ED15 manual was a bit sketchy for newbies, as well.

Minus 2 stars - the CD came with both their Manual/Drivers (USB-uDMX512, XZL Group limited) and ENTTEC (DMX USB Pro). I started by spending a lot of time trying to get it working with the ENTTEC driver. WHY did they include the ENTTEC driver?! CONFUSION! Frustrated, I finally contacted the vendor through Amazon. Within 1 hour, they got back to me and straightened me out. And thank goodness they did for my job was next day. Ah, there's another driver on the CD and another manual, the right driver and manual. I suspect, at one point, they were probably using the same chipset as ENTTEC. Perhaps they still have a few units out there that they were trying to liquidate and decided to put both drivers/manuals on the disk.

Plus 1 star - Much appreciated, FAST tech support! (from pennybuying)

product_title: Hamilton KB90 Traveler II Portable Music Stand
review_headline: Music stand is good but hardware is lacking
review_body:
Reliable, easy to assemble, and very solid. I recently joined a community wind ensemble, in which *everyone* has his or her own stand, and I'm glad I got this one. As good as anyone else's and better than most.

04/06/2014: I have had reason to rethink my review. The stand itself is great but the thumbscrews used to lock it in place are not durable at all. The clamps do not grab the metal well without a lot of tightening and I have stripped all three thumbscrews since buying this stand. product_title: Dean Markley AG15M 15-Watt Acoustic Guitar Amplifier
review_headline: Received the Updated AG15M Amp, with Mic Input and DI Output
review_body: I use this amp with my K&K equipped acoustic guitar.  The four tone controls (bass, midrange, treble, and 'presence' - upper treble) give tremendous control over the sound.  I run my passive K&K pickups without a preamp, as the Ultrasound amp's input impedance is a good match for the pickups.  The AG15 has a very clean and natural sound.  I purchased mine from Woodwind and Brasswind.  The unit that arrived is actually the updated AG15M, which features an XLR direct out, a line out, and a second channel XLR input for a mic.  This was a pleasant surprise!  I am able to connect directly to my church's mixer through the amp, and I had expected to need a DI box for this task.

product_title: Behringer EUROLIVE F1320D Active 300 Watt 12" Monitor Speaker,
review_body:
Starting a new band and bought 2 of these to see how they would sound. Now going back to buy 2 more. I play electric guitar through a Line 6 Pod direct to the board and out through these speakers. Sound quality is great and I can stay beneath the vocalist easily. We used passive Yamaha monitors in the past and considered those THE reference for on-stage monitors. But these match them easily and have more EQ flexibility. Differentiating feature is the compression driver instead of the standard horn. The horns in the Yamahas disappeared at about 2' right/left of axis which made sharing a monitor between two singers difficult. The F1320's drive was stayed the same as far as 4' off axis...a big plus.

And even with a class D amp in them they are lighter than the Yamaha's. A great value.

review_body:
I was drawn to this pedal first because of the price, which honestly, is pretty damned good. The problem is that the pedal has horrible tracking anything between E and A on a standard tuned guitar, and it completely s**ts the bed when you play multiple strings. When I put a capo on and did some scales, I was able to make a lot of cool sounds, but I'm always left feeling like if I had just spent a little more money, I'd get way more out of it.

product_title: Pyle-Pro PDWM2550 19'' Rack Mount Dual VHF Wireless Rechargeable Handheld Microphone System
review_headline: Had High Hopes, but Drop-Outs are Unacceptable
review_body:
I didn't purchase these from Amazon, I got them at a \\"bargain warehouse\\" type place for about half price. That being said, I was willing to take the reduced financial risk of buying a Pyle Pro product.

I took these home, plugged them into my practice rig at home and walked around the house and even out into the yard -- no problems. I was quite pleased with the deal I got.

Fast forward, doing my first wedding gig. I hadn't had a gig were wireless mics were a necessity (birthdays etc.), but for a wedding you need one (at a minimum) for the best man/maid of honor toasts. I got set up, walked around the reception hall and even out into the cocktail hour, no problems, they sounded great. BUT -- when the hall was full of people, and the best man was making his speech, the mic would drop out for a fraction of a second periodically. It wasn't terrible, and fortunately I was the only one scrutinizing the audio quality while everyone else was listening intently to the best man's speech, so nobody else seemed to notice.

The distance from receiver to mic was no more than 125 feet, and there was even line-of-sight. The only possible explanation I can find for the drop-outs was interference from the photographers' wireless flash controllers. It would be consistent with the seemingly sporadic and brief drop outs. However, from my research, most wireless flashes operate in the 340MHz to somewhere under 500MHz range, while these mics are 174MHz - 219MHz (my specific set is 191 and 219 I believe).

Regardless of the reason, people pay good money for a professional DJ, and I'm not willing to accept poor or mediocre performance from equipment. I'll have to do what I should have done originally and shell out the money for a reliable Shure product.

These are great for personal/home use or maybe small church groups, but if you're charging people for your service, they deserve better -- look elsewhere.

Oh and as someone else said... it's rack-mountable, but the mic charging docks are on top? Dumb design. Also, buy some Duracells. Don't use the blank white plastic rechargables that came in the case... no brainer.

product_title: Yamaha THR AMPS THR10C Electric Guitar Mini Amplifier
review_headline: Great, but needs a computer to take full advantage of editing...
review_body:
First, let me say that this is the first practice amp that I've owned that can handle the deep bass that you get out of a hollow body guitar. I've used the Fender Mustang I, Roland Micro Cube and a few others - this amp handles the full range without a hiccup.

The tones are incredible, and it handles pedals well. I use it with a Zoom Multistomp and a Ditto Looper to practice both rhythm and lead. It maintains the clean rhythm sound as well as a crunchy/delayed lead as well.

As I put this amp through its paces, it seem to be able to handle everything very well. So the question is... why the 4 star rating and not 5? There are several features that you can only get to when you have your computer connected. The following effects can only be tweaked with a computer:

* 3 Band EQ - The editor provides 3 band EQ. This is needed if you happen to switch between guitars that have single coil vs. humbuckers, or if you're changing from jazz to blues or rock.

* Cabinet models - the editor lets you choose between American 4x12, American 2x12, British 4x12, British 2x12, 1x12 or 4x10. It would be great to have access...

* Compressor - the ability to choose either a rack or stomp compressor. Tons of versatility, sometimes You I want to add compression on my lead tone on the fly. Can't do that without the computer...

* Reverb - on the amp, you can choose either spring or hall reverb. In the editor you can also select Room or Plate reverb.

* Noise gate can only be selected in the editor too.

I know it might change the overall aesthetics, but I wish I didn't have to connect to a computer in order to obtain these features.

On the positive side, Yamaha provides 35 really great presets and the ability for you to store up to 100. For my taste, they really have captured the most popular sounds out there.

Excellent job, this is now used more than my Eleven Rack or Fender Mustang IIIV.2

product_title: Beyerdynamic DT-770-PRO-32 Closed Dynamic Headphone for Mobile Control and Monitoring Applications, 32 Ohms
review_headline: The last headset I'll ever need
review_body:
I don't consider myself an audiophile, but I do like good sound and can appreciate it when I hear it. My previous headphones were the Grado SR80s. I thought those were fantastic, but I wanted a bit more bass, and decided on these headphones after a bit of research.

The Beyers deliver. It's not just a ton of bass, though; it's clear, natural sounding bass. It won't overpower the rest of the music. While the Grados were considerably brighter sounding, the DT 770 sounds more balanced. It really excels in any genre of music, from Grunge to UK Garage. Add a clip-on mic, and it's an exceptional gaming headset.

In fact, I can hear the imperfections in lower bitrate files too clearly (128kbps mp3 files, Youtube videos with poorer sound quality). It's actually kinda distracting sometimes. For day to day use, this is probably as far as I'm willing to go in terms of sound quality and accuracy.

Just make sure you can drive these bad boys properly if you're getting the 250 ohm version. If you're using this on a mobile device without an amp, you'll definitely need to turn the volume up. My PC's motherboard has an integrated 600 ohm amp, so home use is definitely not a problem. Otherwise, get the 80 or 32 ohm version.

product_title: Odyssey FZGSPIDDJSBL Black Label Pioneer DDJ-S1/DDJ-T1 Midi Digital DJ Controller Glide Style Slim Case
review_headline: Not great for shipping or mobility
review_body: Good build quality, but way too heavy.  Also not as secure as you would think inside.  I had My S1 shipped in this case and it bounced around inside and damaged the unit.  Luckily I got insurance on it.  Ended up selling the case and went with the pioneer soft case.  Much more practical even though it doesn't look as pro, but at least I carry it with me no problem.

product_title: 542 Golden Melody Harmonica
review_body: Love this harp. Fits my hands well, good raspy sound, light weight, won't hurt to get wet. A great pocket harp. And it came with 30 day free online lessons. That's been great. Bought 2 of them a C and an A.

product_title: Mackie PROFX12 12-Channel Compact Effects Mixer with USB
review_body: No issues with the board... works well. Haven't gigged with it yet cuz not enough dead-heads in my area! :).. and I don't want to play the same acoustic tunes everyone else plays just to get gigs... so will "keep on truckin" as-is! :). Has a number of effects, but not a lot of variation between some of them. For solo-acoustic act, will be sufficient I am sure...

review_body: This product is not worth the cost of shipping. Not even good for a beginner child. The only reason to purchase this is to smash it on something while dancing around in fake fog while listening to metal rock. I'd return it, but the box came damaged with poor packaging as well and I shoved it in a closet to calm myself and forgot about it. You get what you pay for folks...and I got just that.

product_title: Lazarro Eb E Flat Alto Saxophone with Music Pocketbook, Case and Care Kit
review_body: This horn arrived in great external condition. The color is even more stunning than the pictures showed. But the pads were slipped and dirty, and needed replacement out of the box. The local music store was happy to do this for $45, but I should not need to have any service on a brand new instrument. I didn't want to return the instrument for a replacement because of the extra time involved and my uncertainty about the general quality of this manufacturer/model.

product_title: Yamaha HS8 Studio Monitor, Black
review_body:
Just amazing.
The room controls are nice, but it is the clarity of the speakers that delivered what I wanted.
Worth every penny if you really enjoy listening to music.

product_title: On Stage MS7701C Tripod Microphone Boom Stand, Chrome
review_body: For the price, it's pretty great. Solid stand, with plenty of adjustments. Best if you are singing while playing the guitar. Need to buy a microphone clip for it.

product_title: Kala MK Ukulele Bundles
review_headline: My experience with the Barre system
review_body: I purchased the MK-B because the seller of the Barre system failed to note in their advertising the system could not be used effectively with a smaller tenor uke. Like others I found the wire wound 4th string noisy with a discordant vibration and wonder why the manufacturer would continue to use it. My impression overall is positive, the instrument appears to be  well made and finished and has a nice sound despite the low price.  I plan to change the strings and would welcome some advice on the best brand  to buy. If you decide on the MK the combination instrument, gig bag and tuner is a great buy.

product_title: Neewer Broadcast Studio Microphone Suspension Boom Scissor Arm Stand with Shock Mount and XLR Male to Female Cable
review_body:
This arm hold the weight of a ATR2100 microphone fine. It stays where you put it and it works as you would expect. The packaging was damaged and it was shipped just in a plastic shipping bag but it works. The shock mount is the same as one of the low end on stage shock mounts. I did have to slightly bend out the lower bit of the frame to allow it to freely move towards and away from me. However it works great. Not too big and gets the job done.

Tip, just take something you can wrap a smaller mic in to get it to fit. My ATR2100 is a 2 inch diameter mic and this shockmount is probably meant for around 3 inches. I just wrapped it with bicycle handlebar padding and it works great.

review_body: I bought these thinking that the added padding on the sticks would dent some of the noise of the drums. It does not do that. They sound just as loud as regular drum sticks. Oh well, they do look sorta cool and my 9 year old likes them.

review_body: Though nearly 500 dollars is a lot to shell out for a VST at first glance, Omnisphere is not your average synth at all. The presets on here, alone, are amazing and you can spend hours just going through the entire list and playing all of the sounds out. The synth engine is great, too. product_title: East West /Quantum Leap Symphonic Orchestra Gold Complete
review_body: BUYER BEWARE EastWest customer support is staffed by a couple of guys who always act like you are interrupting their precious facebook time when you call in to their very hard-to-find studio number in LA. If you wait for email support, you must be willing to wait for snail mail speeds, as they take days to get back to you, which is not good when you are ready to use this sound libary and their player. The software is out of date when you open the box, and in order to get it to install, you need to basically go through the install about 3 full times using different installers in order to install the current player app. The library is over-rated, as there are better sounds on a Kurzweill K2500, or a Korg M50, or even an old EMU Orchestral Proteus. BUYER BEWARE

product_title: TC Electronic Level Pilot, High Resolution Computer-Independent Analog Level Control
review_headline: Awesome, simple. Great addition to my setup
review_body:
The knob is great. Its nice that it's footprint is so much smaller than the Mackie big knob or presonus stuff. It can fit right in next to the keyboard and the mouse. Makes it very seamless.

The turning operation is very smooth and the knob has a really nice tactile feel to it. Sound quality is great and the volume seems very linear from low to high. I love it.

As others have said, the xlr leads are definitely too short to plug directly into powered monitors. But I prefer this, as I think it will actually add to its durability in the longrun. Longer cords would be more fragile and are going to wear out and get mucked up a lot quicker.

I think its better to think of this as a breakout cable and extend them as needed. But it's not a problem for me, as I'm just going from my converters to my amp.

product_title: LOW NOISE IN-EAR BINAURAL MICS - HIGH SENSITIVITY w/ WINDSCREENS
review_body: Great sound quality recording. No regrets! I had been wanting and hearing about these for about 4 years and now I've got some

product_title: BEHRINGER U-PHONO UFO202
review_body: Reasonable cost, compact, and it does what it says: pre-amplifies (if needed) and converts analog signal to digital for input into your computer (where you'll need a program like Audacity to write the file). Only drawback is that there is no gain control for the pre-amplification, so some very loud signals may blast. (The line in/phono switch seems to set preamplification to high or low). Guess I'd need a more expensive unit for that.

product_title: Shure SFG-2 Stylus Tracking Force Gauge
review_body: After doing considerable research on tracking force gauges I ended up settling on this analogue scale. I was quite surprised at the ease of use and accuracy provided by Shure's SFG-2 scale. The mirror provided allows for extremely easy recognition of when your stylus is tracking at the proper force and is a very smart yet simple addition. Highly recommended for the price!

product_title: Promark TXRKW Hickory RK "Rock Knocker" Wood Tip drumstick
review_headline: Speed of a small stick, power of a big stick.
review_body: I usually play (death metal, black metal) with 5Bs, but decided to try the Rock Knockers again, after about 12 years of ignoring my last pair.  I don't think I'll play a different stick again.  I love the speed of the smaller RK, but the power and volume I get from them is something you can't get from a regular small stick.  My toms are louder, the bell of my Ride is clearer.  Love these sticks!

product_title: Electric Acoustic Bass Guitar with Equalizer & Accessories Sunburst

I've had it for a couple of weeks and I think this is a great value that suits my needs. I would not use it on stage though.
I'm using it for sound editing and music recording at low volumes and the reproduction quality is fine. It's sure to deliver good quality voice over internet service as well.
It's a good looking product too, such that I wouldn't be shy about leaving it out at my workstation with company coming.

product_title: Jim Dunlop 6554 Dunlop Ultimate Lemon Oil, 4 oz.
review_body: I never cleaned my fretboard. My guitar is alittle over two years old and I figured I would restring and give it a good cleaning. I couldnt believe the shine and beauty it brought to my guitar. The fretboard seemed alright to me, not until I used this did I notice how lackluster it really was. I am so happy I decided to try this. My guitar looks like new. I liked the fact that you could dispense directly onto the guitar, but I didnt. I put it onto a polishing cloth first then concentrated on cleaning each fret really well. I think using the cloth helps to not overdo the oil too, you dont want too much oil on there. Overall, a great oil for your fretboard, it really restores it to look new again. I would buy again and reccomend to anyone with a rosewood fretboard.

product_title: Alsing Acoustic Guitar Stand, Electric Guitar Stand, or Bass Guitar Stand - Tubular, Black
review_body: I needed a few stands for home and to take around on picking sessions. I decided to buy these based on price and appearance and am well pleased. I have had them well over a week now and used them at home and carried around to several sessions and think I now have used them enough to form an opinion. I don't anticipate any problems at all with these stands. they work as well as any other stand of this style I've used and seem quite durable. I could have paid more and gotten better stands that collapse and may be a little more "convenient" to carry but these do what I want and at a much better price. I could have gotten stands just like these from one of the online music warehouse stores and paid a little more for a little less quality.

product_title: Behringer Mini 9 Band Eq
review_headline: Use for enhancing short wave listening via headphones
review_body:
The design of this unit fits my needs perfectly for use in improving short wave radio listening through headphones.

Short wave audio is typically endowed with a lot of artifacts at different frequencies that blot out the part that we need to hear which is most typically voice between 500 and 5000 cps. Excessive low and high frequency noise can be cut and the most audible portion of the midrange can be boosted to rise above the shortwave clutter. For this use, mono is perfect and the 9 band adjustments are just about what's needed without over-complicating things.

review_body:

I thought that because of the fundamental design, and way these work is completely different from traditional magnet wound pickups, that perhaps they may not play well along side a magnetic humbucker.

I actually found that blending this with another humbucker can create some amazingly acoustic tones with great depth.

I bought this to replace a humbucker in my BC Rich, I'm so glad that I did.

product_title: Samson Meteor Mic USB Studio Microphone (Cardioid)
review_headline: Surprisingly great, gonna stick with it while refining skills
review_body:
I'm really into music and into recording it. I've been watching countless reviews for various cheap condenser mics, wondering which to get: the MX 990, 770, AT2020, AT1A (or whatever)? Well, my mom bought the Samson for voice calls or something and told me I could use it. I have been trying it out recently and...it works pretty great! I've been doing vocals and guitar and it has a surprisngly fuller sound than you would expect. Also, I'm just pleased with the fact that it's a condenser mic, because I have a Shure dynamic mic that I was gonna route through a mixer and buy a USB interface for and all that jazz... but the Samson sounds more \\"finished\\", if you will, like a studio vocal mic. Even as an audiophile, I'm pleased with its simplicity and the way it sounds right out of the box. I'm using Audacity to make multitrack recordings and I'm satisfied for the moment. The best part are the slider crossfader controls - optical .... so almost no wear and tear and that would mean no change of these controls in the long run.
The finishing of the mixer is premium, not tacky at all, and I would say this is a value for money DJ mixer... at par or better than most of it's competing brands.. product_title: Snark SN-2 All Instrument Clip-On Chromatic Tuner
review_body:
In 30 years of playing music, this is the finest instrument tuner I have ever used. I was first turned on to these from my band members. I play in a bluegrass/old-time outfit, and the banjo player and upright bass player both use Snarks. I received my SN-2 as a gift from our guitar player, and have been amazed at how well these things behave.

Making an electronic tuner is all about balance and compromises. If you're making a tuner for a stringed instrument, you'll have to accept that as the string is plucked, it does not ring out at a set pitch. That pitch wavers up and down, and if you make the device too sensitive, the musician will never get a good reading. He'll just watch the LCD dial just swing wildly from flat to sharp and back again.
Also, there is the problem of response. An electronic tuner has to wait until there is sufficient sustain in order to determine what note is being played, but if it waits too long, the musician will become frustrated at the tuner being too slow to respond. This can really become a problem if the musician is bringing the tuning up or down, and goes past the mark as the tuner struggles to catch up with the information it is receiving. Part of the challenge for an electronic tuner is deciding just how much information to discard and what to display. Tuners have to use algorithms to decide how to average the wavering notes it is receiving, and pass that along as useful information to the musician.
In the end, making a tuner is a tricky business. I have had some that were good or fairly decent, and others that were just atrocious. This device is astounding. Part of what makes it so useful is its simplicity. The tuner is very responsive, and presents a very good picture of what your string's average note is, almost immediately.
Being able to implicitly trust your tuner is immensely freeing and satisfying. I use the SN-2 on my acoustic guitar, mandolin, electric guitar (clipping it to the headstock and tuning with the amp off), tenor ukulele, and even my fiddle. For decades I used to tune my fiddle by ear, having never found an electronic tuner that could handle it. I now use the Snark, and have had excellent results. Having played music for 30 years, I like to think I have a pretty demanding ear for intonation, and have never ever had a problem with tuning my instruments by the Snark SN-2.with the amp off), tenor ukulele, and even my fiddle. My light switch is a dimmer ([[ASIN:B000JJYJMM Lutron MIR-600THW-WH 600-Watt Maestro IR Dimmer with Infrared Receiver, White]]) and it works great with this bulb. Instant on (another advantage of LED bulbs) and even at its dimmest mode, the bulb works great. The only thing I noticed is that when the switch is shutting off the light, this bulb flickers for about 1 second, which is not a big deal.

This bulb puts out more light and requires less power than anything equivalent. Compare prices with LED bulbs sold at your local hardware store, and you'll see that this is a steal :)

product_title: Seismic Audio - Enforcer II PW - Powered PA 18" Subwoofer Speaker Cabinet
review_body: It can't be EQed flat even with a 25hz filter rolling off the sub bass.  Convolving it even at low volume just makes it more noisy and less musical.  Clips very early, even with proper phasing to the tops.  Mushy.  Doesn't hit hard.  Huge dip in the 50-60hz range.  Big peak in the 40-45hz range.  Another massive amount of info trying to be played much higher in frequency than a sub driver should be doing.  The low-pass filter built into it is necessary just to flatten the midrange hump on it even with the outboard crossover and sum unit I'm using.  Called Seismic and they recommended various things.  Some of it helped a little, like tightening the toroid inside, but even after I put foam between it and the toroid's plate, there's still too much rattle there and from the heat sink.  The cabinet and the area where the sub driver is screwed is also making noise.  Taped all the unused ports and there's still air escaping the back in spots.  There was also a missing screw with a hole in the middle of the heat sink.  I've heard little 10 inchers that sounded better than this, let alone 12s and 15s.  An 18 in a big box like this with a 120oz magnet and a 1200W RMS amp should not sound like this.  It's as if they didn't use the correct parts or designed it wrong somewhere or are outright lying about the specs... or some combination.  It should be physically and electrically capable of a lot more.  What a sad waste of my money for something so darn heavy.

review_body:
I have had this only a few days so perhaps it is still not good for a \\"full review\\" but here are some of my vital opinions.

Keys feel great, size is perfect.

The largest problem of the keyboard is the screen. It has very narrow viewing angles, to see it clearly you have to view the keyboard from up. But in typical usage scenario (sitting in a chair in studio) you would view the screen from about 45 degree angle and from this angle it is almost impossible to see what is written to the screen. The screen is about 2-3mm below the surface and screen frames will block you from seeing the lowest 5mm of the screen (which often contains low parts of letters and numbers). Fortunately situation becomes much better (although not optimal) by putting something under back feet of the keyboard so that it is in an angle leaning forwards.

Another problem is encoder resolution which is very low. you need to rotate the encoder several rounds to raise value from 0 to 127. M-Audio is not the only keyboard with this problem, Novation Impulse as the same thing. Only keyboard with proper encoders is Akai MPK and perhaps Novation SL MK2

product_title: Sennheiser HD 280 Pro Headphones
review_body: First, the sound quality was very good.  There is no doubt that these headphones have great range. Also, the ear pieces were so large that it completely covered my ears, but in the process they partially rested on my carotid artery so I could hear my own heart beat thumping in my ear.. kinda distracting. Chewing, breathing, the slightest movement would make clunky sounds in my ear.  After a while, it got on my nerves because of all the distracting sounds.  I gave it 3 stars because the construction quality was nice for the price and the sound was good.  I took away 2 of the 5 stars because the noises it would make in my ear were too much for me to use and its total sound-isolation was too much for a work environment.

review_headline: Great practice piano at a very good price.
review_body: We own a U1 upright yamaha with which we are thorougly happy with, however, our eldest daughter has transformed from a budding learner to an talented pianist who practices constantly :) I ordered this electric because of the good reviews and Yamaha's well earned reputation. It was a good choice. Though it will never replace an acoustic piano the Arius is a very good facsimile for headhone(quiet)practice. It also is an acceptable stand-in for the acoustic while playing through the speakers. The action is very good and the material of the keys feels almost identical to the feel of a \\"real piano\\". Alhough I find the voices a little gimmicky having three piano iterations is useful since the 3rd one most approaches our upright, the other 2, as advertised, mimick the resonance of grand pianos. Assembly is very simple but to, my surprise, there is no included assembly manual, the instructions are on the box itself. A word of advice, though the piano is \\"normal\\" sized, the shipping box is huge and heavy, the packaging weighs 50% as much as the piano,  a dolly is a must to move it around. Our pianist is delighted (much better than the practice pianos in the conservatory) with it and now we get a little more quiet time than before. Personally I think this is a great choice for practicing proffesionals and for learners that dont want to invest, as of yet, on an a very expensive acoustic instrument. Id give it five stars but musicians would pummel me for giving a perfect score to something that is not the \\"real thing\\" LOL!

review_body: These CDJ's are just ok. I picked them up because they had good reviews and I wanted something similar to pioneer products. They're mostly plastic, including the play and cue buttons, which can't take the same kind of beating as a pioneer CDJ. The jog wheels are very heavy and nearly impossible to scratch with. They also seem to have a bit of delay on them in vinyl mode. These things also crash so much that I get nervous every time i used them to play a show. They're good for someone who wants to learn to mix on pioneer style CDJ's at home and can't afford name brand ones, but once you get comfortable with the standard CDJ setup you'll most likely want something more.

product_title: La Patrie Guitar, Presentation QI
review_body:
First off, the Presentation QI is really a beautifully built, nice sounding guitar especially for the cost. I doubt you could find another North American manufactured guitar even remotely close to the price. Very nice projection, great factory action, stayed in tune very well and I even loved the sound plugged in to my Crate Gunnison acoustic amp. Overall quality was really nice.

Unfortunately mine arrived with two hairline cracks in the cedar top on the lower bout. Since Amazon was out of stock of the item I attempted to contact La Patrie directly. The guitar is manufactured by a company called Guitabec located in both Canada and the US. After two weeks of emails going unanswered I was forced to just return the instrument for a refund.

Had the guitar had no issues I would have been very satisfied with the instrument. Been playing acoustic steel strings for 25 years and this was my first classical guitar purchase. Was much better quality, set up and sound than anything I played close to that price range in my local music stores.

Guitar for the price is 4.5/5 stars

Company customer service would be a 0/5 stars.

product_title: VHT Special 6 6W 1x10 Hand-Wired Tube Guitar Combo Amp,
review_headline: VHT special 6 is a harmonica players dream
review_body: I purchased this amp to use for harmonica after reading in the harp community about it. It sounds great stock but if using this for harmonica there are many things one can do to improve it because its sooo easy to mod this amp. First the tubes are cheap Chinese ones they use to keep the price low so I replaced both  with the JJ 6v6 and the tungsol 12ax7. Next the speaker is OK but I wanted one specifically for my harp playing so I replaced the stock vht speaker with a Eminence lil buddy because it has a cannabis cone like the mission amps. There are utube vids with this exact set up so you can hear for yourself. I think it sounds as good as if not better than the $800 Harp Gear amp. Harp Gear is a great amp and built much better than this one but also more than twice the price. So $239 for the amp and another $100 for the upgrades and you have a modern, better sounding, louder champ.

product_title: ION Audio Block Rocker (iPA56B) | Bluetooth Portable Speaker with Auxiliary USB Charger [2013 Model]
review_body:
This is an excellent product that performs it's function very well for me. Using the Bluetooth connection on my Galaxy S3 I have walked over 50 feet away from the unit with my phone with no loss sound or connection whatsoever. The sound is rich and full with plenty of volume. Extending drag handle and wheels are handy; just like pulling your luggage at the airport! easy to lift (very light!) with convenient recessed handles. USB port to charge your device (sorry IPhone snobs!) and aux input with cable for your non-apple device. The battery lasts forever, but take care of it. I ran it for 12 hours straight and used less than 1/3rd of the charge. Follow the instructions for the care of the battery which are conveniently written on the side of the unit near the power switch and battery life indicator.

It seems some of the negative reviews here are based on a misunderstanding of the nature of the product.

Essentially, this is only a speaker. That means that the sound you get out of it will be equal to the sound you put into it. Bass, for example, is a function controlled by your music player (if you bought home stereo speakers you wouldn't bellyache that the speakers didn't have bass controls!). The instructions recommend having the volume on your player and the unit at zero when you connect. Then slowly raise both in varying increments to achieve the best sound.

The handle and wheels are not heavy duty; they are for sidewalks, parking lots and other smooth surfaces and perform quite well. You're not going off-roading with the wheels and common sense should tell you that you shouldn't go bashing it around. ION makes another unit for that. [...]

For patios, bbq's, the beach, camping, in the garage, basement, etc I highly recommend.

product_title: Mendini 1/2 MV Solid Wood Violin with Hard Case, Shoulder Rest, Bow, Rosin and Extra Strings
review_body:
I can't say a lot yet to the sound production of this item, since I am just learning. But there are a couple of questions I had prior to ordering that weren't exactly clear from other reviews. I'd like to address them here.

As I received it, the violin was in better shape than I'd anticipated. I was expecting it to require being set up. I'm happy to say this wasn't the case; the bridge was intact and in place (save for needing to be moved about two millimeters lower on one side) and the sound post was firmly in place. It's entirely possible that when shipping, the sound post can get jarred loose, but the manufacturers are making the effort to save us the trouble of having to do this step. If it does, it shouldn't cost much to have it re-set. Of course, the strings did need to be tuned, but this wasn't difficult with a tuner smartphone app. If you're not experienced, go very slow with the pegs, and make sure to push them into the pegboard as you are tightening. Violins do not use the geared peg system like guitars do. If they're a bit slippy, either use peg drops or a bit of rosin. And with new strings (including the ones on the violin), be prepared to re-tune them at every sitting until the strings relax and stretch enough to hold their shape. And, yes, I did break my A string when tightening; replacing it was very easy.

With the rosin, I'm not exactly thrilled with it, but it'll do in a pinch. Before using it, I found it best to go over the block with a small piece of sandpaper to make it easier to get my bow coated. It will take quite a bit because the bow is new and not already rosined; if lightly dragging it across a tuned string doesn't give sound, then it probably needs more. If you rosin it too much; it'll play off as you go.

There were reviews about patchy paint, and I think they must be referring to the underside of the handle. If you look carefully, this is _not_ a manufacturing defect; the lines are quite deliberate and the underlying wood is varnished and clearcoated to protect it. It seems the vendor had said in another review that this was deliberate and had something to do with creating unnecessary friction--I'm not sure here--but regardless it appears to be this way for a reason, and it's not noticeable unless you're actually looking for it.

Overall, I'm rather pleased with this violin. In time, I intend on replacing the strings with a different brand and quite possibly the bow, but for now, it's quite serviceable and does just fine for a beginner. Factoring in the low price, I'd say that I got a great deal.

product_title: Ibanez Artcore Series AF75TDGIV Hollowbody Electric Guitar Black
review_body:
After years of buying and playing a number of entry level guitars, I decided it was time for something nicer. For several years I have been intrigued by the idea of a hollow body arch top guitar. I will confess, in part, that I like the looks of such a guitar, which at one time was fairly common, but today is rather a niche instrument. But in part I was interested in the sonic possibilities of this type of guitar.

I had been researching online various makes and models. I couldn't afford one of the top end models costing thousands of dollars, but the Ibanez line fit in my price range and had several models which interested. So I went to a local music store as I wished to actually try one out before plunking down my hard earned cash. They had one of these hanging on the wall and the clerk got it down and plugged it into an amp. It sounded great and I bought it.

Since then I have become more and more pleased with it. It sound great. The bridge pickup gives a nice, bright sound without being piercing while the neck pickup has a mellow tone without being muddy, even with the tone control turned all the way down. The guitar was well set up, with a nice, easy playing action yet still free of buzzes. The intonation is spot on. In short, this is an easy playing guitar that sounds nice.

My initial impression was that the neck was a bit wider than my old guitar and thus it was a bit easier to avoid having a finger on one string interfer with an adjacent string. However actual measurement reveals no discernible difference in the dimensions. Whatever it is, this guitar does well for playing finger style.

Some reviews I have seen pan this guitar for the placement of the pickup selector switch, which is just below the bridge between the pick guard and the knobs. However, I have no problems with it, I can easily reach it to switch while I have never accidentally switched it by contact by my right hand.

One of the things which attracted me to this particular model was the Bigsby style vibrato tailpiece. I have never had a guitar with a vibrato unit and wanted to have one. It took some getting used to, but it seems to work reasonably well. It does not seem to be well suited for doing 2 and 3 semitone dive bombs and other sorts of extreme techniques that heavy metal shredders do, but for putting some inflection into something, particularly on a chord, does well. At first there was a bit of a tendency for the G string to go a bit sharp after using the vibrato, but it seems that things are broken in now and it holds tune pretty well.

The guitar is a looker too. I have the black model, which is well finished with white binding all around the body, the f-holes, and the fretboard. The pickup mounts are a nice ivory color while all the hardware is gold. Unlike the photo here, mine has a tortoise shell look to the pick guard. The position markers are mother of pearl rectangles augmented by small black dots in the binding on the side of the neck.

The guitar is well made, with no visible blemishes in either the construction or finish.

Since it is a full hollow body, it can be played unplugged. Certainly this is good enough for solo practice, and probably good enough to play for a few friends in your living room. Whether you could play this unplugged in say an acoustic jam session is another thing. Possibly if all your going to do is comp for others, it might work; hard for me to say if it could be up to taking a solo.

If you're looking for something to plug into a wall of Marshalls turned up to 11 and blast away with tons of distortion, this is probably not the guitar for you. If you're looking for something that you could play some country or good ol' r'n'r, or jazz, this could well be the guitar you're looking for.

product_title: Clanrye Bagpipe Chanter Reed
review_headline: good to start with for sure
review_body: If you are a beginning piper and want to get to playing faster rather than later, and are so frustrated with screwing around with blowing in cane reeds only to have them go out of tune, crack, get chipped, etc--then get a synthetic chanter reed. Maclaren, Surefire, and Clanrye are all synthetic and there are different reviews for each one for certain, but the overall issue with ANY of them is that the weaker the reed the more likely to squeal, its just the way it is. That being said, I hurt my back badly on a fall on the ice 10 years ago and just about gave up the pipes as I could not even begin to blow my WEAK cane reed in (it was about med strength to start and I would have had to basically file it to weak which can shorten the life badly), so I bought a blue and a red Clanrye to get me going again after 6 years of no piping. What I found, to my surprise, was that when my bagpipe instructor went to tune \\"that dirty bast*** blue Clanrye 'fake' reed\\" she found...that it sounded EXACTLY like the Apps reed she had been tuning moments earlier...so HA! That was YEARS ago, and I can only imagine the types and building of these have gotten better since 1998. I probably would not recommend them for really trying to sound great in a championship contest, but certainly for my playing Amazing Grace out here in the countryside no one is complaining about a squeak now and then as I relearned, and no one could tell ANY diff with the medium Clanrye EVER that I had going. I've since went to Maclaren, and am eager to see what else comes along. For petes sake, if the drone reeds can be Synthedrone, EEZEEDrone, and the like--plus putting kitty litter in canisters with hoses and piping with ZIPPERS in the Ross and Bannatyne bags now...why bi*** about a plastic chanter reed that supposedly sounds \\"unnatural\\" or is \\"not traditional\\". If you want traditional, get out the sheep bladder, tune in your bog oak drones, and get the canes out. For me meself...I LUV my Clanrye and look to the future with excitement.ture with excitement.

(I have used 3 different computers and it distorts randomly on all three). The first track laid down is usually OK unless there are pops in it, but when overdubbing, the overdub track usually distorts badly. I tried lowering the rate to 32000Hz (from my normal 44100 kHz) on subsequent overdub tracks, which seemed to help, but I want my overdub tracks at the same rate as the first track, and I should not need to change the rate. Am currently using Audacity software..which I hope is the problem instead of this unit. Am now testing with Cubase LE5, the software that came with the unit, and will post results when done.

product_title: TASCAM DR-07MKII Portable Digital Recorder
review_body:
This is my first and only handheld, digital recorder, so that may or may not bias my full opinion.

There is a .PDF list of approved to be used SD Cards on Tascam's website that anyone who is buying should glance at before buying a separate card.
The device comes with a microSD card (2 gb), but in today's market, getting a larger card isn't that expensive.

I do advise to purchase a windscreen if you plan to use this product outdoors or anywhere with a slight breeze. The windscreen really cleans up and protects against unnecessary noise.

All in all, this is a great product that I use currently, and for the future, to record voice notes in various settings (self-use, lectures, interviews, etc.), music (acoustic guitar, live shows), and much more.

Another thing one should note is that the build quality is primarily plastic, so adjusting or moving your hand on the device when recording will produce noise, so I would say it would be best to either plan to delay what you want to record if setting the device down, or using the device's delay feature.

product_title: Schecter Stargazer-12 Electric Guitar (12 String, Gloss Black)
review_body: This is one of the best playing guitars I've ever picked up, and due to its excellent action, it's actually easier to play than many 6-strings.  It arrived with the action and intonation requiring absolutely no adjustment.  Since much has already been written in general about these, I'll give some measurements.  The neck width at the nut is 44mm, with about 1.5mm space between string pairs, and about 4.5mm space between sets.  This makes it easy to reach across the neck and to hold down paired strings, but fat fingers will probably have some difficulty with brushing adjacent strings.  The action height is only about 1mm above the 1st fret, going up to about 1.5mm at the 12th fret...effortless.  The bridge independently adjusts height for every string, with the high octaves strung into the bridge, and the low octaves being strung through the body.  Stringing order is standard, with the higher octave on top, and the last two pairs in the same octave.  Overall construction is heavy, it stays tuned, and I have no worries about neck strain with it fully tuned.  The finish is flawless.  As has been noted elsewhere, Schecter is keeping the price reasonable on these by perhaps not using the most impressive electrics.  The pickups are decent, and they can be split from humbucker to single-coil with noticeable effect.  But the pots and switch are definitely not "mil-spec," and tone and volume control are rather non-linear.  However, that's the way to do it.  You can always change out the electrics on a well-made guitar later, but there isn't much you can do about something that isn't well-constructed.  And this is definitely a well-constructed instrument that plays more like something that might run twice the price.  Summary: Excellent build-quality, excellent action, fair electrics, easy to play but not built for fat-fingers, bargain price for the build-quality.

product_title: Sony MDR7506 Professional Large Diaphragm Headphone
review_headline: Great headphones, but you might as well save yourself some cash and get the V6s
review_body:
These are quickly becoming my go-to headphones. I'm a bit of an audio enthusiast, so much so that' I've developed tinnitus over the years (I play music, mix it, listen to it constantly). I've owned various flavors of Sennheiser and Grado in the $80-$250 range. Since developing tinnitus I can no longer use Grados because they make my tinnitus really flare up and Sennheisers just don't work for me.

Money is tight, so I've been on the hunt for decent headphones in the $80-$100 range. Also, I've been looking for a pair that are easy to drive because I don't want to carry an amp around, plus I like the convenience of using my smartphone as a music player. After much auditioning I've come to these, and I love them!

I need to play my music at about 1/4 volume max to keep the pain away and these are just so silky smooth at that level. As I turn them up they flatten out and some of the finer details start emerging more, which distracts my 'inner-mixologist' because flaws in the music/mix/source start to pop out more, which makes these sound more like monitors. This feature is great for mixing though, so being one who mixes this is a bit of a win/win, but some folks who prefer louder listening levels might find these too flat and fatiguing.

They are more comfortable than my Grados, and this is before I mod them with Beyer pads, which as I understand makes these far more comfortable still. Stock they aren't perfect though. They are nice and cushiony but the pleather gives me hot spots.

Construction seems solid overall. The long curled cord is great for the studio, but awkward on the go.

You should know that there is a hot debate as to whether these or the Sony MDR-V6s are better. Because audiophiles debate this so often that must mean they will sound essentially the same to most of us, and that's because they ARE essentially the same. The grounds are wired a bit differently and the 7506s have a gold-plated plug while theV6s are nickel-plated, but this has no effect sonically, so essentially they are the same thing.

Great headphones! Go audition them at a place like Guitar Center and if you like them then get the V6s. I wish I had known about the V6s before making my purchase, but I never ran across them while auditioning and fell in love with these instantly, so I bought them on the spot. Still a great value at $100 though.

review_body:
..Including your mood.

Being a triumph of ergonomic industrial design as well as an artwork in its own right is all very well, ...but that's of absolutely NO use to me if it doesn't securely retain its settings under load.

\\"Load\\"?

Surely not a 14kg (31lb) Gator GM-4WR rack of four radio mic receivers?

Done.

It turns out to be the perfect height to create a vertical stack of two. Safely. Almost invisibly. With easy access to all sides. Crane's ingenious \\"T-piece tongue\\" simply slides beneath the lower rack so that the pair of front panels align as a neat vertical \\"wall.\\"

The only limit to loading seems to be the strength of an operator's hand and wrist when it comes to levering the beautifully sculpted and brilliantly engineered cams that drive Crane's unique and mind-bogglingly rugged locking mechanism.

Extreme force may indeed temporarily bend the whole assembly, ...after which it simply springs back to its original shape.

Amazingly, it's even secure enough to provide the carpal tunnel alleviating wrist support required for long-term ergonomic benefits.

There's just one problem.

I bought the blasted thing to elevate my laptop to the medically advised height for working on my feet over a standard desk, ...but now I'm also using it for my radio mics (the way others will almost certainly now do, as well as for individually angling secure positions for controllers, consoles, bookshelf speakers and all sorts of other gear) ...and I'd really HATE to front my doctor after going back to my previous arrangement for typing.

Damn. It looks like I'll have to order another one.

So, Dr Crane, these things should carry a health warning.

Maybe something like: \\"Experts advise that prolonged use of the infinitely variable angle-adjustable versions of the Crane Stand may prove to be highly addictive.\\"

review_body:
I use this at work and plug it into a portable amplifier that I wear on my belt to be able to project louder in a noisy environment and save my voice. I have been using this particular microphone for about 6 months now on almost a daily basis (8 hours a day, 5 days a week).

Sound Quality: 8/10 Not incredible but great for the price. Feedback at high volumes. Not as good as the mic I had previously which cost $90, but you get what you pay for. Not bad really. Get's the job done for speaking, but wouldn't be cut out for singing.

Durability: 9/10 Excellent. Mine has lasted months with nearly daily use carried back and forth to work each day, worn most of the day at work as I move around quite a bit. Gets packed an unpacked in the cardboard box I keep it in multiple times a day and shoved in a locker. This unit has lasted much longer than my previous microphone that cost $90. My only complaint is that the windscreens fall off easily. I lost one already (it comes with two) and when this one disappears for the last time, I don't know if I will be able to order stand-alone windscreens but using it with a windscreen is necessary. Without one, letters like "p" are dangerous.

Fit/Design: The length of the boom itself is ridiculously long. I had to bend mine extensively to make it work for my face, and I don't have a particularly small head. It also does not stay put behind my ear consistently when I move (or I don't move) unless I have it tucked into a hat that holds it in place. That's rather annoying, but I can deal with it.

Bottom-Line:

I would recommend this product to others and I will buy it again in the future once this one inevitably wears out/gets damaged from extensive use over time.
