An excellent drum for the price. Just about any issues I could possibly have with this drum are satisfactorily offset by the fact it's priced around $100, which is an excellent price for a cajon.

I also own a regular Meinl cajon.

The slap-top cajon is very nice looking, especially the makah-burl wood-grain top. The plastic cylinder used in the sound project port really seems to improve the sound over the basic hole used on regular cajons.

The slap-top design makes this much easier to play. You can sit and place it between your knees, or place it on a table and stand in front of it (my preferred method). I'm planning to buy a snare drum stand since I've seen a number of videos on the web with people playing it that way. There are nice thin foam pads under each wing to make the drum more comfortable when you're playing with it resting on your knees.

There are four hard rubber feet at the bottom.

The drum surface is divided into three areas: a central area over the central "box", and two small areas over each "wing". The central area produces deeper bass notes....not quite a true bass drum, but decent. A regular cajon produces better bass sounds, but that’s to be expected since it is a larger instrument.

The right area of the slap-top cajon produces almost a bongo sound. The left area has snare wires within it so you can get a toned-down snare drum sound. There's a small hole under the snare area for sound projection. For more on issues with the snare drum, see below.

The sound varies depending upon where you strike the surface, so you can develop a moderate range of tones with practice.

You won't be telephoned by a big name rock band begging you to join but there's quite a bit of novelty appeal and it's really fun to play.

I'll write another review in the future after I've wired the thing with a microphone and amp.

----------

ISSUES WITH THE SNARE DRUM:

I've read a number of reviews on this drum that indicate there is a wide variation in the sound from drum to drum. Most say they are happy with the bass sound but are not happy with the quality of the snare sound. There are a smaller number of reviews that state the reverse. I've actually read reviews by a few folks that said they bought two of the drums....one for bass, the other for the snare sound and higher tone notes.

With my drum, if was the first situation: good bass notes, but hardly any snare sound. I experimented a lot, but just couldn't get that portion of the cajon to produce a good sound.

So, I finally flipped the drum over and removed the 6 Philips screws under the "wing" with the snare. I removed the cover, exposing the inside of the compartment. Inside, there is a small metal bar with 20 snare wires welded to it, creating a brush effect. These wires run along the underside of the striking surface, generating a snare drum sound when the surface of the drum above them is struck. [Put "Cajon Snare Wires" in a web search engine and look at images to see what these look like.]

The metal bar that the snare wires are attached to is held to a wooden brace inside the cajon by only a single wood screw. I removed the screw and took out the snare wires.

The snare wires that came with the drum were only 4 inches long. If you look at pictures of cajon snare wires (on the web), you'll see that they are normally a good bit longer than 4 inches. It made sense to me that the longer the snare wires, the better they would vibrate.

So, I decided to replace mine. I went to a local music store and bought a single package of replacement snare drum wires. The packages range from $10 to $20 (U.S.). This is a smaller cajon so I bought the cheaper package. It's designed for a regular snare drum so the wires have the metal bar on both ends and are 14" inches long.

I also bought a couple of #6 1/2 inch wood screws.

I wanted a clean cut without bending the wires so I had my friend use his Dremel rotary cutter tool to cut the wires. I made the wires 7 1/2 inches long.

I then installed the new snare wires in the drum. There are two round holes in the metal bar so I used two wood screws to hold it down instead of only one. I figured this would keep the snare from shifting around over time. The wooden brace is cut at a bit of an angle so it presses the snare wires against the bottom surface of the drum top as you tighten the screws. I centered the snare in the compartment. Then I replaced the compartment cover and the six screws.

The result? A dramatic improvement in the quality of the snare sound, and a drum I'm very happy with.

As an option, you could leave the bottom compartment cover off. Most people would never notice this unless they stooped down and looked at the underside of the drum. It hasn't happened to me but I've been told that if the snare develops a tinny rattle or metallic 'echo'....which can happen with any cajon.....I can use tape to "tighten" the wires against the underside of the drum. It's a bit of a trial-and-error process.

I hope you enjoy your cajon as much as I do mine.#34; inches long.

product_title: Roland CUBE-40XL 40-Watt 1x10-Inch Guitar Combo Amp
review_body:
Incredible amp. I was looking for something portable to take to smallish jazz gigs so the clean sound was the real appeal. I was hesitant because of the review comments about hiss. Whatever was going on with the hiss has been fixed, as this amp is dead silent in both clean and dirty channels. The clean sound is absolutely perfect, outstanding for jazz, the effects work simply and sound great, and the lead sounds are awesome as well, the Boogie sounds and feels dead on to me. I couldn't be happier, and I can't figure out how this well built marvel can be so affordable. the only thing that bums me out is my $2400 Boogie Mark combo is relegated to the garage, I can't justify lugging all that mess and separate effects pedals etc. Setup with this thing is a few seconds.

As for the power, it has more than enough power for any rock gig I've ever done, not interested in doing anything so loud that this thing couldn't handle!

product_title: Promark SR3BLA Stick Rapp Drumstick Wrap, Black Splatter
review_body:
Beware that this is the solid-black grip tape, and not the splatter pattern shown in the picture. For a splatter pattern similar to the picture, see [[ASIN:B000BJUSMA Pro-Mark SR3WHI]]. It's not EXACTLY like the pic, but it's as close as you can get on Amazon, as of my writing this. Also FYI, each package has four pieces of tape, to wrap two PAIRS of sticks.

Anyway, this is the best grip tape out there, and I've tried them all. This stuff adds a real quality rubberized sort of feel to your sticks that's not as harsh as other grip tape materials. It's damn near luxurious.

FYI, the [[ASIN:B000GE7OE0 Vater]] and [[ASIN:B0002D0HW6 Ahead]] versions are basically the same material, but are much more expensive (the Ahead package only comes with one pair).

It's also reusable a few times, but degrades each time you unwrap it, so you will need to re-purchase it periodically.

It also looks great, incidentally. It comes with a decal to cover the top seam where the tape ends, which just looks awesomely professional, as if the stick was manufactured with the tape already on. People who see my sticks with this stuff on think they came that way.

You have a choice as to how \\"cushioned\\" your grip will be, depending on how much you choose to overlap as you wrap. Doing a complete overlap, so that the entire taped surface has two tape layers, provides a nice cushy feel in addition to providing grip. Doing a wider wrap, with gaps between your overlaps, leaves the stick feeling more narrow and solid. Which way you go with is a matter of preference. I personally always liked the latter option better, mainly because, to me, the double-layer cushioning makes sticks feel unnaturally fat at the bottom, and unbalanced.

Now for the caveat:

Being a somewhat violent drummer, it makes my hands blister faster than naked sticks do. But that's just an incidental truth about all grip tapes, and this tape is actually the most minor offender I could find, so I'm not removing points for it. But I feel it necessary to point out that, due to that issue, I'm actually more a fan of wax these days (see [[ASIN:B0007Y18UA Zildjian Wax]] and [[ASIN:B009LQWVKQ Sex Wax]]), which provides a more subtle grip.

Nevertheless, for many years I was using grip tape, and Pro Mark's version was always the best. I even miss the nice look and feel of it, since wax has neither (even if it is better for my hands). Oh well.inor offender I could find, so I'm not removing points for it. These extenders work well to extend the shelf of our Manhasset stand. From reviews, I wasn't sure if it would work on other stands. The answer is a qualified \\"sometimes.\\" It will not work on our Hamilton stand, because the Hamilton has a lip on the shelf (plus the shelf is too deep). I does work on our folding Jamstand music stand, although it takes a bit of manual dexterity to get it on. On the Jamstand the top of the extenders aren't supported, but they do seem to stay on because of the clamping action of the base.

It's disappointing that Manhasset hasn't figured out a design that would work easily on other stands.

Another consideration: if you want to use a Manasset clip-on shelf to hold pencils, capos, etc., then you can only fit on 1 of the extenders.

The price is double what I would have expected for a plastic item like this.

I usually use Vandoren V-12 reeds, but I have some Rico's which would also fit in the case, as they are the same length as the V-12's (all soprano reeds tend to be about the same length).

This is a great case because it holds the reeds down flat, and tightly. This is essential to making sure your reeds stay flat and do not warp at the tip while not in use. I bought a bigger case a few months ago and am not as pleased with it as this one, because the reeds fit so snugly in the protec case and therefore don't warp. Great case--holds 12 reeds.

product_title: Pyle-Pro PPEQ100 19'' Rack Mount Dual 10 Band 4 Source Input Stereo Spectrum Graphic Equalizer
review_body:
The graphic equalizer works, but this is the only good thing to say. The blue LEDs in the sliders are blindingly bright, so while the unit is on it is impossible to see the scale behind them. The waveform display has two problems. One is that the display is upside down. The segments are lit from top to bottom and I've never seen any waveform display do that. The other problem is that it doesn't display a true frequency spectrum. Not even something close. The waveform does not change much regardless of the frequency composition of the input signal.

Also, the supplied brackets for the 19 inch rack are too small. I had to put 2 washers between the chassis and the brackets on both sides to barely make the screw holes to align (horizontally). I couldn't use more washers, because the supplied screws are too short for more. And the screw holes do not align vertically at all, but the unit is light enough to be mounted with just one screw on each side.

I bought 2 units with the same issues, so there is a design deficiency and not a problem with a particular unit. Well, the first unit had an additional problem (when EQ was switched on, one channel would go silent, left if I remember correctly), but the second unit was free from that defect.

I emailed tech support at Pyle about the problem with this and other Pyle products I bought, but I did not receive any response. This was almost a month ago. I also called and left a message, but no response to that form of contact either.

I'll probably keep it tuned EADGBE for now but have no worries about tuning back up to ADGCEA (tenor ukulele) with these strings when I feel like it. product_title: Left Handed Beginner Black Electric Guitar Package with Amp Case Picks Strap Value Pack
review_body:
I ordered this a couple weeks ago, just before the Easter holiday. I am a beginning left-handed guitarist, and so the low price, high ratings and left-handed orientation of this guitar inspired me to purchase it. It was shipped promptly. However, when I received it, the cable connecting the guitar to the amp was missing so I couldn't play the guitar. I contacted the seller and they responded quickly and were very courteous and helpful. They sent me a new cord and even said that if I did find my original cord, I could keep both of them. I got the new cord in about three days.

The amp works great; it has a lot of power to be so small, and the overdrive function and other effects work perfectly. It has a slight buzz, but that's normal as far as I know, especially for the price. The handle on the amp is a bit tight, but it's not that big of a deal. The guitar itself is a bit simple, but for such an incredibly low price it is in great condition, especially having a nice humbucker pickup. I wish it had a second pickup, but again it's understandable for the price. It keeps its tuning decently well. However, a few days after I got the new cable, I took my guitar to a local music shop and for about $45 had them fix it up. They fixed the intonation, the action and replaced the strings (the originals were a bit big and rough on the fingers), and now it works perfectly (though the sixth string buzzes a little if played hard). I also bought an electronic tuner, simply because a pitchpipe is difficult for a beginner, but at least it came with a tuner of some kind. One other problem I have encountered is the carrying case. The inside of it was a bit marked up and patchy when I first got it, and recently the zipper on the outer pouch broke off spontaneously as I tried to open it, having worked fine beforehand. I just chalk it up to another feature of this being a low priced guitar.

Despite some of my difficulties, I still gave this a five-star rating for threereasons: it's left-handed, which is rare and hard to find; the sellers were quick, helpful and courteous; and it is very cheap yet very nice quality even with some of the problems. God bless. :)

Note: After contacting the seller about my broken carrying bag, they have offered to send me a replacement and responded very quickly and courteously. I greatly appreciate their efforts.

review_body:
These monitors work perfect. They are flat response and are over and above the expectation for my home studio. They are quite large, so make sure to have room for them wherever you plan to place them.

I was shopping for as close to flat response as I could get and at the price, these were my choice. I couldn't be happier with my purchase and these will be the dominant force in my home studio. I also plan on purchaseing the sr-10 to accompany these as I am so happy with them I'll stick to the brand for my subwoofer. I have the gain set on 1/3'rd and they get too loud for my house. These truly help master audio in the home studio, and I'm quite sure would work well on the professional end but have no experience in a professional studio. Questions, email me joefro21@gmail.com

After now another month with these monitors, I have to try and communicate a nuance that I solved by just turning down the gain on the high pass filter on the rear of the monitors. It seemed that the high's were a bit harsh and I hadn't adjusted the gain on the high's at this point. When I moved my chair maybe a foot backwards, they were not harsh or too bright. When I reduced the gain, they were now ok at the distance I sit from them. Although these are near field monitors, I really feel I would gain quite a bit of ease on my ears if I could distance myself another foot or two and create a larger equilateral triangle connecting me and the two monitors(moving my sweet spot a bit farther back than it is now). They sound good, but the sweet spot seems to be just behind me. I don't think this equates to something bad about the monitors, just understand the amount of room needed to operate them correctly in a studio, home or pro.

product_title: rolls CL151 Comp/Limiter Gate
review_body:
I bought a used item to save $10 which covered the shipping cost. No factory box. Item does appear to function normally. Condition looks new.

Metal chassis with rubber feet.

No instructions with the used item but the PDF manual is free online. There's a 2-page and a 4-page version, with the 2-page apparently missing the final paragraph (because the final paragraph is actually first on the page).

No ON/OFF switch, just a wallwart to disconnect.

Input is XLR or balanced 1/4 TRS, Output is balanced 1/4 TRS. Too small a unit for XLR Out.

12V Phantom Power has no switch -- it uses a jumper accessible from the side, with a permanently open hole to insert needlenose pliers.

The input preamp is quiet, other than adding ambient background noise. A supercardioid mic might help if it's a problem.

The output amp adds a little white noise, but not too bad if kept low.

The Gate Release knob adjusts the time the gate remains on before it closes, from 1 second to approximately 1/10th second.

When Input/Output knobs are set quiet, the Gate at first seems useless as there is too long a delay for it to close, which cuts off a portion of the first word no matter what settings are used.

When Input/Output knobs are set close to max, the Gate remains remains closed acting as a 20dB pad, which prevents cutting off the first word. But if the Gate opens beware blowing your speakers or eardrums.

Otherwise the Gate works very well at noise reduction. I hear talk radio stations and networks with a gate setting that likewise cuts off the first word of callers, so perhaps this is a problem with all gates?

If the Input/Output knobs are set too hot both the compressor and gate pop loudly when cutting on/off at high volume/distortion (apparently the Limiter?), but no popping when levels are kept reasonable.

The Compressor Threshhold knob is the main compression control.

The Compressor Ratio knob appears to have only a mild effect, effectively rendering the Rolls a \\"One Knob Compression\\" unit.

For a few dollars more you can buy a mixer with \\"one knob compression\\", plus lots of other features. There's a tendency to play around with too many knobs without positive effect, wasting time. I do have high-freq hearing damage, so perhaps someone with a very selective ear would hear differently.

It uses 12VDC with a wallwart, so a battery pack can be used for remote locations, but you must build it or find one that fits.

If you need the cheapest compressor in the smallest package, for use outside the studio, this unit will do the job best. For studio use a mixer with compression would be a better bargain, with fewer cables. The Yamaha MG102C has compression, and is actually the same price since no cable is required to connect a compressor.

Perhaps all multi-knob compressors are this complicated, in which case the Rolls CL152 is a practical training tool.

If you spend many hours adjusting knobs, it may be possible to find a \\"perfect\\" setting. Like finding the Holy Grail. After 3 hours I did not find it. Not yet.on control.

product_title: Tascam CD
review_body:
I just got my CD200 and wanted to write a much more in depth review then most have, to really give the end user some info about this machine in use.

I have to say I really do like how this player sounds, Note to anyone that for some reason may think this is a recorder, it is in fact a player and has only outputs. If a player is what you are looking for please continue reading my review.

All testing was done on my set of Energy Monitors made in Canada, a Carver M500t, and a Classic Urei 1620 as the mixer preamp set completely flat. This should give you a good idea of the sound to expect.

Lets get right to the sound, so how does this player sound, I would have to say it has a very smooth high end with a really punchy well defined mid and bottom. The D/A Converter in this machine sounds nice and clean. Very similar to what I loved about my classic Natural Sound Yamaha's and that I have not found in other machines.

Even recordings that sound harsh on other players example: \\"Super Tramp Breakfast In America\\" sound smooth and pleasing to this reviewers ear, yet not muted nor muddy in any way, Well recorded vocals have a nice open out in front presence. Piano on Tori's CD \\"Boys For Pele\\" sounds very natural and maintains great depth and definition without a cluttered bottom.

I have also been putting it through some of the simple tests I use to see how accurately a CD Player can cue tracks with little to no servo slop. My favorite CD for this challenge is the Led Zep album from 1969 titled Led Zeppelin, why you ask would this prove anything? well I am going to tell you, yes there is a method to my madness.

This CD is a problem for most CD Players that I have used over the years, because of the way 2 tracks were mastered so tightly together that unless the machine could determine the exact beginning of the song \\"Dazed And Confused\\" it would play a quarter second of the last note in the song \\"You Shook Me\\". My original high end Yamaha CD2000's passed this cue test no problem where most would fail.

Why is this a big deal? The reason is, because this would be totally unacceptable in a pro set up. For example if this was used to cue a song at a Radio Station, Play or Studio. We would want the player to start the track at the exact second, if not it will sound like an audio glitch for some Tracks.

The reason why I wanted to point this out is for some that may use this in a pro setting it is extremely accurate at cuing tracks. I see no mention of this in the few reviews listed here or anywhere else. In fact it excels in this. You cant expect this from just any consumer deck. They are not created equal at all and were not designed to do so. If cuing accuracy is important this is a great choice.

Build quality, some say build is really good. My opinion is average build, and could be a lot better. Yes I am very picky about my gear.

For the money it is acceptable. My comparison on this is based on many other Tascam products I also own where the build fit and finish is much higher. I do not like the overly bright LCD based display at all and feel this was a big mistake on Tascam's part to choose such a display. Really a nice easy to read at any angle standard florescent display would have been the best choice in my opin. I will try and find a way to make this a lot dimmer and am surprised that no dimmer control is provided to set this to your own taste, as Oppo has done with there Blu-Ray decks.

This is nit picking but the logo badge is not in perfect alignment with the model number and it should be, this shows lack of attention to detail. The front panel should be the same epoxy finished aluminum as past products were built with, not plastic as this is.

The remote is really cheep in look and feel, they should have provided a much nicer remote and have skimped on this big time, looks and feels very generic no weight at all even with the batteries installed.

I feel those corners shouldn't have been cut in a pro type deck. Considering some consumer decks still use nice real aluminum face plates. The rotary controls are not of the same Tascam HQ that I am used to, they feel a little flimsy and have play in them. Not the norm for any Tascam I have ever owned. My 122 MK2 controls are rock solid in comparison and still work like new.

The overall cabinet build is better with a fairly thick steel chassis that feels pretty solid considering how most products are built today.

Again I feel the sound is excellent and the cue capability of the transport is very accurate, so on this it is a great buy. I just wish they would have paid more attention to detail and provided a much better display, or at the very least a way to dim this immensely bright LCD display.

If someone has a mod and knows how to dim the display without a lot of fuss please do comment.t all even with the batteries installed.

review_headline: Garbage proudly made in America - beware and never buy!
review_body:
I bought this product after looking at exciting reviews and expecting that the product is really high end and gives excellent isolation.
I received the product in the nice box with \\"proudly made in USA\\" and a lot of proud stickers, and then my troubles began.

First, I was not impressed with sound and specifically with isolation. A cheap $3 ear protectors bought in Harbor freight attenuated sound more.

Second, the headphones are made from un-flexible plastic and they squeeze my head too strong that I cannot wear them longer than 5 minutes.
Third, after the moderate use for a year the joints between the head cups and the top headrest broke today and the spring hurt my head. This pushed me to finally write a review.

Interestingly, some time ago the headphones fell from the desk to floor and fell apart, and what was revealed was even more amazing. In the plastic cup one will find a layer of foam (just the same as in $3 cups, but only one layer - which explains the lower attenuation). And there was yet another headphone (- it was definitely a part of other headphone - and there was a text \\"to open, turn 1/4\\" slowly left\\"), but this headphone was ROUND while the hole in the panel was oblong - so it did not cover the hole eniterely). So this \\"proudly made in USA\\" headphone is glued from a cheap noise isolation cups and some other inexpensive headphones without caring a lot about acoustics. I will post pictures to show my findings.

The only good news I can say - it came with a very convenient gold-plated adapter between 3.5mm jack and 1/4\\" jack for plugging into mixers which tigtly screws on the original jack. The rest is garbage.

product_title: Hohner Inc. 560BX-BF Special Twenty Harmonica
review_headline: Wrong Unit #1 of 3, good Major G Harmonica
review_body:
This was my first attempt to get a good deal on a minor key harmonica from Amazon. I asked for this Special 20 (as a gift - also bought from Amazon) Minor G for Christmas that turned out also to be a Major G. I then ordered a Blues Harp Minor G for $15.98, it's also a great harmonica but also was sent the wrong key (Major G). After that I ordered a third unit, a Minor A Marine band for $20 - which also had been swapped for a Major key.
I'm not how the business works of swapping out cheap Minor harmonica units with much more costly Major ones, but three in a row? There must be something going on. The boxes were clearly resealed with the same factory sticker as the first one. Perhaps they are shipped to Amazon with the cardboard flat and are boxed up by people with no-music-theory. Maybe there's a conspiracy to keep musicians away from Minor key instruments. Maybe Hohner doesn't really make Minor key harmonicas, just refunds for the few musicians who can tell the difference but unlike myself wouldn't rather get a better deal on the purchise. Perhaps the California no returns on breath instruments law has something to do with this. I've no idea.

My advice, if it's under twenty bucks buy it to get a good deal, but don't expect the right key. If it has to be the right key - please support your local music store.

Hohner makes three classes of harmonicas in terms of build quality - toy harmonicas made in China for $5 to $20 (stay away from these), decent German made harmonicas from $20 to $50, and professional musical instruments (usually $40 to $150 - also made in Germany but with a lot more care).
The Special 20 is a strange hybrid that I would say has the hand feel of one of the toy lines - but has the tuning and playability of a higher end decent instrument. The parts are interchangeable with the Chinese made toys - a fun trick if you want to warp musicians minds. If you want an example of of the high end keep an eye out for a sale of the Meisterklasse, Crossover, or a Signature Bob Dylan - they sometimes drop below $50. Note - nearly all harmonicas require a break-in period - a couple of hours of playing without pushing too hard for the reeds to wear in. You can tell if a harmonica hasn't been broken in yet by playing very lightly - you can hear extra tones and ringing that does not fit to the key as the reads are still binding with the plates. Also the instrument might require a slight tuning adjustment after it's been played a while.

product_title: Lanikai NK-C Custom Series Koa Concert Ukulele
review_body:
The Lanikai NK-C is definitely a beautiful Ukulele. Unfortunately I had to return it although now I realize this may have been due to my own inexperience with ukuleles. I'm still not sure. What happened was, when it arrived the strings were taut, not slack. My previous purchase, a Kala Concert also arrived with taut strings and after a few turns, they were in perfect tune. A Koa Pili Koko soprano I ordered arrived with very slack strings so I just kept tightening them until Uke was in tune.
But ..with the Lanikai, no matter how I tightened or loosened the strings I could not get it anywhere close to being tuned. The G string played D, the C string an E and so on. I tried tightening, I tried loosening ... but now I am thinking, maybe I just needed to keep tightening until it was right. I was afraid to do that, afraid I would snap the strings. That may have been my inexperience. With the KPK, it was obvious what to do: keep turning until it is right. If the Lanikai had arrived with slack strings, I would have figured it out as I did with the KPK. if it had been only slightly out of tune, as the Kala was, I could have tuned it quickly.
So a note to Lanikai quality control: either send the Ukes with slack strings, or get them at least close to being in tune. Just my two cents. Or maybe there really was something wrong with those strings, I'll never know. It was a lovely little Uke so four stars for that. Now I'm awaiting arrival of the Uke I ordered to replace it, a Cordoba concert. I don't want to try another Lanikai for now, maybe later.
Thanks to Amazon for an easy return policy!

Gobos are nice and offer a \\"shake\\" mode but no gobo rotation. Light can be strobed and has a nice dimming feature. Power consumption is super low on these fixtures and unit features fan cooling but the light never seems to get \\"hot\\". No duty cycle, run constantly if you like.

Model is getting to be outdated - these lights are ok at best if you are looking for affordable moving mirror scanners at this price point since they can now be had at a third of their MSRP.

I have a total of five of this particular scanner. One has an issue and is in need of service again, support is pretty painful and pretty much no help other than send it back especially when ADJ sells parts consumer direct via internet web site. That's the main reason for my reduction in rating. The other four units continue to work like new.

product_title: Boss LS-2 Line Selector
review_headline: This should be in your pedal train
review_body:
I bought one of these because I have a love-hate relationship with multi-effects pedals. While you can get a really really cool sound and lots of presets, they don't respond like a traditional foot pedal and have a delay when switching between settings. This frustrates me as a quick change from clean to distortion or to add boost to a solo by selecting the next setting is always sloppy when playing live,and I paid a lot of cash for the multi-effect processor. Not to mention the time spent tweaking all that effects power to get that perfect sound and then sounding like an amature when you hit the switch and there's a half second delay when you need crisp changes.

So... I tried to run the guitar through an A-B switch and then through one set of pedals to get a nice clean sound with chorus, delay, etc. Then channel B went through a second effect chain for distortion, with a booster pedal for leads. I had to use two channels in a PA board to do this, which sucks if you have a small board. If I don't run through the PA though, I can't do this and go into one amp and I really don't want to lug two around with me. All I can do is use the clean channel with the built in reverb and the effects all need tapping instead of being set for the distortion sound I'm looking for. It's tough to hit them all at the same time. What's a musician to do?

Maybe your amp has some effects, but they are probably pre-set and not able to really adjustable. AND, the distortion pedals all have gain or volume knobs that make them louder than the clean channel. I don't like compressors, so I'm pretty much angry that I have that beautiful tone that I spent hours getting on the multi-effects processor for the perfect clean sound that I can't really use.

Finally, I saw this pedal for sale on the used table at the local music shop. Problem solved. Effects loop 1 is for distortion sound, with a boost in the chain. Effects Loop 2 goes through the multi-effects pedal which I can now switch to other cool settings to add flange or other sounds when I need them and switch to go through the processor with this cool selector pedal. The Channel Select pedal is an A-B switch for two effects loops. It even has volume for each loop so you can set them to work together perfectly. Feels like a real pedal, responds like a real pedal, is durable like a real pedal: because it is a real pedal. Love it. Love it. Love it.

The reviewer saying it does all kinds of other cool stuff, like two guitars mixed into one amp, and other really really useful stuff that will get you out of a bind if you need some flexibility. I can't believe I didn't know these existed. I give this a full 5-stars with gusto.

I do get sound from regular audio though, which is weird, and there's no support from Avid for this software. I asked around and people told me it was probably because I was running Mountain Lion instead of Lion, which is silly. After installing Pro Tools over and over I just gave up and kept recording on garageband. Pro Tools SE is actually very limited as far as what you can do, you can't even add plug-ins or virtual instruments. What a piece of garbage.

Bottom line, get the interface but skip the software. In fact, just get it used from a reseller and download the drivers from Avid. That DVD is garbage and not worth a single penny.

product_title: Schecter OMEN-7 7-String Electric Guitar, Black
review_headline: Tremendous value -  a Quality Instrument Mass-Produced for a Good Price
review_body:
I've been playing about 25 years, and I will be the first to tell you - I am NOT a gear or tone snob. If I was, I wouldn't be buying a guitar off the internet. Truth is, guitars at this price point are mass-produced, and if you have a modicum of setup ability, there will be very little to differentiate one particular piece from another. These are machine-made guitars, which means there's an abundance of consistency in build quality, aesthetics, and feel, so it all comes down to materials, general craftsmanship, and features.

At this price point, you don't get options. There's no hardshell case here (not even a gig bag), one allen wrench, and little else. The money was spent where it was important: the guitar and hardware, and the packaging. Packaging was a Russian Stackie-doll - it was in three layers of cardboard and styrofoam to keep it safe. Awesome.

The guitar itself is solid and well-built. The finish is a fantastic and thick gel-coat paint, which should be good for a very long and difficult life. The wood all around is really sharp, with the neck and fretboard being especially well done. Tuners are solid and work well, and the nut is grooved well and lubricated well - the strings slide nicely over it.

It needed some setup when I got it. The neck was adjusted well, so no truss adjustments, but I did need to lower the action, and after I string it with my own brand and gauge of strings, I will need to do the intonation, which is off. It feels like it's strung with .11's which is odd.

The neck is thin but VERY wide (this is my first 7 string, so I can't compare it against other 7s, just against a 6 stringer), and has a light satin or bare finish - perfect.

The pickups are tolerable, but I will likely research available 7-string pickups and replace them in the next few months, which I think will make this a stellar axe.

I see Schecter in more or less the same place Ibanez was when I started playing, back in the 80s (and I still have and play all of my old Ibanez guitars from the 80s and 90s) - a relatively young company hungry for the next wave of shredders, aggressively signing endorsements and making high-quality, low-cost instruments, with some stepping up to a mid-level in cost, as well. It will be interesting to see how they grow in years to come.

Overall, my expectations of a $350 instrument were realistic, and this particular guitar far exceeded them.playing, back in the 80s (and I still have and play all of my old Ibanez guitars from the 80s and 90s) - a relatively young company hungry for the next wave of shredders, aggressively signing endorsements and making high-quality, low-cost instruments, with some stepping up to a mid-level in cost, as well. review_body:
When I saw this instrument on youtube I thought, wow, jackpot! now I can play both at the same time. Well, not so fast Jack!
Ok, so the maracas are built well and sound way better than the LP big plastic yellow ones. The wooden "clave" handles are nice and big but they aren't quite true "claves" and hence you won't get the authentic sound. Keep in mind that to obtain a good clave sound, usually there's one stick built from a different heavier and denser wood and that one does the striking, while the other stick is usually fatter and receives all the hits. This last one is called "hembra" female, lol, and guess who takes care of the hitting, the "macho" male. Anyways, enough of the spanish lesson.

Getting to play the maracas and the clave pattern in sync is not a task for the faint of heart, it will take some practice and so far I haven't been able to do it at faster tempos. They work well for slow to moderate tempos. Like a Bolero song for example, but when do you hear claves in Bolero anyways, never! So for Son songs, which are usually moderate to frisk tempos these maracas will be nearly impossible to play and sound well. So, I am keeping them but I don't think I will be using them much really, more as a spare set of maracas or a learning aid for someone, etc. Since, if I want a great maraca sound I might as well play on a standard leather or gourd maraca.

product_title: Dean Markley 1973 Vintage Reissue Electric Guitar Strings 12-Pack
review_body:
A buddy told me a while back that strings are strings and there's little difference between makers. Well with hex cores that may be true, to a point. But when it comes to the old style round core strings, ya gotta know what you're doing if you're gonna sell them and expect them to be bought again later. So what's with round core's? Simple, they \\"bloom\\" when they get plucked, picked, or strummed. I mean they increase in volume after being picked rather than with hex cores that are loudest at first and decay after that. The difference in overall tone is noticeable and for many older players like myself, we know what sounds good. Newer players are \\"discovering\\" this tone as well and have come to enjoy the added smoothness round cores provide.

Dean Markley has been around a long time and I remember these strings from that time. They were good then. They're good now. They know how to build a round core that holds it tuning. Doesn't go dead in a single gig. And most of all they're consistant. You don't get one set that's good and another that comes apart or goes dull in a few hours of playing time. They know how to build strings and they've been doing it right for decades.

A set of strings should be something that lasts for a good amount of time. Stay in tune under hard bends. Keep their tone and not go dull. These strings do that. They give reliable performance set after set with no surprises. Solid body, hollow body, single coil, or humbucker, these sound good with all. I remember them from '73 and in '13, 40 years later, they're still great.

product_title: LIMUSIC Blue G4000 Professional 3.5mm PC Gaming Stereo Noise Canelling Headset Headphone Earphones with Volume Control Microphone HiFi Driver For Laptop Computer
review_body:
I ordered these for a couple of reasons: 1) they looked heavy duty, which I have gone through a lot of headphones for reasons below, and 2) I love the idea of a detachable/removable cord. I also was desirous of having a headphone with really good sound quality.

These Numark DJ phones fulfilled all of my desires.

I received them, pulled them out of the box and had them hooked up within 10 minutes of the UPS man dropping by. The first impressions were good: Beefy construction, fit and finish is excellent, lightweight for the size, nice earpads. Then I hooked them up.

I was not expecting htem to be real hifi phones. Being designed for DJ use, I figured they would be heavy, excessively so, on the bass. What I discovered was that these phones are really excellent across all frequencies. The bass is not excessive, it is simply more clearly defined than with any other phones I've used. The mid frequencies, primarily vocals, are really good. The voices seem to be really inside your head. The higher frequencies, cymbals, violins, etc., are near perfect. I love using these with classical music, which is the hardest music to reproduce due to the complexity. The Numark phones really keep up. I can pick out individual instruments in the orchestra and visulaize exactly where they are in the mental 'soundstage'.

I've been a hifi nut for 38 years, and I haven't heard any phones that even approach what these can do. I've owned quite a variety of headphones through the years, including electrostatics. I'll stick with my Numarks!

One thing to keep in mind. I am 6'4" tall with a 7&7/8ths size head. That translates to the phones being tight over the skull and ears. At first it was uncomfortable, but the headband starts to adjust and relax after a while. At my size, that's just the way the world is, so it is no big deal. My wife is 5'6". so they work fine for her. I did not subtract a star for it, as they are about par for the course.

Summary: I highly recommend the Numark DJ phones for anyone. I'll be getting a pair for my wife soon.

Best regards,

John Pricee course.

I am 32 years old and I am not some kid on here giving a review. Yeah the beats are a lot cooler looking and will give you more street cred, but if you are a mature grown up that wants the best quality audio, get these headphones. The highs mids and lows all sound fantastic with just the right amount of bass. Beats headphones are just bass heavy and do not sound as good all around. If you check the specs you will find these are better in every category except bass, where beats are 106db these are 99 db. They are not that far off, and I believe gives just the perfect amount of bass. If you are thinking about buying beats headphones, don't. Do yourself a favor and pick these up. Because this is really the way artists intended you to hear their music. Unless that is you are looking to make a 300 dollar fashion statement, if that's what you are going for, then get the beats headphones.

product_title: Taylor Guitars Musician's Gear Bag
review_headline: Sherlock Holmes would have loved this bag.
review_body:
This was a replacement for a Fender gear bag that was recently stolen from my car (I've experienced thefts of 3 pianos and a couple of GPS units, but never a stupid gear bag--which contained irreplaceable items like my notebook of musicians' numbers and even several vocalists' song-lists along with the right keys). To lift my spirits I ordered this more elaborate bag (for twenty less from a different dealer, though the price I'm seeing on Amazon has become standard). It's the most intricate, meticulously designed, carefully constructed, amazing (and potentially confounding) bag I've ever come across. After locating a dozen or so smaller, outside pockets, I sensed that I had not gained access to the center of the bag--the main inner chamber designed to hold larger items (piano pedals, electric adapters, my NanoSynth, a Shure SM-58, a Zoom H2, etc). My wife loves puzzles, so I turned the assignment over to her. It took another 5 minutes, but she opened a flap, removed a \\"secret\\" panel, and voila! we had solved the mystery of the bag.

It's a high-quality bag (looks as rugged as the red Nord piano bag I use with a Kurzweil SP4-7), but its owner had better give it a few trial runs before any major, or even semi-serious, gigs. Its high-tech design is only as good, or useful, as the person who packs it. Like mastering a musical instrument, this equipment bag will require some \\"woodshedding\\" for realization of its potential. It can be worn as a knapsack (no way), or slung over a shoulder (way), or carried securely by its large, unbreakable handle (the usual resort). And during an extended break (maybe during dinner speeches by the whole family), you can use this bag to test the I.Q. of any musician who you sense is dragging down the band. Tell him you brought along an extra \\"smoke\\"--in your gear bag. Then set your timer. If, after 15 minutes, he comes back, saying \\"I can't find it,\\" you'll know it's time to replace him with that two-dollar rhythm app you recently downloaded to your iPhone (assuming the first person to take the bait is the drummer). If he comes back within 5 minutes and confidently asserts \\"It's not there,\\" don't let this guy get away. In fact you have good cause to celebrate--but then be sure to start learning \\"West Side Story Suite\\" and \\"Channel One Suite\\" (the two solo showcases favored by Buddy Rich in the last two decades of his life).you recently downloaded to your iPhone (assuming the first person to take the bait is the drummer). review_body:

Here are my reasons why:

1. Quick-N-EZ adapter: Yes, the name is lame but the concept is amazing. 3. The boom hides into the stand for storage.

If you want one steadfast boom stand that will last you for years... this is your stand.

product_title: Korg mini-KP Kaoss Pad Dynamic Effect Processor
review_headline: Not As Well Built As Mini KP
review_body:
Pros:
- Many cool effects like vinyl slowdown and phaser delay.
- Display shows what effect is selected.
- Tap tempo and auto tempo.
- Built-in recorder.
- Can slow down and speed up MP3s using touch slider.

Cons:
- The micro switches under the buttons on the sides are flimsy and prone to break off with minimal pressure.
- It can store three favorites but the memory is cleared if the batteries are low or not installed.
- It loads only one MP3 into memory at a time. It doesn't have a playlist so cannot be used as an MP3 player.
- It uses mini stereo jacks for input and output making it difficult for professional purposes. It should have standard 1/4\\" ins and outs.
- Body is made of thin plastic and is not robust (unlike the mini KP which is better built).
- Doesn't save last selected effect when turned off.

[DW]

review_headline: Fast delivery, sweet, sweet uke/ Update Feb '15
review_body: Yikes!  I was expecting delivery at least four more days down the line, but, BAM!  It arrived on Monday when it should have been  Friday.  I was a bit alarmed when it arrived in the original cardboard ukulele box.  It was inside its soft, canvas case, and I guess that's all it needed for insulation.  I tuned it by ear very quickly, and have strummed about once an hour since.  I put an electronic tuner on it, and the Aquila Nylgut strings seem to be settling in quite nicely.  I'm hoping in a day or two they'll stay in tune.  The sound is as sweet as I'd hoped for, clean and bright, and the volume was what I expected, too - a good mezzo forte with my thumb edge, perfect for practing/self-entertaining.  I can imagine it a bit louder with a felt pick, which is my preference.  The action is a bit lower than I'm used to, but works fine.  All in all, a good little axe.  Wish I had gotten it sooner.  More later if anything changes.  Quick shipping and great quality get it five stars.  Here we go, over two years later:  It still sounds nice, but this is one instrument which would benefit from that tunauke upgrade - tuning from the saddle.  Once I have it in perfect tune, there are a few chords down the fret which just don't fit.  If you tune it to play in G, for instance, it will get you by.  But if you go from a C tune to G without making adjustments, it will play out of tune.  Everything else stands.  Bright sound, ease of portability, and a good little axe to have around if you're fleshing out some chords for your favorite tune.  Great to have along in your car if you just can't be away from a uke, like me.  Good luck, and enjoy.  Music surrounds us constantly - even slience makes a sweet melody when you least expect it.

product_title: Jolida Audio - FX 10 Integrated Tube Amp Black
review_body:
What a surprise this amp is! First of all this amp runs very hot with the glass cover on. That's a no-no; heat is the prime enemy of tubes. I removed the cover and placed 4 rubber feet on the bottom at each corner. The cover is held on by a combination foot/screw so if you don't want to use the glass cover you will need to add rubber buttons at each corner, because the bottom is vented, so you shouldn't place the amp on a surface without some elevation. Without its cover, the amp simply runs warm like any other tube amp.

My source for this review is a Jolida tube CD player and the speakers are Dali Ikon 6 towers (Sensitivity 92dB). They are 6 ohms and sound best on the Jolida's 4 ohm tap. I use Kimber 4PR Biwire speaker cables (8ft). I'm running the stock factory tubes in both the amp and CD player. My room is 2,100 cubic feet.

Sound profile: There is tight and nice lower bass that adds to the bass excitement. The mids are lush and transparent. The highs are extended without being etchy. There is nice air around the instruments. This is a warm sounding tube amp without any tube veiling. Imaging capability places it with the best of the EL84 tube amps I've auditioned. The amp presents a nice, wide sound stage.

One of the nice things about this amp is its current bandwidth. With the Dali's, I get a nice full sound at low background levels. I was never able to achieve this with my Nad C740. The Jolida does not have any tone controls and I don't miss them with this amp. At low volumes, I was always boosting the bass/treble a bit with the Nad.

Overall, this is an outstanding amp for the money. It's a keeper!

product_title: Hercules GS602B iStand Electric Guitar Stand
review_body:
These went on a one-day-only sale at another vendor, I had been looking at this model and wondering if it might do for my purpose, and I thought it was worth taking a chance at the sale price. I don't know that anyone else with this same rather specialized need will ever read this, but just in case...

The Traveler EG-2 guitar has a full-size scale (fretboard) but is dramatically reduced in overall size to work as carry-on luggage, partly by reducing the body size but also by eliminating the headstock, which means that it sure wasn't going to work in my other Hercules stands which grab the neck and suspend the guitar by the headstock, and might not work in some others stands that expect a body with a full-size lower bout.

I've tried it, and this stand does work surprisingly well for a full-size Strat. My initial concerns about being knocked sideways (since the neck is unsupported) seem mostly unfounded, the little arms that hold the lower bout seem to grip well. Yes, I'm sure you could bend the arms that telescope out of the back, and probably get it to fail in other ways if you fell on it or something.. it's a travel stand, and any stand has limits. In any case, the smaller-sized Traveler guitar with its lower center-of-gravity is even more secure on this stand than a full-size guitar.

Somewhat to my surprise, when collapsed this fits just fine in the outer pocket of the (small) EG-2 gig bag with plenty of room to spare. The closed-cell foam padding of the bag is between the pocket and the guitar. Since this stand folds into a rounded, smooth \\"discus\\" shape with no protrusions or corners it would probably take a lot more of a hit for this to damage the guitar than most travel stand designs, some of which seem to be mostly sharp angles and metal rod ends when folded.

As surprise bonuses, the recess left by opening the top \\"flap\\" on the stand accommodates the unusual offset lower strap button just fine, and the rubber \\"puck\\" that contacts the back of a normal guitar body actually drops into the recess for the tuners on the back of the EG-2, making it VERY secure from being knocked sideways- it almost locks into place by default. Seriously, it couldn't work much better if it was specifically designed for this unusual guitar. Traveler should sell these.

Only negatives so far are that while it fits fine in the gig bag pocket, the guitar in the gig bag didn't then fit back into the cardboard box it came in very well- not a problem, that storage arrangement wasn't going to last anyway, I'm surprised I kept the box this long. It does seem a bit heavy in the hand when collapsed for travel, but I think that's mostly because it's so compact- the stated weight is typical of other travel stands. One other design I was considering came in glow-in-the-dark plastic, and I guess that might be a nice feature just to keep from stumbling over the stand in the dark in an unfamiliar small room someday, but that's a very minor point, really stretching as a feature, and there are probably other ways to accomplish it. Also, I have to admit that I really dislike the name. Apple has beaten the whole \\"i\\"-prefix thing to death, and I wish they had picked something a little original, but that's trivial. At least there's no big flashy decal with the stupid name on it.

product_title: M-Audio BX8 D2 8-Inch Active 2-Way Studio Monitor Speakers
review_body:
In the past 48 hours I brought home the M-Audio AV40, BX5 and BX8, as well as the Mackie MR5 MK II. The AV40 was pretty much garbage...:( The BX5 has a very weird compressed sounding upper mid range, almost distorted sounding to me. The BX8 however sounds VERY nice. So why the 2 stars?

Well, when they are on and have no music running thru them, if you put your ear close to them you will hear a very apparent buzz. Since these are primarily near'ish field monitors you will be using them fairly close to your body and you can very much hear the buzz once you've first recognized it. Other than that, they are a very smooth sounding monitor. You can get these heavily discounted right now online from a few different places.

For anyone who is interested, the Mackie MR5 MKII's are the awesome standout in all of these speakers. They can be had very inexpensively right now as well....and they are dead silent when no music is playing thru them. You might wonder how can I be comparing a speaker with a 5.25\\" driver to one with an 8\\"? Well, honestly the Mackie's are super super close to the tightness of the lower frequencies in the BX8...and without the buzz noise in the high end. I did a quick search and it seems this buzz is standard on M-Audio. People either live with it or not. This isn't a review about the Mackie's but they also have a very balanced mid and high end. I'm not sure if I'll be keeping the Mackie's or the BX8's yet. Once I decide I'll try to update this review.

One last note. I had read online about people saying quality control in M-Audio is not that great and all I can say is that on the AV40's and BX5's there is a \\"pop\\" when you turn the power switch off. On the BX5, only one speaker does this, the other one doesn't. The BX8's are silent when flipping power switches but they do have the buzz.

UPDATE 12/23/12
I think I've decided to keep the BX8's. They do sound very good, but sound very much like a hifi speaker,not really a critical monitor for mixing. I bought these to use for listening to music on my computer while I work, not for recording music. I feel they are a very good buy for the money I paid, about 30 percent less than the price here on amazon. The key here is \\"for the money\\". I think if you want a really nice/sweet sounding self amplified speaker that WILL reveal a lot of detail and have a very wide sound stage you will like them. They sound like they have a hip hop or loudness curve sort of \\"built in\\". I don't think they are suitable as a true near field monitor though.

I decided as a comparison to take my Yamaha MSP10 studio monitors that I bought 10 years ago from my living room to compare on my computer as well. These blew the M-Audio BX8's out of the water. I don't listen to music in my living room much anymore and these speakers have just been sitting there, rarely used. Mostly used here and there when people are visiting etc. It's a crappy room with wooden floors so no critical listening could be done there. Anyway, I've been a/b'ing the BX8's and the MSP10's on my desktop for the past day and it's frankly not even close. The Yamaha's are quite a bit better, more revealing, more transparent. They should be though. If I remember correctly I paid $1200 for the Yamaha's 10 years ago. The MSP is Yamaha's pro line. Nowadays you see the Yamaha \\"HS\\" (HS80, HS50) lines everywhere. The HS stands for \\"Home Studio\\" and these speakers are nowhere close to the quality of the MSP line. Long story short, the Yamaha's will be living on my desktop and the BX8's will end up in the living room. The only thing that may stop this is that the Yamaha's are literally about 48 pounds each!!! This is about double the weight of the BX8's for the same 8\\" speaker size enclosure. Not sure how well my desk is going to like it..:)

So, what happened to the Mackie's? Well, I like them a lot, but felt that the BX8's revealed more details in the high's and the extra lows because of the 8\\" driver became more noticeable. The Mackie's are nice but have a darker sound, but without the actual lower frequencies. I still like them a lot, but the 8\\" woofer of the BX8 sort of won me over.

product_title: Numark iDJ Pro | Professional DJ Controller for iPad with XLR, RCA, Mic, and Headphones Connections
review_headline: Fun to use for beginner-intermediate DJs
review_body:
My review after 2 weeks of use:
Pros
+Awesome interface
+Smooth song loading time (using djay by itself produces some lag/skipping)
+3 simultaneous effects per deck
+Loop roll
+Jog wheels & cross-fader are pretty decent, scratching is pretty on point
+Split cue
+4 hot cues
+Master tempo/Key lock (in app)
+Mic & RCA aux inputs that both run independant from iDevice and can be used simultaneously
+Balanced XLR output or RCA output
+1/4\\" and 1/8\\" headphone jacks
+Dedicated filter knobs
+Needle/Strip search (in app)
+Lightweight
+No need for computer (except loading songs to the iPad)
+8 pad sample player (in app)
+Reverse function
+Ability to multiply/divide the tempo

Cons
-Small storage for songs, especially if you have high bit-rate files (depending on the size of your memory bank on the iPad)
-Cannot read key metadata (can be countered by organizing your playlists into keys, but that can take a very long time)
-BPM analyzer is decent, not perfect
-No EQ kill switches
-After moving the track with the jog wheels or viewing a closeup on the waveform you have to wait a few seconds for the waveform to shrink back to use the Needle/Strip search (gets annoying)
-Plastic feels like it can break easily
-No BLEEP function
-Hovered my hands about 1/2\\" above jog wheels and music stopped as if I put my hand on it
-High pitch hum coming from the unit when iPad plugged in, even more prominent through headphones
-No cue on mic/aux inputs
-iPad becomes very warm/hot after even 15 minutes of use
-Taking out the iPad is a little more difficult than inserting it.

Overall, this is an awesome unit, great for beginner-intermediate DJs. This has everything you need to get a party going, possibly even use at a club. The aux input would be awesome to hook up a CDJ/Turntable to, but unfortunately there's no cue to thisfeature so mixing in would be fully reliant to complete and thorough knowledge of what you're bringing in to the mix. Before owning the iDJ Pro, I've DJed using a controller (NS6) at an event where a performer brought his own CD, so we had to use my laptop CD drive; I felt embarrassed but we still got the job done. I have not tested the iCloud feature, as I don't have the 3g version of the iPad. Though it is fun to use, I don't foresee myself keeping it at the moment because I already have a full DJ set-up with either vinyl + Serato Scratch Live or controller + Serato Itch.

product_title: Epiphone DR-212 12-String Acoustic Guitar,
review_headline: Took a Risk on a Cheap Guitar, Got Rewarded!
review_body:
After being on the fence with this guitar for over a year, I went ahead and took the plunge. I was worried that I was going to blow $170 on a child’s toy that didn’t look, play, or sound right, but I was so wrong. This guitar is great! Do not worry about the price because this is a quality Epiphone guitar. If you have been wanting a 12-string, get this one now.

Looks: This is the best surprise. It’s a great looking guitar. The fit and finish are on par with much more expensive guitars. The color of the top on my guitar is very light, and I like that. The back and sides are a nice, dark finish that really pops.

Tuning: Tuning a 12-string is always rough, so considering the challenge, I am pleased so far. When I got it out of the box, the strings were very low and had very little tension. Not sure if this is a function of the cold weather or if it was shipped that way to protect the guitar from breaking. I actually used a string winder to help tighten them up while tuning it for the first time. I tuned it the first day I had it, then left it alone for about a day and had to really tune it again, but after that it has just needed fine adjustments.

Playability: The action is nice. Even for a 12-string, it doesn’t require much more pressure than my 6-string. I played for a while, and my fingers did not feel any more fatigued than normal. The guitar body is big which is fine for me because I’m a big guy, but smaller framed players might struggle. The neck, however, is about as flat as any 12-string I’ve ever played. Players with small hands or short fingers will be pleasantly surprised.

Sound: This is really all that matters, after all. I really like the sound. It’s a little brassy, but it does have some deep rich tones in there. It’s also nice and loud (probably due to the large body mentioned above). I haven’t replaced the factory strings yet (and one of them broke, so I guess I havean 11-string guitar right now!), so I will hold off on a final judgment until I get some quality strings.

product_title: Bach 1866 Stradivarius F-Attachment Trombone Case
review_headline: Fine for regular use.  Fits horn well.
review_body:
The 1866 case is one of the standard mass production cases for the Bach 42x family of trombones. It's designed to accept \\"traditional\\" wrap, open wrap, straight horn, and, apparently, a couple of different valve types. It's about what you'd expect from a factory case--holds the horn snugly, decently but not extravagantly made, and perfectly acceptable for regular use. I would not feel confident about taking it on the road for more than a handful of weeks. I would give it 3.5 stars, but I don't have that option and the people I bought it from did such a great job for me that I'm handing out benefit of the doubt here on that basis.

PROS: Decent-quality handle. Not cartoony looking. Three buckles that are reasonably secure. Fits pretty much any factory Bach 42x horn of the last four decades. Flat on one side, so it doesn't roll over backwards when you open it and take the horn out. Little metal feet on both ends and the \\"bottom\\" of the case allow it to sit on e.g. wet pavement or the floor in an airport bathroom without getting the actual case surfaces wet/nasty. Two internal compartments leave you enough space for a spray bottle, mouthpieces, metronome, slide-o-mix, trombotine, etc. Not too heavy and not too big...will fit in most but not all overhead compartments--watch out on small planes. So far, it seems tough enough to survive/protect through a gate check, but I would think hard before really checking it. (In this connection, Doug Yeo has some great advice on his website about how to use a craft-store-style styrofoam cone to make a kludge that will prevent most bell-folding incidents.)

CONS: The reinforcements on the edges of the case are made of fairly cheap faux-leather plastic with a gooey adhesive under it; the faux leather appears to split wide open with very little provocation--this happened to me after the first gate check--and the goo will get all over you if you don't watch it. There exist no attach points for a shoulder strap, though the case is made of particleboard so adding them should be manageable.) The feet, which are basically little brads with oversized hemispherical heads on them, can be pulled out with your fingernails and, predictably, have a tendency to work loose; my workaround will be to get some screw-in models and see if I can improve on the originals. Some Bach cases have a \\"door\\" that flips up and gives you additional cargo capacity, absent on this model.

Overall, entirely adequate if you don't travel too much, and much cheaper than some of the higher-end stuff you can get these days.lder strap, though the case is made of particleboard so adding them should be manageable.) product_title: AKG M220 Pro Stylist Semi-Open High Definition Over-Ear Studio Headphones …
review_headline: Excellent studio and casual listening headphones
review_body:
I'm going to start off this review by saying this: if you don't have a big head, you might find these unwieldy. These suckers are BIG--much bigger than the AKG K-142 HD's they are replacing.

The build is light yet sturdy, and they feel wonderful on my admittedly large head. I'm a huge fan of AKG's self-adjuting headband, I find that it always sits very comfortably on my head--it's a wonderful piece of engineering!

I also like the little gold accents on the headphones, however, I wish the gold and resin stickers on the end of each of the earcups was replaced with inlaid metal in the same finish as the gold rings around the earcups--it would look a lot more polished and "grown-up". But overall, they're not "flashy" headphones, you won't get any "swag" for wearing them, but they are definitely "elegant". I like the idea of refined, classic style, and I think these K240's fit the bill perfectly. I want my headphones to play music, rather than to play the role of a fashion statement (I'm looking at you, Beats and others!)

The sound is very...neutral? You won't find it blowing you away on house/techno/hip-hop/R&B tracks--until you hit the vocals.

These are very clearly intended for use in a studio for monitoring the various inputs for a track. I personally love the feeling I get from these headphones--it's very realistic for the price.

I haven't tried the Grado S80i's yet, but for now, I'm extremely satisfied with the K240's. I can play music through my phone, computer, and iPad, all at reasonable volume. But I can also plug them into my receiver with the included jack adapter for even better quality sound.

I can say with complete certainty that these headphones were money well spent.

product_title: M-Audio Torq MixLab Digital DJ System
review_headline: Good for both novices and pros
review_body:
Most people will say that this is a controller designed for novice or new DJs, which is true. However, you can also add this controller to an existing setup to plug a gap or make some room for cheap. My favorite thing about this type of cheap midi controller is that you can re-purpose them yourself if you have a little bit of time and know how to program mappings (and have the software necessary to do so--Torq can't do anything of the sort as far as I'm aware).

This controller is small and very light; the only major negative is that it's not lit at all (this may or may not matter depending on your personal setup). They probably could have been even more space efficient with the design. If they chopped off all that plastic around the edges, this would be a 5-star item.
Still, it's a great thing to own for both novices and all you midi mapping ninjas.

From a 2-deck controller with far too basic functionality (for my purposes), I've re-mapped this for 4-deck independent play/pause/cue/hotcue/eq/volume/beatjump/monitor cue, with monitor/mix fader, which is exactly what I needed to round out my setup, save space, and get rid of two older, clunkier controllers that I used for far too long. If I'd been more clever with modifiers (I use Traktor--modifier variables are your friend!), I could have assigned even more functions to it, but that's all I needed this controller to do. So to sum that up, don't underestimate the versatility of this if you know how to leverage custom assignable midi mappings.

A few words on the software--I took a brief test drive out of curiosity. It seems adequate and I think a starting DJ could probably use it for a while as their first piece of software. It actually runs fundamentally well and I wasn't able to confuse it too much during a brief stress test (midi command overload). If you have Traktor/Serato or similar, you probably already know this but there's no reason to even touch the included software unless you're just curious like me.
The fact the Torq software is included with this controller and works relatively well is a huge bonus for newer DJs without software.

Some things I've noted that might be important to know before you buy:
--The sliders offer a fair amount of resistance, which was a major plus for me. Some DJs I know don't like ANY resistance, so keep that in mind if you're in that crowd.
--The buttons can be finicky (decent but not great connections between the button hardware) and my guess is they'll probably wear out before anything else on the controller. That said I haven't really had issues with them yet, it's just an observation.
--The 6 knobs in the middle have a notch at center position so that you get tactile feedback. The 6 knobs on the outside do not and they seem to me to be much looser as well (they're designed to be [0-max] knobs rather than [min-0-max]).
--As you can probably see if you look at the picture, the small buttons (they're pitchbend by default if I remember correctly) and your play/pause/cues are very close together, so those with huge fingers, be careful.are unless you're just curious like me.

I'm not dropping down in the middle of a wedding to check levels.

SOUND: Excellent. Like most wireless mics you have to talk directly into the mic. The top of the windscreen is flat so its more intuative than others. ON DAY TWO I ran into some static while I was setting these up. One mic (2) completely dropped off giving me a taste of verbal static. I turned the system off, restarted, and all was fantastic. I have not run into the problem since. Very Good Sound. I was very impressed by the crispy fullness of these mic's WOW!!

CONSTRUCTION: Very well built. Solid plastic. Battery installation \\"2 AAs\\" requires unscrewing the cap and flipping back a hinged securing flap. Very well made. Slightly heavy for wireless mics.

I just bought these. I'll be sure to update.

product_title: Seiko SAT101 Guitar/Bass Tuner
review_headline: Favorite Tuner by a Long Shot
review_body:
Let me just say, if you are looking for a tuner that just \\"locks in\\" and gives you either a thumbs up or down on tuning, this is not for you. This thing is you true chromatic style tuner that jumps a bit. The reason I love this tuner is I want absolute precise tuning. This gives you the number of cents off you are, sharp or flat. Using this with the Signal Flex Acoustic Guitar Tuner Pickup on an acoustic, and the guitar rings with tuned precision. I have a picky ear and other tuners that just give you a red or green light for \\"in tune\\" \\"not in tune\\" allow for a bit of leeway in how many cents off it can be to be in tune. That works for most people, but not for my ears.

I know there is debate between which is better between this and the Korg CA-40. I bought that one as well and was disappointed to see that it does not give the precise cents off. Is that a great tuner otherwise, sure.

An added benefit to the Seiko/Signal Flex combo is that you can check the intonation at the 12th fret on an acoustic guitar with precision and make minor adjustments, if necessary, by sanding your saddle to make the crest of the saddle (where the string bends over) either closer or further away from your bridge.

All that being said, it takes a bit of time to pull the tuner out. For that reason, I also have a Snark on my guitars for on the fly tuning. I have tried many different headstock tuners and it is the best. One downfall on it, like others I have tried, is it tends to get a \\"rattle\\" after time.

product_title: 5-String Banjo 24 Bracket with Closed Solid Back and Geared 5th Tuner By Jameson Guitars
review_body:
Liked:
* High-quality look (beautiful polished wood back and neck)
* Good sound
* Holds tuning well
* Lowest priced, best value real banjo on Internet and in stores
* Shipped by UPS with no damage, arrived in perfect condition from several states away
* 5-stringed (don't get the 4 string, because eventually you'll want the 5 string anyways, and it's easy enough to play it as if it were a 4-string without the high drone 5th string because it's set slightly lower than the plane of the other four)
* Resonator or closed-back design is louder, better than open-backed banjos, very loud, strong sound
* I found it straightforward to learn basic skills with my guitar background(it's string tunings and configuration are different, but techniques are similar)
* Not too heavy (some banjos I've picked up felt like a sack of bricks)
* Comes with chord chart printed on a piece of paper, a tuning guide with a piano for reference (for most common G-tuning or gDGBD), a diagram of the banjo parts, and a little tool
* Neck and string spacing is not to narrow, it's standard

Disliked:
* Some frets may be a slightly off (I tuned it, but fretting the 5th fret produces a noticeably sharp note that my tuner confirms), or perhaps the bridge is misplaced by a millimeter or two on mine, but I'm not experienced enough to precisely place it for accurate notes-playing all the way up the neck. However, this is not a big deal as you only notice if you have a good ear for pitches, and for the price it's to be expected.
* The tuning peg for the highest drone string that's halfway up the neck is really hard to turn, and doesn't turn smoothly like the other 4 tuners on the head.

Conclusion:
* Buy it. If you want a low-priced, good-quality banjo to start learning and continue playing for years, this is a good find.
* I'm very happy with my banjo, and I don't foresee any repairs needed, and I don't expect tofeel the need to upgrade to a pricier instrument.
* I d also recommend buying a banjo strap, finger picks, a clip-on tuner for guitars/banjos, and possibly a beginner banjo book to get started.

I'm creating a Digital Audio Workstation for home recording and this Mixer does the job very well. I've read others complaining about the FX (including Echo and Reverb). IMHO, I purchased a 12/2 inexpensive mixer. The FX settings are from 00 to 99 and isn't well defined in the documentation. product_title: American DJ Supply LED Party Pak 2 LED Light System DJ Package
review_headline: Amazing Way to Start the Party!
review_body:
I got this for Christmas and it was a huge hit at the New Year's party!!
It comes with three effects: Mini-Gressor Tri LED, Tri Gem LED, and B6R LED.

Mini-Gressor Tri LED
It's the best light in the package. Basically, it's a the \\"son\\" of the Aggressor. (which is an even smaller version of grandpa Dekker)

PROS
-Sound active mode works
-Multiple colors/combos
-sensitivity knob (always kept at max for me)
-LED technology = no duty cycles or heat
-Lights up my whole family room
-Sturdy metal casing
-Logo/name in nice white letters

CONS
-Weak sound active mode
-No off switch
-Only one mode (sound active)

INITIAL FEARS
-Sound active mode would be too weak for anything
+At the New Years Party, the music was cranked up loud and it sat on top of the stereo's shelving, so it was responsive. In my bedroom, I overcame it's hearing impediment by placing my portable speakers literally right behind it's microphone. Now, my Beatles music could be played at reasonable volumes.
-Colors would not line up to form cyan/yellow/magenta
+Well, they did and they didn't: the colors didn't overlap in my large family room, but they do overlap a decent amount in my room, causing yellow to appear as a cool Red-Yellow-Green spot on the wall-I don't mind since it looks cool
-\\"IEC\\" power means I have to buy a cable to plug it in
+No, it came with a grounded U.S cable (or at least the one I got did) and worked upon plugging in

Tri Gem LED
Similar to the MiniGressor, it projects overlapping color spots, but they spin as a group instead of as rows

PROS
-All modes react to the beat of the music
-Three modes: continuous (one-way rotation), stationary (no rotation), and sound active (alternating rotation based on music)
-LED technology = no duty cycles or heat
-Lights up just part of the dance floor area
-Sturdy metal casing
-Logo/name in nice white letters

CONS
-No sensitivity knob (very sensitive)
-Is boring to watch after alone

INITIAL FEARS
-I didn't even know what it was
+I found out :D
-It (and the MiniGressor) need haze
+No, the video on the American DJ site points the camera only at the lights and uses haze to see the beams. While this is cool, the lights projected onto the room are just as cool if not cooler than any pattern of beams, although a smoke machine would be nice...

B6R LED
The light added-in to the package. Looks like a police beacon.

PROS
-Many different patterns: 1, 2 or 4 strips of light clockwise or counterclockwise
-7 different speeds
-LED technology = no duty cycles or heat
-Bright LEDs (not too bright, though)
-Sturdy metal casing
-I hear it's ceiling mountable
-No siren sound effect

CONS
-Not sound active
-DIP switches are tiny and annoying; remote control would be nice
-Ugly appearance when off

INITIAL FEARS
-I thought it would physically rotate
+It basically is 8 strips of light that turn on in succession according to speed and number of strips \\"rotating,\\" allowing it to \\"rotate\\" very fast on speed 7
-DIP switches would be large
+They were not. They are very tiny and appear to be very fragile. All 10 of them are take up about as long as a half of a post-it
-I had a chance of getting a blue beacon
+No, I think all are red (B6Rs, not B6Bs)

product_title: Auralex ProMAX v2
review_headline: I Made It Work For Me.
review_body:
My ProMax panels are used as first reflection absorption and placed on opposite sides of my monitors ... one reflection point being the back of a door. I know, these panels were designed for easy mobility but the tripod stands were too bulky and cumbersome for my home studio; it would've been only a matter of time before I or someone else tripped over them.
