If you are setting up you home studio in a spare bedroom and/or a home office (of average/standard size, with 8ft ceilings) in my opinion these panels wouldn't be a good fit. However...

These panels have been very effective of absorbing my room reflections and controlling wave frequencies. They were the perfect solution for me because as I mentioned, one of my first reflection is the back of a door. The panels are very light and easy to hang using adhesive velcro tape. I much prefer the thickness and the look of the ProMax panels rather than having 2 inch thick multiple foam squares on my door and wall. I gave the product 3 stars because of the large footprint of the tripod stands and cost; Auralex should offer an option of buying these 2 panels without the stands.

product_title: Aiaiai TMA-1 DJ Comfort Modern Fashion Headphone
review_headline: AFTER A YEAR OF USE: Sound quality: 10 stars, build quality: ehhhh
review_body: Sound Quality:    Excellent sound, truly excellent. I listen to mainly electronic music and experimental hip hop plus a bit of psychedelic rock etc (Dubstep, UK Garage, House, Trip-Hop, IDM, Breaks, Juke/Footwork etc etc - generally pretty bass heavy music) so that is what I've tested it on over a year or so.    Bass response is superb. If I was being super picky I'd say the freq's around 40-200 hz or so come in a biiiiiit too strong but that's going by my ear (prolly a heap of wax in there anyway). The bass overall sounds thick, warm and cuddly. Seriously, you'll just want to swim in it when the right song comes on. Mids and Highs are also very clear. These cans give hi-hats, snares etc a lovely crispness. I'm not a DJ so I can't offer any insight into how they perform in a set etc.    Build Quality:    So I've had these things for a year and they still sound amazing, but (and this is a rather large, annoying 'but') the oh-so-lovely matte black film that coats the entire headband piece started to peel about three months into me using them. The entire headband is gradually peeling away and the boring-looking black plastic underneath is really starting to show through. I put these things through pretty intensive use - I commute approx 3-4 hours in a day, 5 days a week, I've taken them overseas twice and I use them at home regularly.  Really quite annoyed at this. I absolutely loved the minimal aesthetic that AIAIAI were going for with this but the quality of the materials simply do not do the design justice. Every time I take them out of the bag I get little black flakes all over my hands and inside the bag - very sad indeed. Also the cushiony sort of rubber thing inside the headband is starting to peel off but only barely.    It should be mentioned that I live in a coastal city (Gold Coast, Australia) so it may be the salty air eroding the adhesive under the film (don't quote me on that, I'm not a chemist)    Apart from that major bummer, it's actual shape has faired very well. Where the earpieces connect to the headband piece in those holes is quite rattly but other than that they are still solid. the semi-leather earpads have lasted incredibly well - still pretty much mint condish'.    What really gets my goat about all this is that in the ads and stuff they put out when the 'phones first came out, they frequently mentioned things like \\"superior build quality\\", \\"resistant to abuse when DJing\\", \\"built like a TOOL\\" etc. - Obviously not. Sure, the headband is strong, but they really should have thought about the materials coating it as well. I expected better, judging from the price tag - was really hoping these things would stand the test of time better than they have.    Side-note: If you are going to buy these I suggest getting the slightly more expensive model with the right-angle headphone jack. I was on the plane with these once and I was getting out of my seat. I left the headphones plugged into the front of the arm, and because the jack at the end of the cable sticks out so far, as I was getting past the arm I accidentally bumped the jack and completely bent it to the point of no return. A new cable is like $20 so I thought I'd buy a spare generic auxiliary (male to male 1/8\\" jack) cable and have been using that since. Of course this is a major instance of clumsiness on my part but it wouldn't have happened if I had the right-angled jack version (that version wasn't out when I bought mine). Also you can't get a replacement cable with the right angled jack so that's a bit annoying.    Conclusion:    Overall I really like these headphones despite the design faults. They sound good enough for me to stick to them. My next pair will probably be a replacement for these or even the studio version - assuming they've fixed these issues. I got my pair a couple months after they came out so I'm still using the not-as-recent model, which means this problem may have been fixed. Not sure though. Judging by the pictures it's the samestuff coating it, sadly. I'd like to hear AIAIAI's word on the coating problem tbh. Might hit up a forum or two. If they haven't fixed these issues I might pick up a pair of the less expensive Capitals - as they don't have the same plastic coating as far as I'm aware.    Anyway thanks for reading. Hope this review was of assistance to you!    Cheers,  Fraser    PS: some pictures of the peeling for those who are interested:  [...]

review_headline: So disappointed... feel like being cheated!!

2. The microSD card does not properly fits in the grove & the cover does not properly close.
3. Very little information on the display
4. Not sure why/how the small red led below the mics blinks even when not recording.. I fear it appears like some loose contact or faulty recording switch?
5. The sound is of very very poor quality.. these days a decent cellphone built in microphone will record sound with better quality.

Really I feel that Samson is trying to make a joke out of this product!! If they are serious of being in the audio market - they should consider stop selling this poor quality product all together. Unfortunately I bought the device when visiting US & I am now back in India were I live. So there is no way to return this product (without visiting US again!!)

Anybody who is considering to buy this poorest quality stuff - I will strongly recommend that you try out H1 in any shop & then only buy it!! review_headline: Completely equal tuning after 18 years of being just a bit off
review_body:
I've been playing the drums for a long time and as confident as I am in my ability to ear-tune a drum it always feels/sounds like there is an unequal pitch across all the lugs.

Fast forward to last week when I received this beauty! I first tested on scratch tom with a collar lock and different sized tension rods. I thought getting equal levels for each lug would be a challenge but that was not the case. Easy to use out of the box with designated "suggestions" for each size of tom or snare. I was able to get the tension equal across all lugs in a few minutes and the sounds was noticeably better than my ear tuned attempt.

This has been one of the best investments I've made in drum equipment and I suggest all drummers get one to take the guess work out of tuning drums. It makes us all look and sound better when we're tuned correctly!

product_title: Seagull Entourage Grand Acoustic Guitar Rustic
review_headline: Beautiful little parlor - modern and traditional elements
review_body: I purchased this guitar, a Seagull Entourage Grand Rustic parlor guitar, from a local music store about a month ago. I went in with the intention of buying a Loar but came out with this guitar instead. It had an overall better sound, feel and was more comfortable for me to play with it's reduced scale length. I'm very pleased with the purchase month later. This guitar is eminently playable. It is a small bodied guitar with a short (24.84'') scale length. It's ideal as a \\"main\\" guitar for everyday use (you do play every day, don't you?) or as a \\"travel\\" guitar for those on the go. It's a small guitar (but full sized, just \\"reduced\\" size) in body but not in tone. While you won't get the bass response in any small bodied guitar that you will get in a mini-jumbo or dread, this guitar has plenty of low end. The highs are silky and clear. It doesn't muddy up when played in the mid-range and has a nice warm bass presence. The overall tone is excellent. The playability of the guitar is off the charts. It's very comfortable, especially for smaller stature players or even kids although I personally wouldn't spend 360 bucks on a kids guitar but that's just me... I found the price to be in line with other instruments in the range and the fit and finish is superior to others in it's class. The best part is perhaps that this is NOT an Asian made guitar (although the Chinese and Indonesians *can* and *do* produce some excellent instruments) but rather is made in Quebec, Canada, by hand, in a shop that has been building acoustic guitars for over a quarter of a century. All Seagull instruments are excellent in quality, fit and finish. This Entourage Grand Rustic parlor is no different. The sunburst vintage finish is gorgeous. It's a beautiful instrument. The body shape is traditional between the wars parlor design that is preferred by fingerpickers everywhere. The bracing is modern and produces a contemporary tone. The headstock is also a modern design which adds to the overall sense (rightfully) that you have a guitar here that bridges the old world with the new - vintage body size and shape with modern bracing, headstock and build techniques. A really great combination, in my opinion and a truly fine instrument. Seagull has done it again... but they always do. You can buy from confidence any Seagull guitar and you will get a fine instrument. If you like parlor guitars (and who doesn't?) then you'd be hard pressed to beat this guitar compared to others in it's price range. An excellent buy and highly recommended.e (rightfully) that you have a guitar here that bridges the old world with the new - vintage body size and shape with modern bracing, headstock and build techniques. A really great combination, in my opinion and a truly fine instrument. Seagull has done it again... but they always do. You can buy from confidence any Seagull guitar and you will get a fine instrument. If you like parlor guitars (and who doesn't?) then you'd be hard pressed to beat this guitar compared to others in it's price range. An excellent buy and highly recommended.

I regret not having paid much attention to the 11 foot cord - it is very bothersome, annoying, and frustrating...it always dangles, definitely not for portable use...Anyways, the overall sound quality is...how should I say this...\\"respectable\\", but lacks in some aspects. At times, the sound quality is not as clear as I would like it to be, and the different background instruments are hard to differentiate and sounded a little muddy. I'm amazed how some people say these phones can rest on their heads for hours without discomfort. I have tried adjusting the length to various sizes, but I can never leave these phones on for more than an hour. Any longer, and my ears start to get really, really sore...I can always feel pressure on some part of my ear, either the top or the bottom, and these phones clamp down fairly tightly. The handband is a little on the big side, although that part at least rests comfortably on my head. On the downside, I get the feeling sometimes that the sound is trapped inside my head...These headphones are fairly comfortable for the first hour or so, but any longer, they start to cause discomfort. One aspect I liked was the thick, albeit long, cable, which is very durable. Overall, there is only a moderate sound quality improvement on these headphones compared to apple stock earphones, and not really any significant improvements. At $40, I would definitely buy them, but at $60, I would wait for the price to go down a bit...

product_title: CB Drums CB5 5-Piece Drumset with Throne, Black (Cymbals not included)
review_headline: Decent for the price I paid
review_body:
I purchased these drums during the Black Friday lightening deal for $300.00. Overall they are not a bad set of drums for a kid/beginner. I wish I would have waited and purchased a better set of Pearls or PDPs that were on sale a week later for only $50.00 more.

Although the hardware is not the greatest, at least it did come with hardware - expect to replace it in the future.

The Chinese made Remo drum heads that come stock with the drums suck. They produce a lot of resonance and make a \\"boing\\" sound when you hit them. Even the tech at Remo told me they were crap. When I inquired about what the best solution would be to reduce the amount of resonance the toms made, his response was not to waste money on dampening pads and the like, but to replace the heads. I ordered the Evans EMAD standard tompack, a Evans REMAD resonant bass drum head, Evans G-Plus resonance standard tompack and a Evans Glass 500 snare drum resonance head. I also ordered gaffers tape, Moon Gel, and a ton of other stuff in an attempt to make these drums sound decent.

I also bought a set of Zildjian ZHT cymbals. I actually spent more for the cymbals than I did for the drum kit, and at least they sound great.

One last note, I can't find any information for these CB drums online. If you want to get any information, you have to contact their customer service.

Yeah, this is one purchase the turned into a money pit. I really wish I would have passed up this \\"deal\\". The drums will more than likely end up in next summers garage sell.

product_title: TC Electronic Nova System Floor Based Analog Overdrive/Distortion with G-System Effects and Dynamics Processing
review_headline: Price drop makes this a no brainer pick up
review_body:
Sure, any pedal over $300 is a lot for a pedal. But what you get here is well worth the price of admission. I picked up the Nova System to fill in some gaps on my pedal board in the effect area. Several of my pedals are analog, which are great, but having a digital delay for pristine cleans and a digital chorus were needs. Especially for songs with more gain. I also needed a tremelo for occasional use. The analog drive is really nice, but I still prefer my amp's gain and separate drive pedals. I also should add I use my compression pedal separate from the Nova.

For live playing, using the Nova with my board is a breeze. If I need to, I can pull the Nova and run it direct into a PA, which is also a nice option. I have some pretty basic presets that I use, especially the delays and run that together with some of my other gear. Live, it sounds amazing...no getting around it. If you are doing home studio work, again, pretty great. I suppose if you are doing a professional studio recording, you may want more individual pedals. But for average players, it's tough to beat the quality of the various effects.

The Nova isn't perfect. At it's original price, Line6, Boss and Digitech make more complete floor units. It also is not super intuitive to use and doesn't just plug into a PC without a Midi converter. Even then, downloading presets or software updates is not as easy as it's competitors. No looper, no expression pedal and a lame tuner round off the negatives. Even after the price drop, it's still more than some very popular floor based units.

I got on this after the price drop and would encourage anyone to give it a look, even the boutique crowd.

product_title: Meguiar's Jazzy Duty Headlight Restoration Kit.5
review_headline: Not bad for a student instrument
review_body: I was looking for a student instrument to practice at home while I took classes at a local community college. I played upright bass years ago, but had not played for many years when I agreed to play in the college string orchestra on a rented bass. I am under 5 ft 4 in with occasional problems with arthritis in my fingers so I did not want anything larger than a 1/2 size. The 1/4 size I did buy is a little small for me, but considerably lighter and easier to manage than the 5/8 one I play at school. (Full size is considered 3/4). First, anyone looking to purchase this bass should know it does not come with the (adjustable) bridge installed and the nut is barely grooved enough to hold the strings, so you are probably going to have to pay someone to set it up for you, usually about $200. Next, the factory strings on it sound very metallic and would be more appropriate on an electric bass than an upright. I plan to replace mine with some synthetic core orchestra strings($100). Also, it does not come with a bow ($60-$100), but if you are going to take lessons with it, you'll want to find out what your teacher prefers anyway, German or French. And last, if you are going to be taking it back and forth to lessons, you'll want another case. The one it comes with has only one zipper that does not reach all the way to the end pin hole and the case is a little short, so it is hard to get the bass in and out of it quickly, but since I plan to use mine at home, I usually leave it out of the case even when I'm not playing.  That said, I bought mine on sale for just under $400, so that makes it about 10% of the cost I'd have to pay to buy the one I'm renting, and barely more than the cost of renting for a year, even after the setup, strings and new bow as mentioned.

product_title: Akai Professional EWI USB Electronic Wind Controller,
review_headline: Official Support only through Windows Vista and OS X 10.6
review_body:
We (this is my wife's Amazon account) recently purchased the EWI USB through an Amazon seller. It arrived promptly and reasonably well-packaged.

The EWI is a really sweet wind controller, when it works. That said, if your experience is anything like mine, it can't really be counted upon to work.

I tried to run the bundled software on a Windows 8 machine (the easiest choice for me, at the moment).

The Garritan (Plogue?) Aria player packaged with the EWI USB would not run at all (well, it would make crunchy noises) until I installed the ASIO4ALL driver. With some tweaking, after installing the driver and pointing the player at it, the system was starting to be functional.

The included sample instruments are OK, but I thought unremarkable.

Invaluable help in getting things working was provided by a nice woman in the official Akai forum and by the very remarkable Jason Knight at ewiusb-dot-com. In fact, I would strongly suggest that non-expert users who want to play the EWI USB on Windows or Linux machines visit Mr. Knight's site before purchasing.

Sadly, just as things were looking good, my EWI experienced an apparent hardware or firmware crash. MIDI monitoring software shows that it isn't sending Note-On and Note-Off messages, just a long string of breath-controller and aftertouch messages -- with no notes.

The official Akai representative on the forum was polite. He or she pointed out explicitly that Akai only officially supports Windows though Vista and Mac OS X through Snow Leopard. It does say that clearly on the landing page for the EWI USB on the Akai site. I guess I should have checked before buying, but it didn't occur to me that Akai would be distributing software only suitable for legacy operating systems.

I'm going back to the site I mentioned above, for guidance in programming and disassembly of my EWI.

~Douglas

product_title: Yamaha QY100 Music Sequencer
review_headline: The only small portable hardware sequencer left on the market
review_body:
The QY100 is the only general-purpose portable hardware sequencer you can buy, at this time. \\"Portable\\" is a bit misleading: batteries will only last about 4 hours. But it is small and powerful. Why use a device like this instead of a laptop? The QY100 has lots of dedicated buttons for the sequencing operations. The software automatically re-harmonizes accompaniment patterns according to the chord progressions you enter. In short, the QY100 is smaller, more fun, and you don't have to deal with a mouse, crappy drivers, slow boots, glitches, etc. The non-velocity-sensitive keyboard is built right in.

I have been using Yamaha sequencers since the QY10. I own a QY20 (now broken) and an RM1X. The RM1X is more powerful as a pure sequencer, but it is missing the nice re-harmonization features of the QY series. If you build purely pattern based music, or primarily rhythmic or electronic music, you might prefer the RM1X. If you like to have automatic accompaniment reharmonization, perhaps even using built in patterns (!), the QY100 is the way to go.

For any Yamaha sequencer, you need to read the manual thoroughly to learn all the shortcuts. There is a yahoo user group discussing the QY70 and QY100.

product_title: Oscar Schmidt OU28T Ukulele - Satin
review_body:
I was a little apprehensive about this model because of the (low) price, but after reading some comments on Ukulele Underground forum about this particular model, decided it was worth a try. I'm really glad I took the chance, this is a well-made, thoroughly-enjoyable instrument with good tone quality and excellent intonation (that is, when you pluck a fretted string, it sounds the note correctly, not a little bit off as a cheap instrument might do).

Some laminated-wood instruments seem to do very well in producing a good tone and rich sound, and this is one of them. Volume is great, and the 8 strings give a nice difference in sound that goes well with some (not all) songs. Mine came with Aquila Nylgut strings, which I highly recommend in case not all of these are equipped with them.

One might think tuning an 8 string would be a hassle, but it's really not much more than normal tuning with an electronic tuner. Just tune one string of each pair with the electronic tuner, then pluck both together and tune the second to the first, listening for the 'wawa' sound to stop as they match up. This even works with the lower two sets, which are an octave apart.

The mahogany laminate construction is an open-pore semi-gloss finish. I have an Islander tenor which has a similar finish, and I've always loved the sound of that uke...very rich and pleasant...so don't think laminated-wood ukes can't be good, indeed as good as many solid-wood ukes I've tried. I think the open-pore finish may be an important factor in the sounds from these ukes, but whatever it is, it works.

The tuners are fine and precise, and I don't see any signs of warping or bridge problems when fully tuned up (that high C string can make you grit your teeth if you're used to tuning a normal 4-string uke, since it's such a high note). In the comment I read before buying, the user didn't care for the close string spacing, and made himself a nut with wider spacing between the pairs, but I like the way it's set up originally and wouldn't want it changed. The action was set properly, not too high or low, so fingering doesn't seem to require any unusual pressure for clear notes.

This uke is lots of fun, has great sound, and for an 8-string tenor at this price, I don't see how anyone could be anything but happy with their purchase.ween the pairs, but I like the way it's set up originally and wouldn't want it changed. product_title: Korg Monotribe Analogue Ribbon Station
review_headline: Awesome waveform filters set, good starter synth for analog experimenters.
review_body:
I have been playing with this for a few days now and I am starting to learn more about how to use it. It really is an awesome little synth / sequencer.

First impression: Wow a retro looking synth - small, (even tiny) durably made, and the knobs have the concentric chrome look from the 1970's.

The Pros: Very simple in function and most importantly the wave filters are FULLY ANALOG which gives the bass lines that old school "thick analog mud" feel like the Daft Punk's first 2 albums. Also any input / sample you can put through the 'line in' can be fed right through the analog filters, which makes for some interesting cool and surprising effects and tweaks when using external keyboards, software synths or other gear to experiment w it... The LFO/VCO/VCF filters can generate -200 to 60000 Hz sound wave frequencies which is just insanely awesome. You can model a very wide variety of sounds with this, the rate knob sometimes makes for some high pitch squelching noises right out of "Outer Limits Episodes" They managed to somehow pack a fully functional 3 waveform filter set in a bite size synth.

Now the cons: There is not enough complexity to the step sequencer and the drum library is very minimal so it's not really enough to do a full jam session or dj set with one instrument, the ribbon keyboard is way too small and imprecise, you can sequence a rough baseline but don't expect to play chords on it. I understand there are cost considerations for it, but I would have preferred that they put a MIDI port instead so that you can use your own 25 key weighted keyboard. The arpeggio is there but it very limited as you only control the speed of the oscillations with the rate knob and not the arpeggio form. Also I wish you could feed not just the waves, but also the drums through the analog filters, it could really expand the very very limited drum library which only has the kick, a dreadful sounding snare and the high-hat. The kick drum is nice and paunchy like an 808 drum #3 or # 4 but the snare is flat and unappealing like a cheap casio keyboard snares which is a real letdown Korg. Also there is no MIDI interface which is somewhat understandable considering it's a very bare bones analog synth. The good news is that it's fairly straightforward to put put a MIDI port in. Lastly there is a FLUX button, that kind of half reverses the sequencer to give you some unexpected and strange variations on your sequence but more often then not it just doesn't sound very appetizing. If I were to design the Monotribe I would replace the FLUX button w another drum like an 808 metal kick or another type snare. All in all ; this is a good instrument with enough waveform complexity to keep you experimenting to achieve that perfect bass vibrato sound you have heard at the rave in 1996. This will not however suffice to become your main peace of DJ gear. product_title: Auralex GRAMMA 2.75 Inches High
review_body:
I purchased this sound isolation riser for use with a subwoofer in my Home Theater set-up. I can attest to the fact that it works, but it is not a miracle worker.

My Home Theater is set up in a difficult room. The house is very old. The floor boards creak. It is built on a perimeter foundation with a crawl space. My big, 12\\" woofer, 75 lb, down-firing subwoofer (Outlaw LFM-1 Plus) wreaks havoc during heavy action scenes.

The GRAMMA helps. It does. There is a noticeable improvement. But, it is a subtle improvement. To my ear, the bass now sounds a little cleaner, a little tighter ... especially on music. But for Home Theater use, the improvement is less noticeable. The subwoofer is now easier to tune and control, but it still has to be turned down to levels well below where the calibration program (Audyssey MultEQ XT32) wants to place it.

Note: I have tried multiple subs in this room, with the GRAMMA, with the same result.

Best Features:
-Sturdy Construction
-Does improve subwoofer sound (cleaner, tighter)
-Size is ideal for larger subs (like my Outlaw LFM-1 Plus)
-Makes sub easier to slide around on hardwood flooring (to evaluate placement options)

Drawbacks:
-Unattractive for a living space (if not fully covered by equipment)
-Sound isolation works, but cannot perform miracles

Summary:
The Auralex GRAMMA does improve the sound from my subwoofer. However, the improvement is subtle to my ear. I am satisfied with the product. I would buy it again. But, I think you need a more discerning ear than mine to fully appreciate it.

review_headline: wonderful item great service value and quality
review_body:
UPDATED REVIEW***
I purchased this flute about 10 months ago and I am learning to play very well on this instrument. I am able to produce clear/full tone consistently as i'm learning to extend the range. The flute is still very shiny and I now polish it on a weekly basis to combat any of the wear I put on the keys. It takes you step by step through the basics and comes with a teacher on CD.

One other note is that this flute does not come with a marking to make sure that the head joint and body are lined up consistently every time you play. I recommend talking a fine sharpie and marking the head and body pieces so that they go on the same way each time you practice.

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

I purchased this flute about 3 months ago and I have been nothing but satisfied. This is the first instrument I have ever learned to play and its easy to play and produces quality sound. The instrument is easy to assemble and maintain. The only thing that I've noticed that looks different from the day I bought it is the tops of the keys have started to lose a bit of their shine. However everyone I've talked to said that this normal for nickel plated keys that are played on a daily basis. In no way does it affect the sound. :) I also find it very easy to tune but out of the box it was perfectly tuned. I keep mine very clean and in the case when I'm not using it has not been damaged in the slightest. The pads are also of a wonderful quality and produce a great seal.

review_body:

review_headline: product OK but beware Karaoke USA service
review_body:
First and foremost, my daughter adores this product. It plays discs just fine, and while overall the machine is a little cheap (mic connections are weak), she's having a ball with it. So if you want a cheap, intro karaoke machine, this works very well. Be sure to buy some karaoke discs to use with it, since the songs included, while voluminous, are short and a little hokey.

The ipod connection is not easy to figure out however, and the manual does not help. So, beware if you try to use the manual and don't understand it, and find the company's website and try to get help via their customer service form. The exchange that I had with a rep was increasingly difficult, as I didn't understand what he was telling me, and I couldn't find the info in the manual. He told me that he didn't see what I was talking about in the manual, and so on. I asked - twice - for a telephone number so that I could talk the issue through with someone, and was finally told that the inquiry was closed. When I went back to the website and tried to find a number to call, I got a recording from Verizon saying that the number wasn't available.

Pity, because when I dug around the website further, I found a helpful FAQ link here [...] that answered my questions. Yes, I could have found it myself. But so could my friend at customer service have directed me there, and we both would have avoided an unpleasant exchange.

The customer service rep at Amazon whom I told about this was very nice, and agreed that this did not sound good. While I can recommend this machine, I suggest you find it sold under the Emerson label, and avoid a Karaoke USA product.

UPDATE: I feel compelled to say that I DID actually find what I needed in the manual after all. So, I hereby withdraw my criticism of the manual, other than to say that it would benefit from a \\"How to get started\\" section. I dxo NOT withdraw my criticism of the customer service at Karaoke USA. The guy could have just said, are you looking at page x? Whatever happened to customer service? It still exists at Amazon, anyway.

product_title: Swan Harmonica Key of C, 16 Hole, 32 Tone
review_body:
This harmonica is surprisingly good.If you are a serious buyer examining this piece at a store,you might not want to buy it.It is a 16-hole diatonic in key of C with a plastic comb and 2 beautiful golden colour metal cover plates;but when you scrutinize it,you will notice that surface of plastic comb is not smooth,edges of holes chipped (mold job not good),metal plates not cut and pressed quite neatly (sheet metal job not well-done).But holding it at a distance,it still looks a beautiful harmonica anyway.First time I took it out of its carton box,I expected to try a somewhat funny harmonica (the reason I ordered it is the price $12.99 +free shipping ,and it has 16 holes,and 1 reviewer gave it 4 stars,and my curiosity ...).I played a song in C with it and instantly got quite cheerfully surprised : It sounds like a good standard diatonic but louder and bearing some echoes (like octave-tuned) and some vibrations (like tremolo-tuned)!..A hybrid...?!! The impression is so strong that I have to take out a Lee Oskar 10-hole diatonic key of C and perform a comparison of Swan vs. Lee Oskar (in about 4 hours with about 16 songs in C,G,A,D). Here are my comments:
1_This Swan harmonica : Reeds are well-tuned and respond great in every hole from end to end,no mute holes (blow or draw).Airtight.
Volume is louder: It has the shape and size of a Hohner 20-hole Otave Comet,but 2 metal cover plates curved
down more (like ones_but not as much_on a Hohner 16-hole Octave Echo).Wider vibration chambers.
Wider range with 16 holes,2 octaves (it can play most songs in major keys,at low or high octaves,when a 10-
hole diatonic cannot do that).
Tremolo-tuned (?) at 2 places :when you blow (not draw) at holes 8&9 and at holes 13&14,it sounds like a
tremolo-tuned harmonica.
2_Lee Oskar : Even though Swan has advantages of volume,range,tremolo...Lee Oskar is still superior in many qualities ( musical
tones,accuracy,delicate and silkymotion of sounds etc...).I would say \\"very,very good\\" to this Swan ;but \\"excellent\\"
to the Lee Oskar.If taking Lee Oskar as a standard of 10 points ,I would score this Swan as follows :
Well-tuned: 9.6/10 Responsiveness: 9.7/10 Airtight: 10/10 Volume(louder): 12/10 Tone quality: 8.5/10
Range(wider): 12/10 Stability of reeds: 7/10 (sometimes this Swan has a \\"hiccup\\" on some reed,causing a broken
sound_quick and faint but noticeable) Silky sound-motion: 7/10 ...etc.
One thing we do not know yet : durability.After 4 hours playing in a normal way,this Swan is still good.In general,against a 5-star
Lee-Oskar,this Swan harmonica may have 3.8 or 4-star rating.I give it a 5-star, considering its low price (Lee Oskar cost 3 times the
price of this piece).

review_headline: Great for begginers, OK back up for professionals

I will start out by saying that I Love DJing, I have used and owned many, many products. I originally bought the mixtrack pro for my girlfriend to learn which is great but we use Serato (for this deck it would be DJ Intro) and it seems that the timecode is not exact which is a big problem for playing in a big venue. also I may be worng but I could not use my headphones to listen to the next Cue'd in song which is a MAJOR disadvantage for using for a crowd, for example; last weeked I played a memorial day club event and since my fellow DJs had already set up I decided to leave my professional DJ gear in the car and used to Mixtrack, I immediately regretted it but I had an hour set so I had to keep going, so along with the lagged timecode, poor sound quality, and the 'blind' beat matching I had a bad set. I decided to never use it again. like I said this is a great piece of gear at a good price but it is not meant near any real venues.

Pro:
good price, lightweight emergency back-up, BPM auto-sync for perfect matching.

Con:
poor sound quality output, no headphone support for listening to next song/s, sometimes laggy timecode using serato.

I will keep this in my trunk in case my CDJs and turntables both fail.

product_title: BEHRINGER XENYX 302USB
review_body: I've been playing around with my new Behringer XENYX 302USB Mixer and so far my impressions are positive.  I was nervous about buying it because there were no reviews at all, so I opened the box carefully and took out only the 302, using my own cable and on-line documentation. That way, if I had to return it, packing it back up would be easy.  I use Audacity (with a single core, Pentium 4 PC running XP Pro) to record, and the program recognized the 302 (as USB codex), no problem.  One thing I wanted to do is record from an iPod Touch 4G to Audacity, then play that Audacity track back and record another track against it from the iPod. I used a mono cable that is 1/4 inch on one end (plugged into the mic jack of the 302) and 1/8 inch on the other (plugged into the headphone jack of the iPod).  I used an app called Chordbot to play a progression on the iPod, which was recorded through the 302 into Audacity. I didn't care that the track was mono, but if I wanted stereo, I could have used the line input on the 302 with RCA cables going to an 1/8th inch stereo plug.  Once my chord progression was recorded on an Audacity track, I played that back by using an RCAs to 1/8 inch plug to connect the line input on the 302 to the headphone jack of the computer. By pushing the red button on the 302, which selects input from the USB (the computer), and the black button next to it, which sends the signal to the headphones, I could hear the Audacity track playing as I recorded a new track, this time using an app called Thumbjams on the iPod.  It worked very well. No hiss or other unwanted noise present.  The 302 assumes (incorrectly, in my case) that I want to hear the mic input through the earphones as I'm recording. I don't. I never monitor myself when singing or playing guitar, but listen only to the backing track.  I got around this by using the pan slider on the 302, panning my live performance all the way to the right. I then removed the right earphone from my ear. I panned thesound coming from the computer all the way to the left. This way I could hear the backing track but not my voice in the headphones.  My Audio Technica AT2020 microphone recorded fine--with no hiss or noise--with the 302's gain set at 12 o'clock, the mic volume maxed, and the main mix volume at about 2 o'clock.  I could generate hiss with the AT2020 if I cranked the 302's gain and volume all the way up, but I can do that with most any mixing deck.  I could not get as loud a hissless track using the 2020 and the 302 as I would like. A preamp is probably called for. But the signal was usable if I increased the gain a bit in Audacity after recording, or if I doubled a track.  In addition to the iPod experiment, I recorded a nylon-string guitar, then recorded a vocal track against it. Used the AT2020 for both tracks. Worked fine.  I have an old Radio Shack dynamic mic with a built-in TSR cable that I tried. It also recorded well, for what it is. (I sound terminally depressed when I record with this mic, so only dig it out for experiments such as this.)  All in all, I'm liking the 302 and plan to use it instead of the XENYX 802/UCA202 USB interface rig I was using.  WOWSERS. Important update. The USB codec that Windows installed when I first plugged in the 302 doesn't play nice with Audacity. Often when I try to play back or play back and record, there is no sound through the 302, even though I can see audio levels in Audacity.  I went to the Behringer website and downloaded the ASIO 32 bit driver. Now things are great. Except. Whatever USB slot you install the driver to is taken over by the driver and can't used by any other audio codec.  This means that if you unplug the 302 and plug another audio device into the same slot, it can only play--if it will--using the Behringer ASIO codec. Other slots are unaffected. It's possible to undo this by running the setup file again and choosing to uninstall the driver.  I'm willing to give up a USB slot to the 302 because I'm liking it so much and will probably use it every day. YMMV.

product_title: TC Helicon VoiceLive 2 Extreme Edition
review_headline: Excellent for Live but too noisy for studio.
review_body:
I'm a keyboard player/singer. I plug my fantom G7 synth workstation into the aux in of the voice live, then and send 2 stereo mic-level L/R XLRs to the mixer. When I do that - I control my keyboard level AND my vocal level. And the audio engineer doesn't have to muck with my keyboard levels. Less channels too! I also recommend using MIDI for tracking (versus audio/gtr in). Finally - use a volume pedal to bring your harmonies in and out while you sing. It's so much simpler than finding button with your foot while you sing.

This unit sounds great live. I love it! Great harmony sounds - it doesn't get better than this. The\\"Extreme\\" version (blue color versus black) has more configuration options (like level choice of mic, mic+6, mic+12, line, etc) and a cleaner and better mic pre-amp. I put my Earthworks SR40V mic and it sounds wonderful. I created 3-4 patches of my own and that' all I use.

PLAN ON LEARNING THIS UNIT WHEN YOU GET IT. Just watch the online videos.

I would caution for studio use - the unit has a high noise floor. Not sure why - they should have cleaned the noise floor on this. Without a noise- reduction s/w for the track - avoid it. For studio vocoder, I'd get the rack version of this unit - assuming it's quieter.

product_title: Boss RC-3 RC3 Loop Station Guitar Effects Pedal with Power Supply, Cables, and Extended Warranty
review_headline: Almost great. Too many small flaws [UPDATED 9/1/14]
review_body: UPDATE 9/1/14:  Two of the issues discussed below were fixed by Boss. The latency when switching from phrase to phrase was eliminated by a firmware update, and the labor part of the warrantee was upped from 90 days to a healthier 2 years.    With those improvements in mind I have changed my rating from three stars to four stars, although I am still not wildly excited about the RC-3. I am currently using it with a Zoom G3X, which can compensate for some of the RC-3's shortcomings. The G3X allows you to dial in a tempo, and it has 40 high quality drum beats (still not enough AFAIC). I've ended up using the RC-3 simply to record and loop what comes off the G3X and have dispensed altogether with the RC-3's inadequate rhythm features. The G3X also has a simple looper that is very convenient and useful when you want to try something out quickly without messing with the RC-3.    -------------    Original Review:    3-1/2 stars, really. It's almost a great product, but considering the relatively high price it's disappointing that Boss cut corners and didn't get some of the details right.    The good stuff about the RC-3 is obvious and easy to find online--it loops, has lots of memory and I/O, is easy to use, and is excellent for practicing and song writing--so I'm focusing on the less obvious bad stuff:    - Various online sources, including, until recently, the Boss and Roland websites, claim you can specify tempo incrementally. Unfortunately this is not true. There is no tempo display and it's tap tempo only, which is a pain in the neck and really ticked me off, because it was one of the few things I was careful to check on the Boss site. At the very least one should be able to fine tune the tempo in 1 BPM increments with the increase/decrease buttons, even if the tempo isn't also displayed, but you can't even do that. And no, you can't use the pedal to tap in the tempo--you have to get down on the floor and use the dinky little button.    - The drum beat and tempo resetto their defaults if you change the phrase number, even if you move to a blank phrase. Sorry, but that is plain dumb--it means you can't record several versions of the same thing, or different parts of a song, without re-setting the beat and tempo. BUT, as noted above, you can't set the tempo numerically, so it's impossible to get the same tempo.    - Built-in time signatures are 3/4 and 4/4 only. No 7/8, 5/4, etc. Boss's marketing department was inspired on how to play this--the web site says, \\"You can also specify the time signature.\\" Uh, thanks, but the choices, which Boss conveniently neglects to mention, are almost as limited as the color of a Ford Model T. (\\"Any customer can have a car painted any color that he wants so long as it is black.\\") I should add that one of the 4/4 beats is a 12/8 shuffle, and that one of the 3/4 beats is a 6/8 shuffle and another is 9/8, but that doesn't excuse Boss's mendacity. It's clear they are trying to hide their product's shortcomings.    - The 10 built-in drum beats are very basic and are not adequate. There's a reason you can't listen to them on the Boss site, but as a public service I have made recordings available [links deleted by amazon. Try searching soundcloud for Boss RC-3 Drums]. There are actually 20 beats, since there are versions for 3/4 and 4/4, but with all the storage space on this thing, surely Boss could have included more. Even the previous model, the RC-2, had 30 (?) beats.    (Yes, you can go to the trouble of recording and importing your own rhythms to get any time signature and pattern, but you lose the pedal's convenience advantage. Besides, recorded rhythms are part of a loop--they can't be re-used without re-importing, the number of measures can't be changed, and the volume can't be adjusted independently of the guitar playback. Maybe there's a way to hook a drum machine up to the second input, but I can't think of how you would sync/trigger it.)    - The 5 year warranty is parts only. Labor is only90 days. Labor rates are $40/hour. Return shipping is on you, and if you choose not to get the repair after receiving an estimate, then you are charged $25 anyway. It seems that warranty information is hidden on purpose. I could not locate it on the Boss site and even the documentation that comes with the pedal does not state the warranty period or detailed terms. It's a wonder of obfuscation: \\"... this product will be free from defect in materials and/or workmanship from the date of purchase until the period of time indicated for this product.\\" Uh huh. And what \\"period of time\\" would that be and where would it be \\"indicated\\"? Well, I eventually found the actual warranty terms on rolandus.com: [URL deleted by Amazon. Try googling rolandus warranty]    - Power supply is not included by Boss, although some retailers include one.    - When you switch between phrases, there is a short lag, so you can't string together phrases to make a song in real time. See this youtube video: TlKDHsauvos    - Buttons are mushy, rubbery stuff like a tv remote. Probably saved on costs, but the durability is questionable.    One other note: I'm using the RC-3 in a Line 6 Flextone I guitar amp effects loop. That way I can overlay loops using different amp effects and amp models. Unlike the Jamman Solo, this is not a mode that is mentioned in the instructions. I think the RC-3 is designed to go before the amp. Amp effects loops are usually line level, while stomp boxes are usually instrument level, so whether it works probably depends on the effect loop's impedance (line level can mean different things and likely varies by amp) and whether the RC-3 can handle the signal coming out of the preamp. Well, nothing's fried yet.    UPDATE 2/21/12:  A minor issue: When a recorded loop is transferred to a computer, a drum/tempo track is not included. You get a Stereo WAV (41.1 KHz, 16 bit) of the guitar. So, if you want to use the loop in, say, Garage Band, or import it back into the RC-3, you willhave to add drums. Getting drums to sync up on the RC-3 is difficult unless the loop was recorded at the default tempo (120 bpm) or is relatively short. If not, eventually the drums go out of sync, because, as noted above, there is no way to dial in a tempo.    UPDATE 7/27/12:  - Supposedly cannot be used with headphones. There is a dire warning in the instructions that the headphones could be damaged, but Boss does not elucidate how. I tried it anyway. It works, but you need a mono to stereo adapter to hear the output in both ears (or something more complicated if you are using both of the RC-3 inputs), and the output is weak. You have to turn the volume up all the way up to get a barely reasonable volume, so I don't see how the headphones would be damaged.    - Do not try using this with a power supply daisy-chained to other pedals or a headphone amp. It generates all kinds of horrible electronic noise, including a high pitched oscillation and in-tempo thunks.

product_title: Ibanez Artcore AS93 Electric Guitar Blue Sunburst
review_body:
Being a jazz guy -- I own a quartet of HERITAGE and GIBSON hollow-bodies worth 10 or 12 times the price of this product -- I needed a semi-hollow body for rehearsing in a studio, where of necessity I'm in close proximity to the smaller 40W amp I prefer to use in such a setting. I've always hankered after something with a blueburst finish, and settled on this modestly-priced, but very pretty and serviceable instrument. Its looks and feel are suggestive of the GIBSON ES-335, although its humbucker-clone pick-ups are not up to GIBSON standards. Given that I only use the neck pick-up, I can live with it. But since this is a hybrid axe that's also aimed at the rock crowd -- trying as it does to do the job of the ES-335 or ES-137, I must admit a rocker would want to swap out the pick-ups for something else -- especially the bridge pick-up, which seems weak to me. Also, I normally play with little or no use of the neck pick-up's treble control, but on the AS93 I find it necessary to crank the treble pretty well all the way up to get the sound I want, which seems a little strange.

On the plus side, though, it's about the prettiest guitar I've ever seen; surprising to see colour-coordinated abalone pearl inlays in the fingerboard. It plays real nice, and -- with the necessary tweaking of sundry EQ settings -- produces a nice jazz sound, with sustain that'll last into the middle of next week, if required. Just as HERITAGE is doing a good job -- from the qualitative standpoint -- of applying pressure on GIBSON from the high end, IBANEZ is doing the same thing at the low end. Japanese guitar, Chinese-made and Korean parts -- a yellow peril if ever there was one. But for my needs, a real bargoon and quite a fine instrument, really.

product_title: SX SST SE LH BGMY Full Size Left Handed Electric Guitar Pink
review_body:
I read the reviews here at Amazon and decided that this was a good bang for the buck in buying a guitar. Also, i saw a review by a very well known music store doing a review. All of these reviews were impressive. I own several guitars and have played many guitars at some well known music stores. When the guitar came, it was very beautiful. It holds in tune very well. I had to stretch the strings out and play them awhile to get them broke in...it's always that way with new strings. Once they were broke in, it held tune very well. The sound is great. The alder is a nice balanced tone. The pickups have a lot of power for single coil pickups. There is nothing cheap about this guitar but the price. I'm very impressed. The only flaw was on the back there are some fine lines in the paint, but you cannot see them unless you hold it up to a light and let the light reflect across the surface...but...who goes around holding the backs of guitars up to the light to check the surface?

The metal hardware feels and behaves very strong. The frets are nicely done. The action adjusts as low as any of the expensive store bought guitars. I might level the frets a little more by hand so I can adjust the all strings to a 16th above the frets. The two middle strings are maybe closer than a 16th at the 22nd fret, but the sides (e strings) are between and 16th and an 8th. Later I might hand level the frets with a straight hand leveler to hone them in to perfection, but I'm pleased. Many expensive guitars from the music store will not adjust to a 16th gap between the fret and string without buzzing. So, i'm happy.

I would gladly buy one of these before paying out hundreds of dollars on something that is not going to be any noticable difference and cost a lot more money.

This guitar compares to guitars costing a few times the price. It's a real good deal.

product_title: PR-20 PR20 Orginal Heil Sound PRO Series Large Diaphragm Dynamic Microphone
review_body: - Sound quality: I like this mic. It sounds darker than the Recording Hack's graph would suggest.  Compared to a LDC, you'll get less fidelity in general. It has too much handling noise for jostling around in general, but shock mounted on a stand is where this mic shines. The proximity effect seems less pronounced compared to the SM57. It allows you to get up close and personal while singing and a tight pattern compared to my LDCs seems to remove the room from the recording at a distance. However, the lowish sensitivity make recording quiet instruments from a distance difficult b/c of the generated noise of the mic and cranked preamp. This is not your HiFi recording vocal mic.  - Reliability / Durability: Built like a vault! Dropped several times, thrown in the back of a truck for months and drove off road while in its case... never a problem. It feels heavy and solid and been around for years.  - Would you buy this again if it were stolen?: Yep.  - Features that stand out: Build quality and less pronounced proximity effect than expected. Also a generally great bass response even from a distance. The case is nice and has several replacement grills with a well fitted clip.  - What I don't Like: Handling noise--for its intended use, that's its only downside as far as I can tell. It would be great if they'd fix that.  - Similar products used: Shure SM57.  Just a workhorse to keep around.

product_title: ION Audio Discover Drums MKII Tabletop Electronic Drums
review_body: Bought this for my godson for his 2nd b-day. My dad was a professional drummer for 50 years. I've been known to chip a stick or two, myself. This is about exactly what you'd expect from an electronic kit in this price range. The sounds are mediocre and the response is about like hitting on Linoleum tile. If you're an adult and thinking about getting into percussion, don't start here. If you're looking to get a gift for a child that they can beat on and drive their folks insane, this'd probably do the trick.   This won't teach you how to play drums, as there's no ability to involve the feet/legs, which is key to playing on a drum kit.   The built-in rhythms are straightforward and easily accessible. You can, also, change the tempo to make it easier to play along with, either on the pad, itself, or on an accompanying instrument.   So, know what you're looking for - if you've got aspirations of actually being a drummer, there are better investments; if you want to bang on something that is the \\"Casio keyboard\\" equivalent for drums, this might be just what the doctor ordered.

product_title: Mendini 1/2 MV Solid Wood Violin with Hard Case, Shoulder Rest, Bow, Rosin and Extra Strings
review_headline: You get more than you pay for -- this is a real bargain!
review_body:
I purchased a this half size violin for my 8-year old daughter who has expressed an interest in the violin but isn't quite ready to start lessons through school. I didn't want to invest in an expensive instrument that might be quickly set aside, but I thought for the cost of one or two lessons (or half of one American Girl doll), I could expose her to the instrument and see if she had any lasting interest.

For the price, I wasn't expecting much. I was a bit apprehensive to open the box, wondering what broken parts I might find inside. But I was pleasantly surprised by the quality of violin I received. And by all the extras -- extra strings and an extra bridge. The violin looked nice, with no obvious problems. And to my surprise, it didn't sound bad at all. The tone was actually clear and somewhat warm. This is definitely not a toy!

On the down side: The case seemed to be cheaply made and a zipper pull was missing -- but not a big deal. And the instrument was very difficult for me to tune. And it doesn't hold its tuning particularly well. The bridge popped out three times when I tried to tune the instrument, which was somewhat startling. But then [[ASIN:B000F3JO7M The Original Peg Drops by Ardsley]], it's been a long time since I tuned a violin. And by the time I got to the G string, the A string was invariably out of tune. But I have never had a brand new instrument before, so I'm guessing that this has something to do with the newness of the instrument. The pegs were also a little slippy at first. Again, I don't really consider this to be a fault of the violin. Just want to share my experiences.

That said, the sound is fine. The bow is fine. The instrument looks great. You're not getting a Stradivarius, of course, and if your child continues with violin you will probably want to upgrade, but for a starter instrument for someone who isn't yet committed, you really can't go wrong for the price. Overall, I'm very, very pleased by this purchase and think it was well worth the money.

UPDATE: Still can't get this violin to stay tuned for ten minutes! Very frustrating to try to tune it.
UPDATE (October 2013): Got some [[ASIN:B000F3JO7M The Original Peg Drops by Ardsley]] and the tuning problem was solved!very pleased by this purchase and think it was well worth the money.

UPDATE: Still can't get this violin to stay tuned for ten minutes! Very frustrating to try to tune it.
UPDATE (October 2013): Got some [[ASIN:B000F3JO7M The Original Peg Drops by Ardsley]] and the tuning problem was solved!

product_title: Hagstrom HJ800 Electric Jazz Guitar (Vintage Sunburst)
review_body:
Pros: Dimensions, neck, action, sound, comfort, playability, value, appearance, resists feedback.

Cons: Bottom contour of the floating bridge does not seem to be a close a fit.

The Bottom Line: Great sound, comfortable size, room up the neck, quality workmanship, nice appearance and reasonable price make this an excellent sub $1000 jazz guitar.

I am returning to playing guitar after not playing or owning an instrument for many years. My interest seems to be jazz and chord melody playing. In the past six months, I've tried out a number of guitars, including Les Pauls, semi-hollow bodies, and a couple of other hollow bodies. The Hagstrom HJ800 is the first one that I have been able to bond with. It is the best playing, sounding and looking guitar that I have found so far.

Here's what I have learned in a few weeks of owning and playing:

1. I love the dimensions of this guitar. The body is just 16\\" across the lower bout, 2-3/4\\" depth at the rim. It is very comfortable to play sitting or standing

2. The neck is 25\\" scale, 22 frets, neck joined at 16th fret with small heel. This was important to me. Lots of jazz boxes have only 20 frets, neck joined at 14th or 15th fret with the heel extending all the way to the 12th fret, resulting in a short-neck, closed-in feeling. Access all the way to the 22nd fret is excellent on the HJ800.

3. Diameter is 15\\", flatter than I'm used to but comfortable. Contour is also comfortable. It is thin -- less depth from surface of fingerboard to back of neck. Width is also comfortable. Graphite nut and smooth tuners.

4. I changed the strings to .10 flats (I'm moving up to .12s in steps) and no plink or buzzes. I was able to lower the action to .050\\" at 12th fret, both E strings.

5. I was worried about setting the intonation on the floating bridge the first time, but it was actually easier than a Tune-O-Matic. With new strings, I tuned the open Estrings with a strobe tuner, fretted each separately at the 12th fret, nudged the bridge back and forth a couple of times until the strobe caged and done. Middle strings were either right on or only a hair off.

6. I am a little concerned about the bottom contour of the floating bridge. It does not seem to be as close a fit as I would hope -- not maximum contact of bridge to body, although it sound is great, even unamplified. After I settle on strings, I'll take it to a pro to work on.

7. It is really a very nice looking guitar. I got the three tone sunburst. Mine has no signature logo on the finger rest and the two screws that appear chrome color in the picture are black on mine. Much more classy in my opinion.

8. The sound is just what I am looking for. After finding the right settings on my amp, I am getting the warm and articulated sound I wanted. Although I mainly use the neck pickup, the bridge and the combination are also excellent.

9. This guitar seems not very prone to feedback. I think I read somewhere that there is something in the sound chamber (a piece of solid material?) that limits feedback.

10. No complaints at all on workmanship. Fit, finish, materials all very good.

I bought mine with the Hagstrom gig bag (\\"Hag Bag\\"), which is much better than any other gig bag I have seen. It has rigid sides and a Velcro strap to hold the neck in place on a removable cradle that can be taken out and used when I'm working on the guitar. The bag seems to provide 80 percent of the protection of a hard case at about 20 percent of the weight. For my minimal transporting use, perfect.

The guitar and bag were purchased directly from Music Farm. Todd was great. Excellent professionalism, communication, shipping. I recommend Music Farm without reservation.

product_title: NEW Portable Digital Roll Up Piano / 61 Key Mini Keyboard / For Music Party Game
review_headline: UNUSABLE! - ALWAYS PLAYS  EXTRA DISSIDENT NOTES!
review_body:
Do NOT buy this piano!!!

What makes this piano UNUSABLE is that, when just 3 notes are
played at once (or 1 note is held down when 2 other notes are played) the piano produces the sound of an additional (unplayed) note. If the additional note were harmonic it could be tolerated, BUT when the notes of a major chord are played, the additional note is the minor-3rd note, which is extremely DISSONANT, thus making the piano produce a sound that is extremely unpleasant!!!

I received a response to my complaints by the company that sold the piano to me and they stated that this additional dissonant sound is NOT a fault or malfunction! That means that this fundamental problem is a built-in DESIGN FLAW! Therefore, this product, as is, should be BANNED from sale until it is fixed.

Here is an example of what happens: I use the notation C1 to mean playing the C note on the first (lowest octave). If I hold down C1 and play (E2 G2 on the next octave up), then the piano adds the additional sound of key D#1. This horrible problem happens across all octaves (e.g. hold down C3 E4 G4 and the piano adds D#3). This terrible dissonance happens for every major chord. For example, if you play D-major (by hitting D3 F#4 A4) that will cause the piano to add the horribly dissonant sound of F3.

The same problem occurs for E-major, F-major, G-major, etc. Imagine trying to play C an octave lower with the left hand on a regular piano while playing only E and G an octave higher with the right hand (a C-major chord) and then hearing D# ringing out! Imagine a very dissonant note ringing out every time you play ANY major chord across ANY octave. It would make any piano UNplayable!!!

The problem is worse if you try to play more than 3 notes at once or if you hold down just one note while playing 2 or more notes.

In addition to this FUNDAMENTAL DESIGN FLAW there are OTHER MAJOR PROBLEMS with this piano:

- When you hold down a key, it often plays the key twice.

- If you try to play quietly by using earbuds, then there is a tremendous amount of static on the line and the piano sounds terrible through the earbuds, with lots of sharp pops and clicks (which will probably destroy your ears and destroy your earbuds!)

A minor complaint: The adaptor (to use in place of batteries) has a chord that is only 3 ft long. With a chord this short I discovered that when I place the piano on a low table and have a wall socket right below the table, the chord will still never reach the socket.

I love the idea of a soft, roll-up keyboard (for traveling) and so I am EXTREMELY DISAPPOINTED with the company's response

Here is their (email) response:
\\"it is unavoidable that compound sounds are heard. The sound is created by the touch of each individual key, with firm hits. Two or more sounds will possibly be made simultaneously when the hits are not consistent. This is not faulty or mal-functioned.\\"

I was VERY careful in my experimentation with this piano. I played the notes carefully, with firm hits with the piano placed on a firm, flat surface. The piano is very consistent in ALWAYS ADDING those, sour, DISSONANT notes! The dissonant sounds are added every time 3 notes are played for a major chord with one of the notes being an octave away. This happens every time the notes are played at once or if one note is held while the others are played. The problem is worse for chords with more notes.

This product should NOT be sold until after this design flaw is eliminated. They should NOT be allowed to sell this DECEPTIVE, FAULTY product to innocent consumers :-(

product_title: CHAUVET DJ Comet LED Effect Light
review_headline: Nice Effect - Cool If an Addition
review_body:
Ordered one of these to go with other Chauvet lights (2 Derby X's, 2 LX-5 Moonflowers and 2 Techno Strobes) for a mobile setup I'm building. Currently have about half of these set up in my basement so I can test and observe. The Comet is smaller than I had pictured from the description, but still a fairly substantial light (external demensinos). Other reviewers have noted the motor noise. It IS relatively noisy, but for my application, with the music turned up loud (mobile DJ) nobody's going to hear it; if you plan on using with low levels, it may become aggevating and may not respond well (or you to it). However, once I got it out of the box and tested it with the others, I decided I needed a 2nd one.......not necessarily because I was crazy about the light, but more or less for coverage, it's got a fairly narrow angle of dispersement.
The light DOES have a pretty cool pattern; the motor reverses itself (based the sound it detects)and consequently the light patterns. The patterns remind me of one of those old kids sparking pinwheels (okay I'm OLD), with red, blue, green and white (no yellow) multiple swirling pinwheel patterns. It has a sensitivity adjustment, but it seems to take a bit of noise to get it started. Once it gets started (on the highest sensitivity setting) it stays fairly active. My other lights have a sweeping effect, so the Comet(s) add a contrasting pattern that wakes things up. It's all LED so it won't get hot, and it is supposed to link to multple Comet's (we'll see how well they work in unison when I get the 2nd one). By itself, the limited repeating cycle would become apparent and boring after a few minutes, but mixed in with other lights/patterns, it's a cool addition.

product_title: Baroq-ulele T, Tenor, Rosewood, Tuners
review_body:
Truthfully I think I was mesmerized by the beautiful laser cut sound hole when I ordered this, and the interesting lute shape. This is not a good first ukulele for anyone, especially since the rounded back makes it difficult to hold. Some people find that using a strap fixes that, others feel a strap does not help all that much. Reviews I watched on YouTube before I bought one indicated that this uke is better for fingerpicking than strumming, given how the rounded back shape cam muffle strumming.

This uke arrived extremely well packed and I was grateful for that. There were a few minor scratches on the back of the neck and some minor problems with smoothness on one of the frets. The biggest problem was that the nut and and the saddle were set WAY too high, and when the uke arrived it would have not been playable by anyone, especially on the first fret. I took it to a luthier, who agreed that it was in unplayable condition. Among other things, the nut was also rough on both sides and had to be sanded. Getting this ukulele set up so it could be played, given the amount of work that had to be done, cost me an additional seventy dollars. I thought about sending it back, but it is beautiful, so I wanted to see if it could be made playable.

The sound quality is alright. And now that it has been set-up properly it is fun for me to play. I am going to buy my next uke from a company that inspects the ukes and makes sure they are set-up and playable before they ship them out. If you want a uke that is unique and beautiful to look at, with average sound, and are willing to accept the possibility you may have to put out extra bucks for set-up (unless you can do that kind of thing yourself) you may find this to be an acceptable uke.

product_title: Fishman Neo-D Passive Soundhole Pickup - Single Coil
review_body:
I have been playing electro-acoustic and acoustic steel string guitars for nearly 20 years. I am also a sound engineer and a producer, and am extremely critical about sound overall, specifically critical about acoustic instrument's sound. I have found that most acoustic guitars with pickups sound terribly artificial, so the past 2 guitars I have bought have been Martins with no pickups. About a year ago I began playing in a band and needed to amplify my steel string, so after researching a bit I decided on this pickup. I was especially drawn by this pickup's ability to blend both a mic and a magnetic pick up. It brings out the best of my instrument. I like to set the knob to halfway between both, which gives me a very natural, beautiful sound. When feedback becomes an issue with the mic, I simply turn the knob to magnetic pick up, and still the guitar sounds beautiful.
The goose neck does move out of place, but only when moving the guitar from place to place. I haven't found this to be an issue.
I highly recommend this pick up.

product_title: AIAIAI Tracks Headphone with Mic
review_body:
I received my Tracks only a few days ago, but it's already clear that they are perfect (for me).

I do not want headphones that attempt to replace a stereo system. I have a stereo system, and like it very much.

I do not want ear buds. I have ear buds (good quality), but do not like the feel of ear buds.

I want headphones that have good clear sound, and are light weight and comfortable. Tracks are perfect (for me). I like their looks, but that is personal. I like their design because it seems simple, durable, and adjustable to fit anybody. The cord is about 55\\".

In a store demo, I tried Monster Beats Pro by Dr. Dre and Bose Quiet Comfort 15. I preferred the Beats Pro, and I think both of them have better sound than Tracks. However, Tracks have good sound, and the other two are not what I want. They're both heavier, less comfortable, bulkier, with joints that can break, and I don't want headphones that require a battery.

Before I bought my Tracks, I sent email to the manufacturer to ask the cord length. I received a prompt reply. Interestingly, it said the cord length is about 3.5 feet (i.e., 42\\"). My guess is that the answer measured the cord to the point where it divides rather than to the ear pads.

review_body: This tuner is exactly as described.  Fast, accurate and easy to use.  Would definitely recommend for all acoustic stringed instruments.

product_title: Roll Up Piano - Yamano Digital & Portable 61 Keys Electronic Keyboard with Built-in Record & Play Back Function, Sustain Pedal and Learning Mode
review_body:
I really had high hopes for this product, but I remained very skeptical. I mean, the idea of a roll-up piano, who wouldn't want one of these? I admit that I play the piano and have high quality keyboards, so my musical expectations of quality are high, however this unit was doomed from the start.

After unwrapping the contents from the box and putting it together (a little assembly work) I couldn't power it because the power cord adapter was broken. I did try it with the batteries and those seemed to work and power the unit. The sustain pedal worked nicely. But there was no MIDI interface which this unit was supposed to have. Also, some of the keys did not work at all. It's only a 61-key board so you really need them all to freakin' work! Also, if you try to play more than a few keys at a time you start to lose the sounds. Like the early rackmounts and keyboards it is incapable of playing a lot of notes at one time. I suppose its a low grade processor and memory available to the unit. Who knows, it's probably running on a 8-bit processor with DOS as the operating system.

After about five minutes of abuse, I repackaged the unit, being sure to include all the broken parts, and went to Amazon to get a refund and return label. I gave this unit a fair shake, but really, unless you're buying this for your 10 year old, don't waste your time or money - it will be a total let down.

If I ever see a roll-up unit made by Yamaha or Kawai or Roland I'd give it a go, but this manufacturer is just pure crapola.

product_title: Shape Graphic Picks 1
review_body: I bought what was intended to be a year supply of picks for a musical therapy program I started at the hospital I work at. These picks are practically useless for acoustic guitar. A pick might last me 25 minutes of playing before there is large gouges in the plastic from strumming. Absolutely the worst picks I have ever played with. I have not tried to use them with electric guitar I would assume they would fair some better but still have less life than others. I think its a shame fender put their name on these.

product_title: Gibraltar SC-QRHHC Quick Release Hi Hat Clutch
review_headline: Great Concept w/ A Few Design Flaws
review_body: I had to purchase this as soon as it became available.  I considered the Remo quick release but, prefered the bearing lock system on the Gibraltar.  However, there are only two bearings. At least two more would put my mind at ease as far as grip and wear.  Also, when I first received it and put it on my legless hi-hat stand it didn't fit.  Then I noticed it would slide on upside down.  Upon closer inspection I saw that the part holding the clamp sticks out over the hole a bit and has a narrow channel that the rod didn't fit through.  This is why it fit upside down since it could get a better angle to the receiver.  Then I tried it on my Pearl 900 series stand and it just barely fit.  So, if you have a light to medium duty stand, your good.  Otherwise, be prepared to file it down a little over the hole.  That being said, this is still an invaluable tool to have if you gig regularly.  It shaves at least two to three minutes off your set-up/breakdown time, which is crucial!  The quick connect is super easy and holds tight.  I expect this to be a headache saver on gigs and will get the Remo clutch to try on my other stands.

product_title: Fender Classic Player '60s Stratocaster® Electric Guitar
review_body:
If you were to buy this strat, it would've been more advantageous to do so back when this line was first released in 2006. That's when this strat came with actual Fender Custom Shop 69 pickups signed by Abigail Ybarra, the woman hired by Leo Fender in 1956 to wind many of the pickups that went into many of those strats that we associate with having that coveted, unique tone that many manufacturers have tried to reproduce but haven't come close. I believe she even wound Jimi Hendrix's pickups, and we all know how great his tone was.

But since then, Abigail Ybarra has retired, and the stock pickups that are in more recent models, I believe, don't have those authentic Custom Shop pickups. Instead, it seems my classic player 60;s strat, which was given to me as a birthday present last year, came stock with 69 pickups that were manufactured in Fender's Encinata factory and not in their custom shop. Therefore, the pickups were neither signed nor wound by Abigail Ybarra. That doesn't mean the pickups that come stock in this model aren't good, but they're not the real deal. It also means something else.

This means Fender, once again, found a way to cut corners by cheapening the pikups while charging the same amount of money for this strat while increasing their bottom line and depriving the consumer of the quality product offered back in 2006. Fender's website states the CP 60's strat comes stock with \\"Custom 69 pickups with gray bobbins.\\" The language is misleading, but upon further research, they're Custom Encinata 69 pickups, not the Custom Shop 69 pickups. Many claim to be unable to tell the difference in the tone between the two sets; others believe the difference is night and day. I belong somewhere in between, as I swapped the stock pickups for the real Custom Shop 69 pickups (signed and dated by Abigail Ybarra) and found the tone to be noticeably brighter and better, whether playing on a clean or lead channel of my tube amp (I have aPeavey Classic 50 212).

In fact, the only changes I didn't make to this guitar were the neck, saddles, and bridge plate (and the body, of course). The neck is real nice and has excellent fret work with a sweet rosewood fingerboard with a 12\\" radius, which makes for a flatter fingerboard surface and easier string bending. The bridge is a two-point bridge, so I definitely wanted to keep that. However, the tuners, trem block, nut (which was horribly cut), and pickups were all swapped out for Fender Schaller locking tuners, a Callaham cold rolled steel trem block, bone nut, and the aforementioned Custom Shop 69 pickups, respectively. All upgrades definitely improved the overall playability and tone of the guitar.

Bottom line: this is a decent strat but way overpriced given the modifications I had to make to this guitar in order for it to play the way I wanted it to. The main selling points here are the neck and two-pivot bridge plate. Besides that, you're better off spending two to three hundred dollars less for either a Deluxe Player's Strat or Mexican Fender Standard Strat and replacing the hardware with better quality material (including the pickups).

Hope this helps guide your decision.
