The way the power cord is designed, people are constantly stepping on it and unplugging it while attempting to cross the room to get to the beer fridge. So just a heads up, this thing is big and heavy, as big and heavy as having another instrument.  If you have a LOT of pedals that you use all the time, however, and have a lot of room in your practice space and on stage, this is a great pedal board.

And someone rated this 1 star because it lacked thorough instructions and suggested it should come with a installation guide with pictures . lol. I'm honestly not sure if there are instructions or not. I think on the back of the package you will find some. So just a heads up. If you need diagrams to figure out how to hold a hanger on the wall and put a screw through the hole. Keep your guitar on a stand and don't rate this product 1 star.

Step 1 find a stud
Step 2 drill 2 small pilot holes (optional)
Step 3 drill in screws.
Done. All the instructions anyone should need.

review_headline: Stinky little bastard, but plays great.

Mine came with the stinky strap problem, and the case stinks too.  I e-mailed Washburn tonight asking for them to replace it, and expect they will get back to me soon.  The strap is kind of junky anyway, I wish they had just not sent one instead of the stinky strap that made the whole case reek. product_title: Behringer EUROLIVE B912NEO DSP-Controlled 1,200-Watt 12-inch PA Speaker System with Neodymium Speakers and Integrated Mixer
review_body:
The B912NEO is an amazing value. I am always skeptical when a product claims to have a TON of features and yet is affordably priced. This speaker is packed with features and performs as well as much more expensive models (I know because I did a head-to-head comparison with the JBL PRX612M currently retailing for $800). The sound quality is very good; so good that untrained ears could not tell the difference between B912NEO and the PRX612M. The difference I heard was very minimal - just a bit more warmth in the PRX612M. $300 worth of warmth? No. In favor of the B912NEO was the ability to mix multiple inputs (two to be exact, with individual gain knobs) directly on the speaker and also several extra options, such as a noise gate (which will cut out lower-volume signal such as background noise, High and Low Frequencey EQ as well as a variable Low Frequency cut, which can help clean up intelligibility of vocals. There is also a selectable contour for speech or music and a timed turn-off.

When it comes to the construction of the speaker, I could not be more impressed. The quality is outstanding, no weird imperfections, it has nice clean seams where the two halves come together, and the finish is a professional black matte cabinet with a heavy duty steel grille in a gloss black. The handles are conveniently placed on the sides of the speaker and are fairly comfortable to grip. I also like the indicator LED on the front which is blue when powered-on and red when clipping - and the speaker still has more LED indicators on the back that indicate clipping and gate functionality.

The only things I didn't like about the speaker are cosmetic - I don't like the stickers on the grille (I can probably take them off easily but haven't tried yet). The other thing I didn't like is the fact that the HF driver has silver/grey color to it and I would have preferred that it be black. That's the only negative things I can come up with - very minimal.

Overall, this is just one great speaker for a great price.l, this is just one great speaker for a great price.

review_body: I have been using this pedal for a few months with my 3 piece cover band (www dontknowjack dot net) we don't use the harmonies all that much, but I do use the octave feature, (pumped up kicks, lonely boy, etc.) and it sounds great. (for solo acoustic gigs, I may use the harmonies more, depending on the songs) don't get me wrong, the harmonies sound good, we just prefer to sing them live. the main reason I bought this pedal was for its \\"tone\\" button, the doubling feature (thickins up your voice) and the awesome reverbs. Everything I watched and read online about this pedal claimed that it \\"puts your vocal above the mix\\", and after using this pedal at about 20 gigs - I couldn't agree more with that statement. I actually just added it to my pedal board as a permanent piece. Another nice feature of the pedal (you have to upgrade the firmware to get it) is the chromatic pitch correction. (just a heads up: after I upgraded the firmware, the knobs stopped responding! I thought the pedal was broken, and was ready to ship it back. A quick Google search for \\"VoiceTone: Re-calibrating the pots\\" found the solution. Very easy fix) At the end of the night, the pitch correction can come in handy. The guitar tuner works very well, very responsive. (when engaged, it cuts your signal out - so your audience doesn't hear you tune) It is built very well. I have read some about people complaining that there is no on/off switch - who cares, I plug it in at the beginning of the gig, and unplug it at the end. If you are having problems with cutting through the mix, or if you have issues with your vocal dynamics (vocals get too loud on some parts, and too soft on others) this pedal will help with that (using the built in compressor when the tone button is engaged - which it ALWAYS should be engaged)

Rated at 4 ohms, in my setup they are powered by a Luxman 50 watt per channel receiver, a clean amp which while not that powerful, drives them just fine at low to middling high volume.

Highly recommended! There is good reason that the Alesis Monitor One MKII have stayed at around $200 a pair for the last three years. You will not be disappointed with these fine reference monitors.

product_title: Novation USB Midi Controller Keyboard
review_body:
This is my second MIDI keyboard. My first one is a very cheap Behringer 49 and I already gave it as a gift to one of my friend. But Impulse 61 is a really fantastic MIDI keyboard + controller.

First, the touch and feeling of the keys are good. The semi-weighted keys are excellent. Besides, pads and keys all have channel aftertouch, so that when you press the key or the pad down, you can push it even harder to create a series of channel aftertouch MIDI events, which is good if your soft-syn can support channel aftertouch.

I use Windows 7 64bit and Sonar X1. I found the Automap 4 is very compatible with Sonar. Only one question is that you have to run Sonar as administrator. If you don't, Automap won't work properly and the keyboard cannot recognize the DAW. If you use other DAWs or use it on Mac, I cannot guarantee it will work perfectly. If you use popular VSTs, such as those from NI, you don't have to configure anything. For other plug-ins, you can create several pages for the mapping of the faders and encoders, so that they can actually control all of your plug-in's parameters. There are two switches to change the controllers from the plug-in mode to mixer mode, and, to traditional MIDI mode.

I bought M-audio's sustain pedal and Alesis F2 expression pedal. Both of them can work perfectly with Impulse. If you want to use expression pedal for this keyboard, make sure to go to the website of Novation to check out which one is compatible, since not every expression pedal will be fully functional when used with Impulse.

Overall, the quality is excellent. It is especially good and suitable when used in a music studio. I only create music at home and never go outside for live performance. 61-keys version may not be good for stage performance, since it is too heavy and bulgy.

product_title: [DISCONTINUED] Line 6 Uber Metal
review_body:
I bought this pedal using Line 6's Tone Dock module method and have had it since early March of this year.

While the tone is meaty it takes a bit to fiddle & find 'your tone' which is that sweet spot in the sound spectrum where it's musical bliss. That tone where even if you play like crap, it still sounds reasonably good. (LoL) However with that said, the three tone settings it offers are okay. My favorite is the middle setting as that most resembles the Boss Metal Zone pedal. The first setting is worthless in my opinion & the last is rarely usable for my style of play. The Gate settings have their uses but typically I leave it at the middle setting.

I'm playing a Squire 72 Tele (dual humbuckers) through a Peavey 212 Transtube amp and at low volumes the pedal is okay but it really shines when you crank some power out of an amp. There's no noticeable hum or noise to speak of. The tone is sweeter at louder volumes & even switching tones is simplistic.

I bought this because I'd plugged into a Line 6 at the music store some time ago & loved the sound but not the amp's price. I figured buying the Line 6 pedal would give me that metal crunch I heard in their amp but not quite. Still I've not sat & fiddled a lot with the controls since I got it. Most of the music I play is more crunchy without mush and the pedal does an acceptable job simulating those tones with my guitar & picking style.

Some complain about the size of the pedal - meh. I don't feel a need to fill up a pedal board with a lot of useless or one-off song effects. If I can't use it for more than one song, forget it. I gave this one 4 out of 5 stars only because it didn't quite measure up to the Line 6 amp that I originally played through at the music store. Otherwise it's a solid deal for the price.

product_title: Zoom G3 Guitar Effects and Amp Simulator
review_headline: I tried every setting, but I still suck.
review_body:
For my situation, I needed a device like this (small, battery power, headphone, variety of effects) and this looked like the best choice. For what it is, I'm happy with it, though I still think digital distortion and amp models generally sound like crap. AMONG modelers, it's nice. I like that it has 3 independent \\"slots\\" to stick an algorithm in, and they all have access to the same library, so you can double up or pick your own sequence...unlike, say, Line6, which has the preassigned sounds and and lets you combine a few effects, but you have no control over the order the effects are applied. In fairness to line 6, their \\"crunch\\" setting sounds the best of any distortion model I've heard.

Knowing that digital distortion is inferior, I really didn't have high hopes for the distortion models. There's about a dozen, or more, different distortion and overdrive \\"pedals\\" to choose from, and they are all slightly different, but they don't necessarily sound like the originals. Same goes for the amp models, each definitely colors the sound, and some will color it in a way you find pleasant, but they don't sound like the devices they were intended to model.

On the subject of the distortion models, standouts, for me were the DS-1, (which sounds really good with the autowah in front of it, but applying an amp/cabinet model on top of that takes it all away again) and the \\"squeak\\" (modeled after the Rat). The unit does have a few compressors to choose from, all of which are usable, EQ, PEQ and a few different noise gates (no expander, or at least I haven't found it yet) The modulation effects are all usable, so sticking this thing in the effects loop of a real tube amp, and ignoring the amp models and tube simulators will probably give you some real nice sounds.

There a bunch of preset patches (sets of effects) that are basically a grap bag. The \\"clean-ish\\" ones generally sound nice, and the more you shoot for heavy sounds, the more that digitaldistortion thing rears it's head, but if you make your own combos you have plenty to work with to come up with a good sound.

It also has a direct out (XLR) that you can set for pre- or post- effects, so you can either bypass it with an AB switch or feed it to a mixer for parallel effects...or just record a clean guitar sound to a different track for later screwing with.

Haven't tried the software. Comes with \\"Sequel LE\\" - I already have the full version of Cubase and my playing isnt worth putting to tape anyway. Had good experience with Zoom before - the HD16 was a nice recorder and has held up well..this is built similarly strong. Metal enclosure, fels solid, not to big or too heavy, but not so small that you can't see what you are doing. Plenty of screen space, and a nice \\"page\\" feature for the parameters.

All in all, far more versatile than Line6, but, Line6's presets tend to sound a little nicer. You can configure your own sounds to be comparable to line6's, but if all you want is presets...more presets with this, better ones with line 6.

The real test will be, like I said, putting it in the effects loop of a real tube amp, which I cant do yet, but plan on it and expect good results, from the dynamics processors and modulation effects, at least.

I still like real analog pedals better, but for a swiss army knife/practice rig im happy with it.

review_headline: Manual incomplete, so I had no choice...
review_body:

(Doesn't matter a lot if you have a dynamic microphone, but it's pretty d*mned important if you plan to plug a ribbon mic into it as the phantom power can severely damage the element! My query to customer support was initially answered that it didn't matter, and subsequent follow-ups were ignored.) After returning the 502, I bought the 802, and now have the switch the manual clearly noted across the entire line, along with a bunch of other inputs I don't need and a somewhat lighter wallet.

It works fine as a cheap mic preamp and mini-mixer, but it wasn't worth the hassle and the delay caused by purchasing the wrong device after researching based on inaccurate paperwork. I wish now I had purchased a mic pre-amp from another manufacturer, one that has a customer support team worthy of the name. Truth is, after the disappointing experience of the last week-and-change with this company and their \\"support,\\" I wish I had never purchased anything from them.

product_title: M-Audio Studiophile DSM2 High-Resolution DSP Reference Monitor, Single Speaker
review_body:
Like the other reviewer, I definitely agree with these monitors being almost too revealing and crisp. I also picked up a pair that were on sale for a huge discount, and while I respect the quality and build of these monitors, I almost wonder when I would have the opportunity to use them. These monitors are so revealing, I went to listen to my \\"reference songs\\" (aka songs I listened to 100 of times on different systems and know so well) and I was hearing things in the song I never even heard before. Like the sound of the bass string being plucked, or the slightest shimmers of drum cymbal, or the subtle pressing of piano keys. These monitors show it all!

Unfortunately, at home though, I use my monitors for both hobby work and pleasure. That means I enjoy just listening to games, tv, or other music with my monitors as much as I will be mixing music, editing audio, or doing sound design on them. The DSM2s just fail hard when it comes to just using them for home entertainment. They reveal far too much about the audio, and trying to listen to compressed to hell TV, game audio, or other low quality audio sources is ear wracking. However, if you are looking for an extremely transparent monitor that will show you every single thing about your mix or whatever other audio you are working on, I could highly recommend these.

product_title: Danelectro CO-2 Cool Cat Drive V2 Effect Pedal
review_body: I had to write a review to balance out the negative review on here.  This is a REALLY great overdrive pedal.  Lots of gain on tap- more than a TS type pedal (but less than a Crunch Box kind of distortion).  It sort of hangs in the space between a tubescreamer and a distortion- sort of like the OCD... (thus the comparisons). You have to hand it to Danelecto for listening to it's customers and providing what we want on the cheap.  What do we want?  Metal enclosures and sturdy true bypass switches at sane prices.  Yes the knob placement is annoying but you get used to it pretty quickly.  This overdrive - and ALL overdrives for that matter - are intended to overdrive the preamp tubes in a VALVE amplifier.  When used as intended, this pedal sounds much better than a $35 pedal has the right to. If you read the negative review on here, the gentleman is complaining that it sounds fizzy going into his solid state Frontman amp.  Of course it does!!  And a Klon Centaur will not live up to the hype going into the frontman either.  There is a reason they call overdrives 'tube screamers'.  It's because they get your preamp tubes screaming- not because they will make your transistors sound like screaming tubes.  This pedal is a 5 star pedal at this price point when used as intended.  I have V1 of this pedal and you can cop the same sounds using the switches under the hood (which is genius on the part of Dano btw...)

review_body: First, let me preface my review with this: this item arrived FAST. I ordered this on a Saturday and got the coming Monday. The shoulder rest is not of the highest quality, but it is very good quality and what I am used to. I have a hard time with the \\"fancier\\" shoulder rests that are made of wood or have bizarre fabric overlays on them. This is metal with adjustable \\"feet\\" and a nice velvet cover. It is not so soft that you're squishing it into oblivion, but is not so hard that your shoulders ache. If you are new to playing violin, try this first. It is inexpensive and does what it is supposed to do. I'm not new to playing, but I've gotten so used to the position of the violin while using this rest that I prefer it so much more than other models or designs. product_title: Marantz PMD620 Handheld SD MP3/WAV Recorder
review_headline: Frustrating, because so much about it is so good.
review_body:
I've had my PMD620 for about 4 years now, and while I would hate to be without it, I agree with those here who have written about its unreliability.

When it works, I have no complaints. I find the user interface to be very easy, the menu screen bright enough to see in most environments, versatile and accurate. The recording quality with its internal microphones is a good solid field quality, not spectacular for music (though certainly fine for documentation recordings of rehearsals or events) but good for interviews. It fits in your pocket and is handy for recording live bands in a reasonably good quality (though sometimes I'm amazed when people's flipcam recordings sound better than the Marantz recordings!). I've had no issues with the input jacks and the metering. And while I agree that the doors on the ports and battery compartment are too fragile, I don't have a major issue with that, because that doesn't effect the performance.

But the damn thing DOES sometime just bail out and go into \\"error\\" mode in the middle of your recording, or sometimes only when you press stop, after appearing to have recorded normally for up to a half hour or more. You can \\"rescue\\" these files by transferring them from the SD card to your computer, but usually if the Marantz has generated an \\"error,\\" the files are corrupt and skip or glitch or are otherwise unusable. And once the unit is confused by an error file on the SD card, it often can't get around the issue and either will not record at all until you replace or reformat the card, or will continue to make errors, as though it is terribly confused by the card itself.

If this happened only rarely, maybe I would be more tolerant, but it really happens too often for my comfort level. If I'm recording something that either I can't get again, or was critical in some way, and the unit just decides that it's time for another of its random failures, it's EXTREMELY frustrating. I've also found it particularly unreliable in .wav mode, which I suppose is because it's having difficulty writing quickly enough to the SD card.

I've used quality SD cards at all times, but it doesn't seem to matter. It just freaks out every so often, no matter what I try. So even though it works normally (and very satisfyingly) 90% of the time, its penchant for panicking and failing to accurately record is too prevalent for comfort. I still use it, because I really find it convenient! But I don't fully trust it....

product_title: Qwik Time QT-7 Quartz Metronome
review_body:
Years ago, a clerk at a local music store swindled me into buying one of these metronomes. The biggest drawback for me, as others have mentioned, is that the meter is limited to 2, 3, and 4, and you can't turn off the downbeat. If there are meter changes in a piece or it is in an unusual meter this is incredibly frustrating.

Additionally, the construction is pretty poor. The stand feels springy and the plastic is sort of light. The three plastic buttons have a give to them that feels cheap and the tempo buttons in the middle require too much pressure to function. There also seems to be a short in my metronome that causes it to turn off or malfunction if I move it while it's operating.

Finally, the sound through headphones is far too loud and only comes out the left ear, which is maddening.

These are all nitpicky complaints, but cumulatively they make for a low quality product. In some applications it will do, but if you want a metronome that will serve you well for life, invest a little more in a nicer product.

product_title: Sennheiser HD203 Closed-Back DJ Headphones
review_body: Ok pros. vs. cons. Pros - the bass, mids & treble can be separated when listening. It is all fairly clear. It meshes, but doesn't all clutter together. These are definitely loud headphones. Cons- these headphones are really loud. :-) Redundant? I know, but I use these for studio/recording purposes (as well as general music/movies). My professor in an audio class stressed the importance of the full range of sounds when mixing your tracks. Monitor headphones are supposed to more or less emulate monitors as in speakers in a studio setting from my understanding. These headphones deliver that yes. They have the power and input levels for lack of a better term. However, they're so loud that I almost cringe when listening to especially dialog. I don't claim to be an expert and doubt I'm the most picky there is btw. I admit I have sensitive hearing, but I also want to keep it that way. The bass is too pronounced in my opinion and might give a false presence when mixing down. Lots of attack on the highs/treb. Comfort is fine for me. I like the fact there is a bit of head room. The ear pads snugly hug the ears so the top plastic part doesn't have to mash down on the dome. I haven't listened to more than a few hours at a time. An improvement from the 201 (which sound muddy and plastic broke fairly quickly), but still I'm not feeling these. Too much attack and they go for about 50 bucks after tax at BestBuy. I'll be returning. I debated Phillips and SkullCandy, (the only other two BestBuy had available in this price range), but am very skeptical.

product_title: Yamaha MG82CX 8 Input Stereo Mixer with Digital Effects
review_body:
I purchased this mixer for my band. We use it for all of our mics (4 of them), the keyboard, and an iPad that we use as our drum machine. The quality of the pre-amps is great and our vocals sound wonderful (as good as they can sound given that none of us is a professional singer by any means), especially with the ability to dial in some reverb or chorus when needed. I also love that we can hook up monitors as well as our speaker system, and because this mixer can be mounted to a mic stand, we can tuck it away on stage and control our own mix.

Keep in mind that while this mixer is indeed an 8 channel mixer, if you have a stereo source (such as a keyboard), it will use two of those channels. With our setup, we max out the inputs. We're going to be buying the 16-channel version soon so that we can mix everyone through the same board, and the fact that we're buying Yamaha's 16-channel mixer is a testament to the quality of this equipment.

Highly recommended!

product_title: Sony MDR7506 Professional Large Diaphragm Headphone
review_headline: Great sound, dissapointed that they broke.
review_body:
I bought these for 172$ roughly three years ago, and now they are broken.

I have had lovely times with these headphones, the best i have owned so far ,
- I have not had many phones and none cost above 40 dollars, so i cannot really compare.

When i first heard them, i though they were too good, i mean, i heard the flaws in the mixing, and had to equalize the music when i heard certain songs in my computer.
It was very special, borderline fun, but also a pain in the beginning - it might be because they were brand new, or that i just had to adjust my ears from mediocre sound to good.

My music-taste is very, very broad, and i see no particular music these fit for, it seems to be an all-rounder.
Some songs can be a bit descant, almost piercing - but i have never been too much into sharper soprano-music, and as i said, i often use a equalizing-program.

Bass is pretty good in these phones, not perfect - but better than my computer-speakers.
All is about taste in sound, these will not fit everyone - what i can say is that both my sister and mother got jealous of these, so that says something.

Yesterday it happened, the left channel left me, only to return, and leave me again.
I think that it was a bit soon for phones in this price-class, at least when i bought it.
Now i see that the price is about half of what i payed for, i also had to pay a juicy bill to customs.

The price i payed was a total of 219$. I would not pay that price for these again.
Now these sell half the price - and they are worth it!

I will not buy another pair of Sony-phones, because Sony builds a lot of electronics - none of them built to last, sadly.
As with a lot of other mainstream-brands.

To sum up: Worth the price, but they will not last - if you want something you can have for years and years i recommend to check out the audio-devoted brands instead.
I would recommendthat actually, before you buy these - that's where im going next.
Goodbye Sony - we've had some beautiful times, but quite a short romance.

Have a nice day, friends!

product_title: Audio-Technica ATH-AD700 Open-air Dynamic Audiophile Headphones
review_headline: I see why everyone recommends these...
review_body: I did a lot of research on the AD700 before finally purchasing them on Amazon. The general feedback on these cans are that they are one of the best (if not the best) entry-level audiophile headphones available for the price due to its great soundstage. The only flaw that people seem to complain about in the forums is that it lacks bass.     I'm not an audiophile but I am seeking better sound quality than my current pair of Logitech G35 Surround Sound 7.1 headphones. When I first received the AD700, I could not help but only notice the seemingly 'non-existent' bass. My current G35 is a closed headphone so the bass was far superior to that of the AD700. As a result I was a little bit disappointed with the AD700 on first impressions. Feeling a bit underwhelmed at this point, I was keen to find out why everyone recommends these headphones. I proceeded with listening to music late into the night.    After about half an hour of listening (I tested with Norah Jones, John Mayer, etc.) I suddenly realised how clearly I could hear the instruments in each song.  The clarity is so good that I was able to pick up subtle sounds from the instruments that I had never noticed before when listening with my G35. For example, when a guitarist changes chords there is a slight squeal when their fingers slide across the strings to play the next chord. I couldn't believe I could actually hear it so clearly let alone hear it at all!      I decided to change back to my G35's to see if there was a difference and to my surprise the AD700 was noticeably better in terms of mid to higher range clarity. At that point, I finally understand why everyone in the forums are recommending these cans. I have been using the AD700 for about a month now and mainly use it for playing StarCraft 2 while chatting on Skype at the same time. For this purpose, they are simply brilliant!    The good:  - Excellent clarity in mid to higher range frequencies  - Comfortable for extended use (doesn't heat up your ears)- Priced well for what you get    The bad:  - If you will be using these with on-board PC sound, might need to pair it up with a add-on sound card (I tried to run the AD700 off my on-board PC sound and I get an annoying buzz when I try to increase the system volume. However, when I ran them through the headphone output jack of my Creative P580 speakers, I was able to get a cleaner volume without the buzz)  - These headphones are NOT adjustable - might be a bit loose for people with smaller heads  - Lacks a bit of bass    To summarise - if you are listening to heavy bass songs such as R&B and Dance music, then these are not the headphones for you. However if you are in the market for a set of headphones with excellent clarity for its price range, then you'll be very happy with this purchase.

product_title: Yamaha CS40 7/8 Size Nylon String Classical Guitar - Natural
review_body:
I bought this knowing it would not be a premium instrument but I wanted a short scale because I am lazy and like easy fingering. I shaved a bit off the bridge to brighten the instrument and adjusted the saddle a bit to lower the string just a little, that helped a lot. I next added some Savarez strings to brighten it further and that really improved it. Not very bassy but I wanted more harmonic content than it had originally and got it. I might shave some mass off the inner bracing and see if I can get a bit more harmonic content out of it. That might weaken the instrument a bit but it didn't cost me too much anyway.
I really just wanted to see if a small scale guitar could give me what I want and now I think it can. I have a full sized classical that sounds excellent but still wanted something that required less effort to play. This would be a pretty decent starter instrument for a young person just beginning and you wouldn't need to do what I did for them to be able to play it.

review_body: If you are mixing in an environment that doesn't allow you to crank up your near field monitors, this little box is quite helpful. I still have not compared a final mixdown made with this tool to something mixed with full studio speakers, but I think it creates a reasonable approximation for post-production, pre-mastering situations, especially for those working with \\"in the box\\" laptop conditions.

product_title: JAM Studio Quality Guitar input for iPad
review_body: Final Updates: 12-23-2014  --I've owned this device now for nigh on three years? My, how time flies! It's still going strong. The only issue I've ever had was one of the gray plates on the sides falls off from time to time. Snap it back on and go about my business. I've carried it around a lot, dropped it, banged it into walls. It's never given me any trouble. Nowadays I use the JamUp app on the iPad with great results. I love this device and would definitely want to buy another if I lost it.    ---END    After reading reviews for other products that plug into the headphone jack, I decided to go midrange and buy the apogee jam.  I received this today and have gathered first impressions.  I will update this review as I draw more conclusions, and the rating may or may not change as a result.    First Impressions:    For 100$, I was expecting an awful lot out of this gadget.  I don't have a lot of money for guitar pedal effects and a really nice amp, so the result of that is that my time spent at the amp tweaking the limited settings at my disposal is frustrating.  The verdict on the Jam?  Nothing!  As in it took no time at all, took no difficulty, no tweaking.  I plugged the 1/4\\" cable in and into the Ipad, loaded the free version of ampkit, and I was getting wonderful sound immediately.  Those first thirty minutes with this new toy melted away in a flash as I played around with the included distortion pedal on ampkit.  Some key features I noted as positives:    Pros:  1) Excellent sound, right out of the box.  No batteries to put in, no complicated setup, no install.  It just worked straight away!    2) No delay, at least as far as I can tell.  This seems to be something people are curious about, and at least so far as I can tell there's not one iota of delay from what I do and what comes out of the speakers.  I simply may not be discerning enough, but to me there's no noticeable pause.    3) Sensitivity is solid.  I was able to modulate my picking style and achievebig differences in the output.  For some reason I was expecting the digital out to be muddy.  It may have been a silly thought, but it's definitely solid in terms of its adjustment to you.    4) On-the-fly gain adjustment works very well, and I love that it gives you a readout of the noise level on the device itself.  It allows you to easily get to a good spot.    Cons:    1) Cost.  Obviously this isn't that much for a good guitar input.  You could easily spend a lot more for fancier gadgets; however, 100$ is nothing to sneeze at when you play as a hobby.  It's definitely worth it since it's no hassle compared to what I have read about other products    That's my list of cons I know for sure so far.  There are other issues that I worry about that cannot be ascertained in a first impression.  I intend to update these at another time.    Potential cons:  1) Output to a larger speaker.  The Jam itself has no way to route your output sound to a larger speaker, and I am not certain that a good solution is going to pop up just yet.  If I want to find a backing track on youtube on my laptop and get the guitar and track to my headphones, I'm not sure I'll be able to.  I expect there is a reasonable solution for this, though    2) Durability.  I have read other stories about the unit failing.  Mine was not DoA, but that's about all I can tell so far.  It seems like it will hold up to shock.  It doesn't feel cheap to me, and it has no little parts to lose (like a battery flap, for example).  Time will tell if this guy goes the distance    All that said, I am elated with my purchase and give it a tentative five-star rating.  I intend to play with it a lot more, and at this stage I am not quite sure which of the several guitar apps I should lay down my money on.  Ampkit seems really good so far with its free effects and amp, so I may go with that.    UPDATE, 12-17-2011    After several months of use, I feel confident in updating my review a bit for those who want some more information!  The device has not given me one iota of trouble so far.  I can now add some more annoyances to the short list.    CONS:    1) Not being able to charge the iPad at the same time while using the Jam has caused a few situations where I had to put down the guitar after several hours of fooling around with recording and whatnot.  I know!  Who says I should take a break, right?!  This has not been a major issue, in reality, but it is a potential one if you are away from somewhere where you can charge up.    2) The digital connection locks tightly into the port, which is good (it's not going to get ripped out of there), but it gets to feeling a little flimsy and makes me nervous about damaging the cable head itself or the port to the iPad.  If you're careful, no issue should ever pop up, but there's that distant possibility.    All in all, any quibbles I have are minor and should not deter you from considering this purchase.  This device along with a few key apps have rendered the Vox AC30 miniamp I bought entirely obsolete.  The apps play a big role in this, for sure.  I'll talk about my setup briefly, as well.    Ampkit and garage band are both awesome for their own reasons.  Ampkit has such a breadth of interesting sounds and presets and customization on your output that it's a must.  The problem is that you lack the smart instruments and the ability to record in an organized way.  Garage band's guitar sounds and interface are a little more annoying to deal with (needing to set the instrument monitoring and the tracklength every time is annoying).  Specifically, the guitar sounds feel somewhat limiting and more difficult to customize.  They are nice, but I like Ampkit a lot more.  The multitrack recording and smart instruments make garage band indispensable for actual generation of musical ideas!  Therefore, I wish I could port my ampkit output sound into garageband.  Too bad!    All in all, the apogee jam is confirmed as an excellent amp input.  Never once have I had a malfunction of the device or any popping or noise that was not setting related.  No issue of detection or anything.  No batteries for the device, no hassle.  The price is the biggest deterrent, but if all the other iPad interfaces have such nasty trouble, then it's best to save your money and grab a good one at the first shot, and the Apogee Jam is definitely a good one!    How about my Potential cons section from before?  Let's see...    1) Ipad can use an aux. cable to output to a larger speaker without hassle.  I can import backing tracks into iTunes no problem.  It's a little more annoying than booting up youtube and flying, but it's not bad.  You can also enable multitasking in the garageband app that will allow you to open up other programs while still getting guitar output, so potential con #1 was not a concern.    2) Durability.  No troubles on my end.  No failure at all.  I have been pretty gentle with it, but it has seen its share of slogging around in by guitar bag.  Solid device!    What more can I say?  I'd buy another if this one broke or got lost without a second thought.  There is no better alternative so far as I can tell without being exorbitantly expensive.

It's difficult for me to separate the two at this point but I believe the two newest features that are part of Reason 5 that I've found useful are the Kong drum designer and the sequencer blocks mode. Reason continues to be the most inspiring music creation program I've ever encountered and the bottom line is it's just plain fun to play and experiment with.

product_title: ROLLS Personal Monitor System
review_headline: THE Monitor System for Singing Drummers On a Budget!
review_body:
Over the years, I have transistioned from loud, hearing-wrecking wedge monitors to isolating full headphones to in-ear monitors. As a singing drummer, monitoring vocals (mine and everyone else's) as well as whatever else I can get from a monitor mix has always been a challenge. A few years ago, I started using a Mackie 1202-VLZ mixer, with an old DBX compressor/limiter and a complicated system of patch cables to get the desired audio (which sometimes included a click track) into my Shure in-ear monitors. This worked well, but required a lot of stuff to carry around, and a lot of time to set up and tear down.

About a year ago, I began to look around for an easier solution, and found the Rolls PM351 Personal Monitor Station. I was familiar with the Rolls line, as I have worked at radio stations that used their other headphone amplifiers, AM/FM receivers and other gear. I ordered one, and when it arrived, I was amazed at how compact--yet well-built--the unit is! The box is metal, not plastic. At first, the \\"jumpers\\" for changing inputs from stereo to mono, turning phantom power on/off, etc., seemed a little strange, but after reading more on their website about why they use jumpers instead of switches (the recessed jumpers are much less prone to breaking compared to switches), it made sense. I just carry some small needle-nosed pliers with me, in the rare event that I might need to alter a setting.

As a singing drummer, being able to quickly use the \\"more me\\" feature to boost or cut my vocal level balance against the monitor input is a God-send! The Line Input uses a 1/4-inch jack, but I have an XLR female-to-phone plug male adapter, allowing me to get a mix back from the board regardless of the output configuration. For some gigs, I also use a click track (which comes from the Tempo app on my iPhone these days!). I simply plug the 1/8-inch-to 1/4-inch stereo patch cable from my iPhone output into the Instrument input on the Rolls, and with the input on that set to mono, I get a great click track feed with its own independent level!

As for set-up/tear-down, I have gone from carrying around the Mackie (in a carry-on suitcase bag!) and a bunch of cables, to a very compact rig: I bought one of those aluminum briefcases they sell for around $25 at Harbor Freight Tools that has the customizable foam rubber cushioning on the inside. I created places to store the PM351, AC adapter, a few cables, my Shure SM-58 bag, and a 20-foot XLR cable (coiled up after the gig). The case only weighs about 5 lbs., and it has everything in one case for my entire monitoring setup! Talk about easy!

I have had to get used to not having any compression or limiting, but that just requires some careful level-setting on my part. I believe Rolls makes a similar-sized compressor/limiter unit to work with the PM351, and I may order one down the road; but for now, I give this 5 stars. It does what I need it to do, the sound quality is great, and the ease of carrying, setup and tear-down has made a big difference in the amount of time I spend assembling and disassembling my monitoring system. I highly recommend it to any gigging musician who doesn't have the big $$$ to spend just to be able to hear properly on stage!t to mono, I get a great click track feed with its own independent level! review_headline: A must if you have a Zoom.
review_body: If you are thinking about purchasing the Zoom h4n do it.  And then also make sure you get this.  I would recommend you get one of the kits, because pretty much you are getting a free sd card.      If you record without this, then you WILL have handling noise.  And it's horrible, super bassy and no way to work around it.  So get this and then you won't have to worry about it. Also, on a side note.  If you do own the Zoom make sure you install the newest firmware.  They finally have separate volume control on the XLR inputs.

product_title: Hercules DS520B Trombone Stand
review_body: Many reviews comment on the difficulty of picking your trombone up from this stand.  Personally, I have not found it difficult.    There are 2 large advantages to this stand:    1.) Outstanding stability and balance.  Unlike the hamilton-style stands, this stand simply will not tip over, even when it's given a pretty good shove.  2.) If you have an older trombone where the bell does not actually screw into the slide (such as those manufactured by Conn or Olds), the Hamilton stands are not safe due to the insecure attachment between the bell and slide sections.  This problem is completely resolved with this stand.    All in all, a good stand.  Great if you have an older trombone.  Probably not worth replacing a hamilton if you already have one for a more modern trombone.

product_title: Blue Snowball USB Microphone
review_body: I did quite a bit of research and watched a few YouTube videos before buying this mic and it paid off, I love the thing. It is very robust, stylish, easy to install and the sound quality is excellent! I use it for both video conferencing as well as music, especially sampling my voice. For voice samples the sound quality is more than adequate. I have several dynamic mics with XLR connections and I wanted to have a Mic that I can easily hookup to the laptop and just sample something without having to turn on all of my gear and this was the perfect solution. I use a Mac and with Garage Band and within the Mac System settings the Snowball was immediately found and I was able to use it. In Propellerheads Reason, which is music production software I use, the snowball was not available for selection in the settings. After doing some research on the issue in the internet, I placed a service email with Blue, they responded quickly with a solution which was to create a so-called aggregate sound device within MacOS. Worked like a charm and with that solution I can definitely use the Mic with any software. I highly recommend this mic. By the way, I have read some complaints about the mic being too quiet; I don't have any issues with that.

product_title: Cremona SV-1750 Maestro Special Edition Violin, Full-Size
review_headline: Please read if you are considering this Violin
review_body: I bought this violin four years ago when I first entered high school and I needed something other than the cheap 100 dollar violin that I learned to play on and played for 6 years. I went to several music stores and browsed around, but when I saw this violin I fell in love. The picture does not do the violin justice. It is a gorgeous instrument with delicately inlaid purfling. It is very unique, and I've received a lot of compliments on it. However, of course the look of it is definitely not all you should focus on in terms of a violin. From my experience in these last few years, the Cremona is a huge step up from the sound of my student violin. It has a beautifully deep tone that is perfect for classical music, but is very adaptable. I personally love playing fiddle music with it because the sound is high and bright, and fun. I used the violin to play in my school orchestra, a smaller Chamber Orchestra in the community and in my violin class at a local elementary school. The price tag is hefty (I know) but I've had this violin for nearly five years, and I couldn't be happier with it's sound and look. It's a violin to keep for a lifetime.     Hope I helped,  Gabryel

product_title: Hohner HC06 Full Sized Classical Nylon String Guitar
review_body: I was looking for a guitar for my 7 year old son who's been wanting a guitar for over a year now.  I spent countless hours searching for the perfect one.  Knowing I was on a tight budget and couldn't afford to spend the $200+ that most \\"guitar people\\" recommend you spend on a good quality beginner's guitar, I wanted to make sure I was getting the best quality for the money I could afford to spend.  I discussed my options with a friend of mine who has been playing guitar for years and knows what a guitar should sound like.  He gave me few pointers, (teaching me some of the \\"lingo\\" along the way) and, after countless MORE hours of internet research, reading reviews, etc., I finally decided this guitar was the one I wanted to buy.  Boy, am I glad I did!!!  I was very pleased with the look and feel of this guitar when it came.  It sounded pretty good to me, too.  But then again, not being a \\"guitar guy\\" (or gal) I was holding off my enthusiasm until I had a chance to have my friend check it out.  He tuned it (all guitars are shipped out of tune so the strings are not overly stressed during the shipping process which would cause them to break) and he played several songs on it.  He was very impressed with the guitar's intonation and sound quality.  He did mention that the action was a little high as you move higher up on the fretboard but for a beginner, this is not a big deal and it can easily be fixed by filing down the saddle just a little bit. (See, told you I learned the lingo!  LoL)  Overall, I would highly recommend this guitar for a beginner on a budget.  You get a good quality guitar that looks beautiful and sounds great!  After seeing this, my daughter now wants one for her birthday next year.  I cannot wait to see my son's face light up on Christmas morning.

product_title: Powerflex Tkl Mandolin Bag

The difference in all three are easily noticeable.   Upgrading from a no-name, no-brand mouthpiece that came with my [[ASIN:B00515AI4C Mendini MCT-30 B Flat Intermediate Rosewood Clarinet w/ Case, Tuner, Stand, Mouthpiece, Box of 10 Reeds, Cork Grease, & a Pair of Gloves]], the C5 brought out my middle register under the bridge (low C up to Bb) and really projects my low E~G range. The upper register is still brilliant, although a little pinched, which can be ironed out through practice.     If you don't have a professional mouthpiece or two, these are decent substitutes. I would recommend investing in all three to test what sort of tone you are looking for based on your play style and literature choice.

product_title: Shure Triple High-Definition MicroDriver Earphone with Detachable Cable
review_headline: Review compared SE535 to Westone UM2
review_body: First, about myself. I am not a audiophile by any stretch. I enjoy music and I primarily use a Zune HD or my PC with ZunePass. (BTW - ZunePass is AWESEOME.)    Prior to purchasing the SE535, I've had the Westone UM2 for about 5 years. The UM2 was my first entry in to the IEM world and it blew my mind at how great music can sound. It was like night and day difference between any earbud headphone and an In-Ear-Monitor (IEM) that completely shuts out ambient sound. The separation between the high and low frequencies were so incredible that I was amazed at the difference.    So after 5 years, I thought I give a 3-driver IEM a try. I could have purchased the new Westone UM3x but I had a great opportunity to pick up the Shure SE535 at a great price so I pulled the trigger. Thus my subjective review is based comparing the SE535 to the Westone UM2.    I listed to three songs on my Zune HD with a 3.5mm audio jack with 2 ports. I plugged in each IEM so I can switch back and forth.    First, I listened to David Guetta's Toyfriend from the One Love album. This is very bass beat driven song. In comparing the two, I couldn't tell the difference.  My guess is because of the over powering bass, whether you have a 2 or 3 driver IEM, it will be difficult to hear the benefit of the 3-drivers.    Second, was Jason Marz's I'm Yours live version. Here I noticed some difference in the overall sound. It's hard to describe but the SE535's seemed more full where as the UM2's seems a bit muted. Don't get me wrong, the UM2 sounded great but I did notice that the SE535 sounded better.    Third, Eric Johnson's Cliff's of Dover live from Austin, TX performance. For those who don't know Eric Johnson, this is a Grammy-winning master piece of electric guitar performance. (Very subjective, I know.) This is where I think the SE535 separates from the UM2. In comparing the two, again the UM2 is great to listen to but I noticed that the SE535 was much more full. I don't know how better to describe the difference other than saying \\"sounds more full\\" but the sound seems more \\"alive\\". I wish I had better vocabulary to describe the difference, but I don't.    All in all, I will give the SE535 5 stars but if I could, I would give it 4.5 stars from an overall value/performance stand point. I feel like I have been spoiled with my first IEM being the UM2 but in comparison, although the SE535 sounds great, it wasn't tremendously better than the UM2. Thus the 4.5 star rating especially given how old my UM2 are and the fact that a 2-driver IEM will probably meet most people's needs.    With that said, the build quality of the SE535 is top notch. The cables are so much better than the UM2. The UM2 had breaded cable and while better than majority of the earbuds out there, the new design of the Shure's cables are very sturdy. However, they are a bit thicker and I haven't quite adjusted to popping in the IEM. I am still adjusting between the more flexible UM2 cable which I can fit in my ear very quickly to the thicker and rotating cable which I have yet to master. But I figure it's just a matter of time.    With that said, if price wasn't an issue, then I probably would have been more brand loyal and picked up the latest Westone IEM. However, like I said, I was able to pick up the SE535 for a very good price so I jumped on it. My biggest problem (if you want to call it that) is how to wind up the cord properly to put it in the case. I have no idea what the center plastic piece and how to use it in the inside of the case. :-P  )      Hope this helps.

product_title: PRS Guitars SE Paul Allender Electric Guitar (Purple Burst)
review_body:
I have both the SE Custom and the Paul Allender and appreciate both guitars for
what they can do.
Both guitars because they are the SE series are made in Korea and have obvious problems.
The biggest being finger/fret boards, nuts, and lack of detail on the finishes.
The Paul Allender is a very powerful guitar with its EMG 81TW and 89R Dual mode (Pot split) active pickups that will give you pretty much any sound configuration you would want.

I have about 60 guitars that I have acquired over the last 20 years and have just recently purchased these two
as Paul Smith finally decided to enter the mid range guitar market (where all the money is) and stop relying on
the sale of 3K to 8K guitars.

I believe Paul has a way to go to catch up with people like Epiphone, Ibanez and Schecter in producing flawless offshore guitars as this does not happen over night and requires specific manufacturing processes be put into place and then strict line inspections be done on a constant schedule.

The first Paul Allender I got, I sent back because of a crack in the Ebony Fretboard which was very dried out.
I am waiting on the replacement as I write this review and will follow up on what I get (It's the purple one).
Received replacement and at least the ebony fretboard is not cracked and is in much better shape than the one I returned. The fretboard does stick out at the neck slightly on both sides and I will grind this away. I have already rounded off the nut (a common part on all SE's) which has sharp outside corners that I will not
put up with.

The Custom had to have conditioner applied to the Rosewood fretboard a few times to bring it back to life and
bring the frets even with the board edge which stopped the fret edges from ripping up my fingers.
The nut was off center and the fretboard was sticking out on one side at the top so I ground this down.

My point in all of this is that at one time you would expect small problems like I have mentioned from mid range offshore built guitars, but that has changed in the last 5 to 10 years and you can expect near perfection from a guitar costing $600.00 to $800.00 made in Korea or China, or Indonesia or wherever.

Actually, I have an Epiphone Nighthawk Custom reissue made in Indonesia (and many other makes)that put either one of these PRS SE's to shame as far as fit and finish are concerned, and they range from under $400.00 to $800.00.that at one time you would expect small problems like I have mentioned from mid range offshore built guitars, but that has changed in the last 5 to 10 years and you can expect near perfection from a guitar costing $600.00 to $800.00 made in Korea or China, or Indonesia or wherever.

review_body: If you don't mind tweaking and adjusting things, this little box has a lot of potential. Once tuned up, the action was very playable right out of the box, the nut height and string grooves were well done. You will need to adjust the intonation by moving the bridge towards or away from the tailpiece. Also a tiny dab of vaseline on each of the tuner gears is a good idea before you start tuning and putting tension on them. These are shipped with the strings loosened, which I feel is the right way given the amount of mileage and stress these instruments must endure between factory and dealer. As a result, the bridge may shift. You may want to change strings to your preferred brand/gauge. It comes with a nice semi-rigid case. A fantastic buy for $130. You can get a comparable instrument elsewhere completely gone over and set up, but it will cost you 2-3 times as much. I didn't want to shell out a lot of dough for a mandolin, because it is not my primary instrument, and this one exceeded my expectations. I have a good A-style mandolin, but I always wanted an F-style. It was hard to find a decent one, new or used cheap until now. I think once I have it completely set up and \\"played in\\" it will hold a respectable spot in any gig or jam session. It may not be a $4000. Stiver, but it is a very good \\"Striver\\".

I took the cable back out and you can see where the spike is making a hole right in the middle of the copper wires- perfect! I pushed it in pretty good and then started to tighten the screw. So easy the screw touches the plug base and that's it. I repeated the other side. The first cable had signal this is a big deal because seriously this has NEVER happened. I always had some issue before with other ones so that right there blew me away. In fact no bs here they all went together and worked the first time.
I need to mention this is a real size cable placing next to my mogami cable they are almost the same width. Also you cant pull them loose its like some chinese finger trick the more I pulled the more it seemed to grab.

product_title: Manuel Rodriguez Caballero 11 Cedar Top Classical Guitar
review_headline: I bought this without seeing or trying it, and I am very happy with my purchase.
review_body:
It's been a very long time since I last picked up a guitar, but I decided I wanted to take lessons and I needed a guitar. I did not have access to a music store where I could try out various classical guitars. I had to order online, so I researched and I made my decision based on the company's reputation and reviews for this guitar that I read online (all over the place - inc. YouTube). I considered a Cordoba model in the same price range (I assumed +/-$300 would be a good range for a decent starter guitar), but the reviews for this one were sightly better and more consistent. I was a bit nervous ... I was clueless about what I wanted/needed, and was buying something sight unseen, and more importantly for a musical instrument, unheard!

I ordered from Musician's Friend, and my guitar and case arrived very quickly and very safely.. it was well packaged.. I was worried because boxes do not always make it through the APO/DPO mail system so easily, but this was securely packed. They even packed the guitar (ordered separately) into the gig bag I chose, which was put into the guitar's box, which in turn was packed into a larger box and padded well!

As for the guitar itself - I don't have much experience at all with comparing instruments (brands, prices, quality, whatever), so take my review with that in mind, but, I can tell when something sounds nice, and, as the daughter of a good carpenter, can tell when things are assembled sloppily!

The guitar is beautiful! A close visual inspection showed all edges, frets, metal work, etc. were very nicely joined, no glue or paint or weird bits out of line. The wood is very pretty. The finish is glossy and even, the metal work and inlay on the headstock are decorative and well made too. Even the inside of the guitar looks nicely assembled.

The tone is mellow, rich and quite lovely. Just tapping the body of the instrument produces a nice tone. It plays nicely and it's truly a joy to listen to... especially when my teacher tuned it up and played a couple of songs on it! (my playing is not so lovely, but that's not the guitar's fault). I don't have the experience with judging various guitars, but when my instructor looked it over he was very impressed with my instrument, congratulated me enthusiastically, and was amazed at how little I'd paid for it.

**update**

I've had this guitar for over a year now and am still just as enthused with it as I was when it first arrived. It holds a tune very well... despite being kept out on a stand where my kids (everybody) can walk by and strum the strings just to hear the pretty tones! The finish is just as lovely and everything has held up very well. The only thing I have altered is to apply small stickers on the side of the neck to mark the 3rd, 5th, 7th, etc. frets to help me with my lessons. I used nice fingernail decals as they are small, stick well, and are decorative. I love this guitar!

review_headline: They're o.k., too.  But apparently not as durable as the Sony V6/7506
review_body:
Edit: The guy at Rat Sound discovered many of the HD280's problems are caused by the flimsy cheap driver housing that vibrates and resonates except when something solid is placed against the housing. This headphone's driver housing needs a re-design with either higher density or thicker plastic, or with (even better) magnesium alloy. The driver in it is capable of good performance.

----

Original review:

I compared them today back to back. I've heard the Sony many times in the past, even owned them for a brief time. Senn had deeper bass, but a dip in the upper bass and a touch wooly in one or two midrange spots. Sony, while it didn't go as deep, lacked any significant dips or wooly aspects from the upper bass to the low treble. The Sony was still potentially a touch too bright, and when the material allowed that brightness to shine though those highs could get hard, especially on dynamically-compressed (I don't mean mp3s) recordings... maybe even harsh. In the past, I found them a lot more harsh, but maybe my hearing isn't what it used to be. The Senns treble, though not quite as bright or at all hard, was still a touch bright over neutral and could be a tiny tizzy or fizzy or something. Not hard, not harsh, but lacking precision. Neither headphones had amazing extension up top or sparkle, but they were both about average in that respect. Neither had fantastic micro-dynamics throughout and both headphones tended to flesh out different frequency regions of low-level detail more than the other. Sony still seemed a little glassy in the mid-band, but its flatness there more than made up for it. The Senns had nice micro-dynamics in the lows, but its upper bass suck-out prevented it from fully exploiting that lack of distortion. This also contributed to a lack of apparent tightness. Sony has the upper bass and while you'd expect that taught quality to shine completely through, its inferior micro-dynamics down there prevented it from fully exploiting it. Still, that Sony upper and mid bass had fair separation when there were obvious layers and didn't blur them into mud, even given this characteristic or its lack of the lowest octaves. The Senn was a touch more open and spread out in imaging, but lost some of the immediacy and engaging quality the Sony grabs you with. I found neither great or fully flat & extended, and both had their strengths and weaknesses. With the appropriate material or sources to match its strengths, the Sony was the easy winner... but you had to be aware of its quirks and limitations. The Senn was more tolerant of material & sources, but never soars as high, metaphorically speaking. The Sony might range from a 5 to 8 in sonics, while the Senn hovers more safely in the 6-7 range... if that makes sense. It did go very low, was more forgiving of high frequencies, and isolated better. product_title: Toca SFMTDK-9AB Doumbek Aztec
review_body:
I bought this model used and its my very first doumbek. It feels great, looks great, and sounds great. The inner rim is a bit egg shaped but it doesn't seem matter much, other than the way it looks. There is also some splintering happening inside the drum, but again, it doesn't seem to matter much. The collar on my drum is currently lopsided, but this may be due to a poor head seating by the original owner. I considered re-seating the head but decided not to as to not deaden the sound and cause excess damage to the Toca goatskin head.

This is a very musical sounding instrument with smooth low end (doums), deliciously warm high-end (pops, teks, kahs), and the slaps, once achieved, are also warm and very percussive. The drum is light weight and durable.

If you are looking for an authentic doumbek, however, I cannot recommend this drum. I would like to see Toca make an attempt at designing an authentic doumbek which would entail an aluminum body, mother of pearl inlay, and a plastic head. Here in the USA it is difficult to find a quality affordable authentic doumbek. There are very few local options and ordering from doumbek heartland (the middle-east) is prohibitively expensive and often brings up quality control complaints.

I recently had a chance to play a couple of \\"Alexandria\\" doumbeks and they are drastically different than my Toca. Their high-end is sharp and very crisp with teks that sound piercing, aggressive and dominant. I found it easier to achieve a good loud slap sound on the Alexandria-style imported doumbek.

Still, this Toca doumbek is a wonderful, expressive, and highly musical instrument. It has its own special unique sound and is more durable and lighter weight than the middle-eastern industry standard. All things considered I highly recommend this drum.

product_title: Snark SN-1 Tuner
review_body:
Clip it on the headstock of your acoustic six string, electric or bass, turn it on, watch the gauge as you tune to pitch. It doen't get much simpler than that.

Although my Digitech RP500 effects processor has a built-in tuner, the Snark SN-1 helps me maintain consistent tuning on my guitars. It works great on acoustics (I have nonelectric types, one with a classical body style and another a full dreadnought). It works great on my Ibanez S series electric and my five string electric bass (the low B string is not a problem to tune, although the RP500 has a more difficult time with that). It is quick to move between instruments, quick to turn on (one button) and easy to use. I leave it clipped to my microphone stand for quick access.

The accuracy is very good. It is at least as accurate as my Digitech RP500 (and more accurate for the bass). For a real world test, I can tune an instrument with it, turn to some random satellite radio station and play along with just about anything post 1970 on there (tunings for 1940s and '50s stuff are inconsistent), in perfect tune with the song. I can record such a practice session and sound like I was part of the original song. Nevermind my improvisational playing skills - there's just no way I could do something like that if I were not in tune!

I only bought it because I had a $10 rebate card that I had received from a recent purchase of something else. I needed a good way to burn that $10 card. I was looking around at Amazon and saw this tuner for less than $10. I got it from BrookMays.com through Amazon - less than $10 for the item, plus shipping. I'm glad I got it now.

product_title: Jay Tercer 1/2 Size Acoustic Guitar Kit with Gigbag - Blue Sunburst
review_headline: Good price, not bad overall, but...
review_body: We received the guitar just last week.  First off, my son was very pleased at receiving it - he's happy.      The guitar arrived in two boxes - the \\"local\\" shipping box and the box I assume it was packaged in for overseas shipping.  I was glad to see the double protection.  The guitar was well-wrapped inside the box it was originally packaged in.  When we unwrapped it we noted there were some minor scuffs on the finish.  As my son is only 7 and I'm sure he's going to bang it up a bit, I'm not fretting over it.    It is made in China (which isn't necessarily bad, however, \\"cheaper\\" goods are usually made there for a reason, and the Chinese are certainly capable of quality product when asked) which I'm sure contributed to the lower price.      The finish scheme is very nice and distinctive and my son really likes that.    If one is new to a guitar and doesn't know anything about the strap, then noting there isn't a second strap button may be cause for alarm.  However, as there are strings on the strap, tying the strap above the nut under the strings seems to be where it goes.  There are no instructions of any kind that come with the guitar, so you are left to guess or decide where you want to put the strap.      The string action is interesting - it seems the guitar is meant to be played more softly as really strumming can cause the strings to rattle against the frets.  As I am also new to guitar, perhaps this half-size gets tuned higher than the standard size - that may stop the rattling as the strings are tighter of course.  However, tuned to standard, it will rattle if \\"over played.\\"    Also, I didn't see that it had an adjustable truss rod - at least there's no readily apparent bolt inside the body.  And the tuning pegs are not sealed (something to note if you have a child who is interested in playing - no pinched fingers please!).    The included CD, in our case, was bad - it had scuffs on it which rendered useless in the DVD player (even after DVD doctoring it).While it is possible it didn't record right off the master (this sometimes happens), physically the disc appeared damaged.  Again, not something I'm going to fret over as we are starting lessons this week and that will take care of what the CD might have taught.  Though my son was disappointed he couldn't start \\"learning\\" right away (as was I as I had wanted to see the content).    Last thing is the case is NOT padded - it is simply a nylon/cordura-type of bag.  So, don't go banging the guitar around.    Overall, for a learning guitar for a 7-year old, I believe this to be a good purchase.  For a more serious player, I don't know that I'd recommend this guitar - guess that all depends upon what you expect from your guitar and how you are going to use, or abuse, it.

Overall a decent microphone for the price. Well built, sturdy construction. Nice extra with the shock mount. But you get what you pay for.

Backing this down to 2 stars.
The shock mount screws as they sit into the shock mount ring will no longer fit as they worse out. I can no longer use the mount with a mic stand because the outer ring wore out.

product_title: Hisonic 180 Watts 2-Way Powered Portable PA Speaker, HS6551
review_body:
My company bought this system because they wanted a wireless PA system for meetings. I work with live sound and PA systems as a side business and was concerned about the quality of this Chinese product. Now I know that China manufactures a lot of electronics for the major PA system players and the quality is very good. I also know China makes a lot of inexpensive poorly-engineered copies of the name brands. This system is one of those low-cost copies. The plastic PA cabinet has an annoying resonance that produces very muddy speech and music. The wireless microphone system frequently drops the signal. The speaker can be standing still and slightly moving the mic as she speaks, and the signal drops out and the sound quits. This is very poor wireless performance. The distance between the receiver and the mic was no more than 15 feet! You should be able to walk 100 feet with no drop-out. The PA system also suffers from a lot of feedback. If a person with the wireless mic gets within 10 feet of the speaker, hitting the right angle, squeeeeel!

Most buyers do not understand gain setting, feedback loops, and the like. These buyers also assume that if someone made the system it must work properly. They also incorrectly assume that a PA system that costs a fraction of the other low-end systems they see on Amazon or elsewhere must be just as good. In fact, if you never had a PA system and bought this one, you may be very happy because everything is louder. But once you hear and work with a real PA system you immediately hear the difference. No squeel, natural-sounding speech that does not cause listener fatigue, and pleasant music reproduction. How cheaply produced is this system and the rest of the Hisonic line? One of my wireless microphones, JUST the microphone, costs $300-$400 depending on the features. You will never see a hotel or school use anything of this poor caliber. Too cheap means corners were cut. If you want a simple PA package and do not want to spend a lot of money (My small PA system costs $3800) check out the JBL EON PA system line. Yes you will have to spend more money for a hassle-free system. Or..you can just rent a system for a one or two day event. product_title: Shure Sound Isolating Earphone Hi-Definition Micro Speaker with Tuned Bass Port
review_body:
I've been on something of a quest to find decent earphones, since foolishly parting with my Shure e2c's. The rundown so far: [[ASIN:B001EZUQ5E Sennheiser CX200]], [[ASIN:B001V9LPT4 Klipsch IMAGE S4]], [[ASIN:B003XU6H8I Bose IE2]], [[ASIN:B000XP8DJC Etymotic HF5]], [[ASIN:B001LNO722 Monster Turbine]], [[ASIN:B0019RBJOE Ultimate Ears TripleFi 10]], and [[ASIN:B003NSBKSC Shure SE425]] have all been run through my Zune, iPod Classic, and Yamaha receiver. So, a wide range of models, on a reasonable range of devices.

Right off the bat, I have to say that I have some bias toward having the speaker wires over my ears. My old e2c's were reinforced to bend around my ear, and I totally loved that. And to date, Shure seems to be the only company around who acknowledges that as a legitimate way to wear earphones. The SE315's are no exception, molding very well around my ears, reducing the rustling sound from a moving wire.

The overall fit of the 315's is excellent. The engineering on this is worthy of a premium price in itself. The speakers themselves don't protrude from my ears, and the above-mentioned wiring is rather discrete. The tubes are a perfect depth, and the foam tips are comfortable enough to wear all day while blocking out the rest of the world. I really don't think I could ask for more on the fit, and the 315's blow away every model I've tried.

And sound quality? It's great. Highs and mids are bright and clear enough that you can pick up loads of detail, but without sounding shrill or succumbing to clipping. I'm hesitant to say they sound \\"natural\\", so much as \\"tuned for recorded music\\". (For truly \\"natural\\" sound, consider the SE425's) On the low end, the SE315's are a huge mixed bag. If you're expecting to listen to Jay-Z and make your head vibrate with bass, these aren't for you (check out the Monster Turbines for that). That's not to say that bass is entirely absent. It's there, and it's actually quite accurate. Listening to songs from Detroit Grand Pubahs and Shiny Toy Guns, there's a lot of detail on the low side that I just didn't notice before. Similarly, the SE315's bring just the right amount of warmth and depth if you're listening to Dave Brubeck or Scala, but on a track like Tom's Diner by Suzanne Vega, you hear the bass line -- but you don't \\"feel\\" it at all. It's a strange sensation.

If you're looking for something particular from your earphones (e.g. lots of bass, absolutely crystal-clear reproduction, overly-pronounced mids, etc.) the SE315's are going to be a compromise in one area or another, or just flat-out wrong for you. But overall, I'd have to say that the SE315's are the best earphones I've used in this price range. Without spending literally twice as much money, you'd be hard pressed to find earphones that are this good all-around.Pubahs and Shiny Toy Guns, there's a lot of detail on the low side that I just didn't notice before. It's a strange sensation. But overall, I'd have to say that the SE315's are the best earphones I've used in this price range. Without spending literally twice as much money, you'd be hard pressed to find earphones that are this good all-around.

product_title: Dampit Guitar Humidifier Super
review_body: Ordered this for my new Taylor GS Mini guitar I got for Christmas. The product is a simple yet functional design, a sponge inside a rubber tube with holes. If you have a guitar you want to last and live in a cold part of the country its crucial to use something like this. Ideal humidity for a guitar is about 47% and in my house during the winter its only around 30%, so I re-wet this about every 5 days. WARNING: It comes with no instructions, but taylor has some great instructions on their website. Big thing to realize is you have to run this under cold water, then squeeze out every last drop and dry the oustide before placing in the guitar. Then should be wedged in between the B and G strings, and allowed to hang in the body. If you don't squeeze out the sponge then it can drip and ruin the guitar. Also recommend buying a cheap digital humidifier to place in your guitar case so you know how often to re-wet the sponge. Highly recommend the product.

review_body: this holds any size mic and has helped out so much. i must have droped em a bunch of times to and theyr very durable! 5 stars this thing is great, and for the price you csnt beat it!

review_body:
I use this with my Kodak zi8, and overall its a great sounding lapel mic.

product_title: Snark SN-1 Tuner
review_body: This item makes tuning a snap.  I especially like how you can twist it to give you a good view at any angle.

product_title: Schecter Model-T Electric Bass (Butterscotch)
review_body: Great looks and even better sound!  The Seymour Duncan pickups are outstanding. They deliver a really strong sound that cuts through in a 5 piece rock band.  The bass itself is very comfortable to play-it balances well on a strap and the neck is very comfortable for me.  The Set-up on the bass was impeccable right out of the box. It was set lower than what I normally use and was almost perfectly in tune when I took it out of the box. I was really impressed by that.    There was only one flaw that I could find. On the front of the bass near the bridge, it seems like something heavy was pressed onto the bass before it was painted. It does not affect the playability of the bass at all and you can only see it up close when you hold it at an angle because the light reflects funny from a small patch thats about 3/4 of an inch by a 1/4 inch.    Overall, this bass is a great value!

product_title: Snark SN-2 All Instrument Clip-On Chromatic Tuner
review_body: this is the nicest tuner I've ever used. It's fast and accurate. There is no waiting for it to reset between checking strings. All I can say is you cant beat it at three times the price

product_title: Vandoren 5RV Lyre Traditional Bb Clarinet Mouthpiece
review_body: WE purchased this for my daughter....and we could not be happier...Its top quality and even her band director praises the sound she gets now. Its the best mouthpiece you can buy and well worth teh $$$$

product_title: Pyle-Pro PDBC10 8 Outlet Rack Mount Power Supply Center w/Each Outlet Switch
review_body:
I have two problems with this item, one with the item and one with the shipping.

I knew that the fake \\"lighted\\" switches did not light up. But, I'm sorely disappointed with the fact that all of the switches have no \\"off and on\\" feel or click sound when you press them, You can't tell if they are on or off. Now as to shipping. The product dimensions are 6\\" x 19.9\\" x 3.1\\" and it was received in a carton of the size that you could have fitted a small 21\\" TV or computer monitor into.

The cardboard shipping box received was 24\\" x 24\\" x 20\\" with the electronic power supply center loose in one side of the carton with 6' of semi-inflated air pillows on the other side of the box.
